# Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique

**Conference:** ICLS 2026

## Abstract & Introduction

### Abstract
Peer critique is a social epistemic practice. Productive engagement in critique requires attention to its affective dynamics. We conducted discourse analysis of two focus groups across two rounds of peer critique. The groups showed different understandings and enactments of epistemic ideals for critique. The negative epistemic affect that emerged signaled differences in students’ epistemic ideals. Yet students strategically managed affect and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

Exploring Epistemic Affect in Middle School Students’ Peer Critique Qiuyu Lin, Rutgers University, qiuyu.lin@gse.rutgers.edu, Ravit Golanduncan, Rutgers University, ravit.duncan@gse.rutgers.edu Clark A. Chinn, Rutgers University, clark.chinn@gse.rutgers.edu Ava Lubin, Rutgers University, ahl120@scarletmail.rutgers.edu Jinzhi Zhou, Indiana University, zhoujinz@iu.edu Joshua Danish, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, jdanish@illinois.edu Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Indiana University, chmelosi@iu.edu Amandesai, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, amanad2@illinois.edu Abstract: Peer critique is a social epistemic practice. Productive engagement in critique requires attention to its affective dynamics. We  conducted discourse analysis of two focus groups across two rounds of peer critique. The groups showed different understandings and enactments of epistemic ideals for critique. The negative epistemic affect that emerged signaled differences in students’  epistemic ideals. Yet students strategically managed affect  and negotiated epistemic ideals, thereby transforming affective tensions into opportunities for shared understanding.

Peer critique provides a forum for scientists to interrogate and evaluate knowledge products and to establish social objectivity (Longino, 1990). This process involves negotiating epistemic aims, ideals, and processes (Chinn & Rinehart, 2016), both in relation to knowledge products and to the critique activity itself. Epistemic ideals are the criteria people use to examine the related knowledge products (Chinn & Rinehart, 2016). In this study, we define students’ epistemic ideals for critique as their criteria for what counts as good peer critique practice and their understanding of their roles and responsibilities as authors and reviewers in the peer critique process. Peer critique can at times produce various emotions and even tension (Thagard, 2002).  Negative feedback, for example, can be upsetting. However, affective dynamics are inherent in and crucial for collaborative knowledge construction in the science community (Jaber & Hammer, 2016). We draw on the concept of epistemic affect to describe the emotions, feelings, and dispositions that are intertwined with, and made visible through, epistemic activities such as knowledge construction, critique, and the negotiation of ways of knowing in sc ience (Jaber & Hammer, 2016 ；Muis et al., 2018). Affect can signal (mis)alignment among community members regarding the understanding and enactments of epistemic ideals. For example, when a scholar feel s frustrated by a critique, it may signal disagreement with the reviewer about what counts as a good epistemic product and whether the work meets those criteria. In addition, affect regulation can foster the negotiation of shared ideals within the community. Before educators can support students in cultivating dispositions that help them “feel like scientists” (Jaber & Hammer, 2016), it is necessary to investigate how students actually feel in peer critique. In this study, we designed and enacted peer critique embedded within a modeling-based inquiry unit. Our study examines the epistemic ideals for critique that emerged in practice and the forms and roles of affect in peer critique. Specifically, we ask: (1) What distinct epistemic ideals for critique emerged across student groups during peer critique? (2) How did epistemic affect surface tensions between these competing ideals? (3) How was epistemic affect managed in interaction? (4) How did affect management contribute to the negotiation and uptake of shared epistemic ideals for critique?

This study was conducted within an inquiry-based learning environment designed to engage students in investigating a locally relevant phenomenon of deer overpopulation.  This unit included two rounds of modeling and peer critique. Students used a collaborative modeling tool, MEME (Danish, 2021), to construct mechanistic, evidence-based models. The tool also supported peer critique, allowing students to give and respond to comments on each other’s models. The peer critique ended in an in-person editorial review meeting, where students evaluated peers’ revised models and decided whether they should be approved for “publication.” The study took place over six weeks in a suburban public middle school in the northeastern United States. In this brief paper, we focus on two focal groups —dyads with the group names Daisy and Rose. These groups 2928 serve as illustrative cases to examine the role of epistemic ideals and epistemic affect in peer critique. During the critique activities, Daisy and Rose reviewed each other’s models, and Rose also served as an editor for Daisy. Our primary data sources included students’ written comments and responses in MEME, screen recordings capturing group dis cussion and their interactions with MEME  during peer critique, and video recordings of within-and across-group interactions. Using discourse analysis across two rounds of peer critique, we identified moments where affect became visible and entangled with peer critique practices through attending to (a) explicit discursive indicators, (b) paralinguistic markers, and (c) physical displays. For each moment, we analyzed how affect emerged, what epistemic meanings it carried, the tensions it signaled, and how participants managed it. To strengthen interpretive validity, we triangulated with earlier within-group practices, including groups’ written critiques and discussion during giving critique, to infer their epistemic ideals for good critique. In the first round of giving critique, each group showed distinct emerging epistemic ideals for critique. Daisy’s epistemic ideals for good critique positioned reviewers as responsible for respecting the author’s perspective while also ensuring that their feedback is clear, specific, and grounded in their understanding of the model and the author’s intent. By contrast, Rose positioned critique as a one-way exchange, where reviewers identify flaws, and it is the author’s responsibility to make sense of the critique and address it; therefore, Rose did not feel obligated to articulate their comments in detail or provide justifications that could aid the authors’ interpretation. In the first round of receiving critique, Daisy displayed negative affect when engaging with comments from the Rose group. When asked to identify the two most unhelpful comments, Daisy  chose two from Rose. Daisy’s strong affective response (i.e., raised voice, rhetorical questioning, expression of disbelief, explicit accusation, and slamm ing hands on the table) suggested dissatisfaction with how Rose understood and enacted the epistemic ideals for good critique. Rose’s practice of critique was misaligned with the ideals held by Daily. Daisy drew on multiple strategies to manage emotions and tonegotiate with Rose the ideals for good critique. First, Daisy engaged in playful venting, which refram ed their negative emotions toward Rose as a form of joking play. This allowed them to express frustration and release social tension in a humorous way without causing harm. Second, Daisy made sincere efforts to collaboratively interpret Rose’s comments. They thus carried their epistemic ideals for good critique into the author role, striving to understand reviewers’ intent before responding. Third, Daisy indirectly negotiated their ideals for good critique with Rose by making Rose experience the unease of lack  of clarity. Instead of summarizing each comment in their letter to Rose, Daisy intentionally listed only the comment numbers, forcing Rose to put in extra effort to match the number to a specific comment, thereby prompting Rose to adopt Daisy’s ideals of providing greater clarity. Fourth, when they met, Daisy openly voiced their dissatisfaction with Rose’s comments, expressing frustration while  explicitly negotiating the ideals for good critique with Rose.  Taken together, affect regulation was more than an individual effort to “manage feelings.” It operated as a shared negotiation through which students establish shared ideals for good critique. Rose gradually took up Daisy’s ideals for good critique. During their in-person meeting, Rose was able to reformulate a specific critique that clearly  captured the main issue in Daisy’s model after rounds of back-andforth. They gradually learned to enact Daisy’s ideals for good critique (i.e., be clear and specific) through repeated attempts to articulate their critiques. In the second round of giving critique, Rose’s comments became more precise and better justified, and the group demonstrated greater met a-level awareness of critique ideals. They used self-mocking humor to reflect on their first round of giving critique. They also drew on earlier practices and reminded themselves to attend to the authors’ needs by providing more specific and well-justified feedback. The affective tensions provided an opportunity to develop a deeper shared commitment to the ideals for critique. Our fine-grained analysis shows that developing and consistently enacting shared ideals for peer critique is challenging for students.  While prior work has framed affect as signaling individual thinking and emphasized regulation at the individual level (Jaber & Hammer, 2016), our findings highlight its inherently social nature. In peer critique, epistemic affect  signals (mis)alignment of epistemic ideals and is best managed interactively. Consistent with Krishnamoorthy et al. (2025), we show that epistemic affect can motivate and guide the negotiation of epistemic ideals. When students attend to the meanings carried in their affective responses, moments of frustration can be transformed into opportunities for seeking alignment, which is an important aspect of meta-affect (Jaber & Hammer, 2016; Muis et al., 2018). These findings suggest the importance of creating space for students to reflect on affect, articulate what they feel and why, and connect these feelings to differing ways of knowing. Supporting dialogue around diverse epistemic ideals and their merits is therefore crucial (Murphy et al., 2025).  Rather than avoiding affect-laden moments, we argue that designing for them can foster deeper engagement with the social and epistemic dimensions of peer critique. 2929 Chinn, C. A., & Rinehart, R. Polman, University of Colorado Boulder, joseph.polman@colorado.edu Abstract: Learning sciences needs a better understanding of how dialogue advances youth identity. In an ethnographic case study, we examined talk story exchanges between a graduate researcher and a Latine youth within an art-making program. Drawing on personal narratives and identity resources, both developed emerging  trajectories of identification. Our findings show relational dialogic work can equitably center identity across roles, fostering the researcher's participant-observer stance and the youth's artist-activist becoming within a collaborative learning community.

Scholars of identity development in education need to further understand the ways ideas are exchanged and advanced in dialogue with youth. We conducted an ethnographic study of Latine youth in a museum program where youth collaboratively created art to tell stories of social justice. For this paper, we  examined how youth interacted dialogically with adult facilitators through  talk story, c asual exchanges of personal narratives privileging multiple viewpoints and creating meaning with a sense of mutuality (Cook, 2023; Simpson, 2012), during art making. We investigated how adult facilitators and youth drew upon identity resources to interactively develop new identifications. We explored dialogic, relationship-centered interactions within a single case analysis of the first author, Mendoza-Maurer (MM), and a youth participant’s talk story process. Our research question is: How can a relationship-centered talk story approach support youth to develop identities as artist-activists?

## Literature review and conceptual framing

Drawing on Vygotsky's (1978) sociocultural view of learning as a social process involving mediated action and dialogue (Bakhtin, 1981; Wertsch, 1998), the zone of proximal identity development (ZPID; Polman, 2012) extends the ZPD to describe socially supported identity development through We pair ZPID with Nasir & Cooks’

(2009) identity resources: relational, ideational, and material, that highlight the critical role of facilitators and

youth relationships, noting its influence in conveying ideational eleme nts supportive of identity trajectories. Stories shape identity through both identification and resistance (Penuel & Wertsch, 1995) and  can capture relationships of self to others (Polman & Miller, 2010). We integrate San Pedro & Kinloch’s (2017) storying, the “merging process that occurs in the space between the telling and listening, the giving and receiving of stories” (p. 377) to better understand the dialogical exchange of listening and giving back to what arises with others through the sharing of stories.

In Fall 2024, 7 researchers and facilitators and 11 youth collaboratively developed multimodal art for a museum exhibit celebrating youth lives in their mountain west city. Over five weekly four-hour workshops at a Latin American art museum, youth ages 13–16 engaged with MM as a participant observer. We developed a case study of MM and a Latina teen, using 9 interview transcripts, 25 hours of audio recordings, fieldnotes, voice memos, instructional materials, and design artifacts. We used talk story, informal, jointly narrated conversations that invite "many voices to proclaim many truths" (Simpson, 2012, p. 41), as a methodology to co-construct knowledge through open, relational dialogue. We utilized Critical Discourse Analysis (Martí nez, 2024; Rogers, 2011) to interpret discourse through micro-analysis of social interaction (Erikson, 2004). MM struggled to translate theoretical goals of supporting youth to recognize and historicize themselves in relation to power. In response, she engaged with the museum as a learner, using talk story with her parents  to reflect on her cultural identity. She learned about her mother’s family prayer rituals as they looked at religious iconography. The project leads (Stamatis and Polman) validated these stories, indicating an alignment with the collaborative dialogue they hoped to have with youth as inspiration for social justice art. 2931 MM thus used the two experiences to guide her program facilitation as a participant observer. In an activity that invited youth to reimagine their self-taken photos of museum art to explore personal connections to the past with future identifications, she used talk story to center relationship building. S he and a youth, Rosa, discussed their rationales for selecting prints and MM contributed her own stories. They shared their joint selection of religious iconography, with MM revealing her mixed feelings toward religion.  This prompted Rosa to describe "so many arguments" with her mother over religion's validity and MM recognizing "the same thing." The dialogue embodied mutuality as Rosa repeatedly completed MM’s thoughts. Together, they concluded  that spirituality might "be explored through multiple means," a meaning neither could have reached alone. This inspired MM to reveal more of her personal experiences during art analysis discussions, which used material resources of socially conscious art to build on the ideational resource that art used to raise awareness about one’s life experiences is a valuable practice. In session 5, the group viewed a painting of migrants making a journey on a mechanical crocodile and MM asked Mariana to elaborate on a symbolic  interpretation. Mariana said, "it's basically, like the person that, like, helps people cross th e border? They call them el coyote." MM then contributed her connection, revealing how “if it meant being barefoot riding on a mechanical crocodile…I would do it if it meant a better life for my daughter and my son, and that’s how strong, like, a mom’s love is.” Mariana took up MM’s mention of “love” when she wrote it in all capital letters to depict her connection to the art in a journal entry  (Figure 1). In a later interview, she expanded on her initial takeaway, reflecting that the museum's art was "about immigration and like coming over" and that she "can really relate to that, but like my family too." She  then used her personal connection to construct an artistic intention, describing a desire to "show that with my art too" by depicting "the process of coming over here and how much that affects families." Her desire to use art to show the emotional struggle of immigration  illustrates progress along an artist-activist trajectory supported by MM’s simultaneous progress along a relational participant observer trajectory.

Art Analysis Connecting to Love Final Collage Contrasting macro-discourses surrounding rhetoric dehumanizing Latine people in the U nited States during the 2024 election also informed Mariana’s artmaking and identity development. She observed that for "a lot of people, especially right now, it's all about immigration and the amount of people coming into the country," and no one "really talks about the effect that it has on the family, and like, how much struggle that we go through." She positioned her art directly against dominant, deficit-based framings that criminalized immigrants and excluded humanizing accounts of their experiences. Mariana shared a story of her grandfather, a government worker in Honduras who came to the U.S. and cleans dishes. She described how discourses ma de it "seem like they're, like, these criminals and rapists and drug addicts” and countered  by declaring, "They're human beings." MM validated and built on Mariana’s story by sharing that her grandfather, educated in the Philippines, made a similar journey. Their mutuality within their talk story was a relational resource supporting Mariana to reimagine artistic narratives toward more humanizing perspectives. In her final art  project (Figure 2), Mariana actualized her desire to tell her family's immigration story. She collaborated with an artist facilitator to layer hearts and stamps over images of brick walls, bridges, fences, scattered bodies along a shore, and a map. She included a family photo and the word "Amor." Her symbology depicted immigration through a humanizing lens, showing how love drives families to endure physical separation while finding ways to maintain their love across distance. T hese artistic choices reflected ideas co-constructed with MM and their learning community.

Mariana's final project marks the actualization of her earlier declaration to "say something," as her desire to create socially conscious art moved from discourse into enactment for a public audience. We argue that through dialogic interactions within her ZPID she: 1) recognized artist-activist models in the museum, 2) imagined herself in that role through talk story  exchanges, and 3) enacted that identity through her own collage work exploring immigration, love, and family. The dialogic interactions between Mariana and MM drew on relational, ideational, and material resources  and were the connective bridges  of both trajectories of identification —Mariana as an emerging artist-activist and MM as a developing participant observer—with each step of identity work creating the conditions for the next.

This work was made possible by  generous support from the Spencer Foundation. The views expressed here are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the foundation. 2933 How Generative AI is used in Learning Games: A Systematic Scoping Review in K-12 Settings Deniz Ercan, School of Teaching and Learning, CLASS Lab, University of Florida, deniz.ercan@ufl.edu Seyedahmad Rahimi, CLASS Lab, College of Lifetime Learning, Georgia Tech., srahimi@gatech.edu Abstract: This systematic scoping review examines the application of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in K –12 STEM learning games. Following PRISMA guidelines, eight studies published between 2017 and 2025 were identified across six databases. Two main uses of GenAI emerged: learning support and assessment/analysis. Overall, Findings showed that GenAI supports learning through feedback and motivation but remains peripheral to core game mechanics.

A persistent challenge in education is preparing students for a technology-driven world while sustaining engagement, particularly in K –12 STEM (NSB, 2023). NSB (2024) reports declining science scores, with only 31% of 8th graders reaching proficiency. Students often perceive STEM as abstract and disconnected, contributing to low engagement (Potvin & Hasni, 2014). Game-based learning (GBL) situates learning in interactive contexts where students actively explore and apply knowledge, supporting visualization of abstract concepts and learning by doing (Gee, 2003; Plass et al., 2015; Aldrich, 2005). Recent advances in generative AI (GenAI), including large language models, expand possibilities for personalized and adaptive learning (Bommasani et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2021). GenAI can generate feedback, examples, and dialogue, potentially enhancing learning games through adaptive and interactive experiences (Chen et al., 2023; Cotton et al., 2024). Despite rapid development, the use of GenAI in K –12 learning games remains underexplored. This review synthesizes existing research to clarify how GenAI has been applied and its role in learning processes. Current study This scoping review examines GenAI in K –12 STEM learning games. Prior reviews emphasize higher education or conceptual applications (Nzenwata et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), with limited focus on K –12 STEM contexts. The following research questions guide our scoping review: RQ 1)  What are the main trends in research on GenAI-powered learning games for K–12 students? RQ 2)  What types of GenAI technologies have been used in GenAI-powered learning games for K –12 STEM, and in what ways have these technologies been applied?

## Method

This systematic scoping review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and MetaAnalyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Moher et al., 2009) to map how GenAI has been used in digital learning games in K–12 STEM contexts. Inclusion criteria were limited to full-text studies published in English between 2017 and 2025 that involved digital games, GenAI applications, STEM subjects, and K –12 mainstream students. Studies were excluded if they focused on non-digital games, non-GenAI applications, non-STEM subjects, higher education, adult learning, or review-type publications. T he search was conducted across ERIC, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, Google Scholar, ACM Digital Library, and Scopus using combinations of terms related to game-based learning, generative AI, STEM education, and K– 12 settings.  One researcher reviewed titles and abstracts, followed by full-text screening of eligible studies using Covidence. After study selection, data were extracted and coded through an iterative process. One researcher developed the initial codes, and the second researcher reviewed and refined them. Through discussion, overlapping codes were merged into broader categories.

Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Two main categories emerged: learning support and assessment/analysis, with learning support focusing on feedback and motivation. RQ 1: What are the main trends in research on GenAI-powered learning games for K–12 students? The final studies comprised 8 studies, including journal articles (n = 5), conference papers (n = 2), and one book chapter (n = 1). Publication activity increased sharply in recent years: all studies (n = 8) were published in 2934 2024–2025, reflecting growing interest following the public release of large GenAI models. Most research originated from the United States (n = 5), followed by Taiwan (n = 2) and China (n = 1). Science-focused games dominated (n = 7), with only one study addressing mathematics (n  = 1). Role-playing games (RPGs) were the most common genre (n = 5), followed by adventure games (n = 2) and mini-games (n = 2). Most games incorporated interactive storytelling, dialogue-based problem solving, or inquiry-driven missions to scaffold conceptual understanding.

RQ 2) What types of AI technologies have been used in GenAI-powered learning games for K–12 STEM learning, and in what ways have these technologies been applied? Based on the analysis of the 8 extracted studies, two major categories of GenAI applications in learning games were identified: (1) Learning Support and (2) Assessment/Analysis. Within these categories, learning support has two subcategories: 1) Feedback and 2) Motivation.

Learning support In this category, most studies (n  = 6) focused on feedback. Chen and Law (2025) and Huang and Chen (2025) integrated ChatGPT-based chatbots into science games to generate real-time explanations and problem-solving hints. Similarly, McLaren (2024) used GPT-3.5 within the Decimal Point game to interpret students’ written self-explanations and generate rubric-based feedback, including identified misconceptions and suggested next steps. Goslen et al. (2025) fine-tuned T5 and GPT-3.5 models to produce goal-aligned problem-solving action plans from gameplay data. Wang et al. (2025) and Zhu et al. (2025) also examined conversational agents powered by Qwen and Llama 3 that interacted with players through dialogue and reflective questioning. GenAI was also used as motivational learning support in two studies. Wang et al. (2025) and Zhu et al.

(2025) designed agents that used supportive conversation, encouragement, and reflective prompts to sustain

students’ interest and perseverance. For example, the Qwen-powered agent “ V” in Planet Rosebud provided personalized praise and questions when students hesitated or made errors. Similarly, Zhu et al. (2025) developed the peer agent CAP, which functioned as a companion rather than a tutor to maintain engagement during gameplay.

Assessment/Analysis A smaller but growing body of work (n = 3) explored GenAI for assessment or analysis in learning games. These studies used GenAI to interpret or evaluate students’ in-game reasoning and actions. Acosta et al. (2025) fine-tuned a T5 model to recognize epistemic dialogue acts in students’ collaborative discussions, identifying moments of reasoning and knowledge exchange during gameplay. Liu et al. (2025) combined GPT-4o with an XGBoost classifier to detect struggle behaviors in gameplay by converting gameplay logs into text replays readable by the language model. McLaren (2024) also used GPT-3.5 to evaluate the quality of students’ reasoning in self-explanations as correct, partially correct, or incorrect. Overall, these studies show that GenAI can be used to assess students’ reasoning and gameplay behaviors and provide insights into learning processes and in-game performance.

This systematic scoping review mapped the emerging use of GenAI in digital learning games for K –12 STEM education. The studies reviewed suggest a gradual shift in game design from rule-based or scripted systems to adaptive, conversational, and data-driven applications of GenAI. Studies used conversational agents' responses in real time (Chen & Law, 2025; McLaren, 2024), yet their integration often remains peripheral to core gameplay. This suggests that current implementations use GenAI to supplement instruction rather than to drive gameplay mechanics. Embedding GenAI into game logic would enable dynamic content, adaptive tasks, and narrative adjustments based on learner progress. As part of the game engine, GenAI could create adaptive scenarios that respond to learners’ behavior and sustain engagement. Such integration could transform GenAI from a feedback provider into an active co-designer of the learning experience. From an instructional perspective, the reviewed studies showed how GenAI can mediate both feedback and motivational support. These applications demonstrate GenAI’s capacity to act as a learning partner that motivates students and fosters their engagement with game tasks. Yet, the interaction patterns with GenAI across studies remain primarily reactive, not proactive. Overall, GenAI supports interaction and analysis in learning games but remains underused as a generative mechanism. Future research should explore integrating GenAI into core design processes to create more adaptive and responsive learning experiences. 2935 Acosta, H., Lee, S., Bae, H., Feng, C., Rowe, J., Glazewski, K.,... & C. Wip: Enhancing game-based learning with ai-driven peer agents. arXiv preprint arXiv:2508.01169. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2508.01169 2936 Being Guided or Becoming? Exploring Learners’ Relational Possibilities and Hazards with GAI Chatbots through Sociocultural Lenses Jusil Lee, Xingxing Xie jjl7118@psu.edu, xkx5097@psu.edu The Pennsylvania State University Abstract: This interpretive qualitative study explores the relational possibilities and hazards that emerge when learners engage with generative AI (GAI) chatbots in reflective writing. While chatbots, as competent and nonjudgmental assistants, create safe spaces for learners, the strong preference for them over peer interactions calls for further reflection. Aligned with sociocultural theories, especially the notion of scaffolding, the study highlights potential risks of prioritizing being guided at the expense of becoming independent and reflective learners. This study explores the relational dynamics of Generative AI (GAI) chatbots, by comparing GAI chatbots support with human peer-interaction in learners’ writing experiences. While there is much positive evidence of GAI chatbots’ influence on cognitive outcomes, such as accuracy and fluency of writing (e.g., Mahapatra, 2024; Mekheimer, 2025), little is known about GAI chatbots’ relational aspects (Polo et al., 2016). These relational dynamics are critical since they could change how learners perceive agency in writing and collaboration (Holland et al., 1998; Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2020). In addressing the aforementioned gap and understanding the dynamics, we aim to identify new relational possibilities and potential hazards that the near future of GAI chatbots may bring to learning environments. In doing so, we aim to answer the following question: What relational possibilities and hazards are explored when learners interact with GAI chatbots in their reflective writing processes?

## Theoretical framework

We ground our work in sociocultural theory, which posits learning as a process of engaging in social practices and emphasizes the dialectic nature of human learning activities mediated through cultural artifacts (Cole, 1998; Vygotsky, 1978). Central to this framework is scaffolding, which is a temporary and contingent support whose ultimate aim is the learner's independent functioning — a graduation from guided participation toward autonomous competence (Wood et al., 1976). Thus, the learning contexts that RW provides will be examined through the sociocultural lenses, comprehensively accounting for the possible and hazardous relational dynamics of mediation and interaction. In other words, we will attend not only to whether GAI chatbots provide scaffolded support, but to whether learners show any trajectory toward independence from that support. Reflective writing (RW), such as reflective journals or self-analytical essays, requires learners to engage in introspective meaning-making, fostering deep reflection, negotiation of identity, and learning (Gibbs, 1988; Moon, 2004; Ryan, 2011). To understa nd the relational dynamics between human-to-GAI chatbots and humanto-human interactions in RW activities, we conducted a comparative case study (Bartlett & Vavrus, 2016). Through convenience sampling (Johnson & Christensen, 2024), we recruited 8 participa nts at a northeastern university in the United States. After each participant’s consent, we conducted a one-on-one interview with each participant to understand their previous reflective writing experiences. Then, we randomly assigned participants to eithe r Group A (interacting with human peers first, followed by GAI chatbot interaction) or Group B (interacting in reversed order) for two one-hour writing activities (either on Zoom or in-person based on their preference). It is also noted that participants selected and worked with a specific GAI chatbot (e.g., ChatGPT 5, Gemini, Copilot, etc) only in the GAI chatbot writing session, based on their own preference and accessibility. In these two writing sessions, participants were given just one prompt, i.e., “ Reflect on an educational experience (personal or historical). Why is remembering it important for imagining your future?” After these activities, we conducted semi-structured post-interviews with each participant to understand their experiences of interacting with both GAI chatbots and their peers as they engaged in the writing activities. 2937 We collected the following five data sources, i.e., participants’ pre-and post-interview transcripts, writing samples, GAI interactional logs and peer interaction videos, and researchers’ fieldnotes. The diversity of data helped the researchers to triangulate the data and maintain construct validity. Then, we followed Emerson’s (2011) three-step analytical coding phases. First, the researchers familiarized themselves with the data and open coded the transcripts line-by-line to identify any recurring pheno mena surfaced on the data. Second, we selected and fine-grained the topical codes that aligned with our research questions and interests in the focused coding. Throughout the coding process, we consistently documented our integrative memos concerning the o bserved phenomena to clarify and link analytic themes or categories (Emerson, 2011, p. 171). In doing so, it helped us build analytical depth in understanding the emerging relational dynamics that pose both opportunities and setbacks as learners engage with GAI chatbots in RW. Here, we present 4 participants as our cases to present the findings.

## Preliminary findings

While the study is still in progress, our preliminary findings through interpretive qualitative analysis (Emerson,

2011) shed light on the dual nature of learners’ relationships with GAI chatbots in a context for profound self-reflection. In the facilitation of deep reflection, the participants’ use of the GAI chatbots suggests the relational possibilities of the GAI chatbot as a competent assistant. (e.g., “The result that the Copilot wrote for me was good, actually.” (Jose)) Furthermore, the participants expressed an enhanced sense of safety and mental comfort as they perceived the GAI chatbot as a non-judgmental and neutral assistant. This was prominent especially when the participants felt less confident about their writte n English as ESL learners (e.g., “ How I felt about the writing experience with the peer? I felt ashamed, a little bit, because I'm not confident in writing an essay in English by myself. My vocabulary is not that good, and sometimes I cannot remember English expressions. I felt more comfortable using Copilot because it doesn’t judge.” (Jose)) or when they had awareness of the privacy of the writing contents.

However, the shared and overwhelming preference for GAI chatbots over human peers, when participants were asked about their future collaboration preferences, calls for further reflection and investigation. While the participants perceived the role of GAI chatbots as an assistant, the way they described and utilized GAI chatbots highlights the theme of guidance from “better” competent beings. To be specific, they asked GAI chatbots for three aspects: 1. Structure & Coherence (e.g., “Revise it to make it soun d smooth and organized. I want it to be concise and clear, with no redundancy” (Dana); “Help me refine this paragraph” (Lucy)). 2. Content Development & Brainstorming (e.g., “Please give me 10 obvious ways and 10 creative ways to select the direction of developing this essay. Then, could you ask me relevant questions to brainstorm about this topic?”  (Donald)).

3. Language & Style Editing (e.g., “Translate what I just wrote in English” (Jose); “Polish the grammar” (Lucy);

“If my writing needs to be improved, please do so right away” (Donald)). These instances resemble “scaffolding” in sociocultural learning theory, which refers to a supportive process in which an expert (GAI chatbot in this case) temporarily manages the challenging aspects of a task so that a learner can focus on achievable comp onents, gradually developing competence to perform independently beyond their initial ability (Wood et al., 1976). However, it is questionable whether the learners would proactively seek gradually diminishing scaffolding. In fact, the participants’ reflection on their own usage of GAI chatbots reveals the already-formed enthusiasm toward being effectively guided by GAI chatbots (e.g., “I even participated in a workshop on how to prompt GAI chatbots well” (Donald)) rather than actually improving the area they have received support. In addition, researchers’ field notes corroborate lukewarm attitudes toward improvement in communication with peers for deeper reflection and learning. In such a context of self-inquiry and learning, purposeful partnership with GAI chatbots provides psychologically safe spaces to reach out for support in various aspects, any time. However, unreflective preference for the scaffoldings that GAI chatbots provide (with the belief of their qualified, quick and quiet nature) may belie the intrusive intervention of GAI chatbots, let alone the nature of static scaffolding. 2939 Assessing Leadership Learning in Youth Participatory Action Research Ben Kirshner, Salvador Ramirez, Beatriz Salazar, Kareem Kalil kirshner@colorado.edu, Salvador.RamirezJr@colorado.edu, beatriz.salazar@colorado.edu, Kareem.Kalil@colorado.edu University of Colorado Boulder Abstract: When students engage in Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) to improve their schools, they practice and develop key habits of democratic citizenship, including critical social analysis, collective leadership, and courage. These habits, however, are rarely aligned with or legible to school assessment systems, which poses barriers for the adoption and sustainability of YPAR programs in schools. In response to this problem of practice voiced by educator partners, our team facilitated a co-design process  for a leadership development assessment. In this paper, we share the rationale, design principles, and key elements of the Habits of a Social Change Leader Assessment. We also share data from a focus group with teachers that elicited feedback and revisions prior to piloting it this year. This assessment contributes to the wider project of designing learning resources that support young people’s agency and critical consciousness.

Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is becoming increasingly common as a vehicle for student voice and leadership development in US high schools (Anderson, 2020). In addition to cultivating academic skills, YPAR cultivates youth development competencies, such as teamwork, critical consciousness, and courage. These developmental achievements, however, are rarely legible to conventional academic systems of assessment. In response to a request from school partners, we developed a resource called the Habits of a Social Change Leader Assessment (HSCL). HSCL enables teachers and students to document youth learning and development in five key areas: critical consciousness, activism, collaboration, self-awareness, and research. This poster introduces the resource and shares results from feedback from teacher partners. Learning and development in YPAR and action civics Research about student outcomes associated with action civics and YPAR has benefited from improvements in measurement of key constructs, including critical consciousness, sociopolitical development, and student voice (Conner et al., 2023; Diemer et al., 20 17; El-Amin et al., 2017; Watts et al., 2011). One challenge, however, pertains to the availability of measures that are aligned with and useful for school instruction (Bryk et al., 2015). Existing survey measures, for example, are not designed to give individualized feedback to students, nor would it be appropriate to link attitudinal survey responses to grades. Also, surveys require partnership with researchers trained in statistical analysis to identify findings that might inform decision-making in the classroom or program. In these ways assessments might be useful for summative measures of growth but not formative uses to improve instruction or classroom experiences. As part of a research-practice partnership, educator partners asked our research team to design an assessment that they could use to document student learning in YPAR. This design paper reports key constructs of the HSCL and focus group feedback from teachers. Construct development We used an iterative approach aligned with  construct-centered assessment (Maul, 2018), which identifies  relevant constructs, describes examples of what they look like in practice, and differentiates different levels of quality. The HSCL development process was informed by a review of qualitative data collected by the TSV team (HipolitoDelgado et al., 2022), then conversations with education program partners, then focus group feedback. Focus groups To get to version 2.0 of the assessment two authors facilitated a zoom focus group with five teachers (four secondary, one elementary). The teachers reviewed the habits and offered feedback via typed comments. Teachers were asked to identify feasibility, usefulness, relevance, other miscellaneous suggestions. 2940 The second author, Salvador, conducted an analysis of teachers’ written comments and the meeting notes. Salvador documented frequencies of comments and maintained a running list to track new or different comments. This helped us focus on predominant themes  while also not ignoring outlier comments. The first author, Ben, reviewed the analysis and then the two worked together to clarify claims and link themes to specific examples. As we finalized themes, we prioritized design implications, such as usefulness and feasibility (Yeager et al., 2014). Habits of a social change leader constructs and prompts The habits are: Critically Conscious, Activist, Self-Aware, Collaborator, and Researcher. Construct maps for each habit include a description, characteristics of  a beginner versus an expert, and a  vignette. These maps were formatted as leader profiles to be shared with students and teachers. Figure 1 shows the top half of the profile of the Critically Conscious leader. The lower half, not shown here, describes qualities of a beginner and expert. Figure 1 Elements of the Critically Conscious Leadership Habit The HSCL includes three types of assessment: Closed response survey items (taken at beginning and end of year), self-reflective writing prompts (throughout year), and for a portfolio (at three points during year). It offers opportunities for formative and summative feedback. Feedback from teachers Teacher feedback about the habits tended to focus on complexities in the descriptions. One of the teachers, writing about Critical Consciousness, wrote: “[I ] [n]oticed that the biggest gap between beginner and expert is that they are interested in knowing why things are the way they are, and the expert knows how. How do you measure what is in between those two (beginner and expert)?” Another teacher named that they “Loved [the] example/non-example” that the habits provided but suggested the addition of an “an intermediate level.” Teachers also raised practical questions about how to facilitate and use the prompts and self-assessment survey. In response, other teachers offered suggestions, such as adding a “Leadership tracker” to the portfolio to “have a way for students to track” their development of Habits of a Leader. The teachers’ proximity to their student’s context and lived realities contributed to questions about inclusivity. One asked “if you were presenting these habits to the students, if you had an introverted student, would they not see themselves in th[ese]?” Another used an example of a student who “creates posters, and that is her contribution, her involvement.” Another said, “I like how there are a variety of ways students are showing the work…Great for catering to a wide range of student learning preferences.” Our work with the HSCL is at an early stage: we are pilot testing it with three teachers during the 2025-26 academic year, which will enable us to gather feedback from students. Nevertheless, our construct maps of the five habits of a social change leader, in tandem with teacher feedback, provides early information about strengths and areas for improvement. The HSCL contributes a resource to the wider field of educators and learning scientists seeking to design and facilitate learning environments that encourage student agency, and critical consciousness. 2941 Anderson, A. ## for Children’s Learning: Perspectives from the United Arab

Emirates Basel Hussein, New York University, baselhussein@nyu.edu Charles Raffaele, New York University, charles.raffaele@nyu.edu Antje von Suchodoletz, New York University Abu Dhabi, avs5@nyu.edu Bruce D. Homer, City University of New York, bhomer@gc.cuny.edu Jan L. Plass, New York University, jan.plass@nyu.edu Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping teaching and learning, yet teachers' attitudes

– particularly in early childhood education (ECE) – remain underexplored. Drawing on survey

data from 315 ECE teachers working with 3–7-year-olds in the United Arab Emirates, we find predominantly positive attitudes toward AI for learning, alongside conflicting and mixed views, and some strong skepticism. These findings highlight heterogeneity in teacher perspectives and can inform efforts to center their voices in shaping AI's role in education. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming central to education, with classrooms integrating both teacher-facing tools – such as for assessment and feedback (Tan et al., 2025) – and student-facing tools for personalizing learning (Wang et al., 2024).  Enthusiasm about AI's potential (Giannakos et al., 2025) is matched by growing concern over its risks and ethical implications (Al-Zahrani, 2024; Yan et al., 2024). Teachers are not merely implementers of AI but key stakeholders whose perspectives should guide its trajectory in educational practice (Luckin & Cukurova, 2019). Early studies reveal a mixed picture: some educators highlight opportunities to reduce workload and enhance learner support, while others raise concerns about bias, privacy, and pedagogical appropriateness (Cojean et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2025; Berson et al., 2025) – a divide reflected in surveys showing wide variation in teacher views (Pew Research Center, 2024; Kölemen & Yıldırım, 2025). According to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM; Davis, 1989), teachers' beliefs about AI's benefits and risks are likely to shape how they integrate it into their pedagogy – choices that, in turn, influence student learning (Bower, 2019; Çelik & Muukkonen, 2023; King & He, 2006). Without understanding these attitudes, education systems risk introducing AI tools that misalign with teachers' needs and values, leading to uneven implementation and excluding key voices from the conversation. We simply do not know enough about how teachers feel and think about AI for learning – particularly given the distinct developmental and ethical considerations around AI use with young children (Berson et al., 2025). Existing research on this population is limited and larg ely based on small samples (Kardeş, Uygun & Türkmen, 2025; Kölemen & Yıldırım, 2025; Lamanauskas & Makarskaitė- Petkevičienė, 2025; Wong, Liu & Yip, 2025), and most studies have focused on Western contexts (Moriguchi, 2022; Valdez & Mendoza, 2024). We address this gap by examining ECE teacher attitudes in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi – a particularly relevant context given the UAE's rapid integration of AI beginning as early as  kindergarten (Gulf News, 2025). We center this study on the exploratory question: What attitudes do ECE teachers hold toward AI, and how do they perceive its impact on young children?

## Method

Participants were 315 ECE teachers in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, UAE, recruited via  our IRB-approved study using WhatsApp teacher networks and snowball sampling. The mean age was 36.51 years (SD = 6.51); 75% identified as women. Nationalities included 26% Indian, 14% Egyptian, 11% Filipino, 8% Emirati, 7% each Jordanian and Sudanese, 6% Pakistani, and the remaining 21% represented other nationalities. Teachers averaged 6.21 years (SD = 3.97) of experience at their current grade level, spanning Nursery throug h Grade 2 (ages 3 –7), and worked primarily in private schools (84%). Instruction was conducted in English (70%) or Arabic (30%). Teachers completed a phone-based survey. Two five-point Likert items assessed AI attitudes. These two items were selected to capture and contrast two distinct dimensions of teacher attitudes: beliefs about AI as a tool  for learning, and perceptions of its broader impact on children's lives. The first asked: "To what extent do you agree that AI-based tools (for example, voice detection or word prediction features) have a positive role in supporting young children's learning in the classroom?"  (Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree). The second asked: "When you think about advancements in technology, such as artificial intelligence, what kind of impact do you think these advancements will have on young children's lives?" (Very Negative to Very Positive). 2943 Overall, teachers expressed largely positive attitudes toward AI for learning (Figure 1). Of the 315 respondents, 127 (40%) were enthusiastic about AI as a learning tool and optimistic about its influence on children's lives, with an additional 27 (9%) expressing positive views and 17 (5%) strongly so. Forty-eight teachers (15%) expressed neutral or uncertain views. Notably, many teachers held mixed or internally conflicting attitudes. Nineteen teachers (6%) viewed AI positively as a learning tool yet were uncertain about its broader impact on children; 28 (9%) were unsure about AI for learning but anticipated positive outcomes for children; and 15 (5%) held the reverse – positive about the tool, pessimistic about its impact. At the negative end, 15 teachers (5%) held generally or strongly negative views across both dimensions. These findings reveal that teacher attitudes toward AI are not simply positive, neutral, or negative – many hold simultaneously optimistic and skeptical views, distinguishing between AI's potential as a learning tool and its broader implications for young learners. Figure 1 ECE teacher attitudes (N = 315) toward AI along Two Dimensions – as a Tool to Support Learning, and its Potential Impact on Students Green indicates positive attitudes, red indicates negative  attitudes, yellow indicates neutral attitudes, and orange indicates conflicting attitudes towards AI. Teachers in our sample expressed broadly positive attitudes toward AI, consistent with some emerging research (Kardeş, Uygun & Türkmen, 2025; Kölemen & Yıldırım, 2025). Our findings extend this work by showing that many teachers hold conflicted or ambivalent views – which may reflect differing levels of AI literacy (Su et al.,

2023) and the inconsistent messages teachers receive about AI in education (Chan & Tsi, 2024). In line with TAM

(Davis, 1989), the generally positive attitudes observed suggest many t eachers may be inclined to integrate AI into their classrooms – though future research should examine actual patterns of use and how implementation shapes children's learning and developmental outcomes (Bower, 2019). The heterogeneity in our sample – strong optimists, pessimists, and many still forming their views – underscores the need for targeted professional development that addresses teachers' differing levels of familiarity and concern. That roughly one in five teachers held conflicting views suggests that professional development must address not only how to implement AI tools, but also listening to teachers' broader ethical concerns about AI and learning. Understanding these concerns more deeply can translate to designing more transparent teacher-facing AI tools. A key limitation is that our study does not capture why teachers hold particular attitudes – a question future interview work will explore. Looking ahead, longitudinal, developmental, and cross-cultural research will be essential for understanding how specific AI tools shape early childhood pedagogy as AI becomes increasingly ubiquitous in classrooms worldwide (Berson et al., 2025).

## STEM Interest as an Entry Point for OST Learning: A Case Study of

the Boys & Girls Clubs of Garden Grove Kylie Peppler, Maggie Dahn, Seth Corrigan kpeppler@uci.edu, dahnm@uci.edu, scorrig1@uci.edu University of California, Irvine Heather White, Boys & Girls Clubs of Garden Grove, hwhite@bgcgg.org Abstract: This paper examines how out-of-school-time (OST) organizations can leverage youth STEM interests as strategic entry points for sustained learning. Drawing on a case study of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Garden Grove, we describe the iterative development of i nterest survey tools to match youth interests with available programming and career pathways. attention to organizational capacity, differentiated mentorship, and intentional connections between interests, programs, and opportunities.

Interest-driven learning has emerged as a critical framework for understanding how young people engage with STEM in informal settings (Azevedo, 2011; Renninger & Hidi, 2016). Unlike formal education, out-of-schooltime (OST) programs can center youth inter ests as starting points for learning –yet identifying, nurturing, and connecting these interests to meaningful opportunities remains a persistent challenge (Ching et al., 2018). This paper examines how the Boys & Girls Clubs of Garden Grove (BGC), active at more than 50 sites across Orange County and serving the 14th largest school district in California, has approached using STEM interest as an entry point for learning. Our central research question is: How can OST organizations develop systematic approaches to understanding and responding to youth STEM interests in ways that support sustained engagement? Interest-driven learning and making connections across OST contexts Interest-driven learning positions learner passions as the organizing principle for educational experiences (Ito et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2018). This approach aligns with self-determination theory's emphasis on autonomy and intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ry an, 2000) and with research demonstrating that interest predicts sustained engagement and deeper learning outcomes (Renninger & Hidi, 2016). In OST contexts, where participation is typically voluntary, leveraging interests is not merely pedagogically valuable but practically essential for retention (Philp & Gil, 2020). However, young people's interests exist in dynamic relationships with available opportunities, social contexts, and identity development (Azevedo, 2011). Simply asking youth about their inter ests is insufficient without accompanying structures to match those interests to opportunities and support identity development (Ching et al., 2018; Dahn et al., 2023). For OST organizations embedded within broader learning ecosystems, the challenge becomes one of strategic brokering—understanding the landscape of available resources and intentionally connecting youth to opportunities that align with their emerging interests and developing identities (Ito et al., 2013; Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). Data were collected between 2023 and early 2025 and included youth focus groups, program leader and STEM specialist interviews, document analysis of survey iterations and program materials, observation of STEM programming, and analysis of approximately 250 initial survey responses from four sites. We employed iterative qualitative analysis with ongoing collaborative reflection with BGC leadership. Problem of practice: The interest matching conundrum Prior to this work, BGC’s STEM efforts –partner workshops, field trips, a community college certification program–lacked strategic coordination. Three interconnected gaps emerged: (a) limited understanding of the STEM initiative landscape; (b) insufficient teen programming, especially around elementary-to-middle-school transitions; and (c) underdeveloped workforce pathways for high schoolers. A common thread was the need to better understand youth interests and match them to available resources. 2946 Tool development: Interest survey iteration Unable to find an existing tool that matched their unique needs and capacity, BGC developed a "homegrown" survey through iterative design. Key components include: a) a five-point Likert scale general STEM interest assessment; b) ranking of eight domain-specific STEM topics tied to existing curriculum capacity at BGC; c) career interest questions; d) identification of competing interests (hobbies, sports); learning preference questions (social, project and temporal preferences); and desired frequency of STEM participation. The survey undergoes ongoing refinement based on partner and youth feedback.

## Initial results: Patterns in youth STEM interests

Critically, this shifts BCG from assumption-based to evidence-based programming decisions. A noted limitation: the survey's eight pre-selected domains render invisible youth whose interests fall outside those categories.

Distribution of STEM Field Rankings by a Subset of Sites Mentorship as connection-making infrastructure BGC treats mentorship as critical infrastructure for translating interests into engagement. Mentors provide both instrumental support (connecting youth to programs) and identity support (helping youth see themselves as STEM-capable). Youth described the importance of authentic relationships: "it feels like you're talking to a person with their own life and their own feelings versus like just another figure to tell you what to do and what not to do." Without trust relationships, youth are less likely to share emerging interests or take risks.

## High-quality programming as interest development context

Interest data is only valuable if organizations can respond to it. BGC's Imagine Science programming—Sphero Robotics, Water Guardians, Power Up!, and Space Quest —offers low-cost, career-linked programs that connect learning to home and community contexts, providing the sustained engagement needed for interests to deepen into STEM identity.

The BGC case illuminates a critical design principle: interest surveys must be calibrated to organizational capacity. Asking about interests only has value when organizations can meaningfully respond. Interest identification alone is also insufficient—huma n infrastructure for mentorship and sustained programming must accompany any survey tool. BGC's emphasis on sustained engagement over one-off experiences reflects understanding that interest development is longitudinal; moving from "triggered situational interest" (sparked by novelty or activity) and "well-developed individual interest" (enduring personal connection to domain) (Hidi & Renninger, 2006) requires repeated opportunities to engage, increasing competence, and belonging within a community of practice. Finally, the case reframes the OST organization’s role: less as a sole program provider and more as a strategic broker connecting youth to a broader ecosystem of community college programs, industry partnerships, and workforce development opportunitie s. Interest-driven learning in OST contexts is less about simply asking youth what they want and more about building organizational capacity to hear, honor, and respond to diverse interests while creating conditions where new interests can emerge and deepe n over time. 2947 Akkerman, S. 2948 Fighting or Learning: Exploring Cognitive and Strategic Practices in MOBA Gamer Communities Tieh-Huai Chang, Cross College Elite Tech Program, National Kaohsiung University of Science and Technology, Taiwan. ironchang@nkust.edu.tw Tsung-Liang Tsai, Department of  Education and Humanities in Medicine, Taipei Medical University, Taiwan. dorami1001@tmu.edu.tw Abstract: This study examines tacit learning competencies developed by MOBA players in high-intensity esports contexts. Drawing on gameplay records, interviews, and player reflections, it analyzes how players demonstrate strategic thinking, team communication, real-time decision-making, information synthesis, and emotional regulation. Findings suggest that MOBA gameplay can cultivate transferable cognitive, social, and metacognitive competencies often obscured by surface-level game mechanics, offering insights for le arning sciences research on informal learning environments.

Digital games have become important informal learning environments in which players repeatedly encounter challenge, feedback, collaboration, and community-based knowledge sharing (McGonigal, 2008; Thomas & Brown, 2011). Prior research has suggested that gameplay can foster strategic thinking, problem-solving, persistence, and systemic reasoning (Gee, 2003, 2007; McGonigal, 2011). Team-based and strategy-oriented games are especially relevant because they require players to manage resources, coordinate with others, and adapt to changing situations (Kirriemuir & McFarlane, 2004; Ulicsak & Wright, 2010). However, the competencies cultivated through gameplay often remain tacit and difficult to articulate, particularly when they are treated merely as game-specific skills rather than as forms of learning (Lin, 2011). MOBA games provide a useful  context for examining these tacit competencies because they combine real-time decision-making, role coordination, information synthesis, and emotional regulation under competitive pressure. High-level players must interpret rapidly changing game states, communicate with teammates, anticipate opponents’ actions, and adjust strategies across uncertain situations. These practices resonate with contemporary educational concerns such as self-directed learning, collaboration, critical thinking, and adaptive expertise, while also raising questions about how such competencies may transfer beyond entertainment contexts (Chang & Chen, 2015; Steinkuehler & Squire, 2014). This study therefore examines how experienced MOBA players demonstrate tacit learning competencies through gameplay actions and reflective accounts, with particular attention to strategic planning, team communication, information literacy, and real-time decision-making.

## Research methodology

This study used a qualitatively oriented mixed-methods approach to examine the tacit competencies developed by experienced MOBA players and their educational relevance. The study extended a previous dataset of 48 MOBA players and additionally recruited several high-ranking players from League of Legends, Arena of Valor, and DOTA 2. Participants were 18 to 30 years old, had at least three years of gameplay experience, and included both university students and working professionals.

Data were collected from gameplay records, system data, player-generated materials, and semi-structured interviews. Gameplay materials included recordings, strategy guides, and gameplay videos shared in online communities. These materials were analyzed to identify critical in-game moments involving decision-making, team coordination, resource allocation, and micro-level strategic actions. Interviews invited participants to reflect on their gameplay experiences and describe the skills or insights they believed they had developed through play. Interview data were audio-recorded, transcribed, and validated through member checking. The analysis proceeded through iterative coding and triangulation. The research team first coded interview transcripts for reported competencies, such as leadership, information seeking, and emotional regulation. These codes were then compared with gameplay records and strategy texts to identify behavioral evidence corresponding to players’ self-reports. Three experts reviewed the preliminary competency mappings for coherence and validity, and participant feedback was used to refine the framework. These procedures informed the construction of a conceptual map of MOBA gamer competencies.

## Research results

2949 The analysis identified four interrelated tacit competencies developed through MOBA gameplay. Pressure-based decision-making MOBA players demonstrated the ability to make high-risk decisions under time pressure. During critical moments, they had to process opponent movement, resource distribution, team positioning, and possible consequences of action. Repeated exposure to such situations appeared to strengthen players’ strategic judgment, information synthesis, and adaptive reasoning under uncertainty. Antagonistic learning and psychological tactics Players also developed adversarial forms of strategic thinking. Tactics such as baiting, feints, and emotional provocation required them to interpret opponents’ behavioral cues, anticipate likely responses, and shape the opponent’s decision-making process (Kordyaka, 2018).  These practices involved tactical foresight and metacognitive monitoring, as players continuously evaluated whether their strategies were working as intended. Team competition and social manipulation strategies Successful gameplay depend s on concise communication, role allocation, consensus-building, and the ability to sustain team morale. Players described learning how to issue instructions, persuade teammates, manage conflict, and adjust the team atmosphere through humor or emotional cues. These practices suggest that MOBA gameplay can cultivate socially situated competencies related to leadership, negotiation, and real-time collaboration. Stress management and emotional regulation Competitive losses, individual mistakes, teammate conflict, and rapidly shifting game states required players to regulate frustration and refocus attention (Gutierrez, 2021).  Players reported using strategies such as cognitive refocusing, controlled breathing, and goal-oriented thinking to recover from setbacks. This self-regulatory process supported both individual performance and team communication, indicating that emotional  steadiness is central to competent participation in MOBA environments.

Overall, these findings suggest that MOBA players’ competencies extend beyond mechanical skill. Their practices involve decision-making, psychological interpretation, social coordination, and emotional regulation, forming a cluster of tacit learning competencies relevant to informal and esports-based learning environments.

## Suggestions and discussion

This study reframes MOBA gameplay as a site of learning rather than competitive entertainment. Findings show experienced players develop cognitive, social, and emotional competencies, including rapid decision-making, strategic anticipation, team coordination, and stress regulation. These competencies are not isolated game skills; they emerge through participation in complex, high-pressure, and socially mediated gaming environments. Integrating complex decision-making into education Pressure-based decision-making observed in MOBA gameplay suggests that time-sensitive simulations may help learners practice strategic reasoning, flexible judgment, and reflective adjustment (Ding et al., 2018). In classroom design, educators may draw from game structures by creating situations in which learners must analyze incomplete information, assess outcomes, make timely decisions, and reflect on the consequences of their actions. Social competencies through community engagement Team coordination in MOBA contexts illustrates how collaboration can be learned through participation, shared goals, peer feedback, and role-based communication. This resonates with situated learning and the idea of communities of practice, where learning develops through participation rather thandirect instruction alone (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998). From this perspective, MOBA communities offer examples of how leadership, negotiation, and communication can emerge through repeated collaborative problem-solving. Future research on transfer Future studies should further examine how gaming-derived competencies transfer across contexts. While this study identified competencies such as psychological tactics, collaboration, and emotional regulation, additional comparative research is needed across different game genres, player expertise levels, and non-game settings. Such work could clarify when gamer competencies remain context-specific and when they become adaptable forms of expertise relevant to education, work, and professional training. 2950 Chang, T.-H., Chen, F.- C.
