2951 Negotiating the Validity of Lived Experience as a Form of Evidence Eowyn P. Wilder, Ravit Golanduncan, Clark A. Chinn eowyn.wilder@rutgers.edu, ravit.duncan@gse.rutgers.edu, clark.chinn@gse.rutgers.edu Rutgers University Abstract: This study explores how 19 undergraduate students negotiat ed the validity of lived as a form of evidence when evaluating multiple online texts  during civic deliberation on an issue of racial equity in education. Data collected from students’ small group discussions analyzed through the lens of epistemic injustice  demonstrates students’ diverse and nuanced thinking around how to evaluate personal testimony when making source credibility judgments. Recent scholarship has called for engaging  students in civic deliberation  in ways that incorporate high-quality factual information, emphasize mutual humanization, build on students’ prior knowledge, engage students with real-world problems, and provide sufficient scaffolding to support students in evaluating sources that represent a diverse range of cultural and ideological perspectives that both reflect and challenge students’ own lived experiences and that of the dominant culture (Lee et al., 2021; Mirra, 2018). While extant research has focused on different approaches to developing students’  capacities for evaluating the credibility of online information sources (Breakstone et al., 2021; McGrew et al., 2018) and the heuristics students use to evaluate source credibility in terms of expertise and bias  (McGrew, 2021; Wineburg & McGrew, 2019), few have examined how students make sense of lived experience as a form of evidence. This study furthers our understanding of  how students negotiate the validity of lived experience as part of evidential reasoning during civic deliberation. Whose lived experiences are allocated more or less weight during evidential reasoning is an issue of power and justice because it indicates who gets to count as a credible knower. To support critical analysis of how students negotiate the validity of lived experience during civic deliberation, we employ the framework of epistemic injustice, specifically focusing on testimonial injustice which occurs when s omeone’s perspective or voice is afforded less credibility than is warranted as the result of prejudice (Fricker, 2007). The research question that is the focus of the present paper is “How do undergraduate students negotiate the validity of lived experience as evidence during civic deliberation on racialized experiences with police and schooling? ” This study was conducted at a public university in the Northeastern United States  in the context of a teacher preparation course which was co-taught by two of the authors and collaboratively co-designed by all authors. All students enrolled in the course were invited to participate in the study. Participants were 19 undergraduate students across different majors who were all interested in pursuing a career in education. The participants were majority white (n=11), with a range of racial and ethnic identities represented among the other students including Asian or Asian Americans (n=2), Hispanic, Latinx, or Latin American (n=3), Black or African American (n=1), one student who identified as more than one race, and one student who preferred not to disclose their race or ethnicity. Data comes from a single class session during which students participated in a semi-structured small group five students and provided with two multimodal digital texts on the topic including one video and one article from a local news source. Students were tasked with deliberating within their assigned groups on the topic with a focus on the claims that were presented across the two texts, the evidence used to support those claims, and the perspectives that were and were not represented by those texts. Students were encouraged to bring in their own lived experiences with for consideration alongside the evidence presented by both texts. Data sources included audio recordings from all groups that were  collected using handheld audio recorders and a student demographic background survey. Qualitative coding was conducted  on transcripts of the audio recordings by the first author to support thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022)  while holding regular coding audit meetings with the team to check for consistency of coding and reach consensus  to build a shared interpretation of the data. Coding and thematic analysis focused on identifying patterns in how students assigned 2952 more or less credibility to particular lived experiences when considering personal testimony as a form of evidence and how such credibility judgments arose during deliberation on race, power, and privilege. This section is organized around emerging themes from the data using examples from a single group to offer an illustrative case of how the same set of students grappled with these issues over the duration of their discussion. Theme #1: Dismissing the lived experience of youth of color Consistently throughout the discussion, multiple students made comments dismissing the lived experience of youth of color  as by attributing their views to their emotional state or mindset rather than to reality, such as by claiming that the only evidence to support the removal of police from schools was that students of color may experience a “mentality” of feeling unsafe rather than viewing their testimony as evidence of SPOs presenting a viable threat to the safety of students of color. However, the same students expressed the view that the personal experiences of  two different representatives of  school police officers  (SPOs) should be treated as compelling evidence and taken at face valu e. One student commented,  “People are like well, the police officer in school is going to get like, get the kid arrested [inaudible] wrong. Like they don't want that, they're not there to arrest their kid. They're there to get the kid out of the trouble.” In neither text is there any evidence to support this claim other than personal testimony; in contrast, both the article and the video offer statistical data on the disproportionate targeting of youth of color  in addition to the personal testimony of youth of color  that SPOs pose a viable threat to their safety, demonstrating a clear tendency to afford the lived experiences of youth of color less credibility. Theme #2: Reconciling differential experiences While students  frequently identified discrepancies among lived experiences in the texts and among group members, students struggled to reconcile those differential experiences and explicate these differences along racial lines. Multiple students voiced that they have never personally had a negative interaction with an SPO, nor heard about anyone else who did. However, when the sole Black student in the group then described his own experience with racial profiling by multiple SPOs at his school, he was met with silence until the group changed the subject. This refusal by his peers to take up his lived experience as a form of evidence in the same manner as they had their White peers’ personal experiences demonstrates how the students were either unwilling or unable to grapple when faced with a lived experience that directly contradicted their own that could not be outright dismissed as a “mentality” given that their Black peer had been outright threatened with arrest and discipline. From the lens of epistemic injustice, this student was done  the greatest epistemic harm by having his lived experience completely omitted from deliberation while others’ testimony was at least taken into consideration if ultimately discredited. Theme #3: Negotiating the relevance of racism in broader society to schooling Students in this group experienced the most tension in their discussion when deliberating on the relevance of individual instances of racism and police brutality in broader society as relevant to policing in schools. Students openly acknowledged the presence of systemic racism in policing outside of school but disagreed about whether broader patterns of lived experiences in society (e.g., instances of racism that occur outside of schools) constitute relevant evidence. One student pushed back on this sentiment by asserting that it is the responsibility of schools to discuss these lived experiences as part of education as a means for educators to communicate, “I see why you're threatened. And I see all this going on in the world. And it’s making those topics a part of the conversation and able to be talked about.”  This student’s argument demonstrated a more nuanced understanding by pushing back against this dichotomy between broader society and the daily reality of students’ lives. This study demonstrates how the credibility of youth of color was frequently undermined and dismissed using language that reduced their lived experience to “feelings” while the testimony of White adults and even White youth were given more weight and taken at face value. When faced with testimonial evidence that directly conflicted with their own lived experiences, students opted not to attempt to integrate this evidence into their deliberation at all. Frequently during students’ civic deliberation, epistem ic injustice was perpetuated against youth of color by undermining their credibility as knowers (Fricker, 2007). Students expressed divergent views around the relevance of patterns of lived experiences  related to racism  in broader society to individuals’ daily realities. Educators and instructional designers seeking to promote more equitable discussions should consider scaffolds that focus students’ attention on the unequal distribution of credibility along racial lines, strategies for reconciling contradictory evidence resulting from differential experiences, and eliciting student thinking around the connections between systemic oppression in broader society and individual lived experiences. 2953 Braun, V., & Clarke, V. Teachers College Record, 121(11), 1–40. https://doi.org/10.1177/016146811912101102 2954 How Networked RPPs Learn: Infrastructuring Data Loops in Developmental Planning David Phelps, Telos Learning, david@teloslearning.net Rafi Santo, Telos Learning, rafi@teloslearning.net, Sara Vogel, City University of New York, Sara.Vogel@cuny.edu Jean Ryoo, Telos Learning, jean@teloslearning.net Abstract: This study illuminates ways that data act as a form of infrastructure, creating wide-ranging forms of value within institutional change processes. Through longitudinal analysis of a networked improvement community of 15 colleges of education focused on int egrating computational and digital literacies across teacher education programs, we demonstrate expansive roles of data that go beyond purposes of measuring outcomes and to act as a key lever in infrastructuring activities (Penuel, 2019).

What role candata play in networked approaches to achieving coherent institutional change at scale in education? One promising approach for network leaders to support institutional change processes is the use of data (Coburn & Turner, 2012). Research on the topic of data use in networked improvement communities typically focuses on the use of data for accountability, theory development, and/or practical improvement efforts in relation to meeting target outcomes of a systems change initiative (e.g. Bryk et al., 2011). The current study identifies an understudied topic of data use in networked improvement communities: developmental planning. Focusing on data use in developmental planning processes makes visible the intricate work that network leaders do to develop networks (e.g. manage, broker, and resource networks), as well as the developmental planning efforts happening within each node of the network (e.g. to design, implement, and course-correct systems change initiatives). The current study analyzes the role of data use in developmental planning processes of a large-scale networked research-practice partnership (RPP).

## Literature review

Studies on data use in education tend to focus on the role of data in implementing solutions and measuring outcomes of those solutions to well-defined problems. These studies highlight the use of data to support accountability via testing how well a solution meets a target outcome or theory development via testing how well the theoretical principles and conjectures that inform a solution actually work in practice (Yeager, et al., 2015). Studies in the context of networked improvement communities reveal the role of data in practical improvement efforts via testing out and iterating upon innovations grounded in the familiar routines of practitioners (Bryk et al., 2011). Yet, there is little empirical knowledge or practical guidance around the role of data in s upporting the developmental stages of a networked improvement community that precede the creation of implemented solutions and outcome measures. In other words, what role candata play in the foundational developmental planning stages of a networked improvement community coming into being, and of network members defining the problem-space, purpose, and vision for their systems change initiatives? To answer this question, the current study leverages the concept of data learning loops (Wenger-Trayner & Wenger-Trayner, 2020). A data learning loop occurs when partners in an RPP analyze data from one or more parts of the network to generate and share insights (e.g. trends, heat maps, worked examples, conceptual frames) to stakeholders connected to other parts of the network. Developmental planning includes the work network leaders do to grow and infrastructure a networked improvement community, and the concurrent work network members do to envision and scale their systems change initiatives. Infrastructuring refers to the practice of redesigning elements, relations, and routines of a system in support of a systems change initiative that will directly impact classrooms (Penuel, 2019).

We explore a large-scale multi-year institutional change project to spread and scale computational and digital literacy (CDLs) pedagogies across a network of 15 colleges of education. Data learning loops were identified as the unit of analysis (Wenger-Trayner & Wenger-Trayner, 2020). Grounded theory (Glaser & Strauss, 1967) was used to identify the value each data loop created for the initiative’s network leaders to engage in coherent institutional change processes. Over two dozen data loops enacted by the RPP during 2022-2025 were analyzed 2955 across six dimensions: the part of the network the data originated from, the analysis that happens with the data, the packaging that happens with the analysis (e.g. to make the analysis sharable with and useful to other stakeholders), the part of the network the packaging is shared with, the transformations to the network that occurred as a result of the data loop, and ultimately the purpose these transformations served (e.g. for network leaders to manage, broker, and resource networks, and network members to design, implement, and course-correct their initiatives).

Once data learning loops were adequately characterized across each of the six dimensions a thematic played in developmental planning processes.  Relevant literature on data practices in supporting systems change initiatives were used to attune to the phenomenon of interest such as using data for persuasion (Coburn, Touré, & Yamashita, 2009) or for diagnostic problem framing (Phelps & Santo, 2022). The current study identified four major types of data use practices that supported network leaders in developmental planning processes. These include: Differentiating needs (of network members that vary across developmental coherence and disciplinary context), Designing Scaffolds (to support network members to create a strategic vision and a strategic plan), Identifying Contradictions  (to engage in diagnostic problem framing or prognostic course corrections) and Establishing Persuasive Frames (to motivate action to those internal or external to the network). Taken together, network leaders leveraged data loops to shift the infrastructure of the network—connecting network leaders, network members, and funders —in consequential ways for institutional change. A brief narrative overview of the development of the networked improvement community will elucidate each type of data use practice.

As the network was being established, it was unclear which next steps would be appropriate for network member teams given their varying initial capacity to start a systems change initiative. To support network leaders and members in determining appropriate next steps, a data loop was created. It was looped from network leaders’ impressions of network members’ initial readiness (and subsequent member checks of those impressions), analyzed via a strategic planning readiness matrix with seven readiness criteria, packaged as a ‘GPS’ (global positioning system) map, and looped back to team leads to help them determine their next steps for planning, resulting in designed differentiated tracks of a strategic planning workshop for teams to self-select into (Differentiating Needs).

After the workshop event, the RPP articulated a theory of change based on the principles of coherent institutional change theory (Cobb, Jackson, Henrik, and Smith, 2020) that centered the change process on teams creating a program-wide vision and then aligning various elements of their program (scope and sequence, coursework, clinical partnerships) to that vision. Leveraging this theory of change alongside a corpus of qualitative data of network members who had agreed to ethnographic observations, interviews, and document analysis, twonew types of data loops emerged. One type analyzed the accomplishments of teams further along in the theory of change to distill their work into a visioning toolkit that other teams could use for guidance and inspiration (Designing Scaffolds). Another type analyzed the challenges teams faced or anticipated in their systems change work and translated these into a handout and workshop retreat activity of productive struggles and pitfalls to support teams’ developmental planning (Identifying Contradictions). As network leaders became clearer about the problem space, they were able to create data loops that were funder-facing to ask for specific supports (such as a funded coordinator role) to help teams that had lower capacity to engage in visioning work (Establishing Persuasive Frames). This brief narrative shows how over time, developments in the network supported new data loops which, in turn, supported new network developments. Developmental planning is a fundamental process for network leaders to build networked improvement communities, and for members within those communities to envision and establish their own systems change initiatives. This research provides a window into the specific ways that data was used to support the developmental planning processes of a network of 15 colleges of education aspiring to integrate computational and digital literacies into their teacher education programs. Although the context is distinct, the findings have implications for other networked improvement community models, as well as relevance to the broader knowledge base of data use in research-practice partnerships in the learning sciences. Specifically, this study complements what is known about data use for solution implementation and outcome measurement activities with developmental planning activities. It further provides practical guidance for how partners can use data to build a networked improvement community.

## Finding Power through Resistance in a Museum Exhibit about

Climate Change Kaitlyn Kinshella, Lynne Zummo, José Gutierrez kaiti.kinshella@utah.edu, lynne.zummo@utah.edu, jose.gutierrez@utah.edu University of Utah Abstract: Museums are uniquely positioned to support climate change education, yet learning unfolds within complex environments where power shapes who feels welcome and able to participate. We examine how power, resistance, and climate skepticism intersect to influence learning experiences. Focusing on a group where power was particularly salient, we analyze how participants navigated dominant discourses of skepticism. Our findings indicate that acts of resistance to discursive dominance can contribute to positive cl imate change learning outcomes.

Objectives Educational efforts that support public understanding of climate change are increasingly necessary (e.g., IPCC, 2023). Museums are uniquely  positioned to engage in such efforts (Hamilton & Christian Ronning, 2020), yet learning in these spaces is shaped by complex social dynamics that influence participation. Prior research shows that power—often structured along race and gender —shapes who feels welcome and able to participate  (Archer et al., 2016; Dawson, 2014).

This study examines how power operates interactionally within a museum climate exhibit and asks:

1. How do participants co-construct power through interaction?

2. How do power, resistance, and climate skepticism intersect in shaping learning?

## Theoretical framework

Power is the ability to shape social and material conditions and opportunities for individuals and collectives (Philip & Gupta, 2020). It is co-constructed through interaction and often operates through taken-for-granted norms. In science learning spaces, power frequently aligns with dominant racialized and gendered identities, positioning science as “white proper ty” and privileging particular forms of participation (Hinsley et al., 2017; Mensah & Jackson, 2018; Archer et al., 2017). These dynamics extend t o science museums, which can reproduce exclusionary structures (Dawson, 2014), and are likely to emerge in social dynamics that unfold at exhibits aimed at supporting visitor learning of climate change.

Climate skepticism is also socially patterned, particularly among conservative white men—described by McCright & Dunlap (2011) as  “cool dudes” who are more likely to express dismissive attitudes toward climate change. Some learning sciences research has  identified similar discourses of skepticism among adolescent boys (e.g., Walsh & Tsurusaki, 2018). When such discourse dominates interaction, it may constrain engagement with climate learning (Norgaard, 2012; Weddig, 2022). At the same time, when learners resist these dynamics, there is potential to create alternative pathways for participation and learning.

## Context and participants

This study took place in a natural history museum exhibit on climate change (see Zummo et al., 2026). We focus on one group of three participants selected for the salience of power in their interaction: Ella (alarmed), George (concerned), and Jerry (dismissive), based on the Six Americas framework (Chryst et al., 2018). Data sources and analysis Video data were analyzed using interaction analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) with Jeffersonian-informed transcription (Hepburn et al., 2017). Power was operationalized as interactional moments in which participants shaped opportunities for participation and meaning-making (Philip & Gupta, 2020). 2958 Learning was conceptualized as uptake or rejection of exhibit framing (e.g., local, hopeful, community-oriented), reflected in participants’ discourse (“side door” and “door closing” moments; Zummo et al., 2026). Ella, George, and Jerry co-constructed power as they moved through the exhibit, influencing the ways that they engaged with each other and how they learned from the exhibit. We offer abbreviated analysis of three moments representing the ways that Ella, George, and Jerry usually shaped power, which in turn shaped their learning. Constructing power through dominant discourse Early in the exhibit, participants were prompted to reflect on their emotional responses to climate change through an interactive display. Jerry frequently centered dismissive perspectives, positioning himself as disengaged from the exhibit (e.g., “that’s how I expect to feel about this entire exhibit”). Ella and George initially responded with laughter and minimal challenge, allowing this stance to shape the interaction. Jerry continued to orient the conversation toward his own reactions, reinforcing a ske ptical frame. These moments aligned with rejection of exhibit framing and constrained opportunities for shared learning. Resistance and agency At a later display highlighting community action, participants begandiscussing whether certain actions were appropriate or meaningful. As Jerry and George debated, Ella attempted to offer an interpretation but was interrupted. Rather than continuing to participate, she disengaged from the interaction and moved to another part of the exhibit. By shifting her attentional and physical engagement, she resisted participation in an unproductive exchange and redirected her learning experience, altering the interactional dynamic and creating space for independent meaning-making.

Making space for positive reflection Near the end of the exhibit, participants were prompted to reflect on what they would share with others. Jerry again emphasized disinterest, but George redirected the conversation toward Ella (“What do you think, Ella?”), creating space for her contributions. Ella sustained this shift by continuing to share her perspective (“I liked everything… I’d bring kids here”). She elaborated on specific aspects of the exhibit she found meaningful, including its interactivity and relevance for younger audiences. In these moments, power shifted away from dominant skeptical discourse, enabling uptake of exhibit ideas and more productive engagement. Interactional dynamics among participants co-constructed power, influencing both participants’ engagement with the exhibit and the extent to which they experienced moments of learning. Jerry asserted power by centering his own disinterest in climate change, aligning himself with other conservative white males, or “cool dudes”, who also evidence expressions of dominant discourse that center climate change denial (McCright & Dunlap, 2011). Initially, Ella and George’s silence, affable reactions, and lack of challenge aided in the co-construction of Jerry’s power. However, Ella also demonstrated moments of agentic resistance through refusal to participate in unproductive conversations with Jerry and George and her own engagement with the exhibit. When given the opportunity, she also spoke her mind and persisted in sharing her takeaways. Ella’s small but noticeable acts of resistance enabled her to center her own experience and engage with the exhibit on her own terms, thereby altering the power toward herself and the exhibit. This benefited her learning in the end, as demonstrated through her final reflections on the positive experience she had in the exhibit overall.

## Scholarly significance

This work offers insight into how co-constructed power can influence climate change learning in museums. Powered interactions that favor dominant voices can inhibit learning, while opportunities for agency and resistance against dominant power structures can aid in learning. This finding presents both a challenge and opportunity for museum professionals seeking to promote climate education—that is, to create ways to deconstruct and reconstruct imbalanced power dynamics that can take place in many social rel ationships, particularly within relationships where intersecting identities are at play and the group holds conflicting views on climate.

2960 Testing a Graph-Based Intervention to Support Belief in Climate Change: Potential Roles of Numeracy and Surprise Rina Miyata Harsch, University of Minnesota, harsch@umn.edu Vijay Marupudi, University of California, Berkeley, vijaymarupudi@berkeley.edu Amber Armstrong, University of Minnesota, armst417@umn.edu Alyssa Kasahara, University of Minnesota, kasah010@umn.edu Maha El Ouaer, California State University, Dominguez Hills, melouaer1@toromail.csudh.edu Lila Flores, California State University, Dominguez Hills, lflores249@toromail.csudh.edu Marlen Nava, California State University, Dominguez Hills, mnava41@toromail.csudh.edu Jennifer Hernandez, California State University, Dominguez Hills, jhernandez1248@toromail.csudh.edu Jeffrey Kramer Bye, California State University, Dominguez Hills, jkbye@csudh.edu Abstract: In this in-progress study, we developed an intervention that uses graphs of climate data to engage participants’ in reasoning about causal invariance, highlighting fossil fuels as a primary cause of increases in CO₂ levels. We examine changes in climate knowledge as a result of the intervention, as well as the potential moderating role of numeracy. Data collection will be complete by May. We predict that numeracy and graph literacy will predict students’ change in climate beliefs.

In the learning and cognitive sciences, recent projects have made efforts to leverage what we know about STEM education toward improving people’s understanding of climate change. In particular, Thacker and Sinatra (2022) examined the role of numerical estimation and epistemic prompts, Schotsch and Powell (2022) examined people’s intuitive causal theories, Lee et al. (2023) examined instruction in causal invariance and moral framing, and Cho et al. (2024) have shown that numeracy overrides polarization to help people understand the math of climate change. Collectively, these suggest that people’s numeracy, understanding of graphs, and intuitive reasoning about causation, might moderate their ability to learn about the scope and scale of climate change. Particularly striking is the finding that participants receiving a causal invariance (Cheng & Lu, 2017) intervention persisted in self-reporting more actions to support the climate two years after the initial intervention (Lee et al., 2023). These efforts are needed, in part, because of the widespread difficulty most people have in intuitively understanding very large numbers (Landy et al., 2013; e.g., measures of climate impact) and super-additive functions like exponential growth (Ciccione et al., 2022; e.g., the rate at which plastic production has increased). The present study seeks to explore ways that people’s sense-making of graphs may help them better understand the severity of the climate crisis (RQ1)–and how that may be moderated by their numeracy (RQ2) and reasoning about causal invariance in graphs (RQ3).

## Method

Undergraduate participants are being recruited to complete this lab-based experiment at an urban public university in the Los Angeles metro area in the United States. Data collection is ongoing and will cease by May after the full target sample of 75 participants. Below, we report tentative analyses on the 40 participants so far.

## Materials and measures

The pre-test was comprised of seven measures: Subjective Graph Literacy (Garcia-Retamero et al., 2016), Berlin Numeracy Test (Cokely et al., 2012), items from the Test of Science Related Attitudes (Fraser, 1981), Willingness to Take Climate Action items (Lee et al., 2023), Human Induced Climate Change Knowledge (HICCK; Lombardi et al., 2013), Climate Change Estimation, Prefer, Incorporate Feedback and Change Preference (EPIC; Ranney & Clark, 2016), and the Six Americas Super Short Survey Yay measure (SASSY; Chryst et al., 2018). The post-test included two of the seven: the HICCK and SASSY, which we predicted would be most sensitive to changes in attitudes following the intervention. We also measured participants' arithmetic fluency (Loenneker et al., 2024) and fraction comparison ability (Obersteiner et al., 2022) as additional measures of numeracy, which we predicted might influence the effect of the intervention (RQ2).

In the intervention, participants first were introduced to the topic of climate change and emission of greenhouse gases like CO

2. Then, participants viewed a series of labelled graphs depicting CO₂ levels recorded

over different timespans. Participants were asked questions to check their understanding of each graph. Then, they 2961 received a paragraph explaining the graph before the next graph was presented to them. The first graph depicted CO₂ levels over the past two years, the second graph, CO₂ levels over the past 65 years, and the third graph, CO₂ levels over the past 800,000 years, but with the last 100,000 years hidden (Figure 1, left). Participants were asked to use the graph to predict CO₂ levels for the last 100,000 years (the gap in the graph). After participants drew their predictions, they were shown the entire graph (Fi gure 1, right), depicting an unprecedented spike in CO₂ levels. We predicted that participants might show greater pre-to post-test gains if their predictions were further from the actual levels (RQ3). Next, they viewed graphs depicting CO₂ emissions caused by volcanic activity over time (which remained constant), and CO₂ emissions caused by fossil fuels over time (which increased). Thus, these graphs together used causal invariance to show that somethi ng must have caused the spike, but that natural contributors of CO₂ must not be the primary cause; this causal attribution is the learning target. The study was completed on a lab computer on a custom web interface in around 45-60 minutes. Figure 1 Two of the Crucial CO 2 Graphs in the Intervention Sequence.

Below each graph, participants wrote an open-ended response and read a scientific explanation for the graph.

To address Research Question 1, we conducted a one-tailed paired sample t-test on HICCK sum scores for each participant in the pre-test and post-test. We found improvements in HICCK sum score from pre-test (M(SD) = 22.13(2.78)) to post-test (M(SD) = 22.98(2.72), t(39) = 1.96, p =.029). On average, HICCK scores increased by 0.85 points (SD = 2.74; 95% CI [0.03, 1.68], 10,000 nonparametric bootstrap). A Stuart Maxwell test suggested some potential trends towards pre-to-post shifts in SASSY (χ2(2, N = 30) = 9.53, p =. 009). In the analyses for Research Question 2, we examined the potential contributions of participants’ numeracy during the intervention on this trend toward a pre-to post-test increase in HICCK, standardized across participants. We fit separate models for the math tasks, as the incomplete sample lacks power for a combined model. We found no evidence that pre-to-post HICCK improvements is predicted by arithmetic fluency accuracy (β = 0.15, bookstrapped CI [-0.07, 0.39], p =.363), fraction comparison accuracy (β = -0.05, bootstrapped CI [0.49, 0.18], p =.749), or the Berlin Numeracy Task accuracy (β = 0.15, bookstrapped CI [-0.21, 0.45], p =.368). Thus, these preliminary results suggest no evidence in this incomplete sample of any effect of numeracy on the improvements in HICCK.

To address Research Question 3, we constructed a linear regression model with z-scored HICCK difference score as the outcome variable. To test the hypothesis that the discrepancy between participants’ expected carbon dioxide concentration and the correct c oncentration would predict changes in HICCK score, we computed the signed error between participants’ prediction about current-day carbon dioxide concentration levels (the y-value of the rightmost pixel of the graph they drew in the function prediction task) and the true concentration value, 426, which was presented to them after they drew their prediction. The signed error between prediction and true value, standardized across participants, was not found in this preliminary analysis to predict changes in HICCK score (β = 0.19, bookstrapped CI [-0.14, 0.48], p =.244). In summary, we developed an intervention using graphs and explanations designed to guide reasoning about causal invariance to support the enrichment of knowledge and changes in attitudes about human-induced climate change. We hypothesized that this intervention would result in improvements in knowledge and beliefs related to climate change. An analysis of our incomplete sample showed trends, though no conclusive evidence, towards the efficacy of this intervention. Furthermore, we hypothesized that pre-post learning would depend on participants’ numeracy and discrepancies between their predictions and the facts depicted in the graphs, though our analyses of the incomplete sample do not corroborate these hypotheses. Once data collection is complete, these results will determine whether this intervention is likely effective, and if so, for whom. 2962 Cheng, P. W., & Lu, H. (2017). ## Acknowledgments

We would like to thank our participants for their contributions. 2963 Queering STEM: Envisioning Disruptions to Normativity Nickolina Yankova, University of Southern California, yankova@usc.edu Abstract: Though commonly perceived as neutral and unbiased, undergraduate STEM contexts are steeped in exclusionary practices. Situated in an interdisciplinary elective course, designed as a queering  of STEM, this qualitative study examines students’ past  experiences with normativity and what they envision as possibilities for transformation. Findings surfaced themes depicting students’ lived experiences in STEM, with implications for design. Despite being commonly perceived as neutral and unbiased, STEM fields are grounded in exclusionary practices across gender, racial, and other lines of division (e.g., Denaro et al., 2022; McGee, 2020), perpetuating systems of oppression which privilege who is white, cis, male, and straight (e.g., Leyva et al., 2022; Kersey & Voigt, 2020). Interrogating inequities in higher education STEM has permeated academic discourse for some time now, yet there is an underexplored opportunity in taking a design-based approach (Brown, 1992) to addressing present disparities, aimed at transforming and queering current curricular practices in STEM and reimagining possibilities. Prior work has investigated efforts to queer STEM culture and practices across disciplines (e.g., Yankova & Peppler, 2025; Cross et al., 2022; Paré, 2021), with the goal to deconstruct and disrupt what is normative toward more equitable outcomes. The present study contributes to such efforts, with the goal of understanding students’ experience with normativity in STEM along with envisioned possibilities for disrupting what is normative. Thus, I asked, How  have students experienced normativity in STEM over the course of their academic careers and what are some envisioned possibilities for unsettling present inequities? This study takes on queer theory perspectives and is further grounded in queer pedagogy (e.g., Butler, 1999; Halberstam, 2005; McWillims & Penuel, 2016; Pennel, 2020; Sumara & Davis, 1999). The term queer in this study, in addition to pertaining to one’s gender or sexual identity, is used as a verb, meaning to deconstruct and challenge what is normative. Embracing notions of queer pedagogy and queer curriculum has predominantly been taken up in areas that are intuitively more “queerable” like the humanities and social sciences, though perhaps there is even greater need to consider a queering in STEM toward creating more equitable spaces where students can thrive (e.g., Britzman, 1995; Dubbs, 2016). Emergent tenets of queer pedagogy focus on questioning norms toward subverting them, disrupting dominant narratives and heteronormative structures, and illuminating new ways of learning and knowing (e.g., Sumara & Davis, 2002). This qualitative study is situated in the context of a 10-week-long elective, undergraduate course at a minority serving institution in Southern California, at the intersection of mathematics, robotics, and weaving. In the course, students who were primarily Informatics majors  worked in groups of 3-4 (N = 23) to first construct their own robotic loom and then, to design and weave their textiles, leaning on mathematical principles in the process. From the start, the course was framed as a queering of mathematics, and STEM more b roadly, with students learning about the underpinnings of queer theory and queer pedagogy as one framework to challenge dominant practices in STEM and call into question what is normative. It was important to position the course in such a way, with the explicit goal of disrupting curriculum designs that perpetuate inequities toward better outcomes, as to prime students to reflect on the ways in which they had – or had not – experienced normativity in their prior educational STEM experiences.  To understand how students ha d experienced normativity in STEM, I draw on individual reflection data from Week 2 of the course. S tudents were asked to reflect on their prior educational experiences in STEM and answer: What are some normative or oppressive practices you have encountered in STEM contexts? What might be some potential solutions? I engaged in iterative thematic analysis (e.g., Creswell & Poth, 2016) to gain understanding of the student experience with normativity in STEM  and how they envision a path forward, mining for emergent themes through my analysis.

Out of the enrolled students in the course, 39.13% (n = 9) had experienced normativity and/or oppressive practices in STEM firsthand while 60.87% of students (n = 14) had not. Unsurprisingly, most students who had first-hand experience belonged to one or more minoritized groups in STEM (i.e., female, non-binary, queer, Latinx/e), with two students, drawing on their intersectional identities. Even so, the remaining students had an awareness of 2964 existing biases in STEM which came through in their responses. Following an iterative thematic analysis of student reflections, four themes emerged depicting the student experience with normativity (see Table 1). In the interest of space, I discuss one of the themes in further detail below. Table 1 Students’ Experience with Normativity in Higher Education STEM Theme Description Data excerpt % of Reflections Gender imbalance Awareness of or first-hand experience with STEM as male dominated.

“Gender bias in STEM is an oppressive practice that has affected many women, including myself.” 69.57% Class structures Instructors perpetuate inequities via class structures and/or content.

“I have witnessed professors who are set in their ways and refuse to adapt to students’ needs.” 21.74% STEM culture Competitive and/or toxic STEM culture as the norm ⇔ not feeling “good enough.” “Everyone is always trying to get ahead of each other, and people forget what really matters.” 26.09% Diversity and equity Issues of equity across other axes for minoritized groups (race/ ethnicity, LGBTQ+, disability).

“Due to my ethnicity and sexual orientation, people do not immediately think I love to code.” 30.43% One way s tudents in the course had experienced normativity was through fixed instructional practices (e.g., course content, class structures – group work), privileging dominant groups in the field, with 21.74% of students bringing up the theme of class structures in their reflections. Reflecting on their experience with a class project as part of a major class, Jazzy, a senior in Business Information Management who identifies as queer and non-binary, said: Reflecting on my own educational experiences, some normative and oppressive practices I have encountered in STEM would be in the language used in a lot of the projects we were given. I distinctly recall a project where we were told to create a program that paired women with men for marriage based on both of their rankings of their top three candidates. This project made me very uncomfortable as a queer person because I felt this was objectifying, heteronormative, and sexist.

In their response, Jazzy sheds light on the importance of language for creating environments that would allow students to thrive, or conversely, feel excluded from STEM spaces, with their identities unaccounted for. Fixed instructional practices where the language or wording of a prompt gets outdated over time can, as in Jazzy’s case, perpetuate inequities that go unrecognized. As Jazzy pointed out, the project takes as a starting point an ingrained narrative of heteronormativity, which came in conflict with their identity. Yet, beyond that, the prompt’s wording had no value added and little to do with the actual learning goals of the project. Being cognizant of inequities perpetuated by language could thus unfix  what has been fixed  by dominant groups in the field toward recognizing student identities and fostering more inclusive spaces. Three other themes outlined salient next steps toward imparting change in STEM spaces with respect to disrupting normative practices, in line with existing research (e.g., Schipull et al., 2019). Most prevalently, about half of the students in the class (52.17%, n = 12) found that a key first step was an awareness of and education about the normative practices that have been perpetuated in STEM, especially as it pertains to equity and inclusion. Another theme centered around efforts to broaden participation of minoritized groups by engaging in early education, programs that spark student interest, or mentorship opportunities. The last theme focused on finding community in STEM spaces and growing safe spaces where one’s voice can be heard. Drawing on reflection data from an elective undergraduate course designed as a queering of STEM, this study examined students’ prior experience with normativity in STEM, on one hand, and how students envision a path ahead, on the other. In mining for emergent themes, this study surfaced many of the inequities and normative practices already permeating STEM discourse such as issues with gender imbalance, a toxic STEM culture, and other issues around diversity and representation, centering the experiences of minoritized students in the field and affirming the pertinence of addressing these issues. Implications lie in the design of queered  STEM learning environments that tackle present normative practices as surfaced in this study, and others, toward disrupting them. 2965 Britzman, D. (1998). 2966 Designing Learning Environments to Absorb Social Risk Lee Martin, UC Davis, leemartin@ucdavis.edu Angela Booker, UC Sandiego, a1booker@ucsd.edu Abstract: All learning environments involve risk, and patterns of risks can create profound and inequitable exclusionary pressures, inviting in some participants while excluding others. This conceptual paper introduces the idea of absorbing social risk and three design moves: framing, creating structures, and e nhancing visibility. The paper considers the nested and uneven ways learners face risks, considers recommendations for designers, and calls for further investigation. A Focus on social risks in learning Learning is inherently social, both in the sociocultural sense of learning as participation (Lave & Wenger, 1991), and in the practical fact that many learning activities must include other people (e.g., debate, soccer, jazz band). We posit that learning also involves intrinsic risk, as learning environments ask learners to act beyond their competence, as in Vygotsky’s (1978) notion of the zone of proximal development. Learning in social settings can provide many forms of support, including social scaffolding (Pea, 2004), friendship (Takeuchi, 2016), and access to creative ideas from others (Pierroux et al., 2022), but learning with others also presents social risks that incur specifically because the learning is taking place in a social group – in the presence of others and subject to cultural historical conditions. Learning alone poses certain risks (e.g., practicing dance alone still poses risks of injury or frustration), but learning in a social setting adds risks of embarrassment  (DiSalvo et al., 2014), microaggressions (Nasir & Vakil, 2017), and marginalization (Bell et al., 2017), among others. The presence of risks can limit students’ willingness to engage in learning activities, and uneven distribution of risk among learners can create inequitable exclusionary pressures, inviting in some participants and excluding others. As designers then, we have an imperative to consider the landscape of risks facing learners and how to manage them. One approach to risk is to focus on solutions at the individual level. For example, an intervention might aim to bolster students’ self-efficacy (Bandura, 1982; Pajares, 2006)  or increase their interest in a domain (Hidi & Renninger, 2006)  to make the value of the activity higher, or their assessments of success likelihood higher (Wigfield et al., 2004). Interventions might change students’ attributions around failure (Dweck, 2000), or might try to build “grit” so that students are persistent, holistically, regardless of risks (Duckworth et al., 2007). In this conceptual paper, we look beyond the individual to consider absorbing  social risk in ways that

(1) relate to the inherent social risks and (2) do so at the level of design choices in the learning environment. By

absorbing, we meandesign choices that “soak up” or remove risk from the environment. We build on research that takes an organizational perspective on risk (Edmondson, 2008), adding attention to overlapping cultural and historical contexts. We offer three hypotheses for how designers can absorb social risk. Framing to absorb social risk First, an activity can be framed  to absorb risk (Goffman, 1974). Consider the effect of framing a meeting as a brainstorming session – a “no bad ideas” framing can reduce risk of embarrassment from presenting one’s ideas. Or consider Black Surf Week (Rubalcava, 2023), an initiative that offers a surfing learning environment that is open to all UC Sandiego students, simultaneously framing it as (1) definitely involving some Black participants and (2) addressing “Black and Africandiasporic relationships to land and water.” This framing absorbs some of the social risk —embarrassment, microaggressions, and marginalization that are disproportionately experienced in surfing which can be a highly specific intersection of race, ability, culture—that limits access and participation frequently constrained and surveilled through racial identity. Creating structures to absorb social risk Designers can create structures (real or virtual) to guide people around or through socially risky spaces. The jigsaw method (Aronson & Patnoe, 1997), for example, was designed to mitigate racialized and social class divisions through division of labor in a classroom activity, facilitating more equitable participation in classroom discourse. School PE programs, in contrast, use physical barriers (gender-segregated locker rooms) to mitigate risks of boys and girls intermingling in a state of undress, but do little to mitigate risks that might be felt by LGBTQ+  youth. Alternatively, consider youth theater companies that require all youth to wear black shorts and a tank top at all times while changing).

Enhancing visibility to absorb social risk 2967 In addition to creating frames, norms, structures, and so forth, designers can make those choices  explicit and visible to current and potential participants. Visibility moves may include providing mission and vision statements, announcing “curricular” choices (e.g., reading lists), or other branding/marketing moves. Visibility moves offer a kind of map that allows participants to see the landscape of risks and opportunities in a learning environment and the ways in which the design of the space is working to make participation less socially risky for them. Maps may help people know whether approaches to absorbing risk are partial  (e.g., statements of solidarity), or more complete (e.g., comprehensive structures to absorb risk). Participants can also make and share their own maps, providing insight on risks that may be invisible to designers. Why absorbing social risk matters When we bring people together, and especially when we do so in ways that connect people across social divisions, such as generation, gender, race, and political sensibilities, we inevitably introduce social risks. When those risks are not designed for, the y can become exclusionary forces that limit the potential for people to fully participate. While we can celebrate when individual  resources (e.g., bravery, strong social networks) are sufficient to overcome such exclusionary pressures, we should not rely on them. We must instead design to absorb risks to encourage and allow for full and meaningful participation. It is helpful to think about social risks as layered, unevenly encountered, and nested, from the individual right in front of you, to the social group surrounding you, to the layered exo-and macro-systems that form the sociocultural and sociopolitical contexts of learning (Barron, 2006). Social risks are  unevenly noticed and experienced across social and cultural identities (Nasir et al., 2020). Risks are simultaneously immediate and historicized. Risk is temporally complex, looking different in established community settings (Rogoff et al., 2003) than it does when a new group spends 10 to 20 minutes building  rapport before beginning an activity. We argue it is essential to attend to the active presence of social practice  steeped in sociopolitical conditions about which some participants may be highly aware and involved, while others may be ignorant. We offer a visual of these overlapping layers in Figure 1, to portray the idea that individual, social, and sociocultural/sociopolitical dimensions are (differentially) at play and bear on issues of risk. We ask, at what level, and over what period of time, have participants unevenly been navigating consequential social risks? Likewise, can we recognize the consequences where social risk has not effectively been absorbed? Figure 1 Nested and Layered Forms of Constraint and Risk.

We see substantial variation on whether and how learning environments attend to social risk. Some do little, offering no clearly stated commitments, no infrastructures where practice-expectations are embedded, and no educators well-prepared to recognize how social risk arises and how it can be socially navigated in alignment with clearly stated and community endorsed commitments. Other environments offer partial support – perhaps social commitments are clearly stated, yet infrastructures (such as framing, structures) to absorb the actual risks are absent, invisible, or only in place for some learners. Others are more comprehensive, yet we note that no learning environment can absorb all risks for all people. Nor do we think that all social risk is detrimental, as there are times when it can be a powerful motivator (Martin et al., 2009). We do believe that educational designers interested in fostering meaningful participation should attend to social risk, its exclusionary pressures, and how designs can intentionally and strategically absorb social risks. We offer this paper, o ur hypotheses on how designers can absorb social risk (through framing, structures, and visibility), and our urging to attend to the contextually nested, temporally complex, and unevenly distributed nature of risk, not as a mature or final framework ready for use, but rather as conversation starters. We hope this paper opens a discussion in the learning sciences community about how and why we design to absorb social risk, inviting further research around a shared set of concerns. 2968 Aronson, E., & Patnoe, S. 2969 A Shifting Mosaic of Student Feelings: Experiences within and Reflections toward Productive Failure and Productive Success Designs Zack Carpenter, Regina Lisinker, Chelsey Legacy, David DeLiema Carpe787@umn.edu, lisin003@umn.edu, legac006@umn.edu, ddeliema@umn.edu University of Minnesota—Twin Cities Abstract: Productive Failure (PF) asks students to engage with complex, open-ended problems before formal instruction — embedding “failure” as a design feature. Despite PF's learning benefits, students' emotional experiences across its components remain understudied. Emotion surveys and interviews in an undergraduate data visualization course revealed consistently higher frustration in PF than Productive Success (PS), decreased enjoyment during solution revelation, and interview themes of discomfort, valued struggle, and preference for PF as a strategic supplement.

Caring for students' emotional experiences in failure-laden learning environments is a growing priority in the learning sciences (e.g., Jaber & Hammer, 2016; Lanouette, 2022; Radoff et al., 2019; Scipio et al., 2025; Vea, 2020; Vescio, 2025). This concern becomes especially salient when failure is intentionally designed into learning, as in Productive Failure (PF). In PF, students engage with open-ended problems — failing to produce the canonical solution by design — whereas Productive Success (PS) designs often have step-by-step guidance and produce success through the activity itself. Although PF's learning benefits relative to PS designs are well-documented, less work examines the emotional nature of learning in PF (see Savelson & Muldner, 2024; Sinha, 2022; Gashaj et al., 2022), especially students' overall feelings toward the design. Understanding students' experiences during PF could open new research horizons, inspire design refinements, and improve learning outcomes. Such insights matter for ensuring PF's learning gains don't come at the cost of intense negative experiences that risk turning students away from learning in a subject (c.f., Heyd-Metzuyanim, 2015). PF is a subset of problem-solving-before-instruction designs (Loibl et al., 2017; Sinha & Kapur, 2021) structured around four mechanisms—activating prior knowledge, highlighting critical features, promoting elaboration, and organizing features into coherent concepts —across two phases and three environmental layers (activity, participation structures, social surround). In the generation phase, students tackle open-ended problems and rarely solve them completely, creating productive failure moments; in the consolidation phase, instructors guide comparison of student-generated and canonical solutions (Baumgartner et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2024; Kapur, 2008; 2010; 2014; 2016; Kapur & Bielaczyc, 2012). Meta-analyses show PF leads to higher conceptual learning and transfer when design principles are closely followed (Sinha & Kapur, 2021). Prior research on emotions in PF is mixed: some studies find little correlation with post-test performance (Savelson & Muldner, 2024); others link negative emotions to positive outcomes (Sinha, 2022). Furthermore, Gashaj et al. (2022) found that PF can intensify math anxiety and lead to disengagement, while Suriyaarachchi et al. (2025) found that students appreciated structure in PS and challenge in PF. We extend this work by linking emotion questions across PF's three design layers and exploring students' reflections toward the design through interviews.

## Method

This IRB-approved study took place in an undergraduate data visualization course (N = 44) during Fall 2024 at a large Midwestern university. PF activities were "recreate" tasks — students collaboratively deduced how to reproduce a target graph in R, activati ng prior knowledge while introducing novel elements, with multiple valid solutions, followed by instructor-led consolidation. In PS, activities were step-by-step tasks with explicit guidance and active instructor support. Emotion surveys (adapted fr om Watson et al., 1988) were administered after each of three PF and three PS sessions; the first author wrote ~6,000 words of field notes; instructors recorded 14 audio memos; ten students completed 30-minute end-of-semester Zoom interviews. Surveys were analyzed using paired t-tests with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), and interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022). 2970 RQ1: Feelings within PF and PS design components The most notable finding was significant and marginally  significant elevated frustration in PF across all three components: within the activity (t(29) = 3.47, p =.005, d = 0.63), within the group (t(29) = 1.79, p =.083, d = 0.33), and during solution revelation (t(26) = 2.04, p =.077, d = 0.39). In the solution compone nt, students also experienced significantly less enjoyment (t(26) = −3.09, p =.014, d = −0.59) and marginally more boredom (t(26) = 2.27, p =.095, d = 0.44). Within the activity, PF students reported marginally less confidence (t(29) = −2.33, p =.08, d = −0.43). Overall, students experienced fewer positively valenced emotions and more negatively valenced emotions in PF than in PS across nearly all emotions and components. Figure 2 Bar Graphs of Emotions Experienced in Productive Failure and Productive Success RQ2: Feelings toward PF and PS designs Four themes emerged. (1) Diverse preferences shaped by structure, exploration, and interdependence: some valued PS's step-by-step structure; others preferred PF's exploratory nature; still others described the designs as mutually reinforcing—PS built foundational skills that made PF enjoyable. (2) Complementary roles and value of struggle: PF and PS supported different learning types; one student noted that "having to figure stuff out on my own…ingrained it into my brain more." (3) Structural differences shape error experiences: errors in PS felt low-stakes because help was available; errors in PF felt "high-stakes" because students had to wait. Paradoxically, PS errors could also be stressful —students felt they "should know it already." (4) Support for PF w ith strategic integration: students broadly endorsed PF in other classes but wanted it "sprinkled" —at unit transitions or before assessments—rather than as the dominant mode.

Students' experiences in PF and PS form a mosaic of varied feelings depending on where within the instructional sequence we look. Frustration extended beyond problem-solving to group work and the revelation of solutions, suggesting its object is broader than merely failing to find the canonical answer. Decreased enjoyment and increased boredom during consolidation suggest that solution revelation may be associated with a shift from active to passive processing. Notably, PF's frustration stems from structural withholding of support —yet this same feature is what students credited for deeper retention. Students described PS and PF as interdependent: PS builds the confidence that makes PF's ambiguity tolerable. Though surveys were discrete, interviews retrospective, and not just the moment of "failure" but the whole design, and bringing us closer to PF where student experience becomes "a target of teaching and learning in its own right" (Vea, 2020, p. 311). 2971 Baumgartner, V., Daguati, S., Trninic, D., Akveld, M., Caspar, A., Hungerbühler, N., & Kapur, M. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(6), 1063 –1070. 2972 How a Site Walk Near Lake Victoria Helps Engineers Learn Jessie Zarazaga, Southern Methodist University, jzarazaga@smu.edu Max K. Sherard, University of North Texas, max.sherard@unt.edu Abstract: A community-led site walk introduced engineering professionals and students tonew understandings about space/place, which in turn, improved participatory co-design practice. We present a framework for exploring how site walks made different objects of reasoning visible (material and spatial) and subverted social hierarchies (between engineers and community members), and close by discussing the value of such site walks for engineering education. Community engagement processes in engineering and engineering education are a collection of practices which stimulate dialogue between community members and professional or student engineers, for the purpose of producing more sustainable and effective engineering outcomes (Taylor & Kent, 2014). These processes support material-based technical exploration, collaborative problem-solving, and understanding spatial/temporal qualities of a community (Keshwani & Adams, 2017; Sherard et al., 2025). However, there are a variety of pitfalls in such community-based engineering experiences. Traditional engineering education tends to prioritize abstracted problem-solving processes supporting an assumption of technical and design superiority (Lucena et al., 2010; 2024). Local communities may respond passively, either through lack of power, expectations of ‘outside expert’ control, or lack of confidence and language for technical collaboration (Natarajarathinam et al., 2021). Participatory co-design is one approach to community-based engineering which attempts to rebalance this dynamic. Here engineers are taught to prioritize community knowledge and capacity-building, while the community is given a central role in designing, prototyping, and evaluating solutions (Murcott, 2016). Site walks, community-led walking tours to teach “outsiders” about important community spaces, are one participatory codesign practice which foregrounds community understanding and authority, enables mutual learning, fosters trust, and grounds research in community priorities (Hagen, 2011, Rojas, et al. 2021). In this this study, we explore the dynamics of a community-led site walk that took place in an engineering co-design project in rural Tanzania (TZ). The Kijiji Project Kijiji Project is a participatory co-design engineering project that brings together: (a) Kasisa village community members (TZ); (b) a local non-profit organization (NGO); and (c) professional and student  engineers from the United States (US) and TZ. Each year participants gather in a field site on Lake Victoria to collaborate on an intensive 6-day co-design process focused on sustainable rural development. Mixed teams of community members, students, and professionals focus on micro research projects such as sustainable construction materials or water procurement, projects imagined and selected by the community during a series of focus groups. Critically aware of how hierarchies between engineers and community members continue to emerge in each micro project, we planned a series of design exercises to subvert these hierarchies. However, on arrival this past July a community team-leader shared concerns about impacts from recent climate-related flood events. The team was redirected into a walk across the 600m rural site, structured around community stories of storms and water and their effects on soil, planting, boundaries, and technology. The site walk was documented with video and audio, GPS walk-traces, field-notes, and video recordings from a post-walk reflection. Researchers watched videos, took notes, and discussed emerging themes. This study is a qualitative analysis of a single case (Ragin & Becker, 1992), the site walk, and draws on analytical techniques from interaction analysis (Jordan & Henderson, 1995) and ethnography (Emerson, 2011). Analysis is still unfolding; we present here an initial rendering of our findings. Describing the site walk The site walk was led by one community-member (Saleh, a pseudonym) and involved 22 others, of which seven were engineering students, five faculty, one member of the NGO, and eight community members. The hour-long site walk transversed the project site from the high point near the road, to the lowest point near the  lake shore. Saleh initiated and led the walk, following his memory of the climate-impacted path of stormwater drainage. The group paused at places of heightened importance in terms of water and flooding, safety and trespass, or construction, planting and development. While some pauses were marked by clearly visible objects (a living fence), others were marked by more subtle landscape changes, such as changes in plant growth or topography, previously invisible to the professional and student engineers. The primary conversation was led by Saleh in 2973 Swahili, translated to English by a student engineers. The secondary conversation, led by professional engineers, connected this information to the future work of different project-teams. Theorizing learning on the site walk As the group moved across the site, the process of walking, pausing, and discussing provided opportunities for the group to learn about land, community, and design. To better understand what was learned on the site walk, we crafted an initial framework to differentiate two broad objects of reasoning (Table 1): (a) knowledge about physical qualities of land, gained through the body while walking, pausing, and discussing; and (b) knowledge about social dynamics of the community, conveyed in Saleh’s stories. We broadly describe the two forms of knowing that occurred here, and discuss specific learning related to the projects. Most fundamentally, the physical pace and rhythm on the land allowed an embodied measure of place, experienced in the horizontal repetitive sequence of steps in motion. Similarly, through the foot and the eye, the vertical slope dimension was measured by the body through visual change  in the lake-horizon parallax. Next, students experienced a material inventory; sandy soils, and rough clay were identified by the foot; lake-side plants, sisal cactus and eucalyptus marked boundaries. Changes in landform and material added richness to the variable of time, interacting with motion to alter the sense of distance (Scott, 1998). While impacted by variables like wind and heat, these body-measures were consistent and shared. In addition to this physical site-knowledge, participants learned about the social dynamics of the space, gaining a more layered understanding of site. The site walk helped participants understand differing notions of land ownership and local knowledge about the land and its memories. Students learned that specific land-uses and knowledge varied across community groups, and how those understandings were given greater or less value, open-endedness or certainty by particular participants. Taken together, the site walk engendered a complex physical and social understanding of the site that became, for the micro-project teams, a touchstone for their week’s work. Later in the week, design discussions referred to the site walk, not only for individual projects, but also for interconnections between projects. For example, a shared conversation between the water filter team and the site-landscape team, regarding specific filtration properties of reeds identified near the lake. Finally, and most unexpectedly, the process of learning through active participation opened up a more interactive attitude to the design process.  Compared to the previous year, students were more likely to leave the site to visit sites of knowledge with community members, and to do so at an earlier stage in the process. The shared physical site-learning helped students find earlier confidence in collaboration and in doing less themselves. Justifications for creative changes on a ‘stuck’ design decision, such as choosing to remove a whole water-filtration element, or test two different drainage control ideas, partially referenced that walk-experience. Table 1 Knowledge Uncovered through the Site-Walk Projects Physical Knowledge of Site Social Knowledge of Site Distance Flow Materiality Community Connectedness Exploration Climate Project design at pause-sites Slope drainage palate of plants, soils authority & expertise reference all decisions confident interventions Water Project filtration network slope, gravity, tank distance cost listen local, take time circularity of projects confidence doing less Engineering Knowledge measure body, time vertical flow material knowledge community knowledge connected projects grounded innovation The intention in reproducing this experience is not to efficiently teach professional or student engineers to know a site; but rather to explore a way of knowing that allows more familiar, measurable aspects of site-learning to be integrated with less familiar conceptual learning of special community qualities. As an approach to community-based work, such an experience-prior to active co-design practice-has three values: (1) it prioritizes embodied measurement over cartesian measurement, grounding the engineer in the local knowledge of the site; (2) it constructs an understanding of place rooted in the perspectives and pathways of the community, prioritizing their authority and expertise in  land-knowing; and (3) it embodies  processes of movement, exploration, and interconnected networks between project materials. Bounding of project knowledge gives comfort to student-engineers. International learning experiences break such limits, a benefit that comes with challenges. Grounding an open-ended design experience within the physical certainty of land-walking may have assisted students to remain more comfortable in that new unbounded thinking-space during their week-long collaborative practice. 2974 Emerson, R.
