## Acknowledgments

We thank the community members from Kasisa for their engagement, teaching, and wisdom. 2975 Immersive Virtual Reality in STEM Education: A Systematic Review of Theoretical Constructs Giomara Sevilla-Campoverde, Guillermo M. Chans, Genaro Zavala giomara.sevilla@tec.mx, guillermo.chans@tec.mx, genaro.zavala@tec.mx Tecnológico de Monterrey Abstract: Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) has shown a positive impact on teaching and learning processes within STEM education; however, limited knowledge still exists regarding the factors that influence and interact within this process. Accordingly, the present study focuses on reviewing the affective and cognitive aspects examined in recent literature and analyzing the relationships established among them. The findings indicate that factors such as immersion, interactivity, control, presence, and graphic quality s ignificantly influence variables like motivation, enjoyment, self-efficacy, and learning outcomes. Nevertheless, there remains a need to consolidate a theoretical foundation that explains how these elements interact to foster meaningful learning in immersive environments. Therefore, future empirical research should further explore these factors and their causal relationships to deepen the understanding of learning processes in IVR-based education.

The integration of virtual reality (VR) into higher education is transforming how students engage with STEM disciplines, enabling immersive environments that enhance interaction and promote deeper engagement ((Marougkas et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2021). Despite its potential to improve understanding of complex concepts, the effectiveness of immersive virtual reality (IVR) depends on multiple affective and cognitive factors that remain insufficiently explored. Understanding how these factors interact is es sential to optimize instructional design and maximize learning outcomes  (Matovu et  al., 2023). To address this gap, this systematic review synthesizes the affective and cognitive constructs most frequently investigated in empirical studies on IVR-based STEM education at the higher education level.

## Method

This study forms part of a broader  systematic literature review. The review followed the PRISMA framework, drawing on articles retrieved from the Scopus and Web of Science databases.  The search string used for this study was (("immersive virtual reality" or "immersive virtual learning environment" or "IVR" or "immersive learning" or "CAMIL" or "the cognitive affective model of immersive learning") and ("teach*" or "educ*" or "learn*" or "knowledge") and ("science" or "technology" or "mathematics" or "art" or "engineering" or "steam" or "stem") and  ("higher education" or "undergraduate students" or "university”)). The inclusion criteria were as follows: a) full-length papers published in peer-reviewed scientific journals, b) empirical studies employing Structural Equation Modeling (SEM)  as the primary analytical technique  because the study aims to examine the causal or predictive relationships among the constructs  compared to other studies that seek to validate instruments or modify variables to observe a change, c) use of IVR through Head-Mounted Display (HMD) devices, and e) publications dated between 2019 and 2025. Studies were excluded if they focused primarily on the technical design of immersive environments, or if they were non-peer-reviewed publications such reports. Likewise, papers were excluded if they: (1) discussed only theoretical or conceptual frameworks without empirical validation through experiments or case studies; (2) employed non-HMD immersive technologies; or (3) involved participants  with medical condition s that  could affect cognitive processes. Following this screening process, 17 studies met all criteria and were included in the final analysis. The analysis revealed multiple  direct and indirect relationships underlying learning processes in  IVR environments. A direct relationship refers to an immediate effect from one observable variable on  another. In contrast, an indirect relationship occurs when one or more intervening factors mediate the effect of an independent variable on a dependent variable.  Several studies have used structural models within IVR-mediated learning to analyze how cognitive, emotional, and technological variables  interact. The following summarizes the mai n 2976 Direct relationships The reviewed studies identify immersion, interactivity, control, presence, attention, and pedagogical orientation as key factors shaping IVR-based learning. Immersion and interactivity consistently enhance engagement and learning outcomes by enabling active manipulation and meaningful interaction with virtual environments (Makransky & Lilleholt, 2018; Yang et al., 2023; Agbo et al., 2023). Similarly, presence and attention are positively associated with emotional engagement and cognitive focus (Petersen et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024; Makransky et al., 2020).

However, these relationships are not purely linear. While immersive features promote participation and learning, excessive sensory or informational input may increase cognitive load, thereby hindering learning efficiency (Petersen et al., 2022; Fokides & Antonopoulos, 2024; Yang et al., 2023). This suggests that immersion functions as a double-edged factor, requiring a balance between sensory richness and cognitive processing demands. Across studies, a consistent pattern emerges: immersion-related features enhance presence and engagement, but their impact on learning depends on cognitive conditions and instructional design. In this process, pedagogical orientation plays a central role by aligning immersive features with learning objectives and supporting cognitive regulation (Matovu et al., 2023; Agbo et al., 2023; Makransky & Lilleholt, 2018). Approaches grounded in constructivist and experiential learning frameworks further reinforce the role of pedagogical design in enhancing learning, presence, and enjoyment (Agbo et al., 2023; Makransky & Lilleholt, 2018).

Additionally, instructional scaffolding supports cognitive regulation and prevents overload, while structured design improves perceived usefulness and behavioral intention (Petersen et al., 2022; Villena-Taranilla et al., 2023; Cheng & Tsai, 2020). Although IVR can support both individual and collaborative learning, evidence suggests that performance may decrease as group size increases, highlighting the need for appropriate interaction strategies (de Back et al., 2021).

Indirect relationships Indirect relationships highlight the role of mediating variables in IVR-based learning. Factors such as feedback, goal clarity, usability, and challenge influence learning outcomes through their effects on attention, enjoyment, and motivation (Cheng & Tsai, 2020; Agbo et al., 2023; de Back et al., 2021). Conversely, poorly designed environments—characterized by low-quality feedback or excessive visual complexity—can increase cognitive load and negatively affect learning performance (Fokides & Antonopoulos, 2024; Petersen et al., 2022). The findings of this review deepen our understanding of how individuals respond to and adapt within immersive learning environments. By examining both affective  (e.g., motivation, presence, enjoyment) and cognitive (e.g., attention, self-efficacy, cognitive load) dimensions, this study highlights the dynamic interplay between emotion and cognition in IVR-based learning. This integrative perspective  supports the development of a conceptual framework explaining how learning unfolds in immersive contexts and informs the selection of appropriate pedagogical approaches, instructional strategies, and assessment tools. When instructional design  aligns with learners’ needs and interests, it fosters a balance between affective engagement and cognitive processing, thereby promoting meaningful learning.

From a practical standpoint, the se findings offer actionable insights for  designing immersive environments that minimize cognitive overload while enhancing motivation and engagement. They also provide guidance for educators in selecting and adapting resources that align with specific learning goals, ensuring that the integration of technology remains pedagogically grounded. In this way, immersive technologies can enhance learning by connecting technological design with instructional intent.  Overall, the reviewed studies confirm that IVR can significantly improve teaching and learning, particularly in STEM education, yet its impact depends on complex interactions among technological, cognitive, and affective components. These findings contribute to theoretical models such as the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL) by supporting the interaction between affective engagement and cogn itive processing. This review extends these models by highlighting the moderating role of cognitive load and the central importance of pedagogical design. Future research should advance toward empirically validated models that explain these interdependencies and support more precise instructional design.

Frontiers in Psychology, 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.1081372 2978 The Progression of a Research Practice Partnership from Opportunity-Based to Collaborative: Lessons from a Rural Partnership Centered on the Co-Design of STEM Curriculum Srinjita Bhaduri, Jennifer Jacobs, Quentin Biddy srinjita.bhaduri@colorado.edu, jennifer.jacobs@colorado.edu, quentin.biddy@colorado.edu, University of Colorado Boulder Abstract: Although studies have examined the early development stages of Research Practice Partnerships (RPPs), there is minimal literature on partnerships in rural areas that have successfully evolved beyond these initial efforts. This paper explores  the intersection between RPP development and curricular co-design, focusing on how these interconnected aims can be jointly leveraged to promote STEM education. We articulate the processes by which the RPP engaged in pre-development and development phases  of curricular co-design, along with activities that helped align goals  and accelerated movement from an opportunity-based to a collaborative partnership. We share lessons learned regarding cultivating and sustaining partnerships, particularly those that seek to generate inquiry-based curricula. Rural communities offer rich contexts for innovative teaching and learning (Avery, 2013), and rural Research Practice Partnerships (RPPs) hold potential for continuous improvement based on partners’ overlapping interests and goals (Wilcox & Zuckerman, 2019). This study builds on and expands an existing RPP (Bhaduri et al., 2022) to create a curriculum that incorporates a locally relevant engineering design challenge (How can we increase the amount of food our community gardens can grow?), involves programmable sensor technologies and data science, and emphasizes local career connections. Collaboratively designing (co-designing) this curriculum serve d as a convergence point in bringing together teachers, district administrators, nonprofit organizations, and the research team by joining forces and collaborating to meet shared goals (Lee et al., 2022).  Guided by a partnership typology lens (Allen et al., 2020; Noam & Tillinger, 2004), the study addresses the question: How do intentional predevelopment and joint curricular co-design activities serve as mechanisms for advancing a rural RPP from an opportunity-based to a collaborative partnership?

Theoretical Framing Partnership development in rural environments This study leverages the cultural wealth of rural community members (Crumb et al., 2023) through partnerships with engaged organizations that agreed to collaborate on the development of a new STEM curriculum. RPPs typically evolve in stages over a period of several years (Booker et al., 2019). In this paper, we build from the partnership typology terminology developed by Noam and colleagues (Allen et al., 2020; Noam & Tillinger, 2004). Our study took place within an established RPP that is best described as  an “opportunity-based” (level 1) collaboration. The partner organizations in the rural community had overlapping interests, but their interactions were relatively infrequent and fragmented in nature. We articulate the processes by which the RPP became mor e “collaborative” (level 2), especially as the organizations engaged in the early phases of curricular co-design. Curricular co-design leveraging rural cultural wealth Curricular co-design can serve as a lever for RPP development, as it brings together the partners to ensure a common understanding pertinent to the problem at hand and generate innovative learning materials (Penuel et al., 2017; Roschelle, Penuel & Shechtman, 2006). As curricular co-design within the context of RPPs becomes increasingly common (Ni et al., 2022; Novak & Khan, 2022), there is a need to further unpack components of this process, including how community partners can become engaged and leveraged to provide critical support. For example, Lee and colleagues (2022) have identified the need to “design for co-design,” arguing that a layer of pre-work is necessary to ensure that co-design efforts will be successful. In this paper, we highlight what partnership-focused pre-work entailed in our rural RPP, how it contributed to a successful co-design workshop, and the subsequent transition of the RPP from an opportunity-based to a collaborative partnership. 2979 This study took place in a rural mountain town community in a Midwestern state in the United States, served by a school district comprising approximately 7,000 students. The district’s student population is 52.1% Hispanic/Latino, 44.2% White, and small percentages from other racial and ethnic groups; 38% are economically disadvantaged, and 33.9% are English language learners. Currently, the RPP includes individuals from the local school district, community college, environmental education nonprofit, community garden nonprofit, and community market (food bank) nonprofit.

This paper presents a descriptive case study (Yin, 2003) using an interpretative approach to analyzing project data to construct a detailed understanding of the dynamic and situated nature of our partnership development and codesign processes (Putnam & Banghart, 2017). Data included field notes from pre-development meetings with community partners (January-July 2025), a week-long co-design workshop (late July 2025), and follow-up exchanges with the community partners (August-October 2025). Pre-development work: Landscape analysis to orient and expand the partnership Prior to co-designing the curriculum, the research team conducted a six-month planning phase to expand the RPP by engaging in a landscape analysis (Mak et al., 2025) and targeted partner outreach. This process strengthened existing relationships, added a new partner organization, and clarified community assets, needs, and existing collaborations—facilitated by the close-knit nature of the rural context. Findings from these early discussions provided insight into the nature of each partner’s goals and how they aligned with the project’s goals. Four shared RPP goals emerged that helped to guide the co-design work: (1) integrating computer science and gardening education and outreach, (2) promoting sustainable gardening to provide access to local fresh food, (3) highlighting career pathways, and (4) cultivating partnerships within the rural community. Curriculum co-design: Development work with a collaborative partnership The project convened a workshop that included teachers and the partner organizations to develop an initial version of the curriculum and deepen partnership collaboration. Held at a community college adjacent to the community garden and community market, the workshop facilitated cross-organizational learning in both planned and organic ways. Partners contributed domain expertise (e.g., garden operations, food systems, career pathways) and collaborated on initiatives such as installing sensor stations in additional gardens that served the community market. The workshop yielded a detailed storyline overview (Reiser et al., 2021) of the curriculum with driving questions to motivate each lesson, as well as draft lesson resources (e.g., slides, student handouts). Ongoing partnership activities after the co-design workshop After the conclusion of the co-design workshop, additional cross-partner collaboration was required to produce a pilot-ready curriculum for implementation in Spring 2026. These collaborations included expanding the sensor setups, ensuring functionality and access, collecting video footage, and conductin g follow-up workshops. They helped to shift the RPP from a primarily researcher-driven, cooperative structure to a more “collaborative” model characterized by shared ownership, distributed responsibility, and partner-initiated engagement, as stakeholders actively contributed time, expertise, and resources toward advancing the project’s curricular goals.

## Lessons learned and conclusion

This study traces the evolution of an RPP expanded to co-design an inquiry-based STEM curriculum, offering insights into how partnerships can be cultivated and sustained over time. A key takeaway is the importance of intentional pre-development work—such as landscape analysis, goals alignment, and surfacing uncertainties — which can be understood as building a boundary infrastructure (Farrell et al., 2022) to support mutualism, shared goals, and coordinated action. Three core lessons emerged: (1) intentional pre-development phases are critical for ensuring alignment, identifying gaps, and sustaining engagement; (2) rural contexts can uniquely support RPP growth due to existing social networks and shared community investment; and (3) partnerships can progressively deepen across projects when grounded in stakeholder needs and supported by continuity in resources and collaboration. This work highlights the importance of studying RPPs as dynamic, evolving systems rather than static entities, emphasizing that alignment, multidirectional communication, and responsiveness to local goals are central to long-term success.

Any opinions, findings, or conclusions expressed in this material are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the National Science Foundation. 2981 From Root Cause to Action: Addressing Barriers to Computational Thinking Integration Alessandra Rangel, Digital Promise Global, arangel@digitalpromise.org Merijke Coenraad, Digital Promise Global, mcoenraad@digitalpromise.org Lisa Milenkovic, Broward County Public Schools, lisa.milenkovic@browardschools.com Sheryl Arriola, Broward County Public Schools, sheryl.arriola@browardschools.com Annmargareth Marousky, Broward County Public Schools, annmargareth.marousky@browardschools.com Sherenna Bates, Digital Promise Global, sbates@digitalpromise.org Kyle Dunbar, Digital Promise Global, kdunbar@digitalpromise.org Abstract: As school districts pursue computational thinking (CT) integration across their curriculum, it is important to examine barriers that may limit access to computing learning experiences. This paper examines a root cause analysis of factors limiting access to  CT and computer science (CS) for students in a large, urban school district and actions to mitigate barriers. We hope to support research-practice partnerships using root cause analysis to overcome challenges in making CS available to all students. To improve access to computing experiences for all students, school districts are increasingly moving towards integrating computational thinking (CT) and computer science (CS) into core curriculum, such as math, reading, and science (Adler & Kim, 2018; Barr & Stephenson, 2011; Dunbar et al., 2025; Orton et al., 2016). Exposure to CT can broaden student interest in STEM and CS fields and ensure that students who may not have access to CS courses or electives still have opportunities to engage in CT learning experiences (Orton et al., 2016). However, efforts to integrate CT into core curricula face barriers at classroom, school, and district levels. Teachers report limited CT expertise and limited time for implementation (Israel et al., 2022). There is limited  time to support teachers in building their capacity for embedding computing learning in their classrooms and ongoing priorities within school districts that create tensions and necessary trade-offs to balance different district-level needs when developing a district-wide CT initiative (Coenraad et al., 2021; Fletcher & Warner, 2021). While these challenges have been identified, less is known about the root causes of the challenges educators are facing, particularly as they are likely contextualized based on the unique situation of each district. Root cause analysis is a tool that can be used to more deeply understand a challenge by identifying not only details such as what and how, but also why it is happening (Rooney & Vanden Hauvel, 2004). Root cause analysis can surface causes for systems-level challenges (Phelps & Santo, 2022) and, in doing so, can allow researchers and practitioners to go beyond focus on curriculum and programmatic-level foci when focused on ensuring the inclusion of all students to address deeper, systemic factors (Erete et al., 2021). We approached the root cause analysis through the framework of Water of Systems Change, seeking to explore the conditions within the system that hold the challenge in place (Kania et al., 2018).  Root cause analysis can help us consider causes across the conditions that impact system change from explicit conditions (e.g., policies) that will lead to structural changes, to semi-explicit conditions (e.g., power dynamics), and particularly implicit mental models that, if changed, can lead to transformative change (Kania et al., 2018). Root cause analysis is a general methodology and the Water of Systems Change framework helped us identify the complex nature of root causes that could be contributing to the problem faced by the district and to focus conversations  on root causes at different, and preferably higher, levels of transformation.

In this paper, we share findings from work within Broward County Public Schools (BCPS), a large, urban school district, focused on expanding their CT Pathway and building on CT and CS work that has been occurring within the district for over a decade. The district is part of a large-scale, 4 year research-practice partnership (RPP) with six partner districts across the United States working to scale CT pathways for all students. The district’s STEM+Computer Science (STEM+CS) Program has worked for over 10 years to bring CS/CT to all students through student programs, teacher training and professional development (PD), and curriculum integration. The need for a root cause analysis emerged from both a district landscape study of their current CT Pathway and collaboration within our RPP. Through the landscape study analysis, the STEM+CS team lea rned that there was limited knowledge of the CT initiative across the district. Since then, STEM+CS leaders have led efforts to build awareness of their CT initiative, including utilizing an interactive infographic tool made to engage various stakeholders such as teachers, students, and district leaders (Rangel et al., 2024). In conversations with the research team, the STEM+CS team hypothesized that there may be challenges in how CT and CS are messaged 2982 across the district. Without a district mandate for CT integration, CT is a “nice-to-have” across curriculum. We seek to answer the research questions: 1) What are teachers’ perceptions of and experience with CT, CS, and the district CT Pathway? 2) What ar e the root causes of limited access to CS and CT for students in a large, urban school district?, and 3) What actions are predicted to overcome these root causes? Our process of conducting a root cause analysis included: 1) organizing a Core Team of 22 educators and community partners, 2) identifying the challenge statement, 3) identifying the root causes of the problem, 4) conducting data collection, and 5) developing an action plan. The root cause analysis process took place across 9 meeting sessions beginning in the summer of 2024 and through the 2024-25 academic year. In our first two sessions, we introduced the Water of Systems Change as the framework for understanding the conditions that enable systems change (Kania et al., 2018), with a focus on challenges educators face with integrating CT and overall awareness of CT. Then, the Core Team reviewed and provided feedback on an early version of a challenge statement drafted by the STEM+CS and research team (see Findings below). In the third and fourth sessions the Core Team identified key root causes they believed to be driving the challenge utilizing diagramming tools such as a cause and effect (or “fishbone”) diagram (Doggett, 2005) and exercises such as the Five Why’s activity. The fifth and sixth sessions were used to brainstorm data collection and survey development. Survey data was collected to learn more about these root causes from a broad group of educators in the district (n = 125). Finally, in session 7, we co-analyzed the survey data and developed an action plan to address the challenge to mitigate the root causes. The remaining meetings focused on finalizing this action plan. To begin, our RPP team utilized data from the landscape study and the district leaders’ experiences to identify and draft a challenge statement related to students’ access to and participation in CT and CS learning experiences. This challenge statement was  refined and finalized by the Core Team as: “Challenge is messaging at the instructional curriculum director level and district department level. Schools that may benefit the most from CS PD prioritize math and reading (Science of Reading). Even when training and support is offered, teachers may sign up for PD but not attend due to building level conflicts that arise (messaging is a nice-to-have, but not a needto-have without a mandate). How do you convince instructional curriculum directors that CT suppor ts reading and math priorities so that building administrators can support CT integration?” The Core Team identified causes that limited access to CS and CT for students, including communication (“CT needs to be rebranded: just like we said every teacher is a reading teacher; finding a way so that CT is at the forefront of our classroom and culture”), competing priorities (“CT would be included in all content areas as part of the instructional, content-focused calendar”), and knowledge/lack of understanding (“People don't know what computational thinking is”). The Core Team dug into each of these causes until they reached the root, which included two priority areas to focus their action planning on: 1) teacher training and ongoing support, and 2) accountability systems within the district. To learn more about the identified causes, the Core Team su rveyed teachers across the district (n=125) and found that teachers were mostly unfamiliar with CT, confirming the challenge of awareness. However, when asked about CT messaging in the district, teachers familiar with CT knew its importance, including how to use it in class, its role in preparing students for college or the workforce, and as a foundational skill for 21st century learners. One teacher shared, “That it is a shift toward making students more able to tackle not just academic but social and real-life situations in an effective manner and that it is beneficial for the whole picture of the student, not just their performance in my class or subject.” The Core Team developed an action plan to address the initial challenge of building awareness of CT, including conducting further analyses of the survey data collected to understand findings by geographic district zones and specific areas of need; building out curricular resources that would support teachers and school leaders with explicit connections between CT, math, and ELA; and leveraging existing partnerships with external partners to bring CT/CS integration into learning experiences with partners (e.g., field trips). The lessons learned in conducting the root cause analysis have broader implications for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers seeking to improve access to CT and CS for all students and conduct a root cause identify current challenges, explore root causes for those challenges, and develop an action plan to overcome them. Utilizing a root cause analysis process to identify specific challenges, causes, and actions can support RPPs and districts to identify needs within initiatives and work toward ensuring all students have access to CT and CS learning experiences. Every district presents a unique context, meaning that district-specific exploratio ns of needs and root causes are essential for ensuring that both the research-side and practice-side of RPPs fully understand challenges and can work with community members to take action to overcome them. 2983 Adler, R. 2984 Disciplinary Computational Thinking in AI-Mediated Problem

## Framing: A Rural Ag-STEM Context

Tugce Aldemir, Selcuk Kilinc, Vivek Sabanwar, Ali Bicer, Donggil Song taldemir@tamu.edu, selcuklnc@tamu.edu, sabbanwarvivek7@tamu.edu, alibicer@tamu.edu, creative@tamu.edu Texas A&M University Abstract: We examine how disciplinary computational thinking (CT) emerges during AI‑mediated problem framing in an Ag‑STEM pilot. Eighth‑grade teams used a chatbot while revising research questions /hypotheses in a sense-analyze-act cycle. Video, journals, and chatbot logs were coded for CT micro‑moves and cognitive‑apprenticeship methods. Students’ CT was emergent, concentrated in preparing problems and reasoning about system relationships; modeling/coaching supported these moves, with limited fading and co‑construction. We share design implications for AI-supported problem framing in class. Disciplinary computational thinking (CT) integrates computing into the core practices of STEM, such as framing researchable questions, operationalizing variables, working with data, building and evaluating models, and communicating evidence‑based claims, rather than coding for its own sake (Weintrop et al., 2016). Positioning CT in authentic, problem-driven science contexts can broaden participation by reframing computing as a tool for doing science, not an end in itself (Greenwald & Krakowski, 2020; Krakow ski et al., 2024). In rural Agriculture STEM (Ag-STEM), locally meaningful sustainability challenges can further make inquiry consequential for learners. Yet classrooms often stall at the outset, i.e., problem framing, where learners need to coordinate domain and computational representations, decompose problems, and align measures with claims (Basu et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2020). Progress in evidence‑centered CT assessments has improved what we can measure, but early‑phase reasoning is still hard to capture, and CT is often conflated with programming (Cutumisu et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020). Emerging AI scaffolding can surface and respond to micro-moves (e.g., tightening a question, operationalizing a variable) and may help make students’ emerging reasoning more visible during classroom orchestration, but fine-grained accounts of how such support shapes the substance and sequence of framing remain scarce (Morales-Navarro et al., 2025; Troiano et al., 2025).  In response, we report a small-scale analysis from a rural Ag-STEM pilot where middle-school teams engaged in a sense-analyze-act inquiry cycle around a locally relevant sustainability problem using low-cost tools and a discipline-trained AI chatbot as a peer mentor. We adopt Weintrop et al.’s (2016) taxonomy, Data Practices  (DP), Modeling and Simulation  (MS), Computational Problem Solving (CPS), and Systems Thinking (ST), as our definition of disciplinary CT. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship (Collins et al., 1989), the chatbot instantiated modeling and coaching/scaffolding (with fading), and prompted articulation and reflection. Analytically, we linked the AI’s moves to the disciplinary CT practices they supported and examined how those links played out during problem framing. Accordingly, we asked: RQ1. How did two middle‑school teams enact disciplinary CT during problem framing? RQ2. How did the AI chatbot facilitate those practices?

This study draws on one focal week of a 16-lesson Ag-STEM unit implemented in a rural Texas middle school. The unit engaged eighth-grade agriculture classes in a sense-analyze-act inquiry cycle around a local sustainability problem using low-barrier tools (e.g., Arduino sensors, Google Sheets/Docs). Two focal teams (3-4 students each) were selected from six class sections (~86 students total; 50% female; majority White/Hispanic). During the focal week, teams revised their research questions and hypotheses about measurable relationships among environmental conditions (e.g., soil texture/moisture) and plant outcomes (e.g., height/leaf color), with process-level support from a domain-tuned AI chatbot configured as a peer mentor while the classroom teacher managed overall lesson flow. Data included (a) small-group video and audio recordings of the framing lessons, (b) verbatim transcripts,

(c) group journals documenting original and revised RQs/hypotheses plus rationales, and (d) individual chatbot

logs. Each dataset was time-aligned by episode to trace links among talk, written revisions, and AI interactions. and coded student talk and journals using Weintrop et al.’s disciplinary CT taxonomy, focusing on early problemframing practices such as preparing problems for computational solutions and reasoning about relationships within 2985 a system. Next, within the same episodes, we coded AI turns for cognitive  apprenticeship methods (modeling, coaching, scaffolding/fading, articulation, reflection, exploration) and linked each AI move to the immediately subsequent student CT move to examine facilitation patterns. Finally, we applied pattern coding (Saldaña, 2016) to identify cross-case themes in what the chatbot appeared to support and where support remained limited. All coding was iterative and collaboratively reviewed by three researchers, with >85% agreement.

## Key findings and implications

RQ1. How did two teams enact disciplinary CT during problem framing? Across both teams, disciplinary CT appeared at an emergent level, that is, in brief, individual turns rather than sustained, co-constructed group episodes. The practices that surfaced most consistently were (a) preparing problems for computational solutions, such as naming and clarifying variables and making questions testable, and

(b) reasoning about relationships within a system, that is, articulating plausible causal links among variables. In

preparing problems for computational solutions, both groups moved from vague propositions to more testable statements by specifying independent and dependent variables or adding concrete levels. For example, Team 1 shifted from “If soil texture increases, then plant height will increase…” to a version that named contrasts among soil types, “shifting from sandy to loamy” (S1-T1, chat log). In discussion, S1-T1 similarly noted the need to “specify what soil textures and the kind of plants… [and] how I can measure plant height,” marking a targeted move toward operationalization. Team 2 likewise refined “the color of the leaves will change” to “turn yellow or brown,” explicitly specifying expected outcomes and direction of effect (S1-T2). These moves tightened variable definitions and testability, but they remained brief and local rather than sustained decomposition, students seldom elaborated measurement scales or decision rules beyond the immediate utterance. In reasoning about relationships within a system, groups also produced short causal warrants linking variables. Te am 2 tied moisture to plant physiology, noting that “reduced moisture can affect photosynthesis… indicating stress on the plant” (S1-T2, S2T2), thus linking soil moisture, photosynthesis, and leaf color. Team 1 similarly connected soil texture to growth through drainage and nutrient retention in chat (“loamy retains moisture and nutrients better than sandy”), then predicted greater height in loam. These causal links were plausible but cursory, with little discussion of competing mechanisms or boundary conditions.

RQ2. How did the AI chatbot facilitate these practices? Across both teams, the chatbot enacted core cognitive apprenticeship methods, most often coaching/scaffolding interleaved with modeling, with frequent articulation prompts and lighter instances of reflection, exploration, and fading. In Team 1, the chatbot  modeled what a stronger hypothesis could look like (e.g., a worked revision contrasting soil types) and then scaffolded S1-T1 to supply specifics (“sandy, clayey, loamy” and their drainage properties) before asking her to write her own version, an articul ation move with light fading as responsibility shifted to the learner. S2-T1’s exchange similarly showed stepwise scaffolding (“identify the main idea… simplify the relationship… remove unnecessary words”), followed by a self-authored formal statement and brief reflection (“How does this fit with your ideas?”). In Team 2, coaching paired with modeling nudged S1-T2 from “the color… will change” to specifying “yellow or brown” and a possible mechanism (“decreased photosynthesis”), while exploration-oriented prompts with S2-T2 extended to measurement planning (e.g., moisture meter, tensiometer, “squeeze test”). Overall, these support moves were most often associated with the practices documented in RQ1. Modeling and coaching around variables, levels, and wording helped students make questions more testable. Articulation prompts (“try your own version,” “what measurements will you use?”) consolidated those local decisions. Mechanism-seeking questions (“because…?”) elicited brief causal warrants (e.g., moisture → photosynthesis → color change; loam → moisture/nutrient retention → height). Notably, these interactions were focused on revising research questions and hypotheses and occurred largely as brief one-to-one turns with the AI. This task focus, together with the lack of prompts for coordinating peer deliberation, may help explain why CT appeared mainly as individual micro-moves rather than sustained, co-constructed reasoning. These findings suggest that AI modeling and coaching helped tighten variable definitions and testability and elicited concise causal warrants but seldom produced sustained group-level reasoning or strong fading. Two implications follow. First, AI-mediated framing should be designed to better support co-construction. This could include prompts that require peer deliberation and consensus writing, measurement-planning checklists with decision rules, and simple teacher-facing supports for identifying where groups are stuck. Second, in rural AgSTEM contexts, pairing low-barrier tools with locally relevant problems can position computational thinking as meaningful, consequential work that students can take ownership of. Future research should compare adaptive AI prompting with simpler static supports, examine fading trajectories across teams, and trace effects on later data use and modeling.

Journal of Science Education and Technology, 25(1), 127-147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-015-9581-5 Acknowledgment This work was supported by two internal grants from the College of Education and Humandevelopment at Texas A&M University (AI Emerge Program and Catapult Program). 2987 Uncovering the Value of In-Person Field Trip Experiences for Students Ana Saavedra, Daniel L. Schwartz anamar@stanford.edu and daniel.schwartz@stanford.edu Stanford University Abstract: Field trips are considered an essential experience in school. While their  benefits for various outcomes are well documented, less research exists on how students perceive the value of field trips. We conducted an initial study with 39 tenth-grade students who attended a field trip to the Amazon rain forest. Students completed a paper-and-pencil survey at the end of the field trip. Results suggest that when reflecting on the field trip,  students tend to prioritize their internal experiences over external features. These findings  invite consideration of field trips’ potential for supporting components beyond knowledge, such as socio emotional learning. This study contributes to our understanding of how students construct meaning from field trips experiences and may inform future design of field trips to maximize their beneficial impacts. Many schools have students take in-person field trips  (FTs) ranging from day trips to farms in pre-school, to overnight programs in higher levels and g eology trips in college. The benefits of field trips have been studied using frameworks of knowledge acquisition, connectedness, and stewardship, among others (Ardoin et al., 2018; Mullenbach et al., 2019). For instance, we know that after attending a field trip, students report higher levels of nature stewardship (Rijal et al., 2018) and increased connectedness to nature (Vande Wetering et al., 2022). However, there is limited research on how students construct meaning from field trip experiences. In this research, we ask: What experiences do students emphasize in their own recollections. Specifically, what is their relative emphasis on internal psychological states like perseverance as compared to external features such as spectacular waterfalls? When students participate in field trips, they transition from a familiar environment (the classroom) to a relatively novel and rich environment (the field  site). In both contexts, students encounter both external stimuli (new environments, activities) and  internal stimuli (their own thoughts, emotions, and bodily responses). Do students find the value of field trips primarily in knowledge gained (e.g., learning about new animal species or cultures) or in the  psychological experiences and dispositions they employ to adapt to unexpected situations?

We further examined which experiences students view as beneficial for their learning when they return to school. We surmised that the way students experience a field trip could influence its perceived value and how they connect it to school learning.

## Participants and Procedures

Thirty-nine tenth-grade students from a  school in Bogotá, Colombia, participated in a five-day field trip to the Amazon rainforest. The study was approved by Stanford’s Institutional Review Board. The field trip was a schoolsponsored activity operated by a Colombian outdoor education company. Students engaged in different activities including cultural exchanges with local communities, jungle hikes, and wildlife observation. At the end of the program students individually complete d a paper-and-pencil survey. F ield assistants  were trained  in research ethics and data collection  protocols. To ensure fidelity of implementation, we created a  manual with guidelines for data collection.

## Measures

We administered two different measures for this study: 1. Value of experience (open-ended responses): Students responded to open-ended questions about the value of their field trip experience. We analyzed responses using grounded theory analysis (Thornberg & Charmaz, 2014; Willig, 2014) to identify emergent themes; 2. Field trips benefits (Likert-scale items): students rated 11 items in a four-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 4 = strongly agree) assessing field trip benefits including connectedness, emotions, personal growth, and social interactions. For example: “I shared a positive emotion with someone else.” 2988 of a field trip experience into recommendations for another group of students. To address this, we asked students to share specific advice to other students. Table 1, section 1.1. presents the most frequently mentioned categories that emerged from students’ responses, organized in alphabetical order.  Percentages are calculated for emergent category and represent the proportion of students who mentioned that category in their response. Another question is related to where students found value of their experiences for school. Section 1.2. (Table 1) presents the most frequent categories of response in alphabetical order.

To answer this question,  we combined data from the two measures. We found that suggesting a positive attitude in the advice to others is positively associated with: feeling a stronger connection to other people that are part of the FT (r =.32, p =.045), as well as with sharing a positive (r =.33, p  =.038) and negative (r  =.34, p =.034) emotion with someone else. Interestingly, there was a negative correlation between students’ agreement on sharing responsibility toward a group goal (r = -.55, p =.000) or learning something about someone else (r = -.59, p =.000) and their tendency to provide recommendations related to trip logistics. Students who disagreed more on these aspects were more likely to  offer advice on practical matters  such as what to bring and time management.

Field trips are complex cognitive experiences where external and internal components of experience interact to shape students learning (Richmond et al., 2018). Results from this initial study reveal that when students describe the value of a field trip, the majority emphasize impacts  on their internal psychological experiences rather than external content acquisition.

Additionally, our analysis revealed significant associations between students’ internal psychological experiences and their social engagement with peers during the field trip. While previous research has established how social interaction  influences reasoning and behavior, these findings  extend this understanding by demonstrating the role of peer engagement in the constr uction of personal expe riences during a field trip  (e.g., Spang et al., 2025). This study examined a single field trip location with a specific age cohort, limiting generalizability. One potential limitation of the results is that we asked students to give advice about a field trip to a place they had never been. This may have led them to write about their internal states, because they had little knowledge of the Alaskan environment.

Schwartz anamar@stanford.edu and daniel.schwartz@stanford.edu Stanford University Abstract: A common characteristic of adventures is that they are often shared experiences. Camps, for example, arrange adventures for groups of students. This study investigated the degree of shared emotions during an adventure, focusing on a  group of Colombian fifth-grade students (N=41) during a field trip to the Chicamocha canyon. Participants reported their own emotions and those perceived in their peers. Results indicate that students tend to attribute more positive emotions to  themselves than to  others at the beginning and middle of the  shared adventure, with a converge observed towards the end. These findings raise questions about the discrepancy between self-reported emotions and those perceived in peers during shared adventures. Future research is needed to explore the underlying factors contributing to this phenomenon and its implications for group dynamics in different learning environments. Shared adventures, often  realistic and demanding, are inherently social experiences in informal learning environments. Many camps and field trips are designed to provide  participants with peak experiences, pus hing them beyond their comfort zones to encounter novel situations in a group setting (Leberman & Martin, 2002). As part of the peak experience, participants usually achieve a collective goal. For instance, going on a mountainous hike with friends. While research on field trips  has largely focused on individual outcomes (self-attributions) or changes in beliefs and behaviors  (e.g., Růžičková et al., 2023; Zeivots, 2018) less is known about the role of “sharing” in these adventures. A recent study found that participants reported higher confidence and self-esteem after experiencing a shared adventure (Kuban et al., 2014), but the interpersonal dynamics remain understudied. Studying emotions in shared adventures is particularly relevant to bridging the gap between informal learning experiences and the value of socio-emotional shared situations. Understanding the emotional dynamics of these shared experiences can provide valuable insights into how learners  engage with and process novel, challenging situations while interacting with others. Outdoor Education Programs have long incorporated challenging experiences (Schoel, 1988), with peak experiences considered a gold standard. While a field trip itself could be considered a form of shared adventure, the peak experience has a much shorter duration and therefore it is easier to measure. In particular, we measure affective responses – what are the emotions that comprise the peak experience? Moreover, we wanted to see if participants see these emotions as shared. T his study addresses two main research questions. First, is there a stereotypical emotional arc in a shared adventure? Second, do participants perceive their affective experiences converging with others over the course of a shared adventure?

## Participants

Forty-one fifth-grade students from a Bogot á, Colombian school participated in a field trip to the Chicamocha Canyon. The study was approved by Stanford Institutional Review Board. Parents/guardians provided consent during trip registration, while students gave oral assent on the first day of the field trip. Procedures The peak experience, a hike along the Chicamocha  canyon, occurred mid-program. Students hiked from approximately 1,600m (5,249ft) elevation, descending to 500m (1,640ft) at the canyon  bottom, then ascending back to the starting elevation. After hydrating and enjoying canyon views, students completed surveys administered by trained field assistants following a standardized protocol.

## Measures and coding

We de veloped a measure to assess students’ affective states at the beginning, middle, and end of the peak experience. Due to environmental challenges and safety considerations in outdoor settings, students completed 2991 the measure retrospectively, 1-2 hours after the experience  concluded. S tudents reported their own affective responses at each time point, with the option to list multiple emotions. They could write more than one emotion. Students also reported their perceptions of other students’ emotions at each time point. We employed the valence dimension (positive or negative) to classify emotional states (Trimmer et al. 2013). Each reported affective state was individually coded.

We present data for self-reported and perceived emotions of  others at three stages of the peak experience (beginning, middle, and end). Due to space constraints, we focus mainly on positive affective responses. Figure 1 shows the average number of positive responses reported for self and others. Students consistently reported more positive emotions for themselves than for others across all three stages. While the difference in positive affective responses tends to converge  descriptively at the end, significant differences persist from beginning to end (p <.05).

Figure 1 Average of Positive Affective Responses for Myself and Others We conducted one-way ANOVAs for each of the three stages, comparing the frequency of positive affective responses for self and others. Beginning: [F (2, 38) = 5.34, p = 009], middle: [F(3, 37) = 3.39, p =.03], and end: [F(2, 38) = 11.97, p =.000]. The challenging nature of the peak experience may incline students towards a self-serving bias to overcome personal struggles (e.g., Kashima  & Triandis, 1986). One interpretation of these affective responses this was not the case for the middle and end stages. These findings suggest a more complex emotional dynamic during shared adventures, warranting further investigation. Shared adventures are a form of informal experience that provide memorable interactions with others. This study focused on the shared nature of the experience and the affective responses that may contribute to this sharing. self-reports suggest similar rates of positive affective responses across participants. One limitation of our study is familiarity bias: M ost students knew each other since preschool, potentially  influencing their emotional interpretations of peers. A second limitation is relating to the timing of the reporting, retrospective reporting: Affective responses were collected 1-2 hours post-experience, which may impact accuracy. A follow-up study is underway to address the second limitation by collecting real-time affective responses during the peak experience. Our initial findings suggest that students may employ affective mechanisms to overcome challenges during the peak experience, such as attributing fewer positive emotions to others as a way to bolster themselves during the adventure  (self-bolstering strategy). Using narrative analysis, findings from eleven participants reveal that while online learning offers flexibility and access, it often lacks cultural safety, community, and re cognition of Métis identity. Participants described isolation, microaggressions, and expectations to educate others, yet emphasized the transformative value of Indigenous-only spaces. Métis identity shaped belonging, resilience, and feminist perspectives rooted in relationality, collective responsibility, and cultural continuity. This doctoral study explored eleven Métis women’s experiences with post-secondary education, focusing on any online courses or programs. The research questions included: (1) How do Métis women’s cultural identities and self-concepts shape their access to and experiences within online post-secondary education?  (2) What role do online instructional practices have on Métis student success? (3) How do colonial assumptions, embedded within learning management systems, impact and influence Métis women’s experience in online discourse? (4) How do Métis women’s cultural backgrounds impact their participation in online learning communities? (5) What are the experiences of Métis women engaging in online discussion spaces?

## Literature review

Because a literature scan of Métis women’s experiences in online post-secondary education did not surface relevant literature, the search was broadened to include empirical studies examining how culture shapes the experiences of marginalized students in on line contexts. Within this broader body of literature, scholars suggest that digital technologies hold the potential to expand access and opportunity for diverse and historically marginalized learners (Dunn & Brown, 2021; Eady & Woodcock, 2010; Kral, 2010; Phirangee, 2016; Simon et al., 2014; Sisco, 2010; Zou et al., 2025). Increasing enrolment in online learning (Allen et al., 2016; Seaman et al., 2018), alongside national priorities such as the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s Calls to Action (2015a, 2015b), has fu rther prompted educators to design digital environments that foster connection and engagement (Kral, 2010).

However, a consistent tension emerges regarding the difficulty of cultivating meaningful community in online spaces. Online environments are not neutral or culture-free (Gunawardena, 2020); rather, they often reproduce dominant paradigms that shape how int eraction is structured and evaluated (Carr-Chellman, 2005; Caruthers & Friend, 2014). While frameworks such as CoI and Communities of Practice emphasize interaction and participation, they do not fully account for relational accountability and cultural saf ety, which emerged as central to Métis women’s experiences. In many online environments, community is operationalized through structured activities such as discussion posts and group work, privileging visible and measurable forms of participation. As a result, interaction may be present, but relational depth remains limited  (Du et al., 2022; Hew & Cheung, 2014).

These tensions help explain why, despite claims that online learning increases access (Eady & Woodcock, 2010; Kral, 2010; Simon et al., 2014; Sisco, 2010), inequities persist within digital spaces (Ikebuchi, 2023; Kar, 2026; Resta & Laferriére, 2015). Flexibility alone does not ensure that learners experience community in ways that are meaningful or culturally congruent (Aragon & Johnson, 2008; Jaggars, 2011; Mello, 2016). Together, this literature underscores the need to move beyond participation-based notions of community toward approaches that centre relational accountability, cultural safety, and Indigenous ways of knowing. This study follows a grounded theoretical approach informed by Métis research methodologies (MRM) (Davey, 2023), including gathering and visiting (kiyokewin) (Flaminio et al., 2020) and keeoukaywin (the Visiting Way) (Gaudet, 2019). Guided by a Métis feminist lens, eleven participant interviews were analyzed thematically to understand experiences in online post-secondary education. Interviews were conducted using a semi-structured format, with both researcher and participants engaging in beading to foster culturally safe, relational conversation. Participants shared rich narratives about their experiences in online discussion spaces, including the barriers and challenges shaped by their Métis identity.

2994 A relatively homogenous group was recruited who shared an identity with the researcher—Métis women between 25 and 80—who ha s engaged in online post-secondary courses. Participants were selected by using the criterion-based approach of purposive sampling (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Patton, 2015) followed by snowball sampling (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Noy, 2008; Patton, 2015). For this paper, I focus on two intersecting findings: (1) lack of community and connection, and (2) education as transformative. Although participants completed their post-secondary degrees, their experiences were often marked by significant challenges.

A pervasive theme across narratives was a strong sense of isolation and disconnection. Participants described online courses as mechanical and performative, with limited opportunities for meaningful community building. As one participant noted, “I need my community. I need an instructor. I need that classroom,” while another reflected, “I would never do another online degree again. I was so isolated and so out of connection with my learning cohort.” The absence of Indigenous content, relational pedagogy, and culturally responsive facilitation contributed to feelings of exclusion. Intended sites of interaction, such as group work and discussion forums, often reinforced this isolation—particularly when peers disengaged or ignored Indigenous perspectives. Participants also encountered microaggressions and epistemic violence, including having their Métis identity questioned or invalidated. One participant described being asked, “What does Métis mean?” and being required to justify her lived experience. Such interactions undermined credibility and belonging, reflecting Dotson’s (2011) concept of testimonial quieting. Participants emphasized that instructors often lacked the cultural competency to recognize or intervene in these dynamics, leaving students to navigate them independently. Despite these barriers, participants consistently described education as transformative. It created opportunities for economic stability, leadership, and advocacy. As a participant noted, “Education made it so I am not in poverty in retirement.” Beyond material outcomes, education also supported cultural resurgence and self-determination, functioning as a site of both resistance and renewal. that challenge Métis women’s sense of belonging, epistemic agency, and cultural safety. A central issue was the lack of meaningful community.  Participants described discussion boards and group work as mechanical or performative, offering limited opportunities for relational connection. Many experienced isolation and a lack of cultural recognition, reflecting research that online environments often fail to support the relational and affective dimensions essential for Indigenous learners (Battiste, 2017; Pidgeon, 2008). From a relational accountability perspective, these findings suggest that interaction alone is insufficient; meaningful engagement requires reciprocal relationships grounded in trust, responsibility, and cultural safety. While frameworks such as CoI and Communities of Practice emphasize interaction and participation, they do not fully account for relational accountability and cultural safety, which emerged as central to Métis women’s experiences. The absence of Indigenous content and culturally relevant pedagogy further compounded disconnection, while microaggressions and identity challenges required participants to justify their Métis identity. These dynamics align with e pistemic violence  (Fricker, 2007), where marginalized learners’ knowledge and credibility are undermined. Instructors’ failure to intervene allowed these inequities to persist. Despite these barriers, participants demonstrated resilience through acts of reclamation. Education, community, and cultural practices such as beading and storytelling became pathways to reconnect with Métis identity. Reclaiming identity functioned as both personal healing and political resurgence, restoring epistemic agency—the authority to produce and share knowledge grounded in lived experience. For many, education extended beyond economic mobility to become a site of transformation, enabling critical aw areness of power structures and supporting self-determination. In this way, participants’ experiences illustrate how education can function not only as a colonial institution, but also as a space of resistance and resurgence. In summary, the findings reveal that while online education expands access for Métis women, it often replicates colonial dynamics that marginalize Indigenous learners. Participants’ stories underscore the necessity of designing online environments that are culturally safe, relational, and led by Indigenous educators. When grounded in Métis values of kinship, reciprocity, and community, online learning can move beyond access to become a transformative space for empowerment, identity affirmation, and social change. 2995 Aragon, S. Educ. 10(1562391). https//doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1562391 2996 Enhancing the Transformational Coaching Framework Kareem Kalil, University of Colorado Boulder, Kareem.Kalil@colorado.edu Abstract: This study unpacks the author’s experience leading a high school varsity basketball program through both a successful and an unsuccessful season. Framed by Bronfenbrenner’s Ecological Systems Theory and drawing on coaching reflections and artifacts, this piece argues that Côté’s Transformational Coaching Framework can be improved by attending to the power of the coaching environment, which acts as a prerequisite to transformation. Before achieving transformational leadership, out-of-school-time leaders must first cultivate an ecosystem grounded in shared goals, values, and support. Learning scientists are thus encouraged to view leadership in educational settings as ecological by nature.

Keywords: sport, coaching, leadership, ecological systems theory, autoethnography Paper objectives Although youth sports are a part of the Outside of School Time (Rogoff, 1994, 2003; Kirshner, 2015; Hirsch,

2005) world, knowledge of the role sports coaches play is limited by the incongruence between the most common

metrics used by researchers to analyze sports coaching success (on-court/field performance) and the more holistic goals of positive youth development (Gearity, 2011).

In this conceptual paper with illustrative examples, I draw on theories of learning and development developed in OST settings to gain a deeper understanding of the role of coaches. Specifically, I extend a dominant theory of sports coaching—the Transformat ional Coaching Framework (Turnnidge & Cote, 2016) —to examine the contextual determinants of coaching. I am motivated by the need to contextualize the experiences of a coach and the impact of the broader team environment on intended learning outcomes.

## Perspectives and theoretical framework

Some learning scientists have used sports as a lens to build on the sociocultural approach to learning in that particular setting (Nasir & Cooks, 2009; Nasir et al, 2020). Others have argued for us to broaden the boundaries of who we normally view as educators beyond the traditional schoolteacher, and also to give greater credence to educational spaces in out-of-school contexts (Germinaro, 2022). An aggregation of these views is evidence for the need to better understand athletic coaches and their pedagogies as a key lever in the development and learning of young people.

Effective coaches aim to integrate professional, interpersonal, and intrapersonal knowledge to improve the competence, confidence, connection, and character of athletes (Côté & Gilbert, 2009). Coaches have a positive influence on young athletes’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation (Mageau & Vallerand, 2003) by utilizing a variety of different leadership styles (Chelladurai, 1978). Nonetheless, there has been limited research on how contexts – micro, meso, and macro –shape coaching practices. For example, why do  coaches achieve positive outcomes in some years, yet face staunch criticism in other years while employing similar strategies? “Embedded contexts” are key to development, and different success levels for student development are possible despite similar programming (Cole & Nicolopoulou, 1993). Bronfenbrenner’s (1979) Ecological Systems Theory can be used to explain the contextual factors within sports teams that impact development. This study is autoethnographic, drawing on two years of data from my time coaching a high school varsity basketball team. During my time as head coach, I acted as a participant-observer (Merriam, 2016), both leading the program and also engaging in my reflective study of my coaching practice as a doctoral student. I drew on these experiences to compare and contrast one year of perceived success with the following year, when I experienced many challenges and did not meet the previously mentioned criteria of coaching success (Côté & Gilbert, 2009). I used a bottom-up approach, aiming to dissect my own experiences as a practitioner. In doing so, I gravitated to the distinct nature of my experience in the two seasons. I then began to explore how shifts in leadership decisions, team culture, coaching practices, and environmental and team-related factors may have influenced the disparate performance and cohesion of my teams during these seasons. Data sources neutrality (Smith, 1999). Data sources included reflective journals, practice plans, team documents, and 2997 communication with administrators and families, which were analyzed to identify patterns related to team dynamics, trust, and organizational support.

Of the two seasons analyzed, the first was perceived as successful, while the following season involved inconsistent performance and significant player and parent dissatisfaction, despite consistent coaching practices. Two key artifacts illustrate the challenges of coaching a team with an unhealthy ecosystem. The first is an email between the school administration detailing an unsubstantiated accusation of a facilities protocol violation. The second artifact is a text ex change between the head coach and a parent of one of the players, who later came to the school principal with a litany of grievances about the head coach. This autoethnographic reflection revealed that the mediating factors in the environment dictated our staff’s capacity to coach transformationally. The analysis shows that the effectiveness of my coaching was correlated with the overall health of the broader team environment. This shows that ultimately, it is not enough for coaches to approach coaching with a transformational lens. By examining the artifacts presented, we also see that when one part of the ecosystem is unhealthy, there is a ripple effect that undercuts the relationships foundational to a coach’s ability to be transformational. The complex ecosystem of a team, shown in Figure 1, includes coaches, players, parents, and administrators, each with blind spots and interdependent relationships. Figure 1 The Ecosystem of a Sports Team Each participant in the team ecosystem influences organizational health, and transformational coaching depends on the alignment and trust among these participants.. For example, breakdowns in the parent-coach level of the team ecosystem will also put coach-player relationships at risk.

## Significance

Coaches play a meaningful role in the lives of young people and operate in an environment that affords them the ability to transform lives. Coaching research has largely been ceded to researchers who take a less contextual approach to humandevelopment. As  an emerging scholar and graduate student in the LS, there is an important opportunity and need to leverage the insights of the LS for improving the coaching profession The Transformational Coaching framework (Turnnidge & Côté, 2016) is an excellent starting point for researchers to understand how coaches can improve the competence, confidence, connection, and character of their athletes. Nonetheless, there is room to build on this initial concept and provide additional nuance. This autoethnography provides evidence for the following key findings that can serve to enhance the Transformational Coaching Framework:

- Viewing the practice of Transformational Coaching in a vacuum is insufficient and fails to acknowledge

the support that coaches need to best impact their players transformationally.

- Transformational Coaching is not achieved by a certain kind of person or merely through a dyadic

relationship between a single party and another.

- Transformational Coaching is more likely to be realized when there is alignment and trust among all parties

within the complex team ecosystem.

The shift away from viewing the leader as the center of an ecosystem to just a member of the ecosystem is also relevant to OST settings outside of sport (Akiva, 2022). For instance, after-school program directors are also likely to see greater impact when operating in unison with members of their ecosystem. All OST spaces can benefit from viewing their leaders through a dynamic, ecological lens that prioritizes the relational nature required by high-impact coaching and leadership roles.

International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology. 16. 1-16. 10.1080/1612197X.2016.1189948 2999 Beyond the Code: Supporting Beginners with Interactive Data Science Labs Amanda RK Jotte, Amy Nussbaum, Atticus Ginsborg akube@uchicago.edu, anussbaum@uchicago.edu, aginsborg@uchicago.edu University of Chicago Abstract: Lab materials provide students opportunities for practice in new domains. However, existing tools for implementing interactive data science labs require installing software, which distracts from core lessons. We leverage R’s instructional ecosystem for bro wser-based, selfguided Python tutorials for data science courses. These tutorials require minimal setup, ideal for use across different classroom modalities. R’s framework can be successfully adapted for Python labs, lowering barriers to entry and strengthening student learning of core data science concepts.

The field of data science has rapidly expanded in recent years, and approaches to designing introductory data science course materials vary widely (Hardin et al., 2015). Many courses, such as Data Science in a Box (Çetinkaya-Rundel, 2024), grew from Statistics departments and use the programming language R and its extensive range of pedagogical tools (Hardin et al., 2015). Others born from Computer Science departments have adopted Python as their primary language (Brunner and Kim, 2016, Hardin et al., 2015). Still others have eschewed choosing a language entirely and use tools that abstract away from programming to focus on key statistical topics (Hoyt and Wangia-Anderson, 2018; Nair et al., 2020). For data science courses introducing students tonew concepts, there is an inherent tension between the challenges associated with teaching students to set up their programming environment and allowing students to investigate statistical content and implement data analysis computationally. This tension is particularly painful in introductory classes where students from non-technical backgrounds may initially be intimidated by the technical learning curve (Veilleux et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2011). Providing a welcoming environment and materials to stave off that intimidation is a key recommendation of the 2018 report on "Retention in Computer Science Undergraduate Programs in the U.S.: Data Challenges and Promising Interventions" (Stephenson et al., 2018). One approach to creating such an environment is utilizing problem-based teaching strategies that encourage student collaboration and self-directed learning (Yew and Goh, 2016). Many Python-based courses rely on Jupyter for interactive work. R’s more mature teaching libraries (e.g., learnr, gradethis) do not run in Jupyter, and comparable Python tools may be unfamiliar to statistics faculty new to teaching Python (Brunner & Kim, 2016). Jupyter courses without a managed cloud still require substantial environment setup before students write code. By contrast, Shiny (Chang et. al, 2025) combined with PositCloud supports simple, interactive assignments, lowering barriers for beginners  (Çetinkaya-Rundel and Rundel, 2018; Stoudt et al., 2022).

As data science educators teaching with Python, we see a need for tools that provide a low-friction experience, without the heavy setup common in many courses. The reticulate package (Ushey et al., 2025) lets R-users embed Python in R workflows (Navarro et al., 2024). We have therefore leveraged the more mature instructional framework of R to teach Python skills. Our work is guided by the following questions: ● RQ1: Can frameworks developed for R-based courses be adapted for teaching data science in Python? ● RQ2: Do browser-based, interactive labs improve understanding of data science concepts? ● RQ3: Do such labs reduce barriers for students from non-coding backgrounds and increase confidence and self-efficacy?

These questions will help us assess how frictionless  data science labs — lightweight, browser-accessible environments requiring minimal setup — can support student learning and retention in data science. Technical set-up In pursuit of these research questions, we have developed a series of interactive labs that leverage the ability to run Python code within an R environment. Through this integration we take advantage of established pedagogical tools such as learnr (Aden-Buie et al., 2023b), a package for interactive quizzes with coding, multiple choice, and free response question types, and gradethis (Aden-Buie et al., 2023a), a package for improved grading of 3000 learnr-style questions. Combined with PositConnect (Posit Team, 2025), a publishing platform that hosts our interactive assignments, these labs place students a click away from coding, eliminating setup barriers and enabling them to focus on programming and data science concepts. Instructional content and questions are written in R Markdown and formatted using the learnr package, and grading is customized via the gradethis  package. Within labs, designated code chunks are configured to run Python code through the reticulate package. All required R and Python libraries are pre-installed on the cloud server and imported in advance, allowing students to focus on problem solving and practicing coding concepts. An example of coding, free response, and multiple choice questions is  depicted in

Figure 1.

Figure 1 Example Questions from a Data Wrangling Lab Topic coverage and implementation Using the technical set-up as above, we have developed 24 interactive lab assignments that can be used across our introductory data science sequence to support a wide range of concepts, both computational and statistical. These labs are designed primarily to support course-specific content (e.g. lectures and assignments) or provide opportunities for practicing more general data scientific skills (e.g. debugging, using the command line, etc.). Each can be completed in around one hour with minimal external support, serving as self-contained resources for exploring topics in greater depth than lecture allows or providing additional practice before homework and exams. Although the labs can be completed individually, collaboration is encouraged. Discussion prompts and open code cells are included to promote exploration and peer-to-peer learning. So far, these labs have been used in multiple sections of the Introduction to Data Science II course over the last two years at the University of Chicago. They have been used by 300+ students and received positive feedback. Having piloted these labs, we are confident in our response to our first research question: Frameworks developed for R-based data science can be adapted for teaching introductory data science with Python.

## Future work and conclusion

This project is a work-in-progress. We have obtained IRB approval to evaluate how the labs (i) reduce barriers to entry, (ii) support learning of computational and statistical concepts, and (iii) build student confidence and are in the process of collectin g pre-and post-quarter survey data and analyzing preliminary results. Future work will involve refining design based on both student feedback and empirical results from our ongoing study. Existing lab materials, including a template for creating frictionless data science labs in Python, are available upon request from the authors; our goal is to release them as open-source resources, enabling other data science faculty in other institutions to adapt our approach to their own teaching contexts. We believe that this approach could also be particularly useful in courses in related disciplines where instructors wish to integrate Python into select lessons without devoting substantial time to programming instruction. By adapting R’s instructional ecosystem to deliver browser-based Python labs with minimal setup, we offer a practical path to lower entry barriers and improve learning at scale. We welcome collaboration and community feedback as we iterate and broaden adoption.
