Health Professions Education, 2(2), 75–79. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hpe.2016.01.004 3002 Attending to Relations of Care as Learning Through Collaborative Design with an Alternative School Community Eli Tucker-Raymond, Beth Warren, Maria Olivares etuckerr@bu.edu, bwarren@bu.edu, mariaco@bu.edu Boston University Brian Gravel, Tufts University brian.gravel@bu.edu Rayna Briceno rayna.briceno@gmail.com Who’s Got Morale Ann Rosebery, Independent asrosebery@outlook.com Abstract: We describe a collaborative community-based design research project with the purpose of reimagining education alternatives rooted in care. In the poster, w e share data from a discussion of a multimodal text among students, teachers, staff, researchers, and community partners from an alternative school community to argue that collective sense-making of how care is offered and received is dialogic, articulating multiple simultaneous meanings. We explore a collaborative design research project involving an alternative public school, university researchers, and a community non-profit that attempts to reimagine how alternative education might be different, intent on cultivating relationships of care at an alternative urban public high school serving students who have not thrived in traditional school settings and who are living with ongoing histories of trauma. We focus on webs of relations between people, more than humans, time, and space that cre ate the material, political, and ethical conditions for overlapping, reciprocating cycles of care. Our collective work involved building a garden together on school grounds as a model of care and shared among human and more-than-human beings. To bring relations of care to life, we engaged routinely in a collective practice of attention (Burnett & Strauss, 2022) we call “text-image work” in which the community of educators, youth and researchers made meaning of a paired short written passage and an image in rounds of layered noticing and interpretation.

## Theoretical framework

Understanding and cultivating care in education has a long, albeit unprioritized, history (e.g., Antrop-Gonzalez, 2006). We understand care as a relational sensibility – grounded in ethical commitments to dignity, humility, mutuality, reciprocity, and respect – towards human, social, and natural worlds and their multiple orders of connectedness. Care is personal while als o extending into the deepest reaches of our collective ecologies along social, ethical, and political dimensions (Darder, 2002; Freire, 2005). Educational spaces grounded in an ethics of care and responsibility provide educational sanctuary as a break with normalized practices of subjugation and an opening into the possibility “to speak, to opt for life, to exercise the nonviolent and creative option” and “to see space as a tool —something creatable, malleable, and shareable” (Espinoza, 2009, p. 61). In that create-ability, malleability, and shareability, we argue that care takes many forms. Commitments to dialogism and heteroglossia were central in our attention to text-image pairs (Bakhtin, 1981; Warren et al., 2020). Drawing inspiration from the pedagogical work of a colleague (Lynn Brown; see Warren et al., 2025) who developed the protocol we are using and Radical Attention movements (e.g., Burnett & Strauss, 2022) we are committed to processes of slowing down and directing our attention to the world and to each other in ways that are not commodified. The practice  acted dually, a)  as an anchor activity for the partnership–to level the ground for each participant to contribute what they saw in the text, and b) to satisfy school district goals of creating opportunities for “equitable literacy practices.” Ultimately it was meant to imagine and animate relationships of care in alternative school settings. 3003 Throughout four years of work, we co-developed several practices for building relationships and pursuing project goals. In the third summer we introduced the text-image circles.. In keeping with our relational commitments, we engage in collaborative community-based design research (CBDR) (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). For four weeks, beginning in early July, we met three days a week for five hours a day to work on the garden and reima gine learning. Nineteen people engaged in gardening, making, designing and crit iquing. Every day the group participated in what we call “text-image work.” In rounds, each person in the circle contributed a noticing about the image and/or the short passage. Noticings in turn gave rise to resonances, including extended stories. The circle closed with this question: “What stories or relations of care can we draw from our responses?” Data came from one short exchange during our first time engaging in this collective practice of attention. We focused on an image only, with no paired passage, to introduce the practice in a way that would feel less like school. The image was by a local artist, Ekua Holmes, and depicted three figures in a familiar city landscape adorned with imagery, symbols, and texture. The excerpt is representative of the ways in which  multiple forms and relations of care are collectively manifested in ongoing partnerships.

The exchange opened  with Johnson making a personal connection to the figures in the image: “They look like me.” What followed were agreements, disagreements, offerings of confusion and uncertainty, support for each other’s contributions, and playful and joyful interrelations. The group notice d visible elements of the collage – skin color, symbols of commercialism, words, and facial expressions – and shared wonderings about politics, families, relationships, and values, their own and those represented in the  picture. They also noticed the process of naming, sharing, and connecting what is visible as they navigate this together. The noticings we re collective sense-making of the image, world, each other, and the process itself. Sitting in a circle, each facing the others, we were working toward bringing care to life collectively. The project amplified conversations about care, the school, the garden, ourselves, and each other.

James layered Johnson’s felt connection to the people in the pictures because of their skin color, and connected their skin color with the words “must be” and “free” (words not next to each other and oriented in different directions)–making an implicit allusion that freedom was imperative to Black people, adding political, and perhaps spiritual, meanings to Johnson’s identity making. Brian, a white researcher further built off of James’s practice for looking at the image, holding the paper at different angles; he built his relationship to James. He could learn from James. Implying that the youth have something to offer the adults, and in doing so Brian began to build the practice of attending also to each other.

The group articulated  differing meanings in the relationships between the figures in the image. Hak, a member of the safety staff at the school, attended to the relationships between the people, and in doing so made a bid for the group’s serious attention. He suggest ed that the man and the boy, father and son are together – an ostensibly caring relationship in itself – and at the same time, he suggest ed that they should stand up and offer their seats to the woman –a display of ritualized, gendered caring. His contribution wa s immediately met with questions and arguments from at least three of the women from the school. They questioned whether Hak inferred the woman was expecting them to stand up–that the morality and bid for the father and son to offer their seat was stemming from her. Besides just being a disagreement over the meaning of the image, it was also a disagreement over care. How one offers care and thinks others should be cared for is not always how people want to be cared for, nor how they receive it.

The excerpt above brings attention to investigating the many dimensions of care, discerning between the kinds of care that are offered or not, received or not. It also marks and anticipates that the journey of the partnership will surface and perhaps pursue unanswerable questions. What are the relationships between the woman, man, and boy in the image? What are the relationships between the figures and words in the image? How will our group care for one another? How will we sustain this practice in the spac es of the school? Discussions like these create our partnership in ongoing ways. Sitting and attending to texts in a circle, each person sharing what they notice, allows for multiple meanings, heterogeneity, poetics, and imagining different worlds. In the circl e there is room for multiple interrelated truths. They build on one another, toward care, because they are allowed to exist in shared space, protected and embraced by one another. Sense-making in a circle during text-image work creates something democratic and makes for more worlds to live than the totalizing one of school. Care is not something people carry around with them,  and it is not a service to someone else. It evolves from relations among beings. It all contributes to our design-in-the-becoming, our knots of relationships-in-the-becoming. That is, we create not current partnerships or relations of care in our activities, but future ones. 3004 AuthorsD Warren AERA Antrop-González, R.  (2006). 3005 Embodied TEA: Healing, Art, and Collective Knowledge In Learning Spaces Marlene Palomar, Kalonji Nzinga Marlene.Palomar@colorado.edu, Kalonji.Nzinga@colorado.edu University of Colorado Boulder Abstract: Healing can be understood as a form of learning that centers cognitive, emotional, and relational processes. This case study focuses on one young woman of Color from a larger project of five participants to examine how healing extends beyond recovery, operating as an active epistemic practice showcased through technology. Drawing on the Lyripeutics Storytelling Project (LSP), a high school ethnic studies and Hip-Hop education collaboration focused on wellness, we examine how art and storytelling foster heal ing-centered learning.

Using the TEA (Technology, Engineering, and Arts) framework that draws heavily on Anzaldua’s concept of conocimiento, we explore how technology can support reflection, creative expression, and connection. Findings showcase that through storytelling, artistic creation, and community engagement, the participant transformed experiences of loss and isolation into pathways of healing and connection. These insights highlight healing as a dynamic relational learning process, inviting educat ors to integrate emotional and creative dimensions into educational practice.

Learning sciences have explored socioemotional, transformative, and identity-based learning, yet often overlook healing as a core dimension of learning. While healing has long been central in femme of color scholarship (Anzaldua; hooks; Lorde), it has only recently gained traction in learning sciences (Jurow et al, 2025; Mendoza et al., 2024). This emerging work calls for deeper engagement with healing as both concept and practice, particularly in designing learning environments rooted in accountability, r espect, and relationality. Jurow  et al., (2025) ask, “how might we better understand healing and its connections to learning?”, a question this study takes up through the Lyrupeutics Storytelling Project (LSP), which centers healing as both personal and collective.  Healing is inherently communal, intergenerational, and embodied. Scholars emphasize that healing rarely occurs in isolation (hooks, 2018) and involves histories, and relationships that sustain transformation (Bang et al., 2015; Teeters et al., 2022; Meixi, 2022). At the same time, self-preservation remains central (Lorde, 2023, p. 103). Healing engages mind, body, and spirit, challenging institutional separations that can enact harm (Nzinga, 2023). Emerging research also highlights how technology and creative spaces can function as sites of healing, enabling learners of color to reimagine identity, justice, and collective wellness (McKoy, 2025; Germinaro, 2022; Tanksley & Hunter, 2024).

Creative expression is central to this process. Writing, music, movement, and digital arts allow for the transformation of stored emotional energy into healing practices (Tran et al., 2023; Meixi, 2022; Palomar, 2025). Anzaldua’s stages of conocimiento conceptualize healing as nonlinear, relational, and action-oriented, emphasizing transformation through both reflection and creation. This paper explores how a young girl of color images in healing as a process of learning  during the COVID-19 pandemic, using digital art and community. In this paper, Healing is understood as an “ongoing, relational process rooted in wellness, connection, and culture” (Palomar, 2025).

Theoretical lens This study uses Palomar’s (2025) TEA (Technology, Engineering, and Arts)  framework, a living theory grounded in Anzalduan conocimiento and informed by Chicana and Black feminist thought. TEA positions healing and the arts as central to learning, transform ation, and growth, emphasizing relationality, creativity, and cultural expression.

Within TEA, technology functions as a tool for reflection and connection, engineering is reimagined as creative, everyday problem solving, and art becomes a vehicle for expressing, processing, and transforming lived experiences. The TEA framework highlights four key dimensions of healing-centered learning: 3006

1. Storytelling as healing-validating lived experiences and resisting dominant narratives.

2. Engineering as Everyday Problem-Solving-emphasizing relational, collective knowledge-building.

3. Embodied Practices and cultural knowledge-recognizing intellectual, spiritual, and physical dimensions

of healing.

4. Decolonizing Learning Environments-centering non-western epistemologies and holistic approaches to

knowledge.

Across the various branches, healing is both a process of transformation, restoration, and embodied learning. The LSP, conducted from 2020-2022 with approximately 60 participants, served as the research site. From a subset of participants, one young girl was selected for in-depth case study analysis using purposive sampling aligned with the study’s focus on healing and conocimiento among girls of color. Data included semi-structured interviews (30-45 minutes), audio-recorded and transcribed, alongside arts-based artifacts such as visual media, music, and storytelling projects. Participants also produced artist statements reflecting on their work. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, combining deductive and inductive coding. Regular team discussions supported the development and refinement of themes, allowing both overarching patterns and emergent insights to shape the themselves through reflection, creativity, and community. Ruby, the focal participant, created a three-and-a-halfminute cinematic video documenting her healing journey during COVID-19. The video begins with news footage of the pandemic, transitions to personal narratives of isolation and a breakup, and concludes with scenes of connection and joy through friendships formed online. She identifies these relationships as her “chosen family”, marking a shift toward healing and belonging.

Through storytelling, Ruby transformed personal pain into creative expression, using reflection as a way of understanding her emotional experiences. Revisiting and editing her footage allowed her to reinterpret her past, positioning her healing as an epistemic and learning process. Through the engineering dimensions of TEA, her video editing functioned as everyday problem-solving. By juxtaposing sorrowful music with joyful imagery, she constructed a narrative rainbow of grief and hope, demonstrating how cr eative production itself is a form of learning. Technology also supported relational learning. Online friendships became sites of connection, vulnerability, and care, helping Ruby reimagine belonging beyond traditional familial norms. Through these interactions, she learned to express emotional needs, build community, and engage in reciprocal care. Healing, in this case, emerged as communal and relational process grounded in shared meaning-making.

## Implications

This study positions healing as a central dimension of learning, expanding how knowledge, emotions, and transformation are understood in the learning sciences. Ruby’s video-making process illustrates how storytelling, technology, and creative practice support emotional literacy, reflection, and community building. These findings highlight the importance of integrating digital and artistic practices into learning environments to support healingcentered education. Drawing from Black feminist thought and Chic ana feminist epistemologies, this work reframes learning as an embodied, cultural, and relational practice rooted in lived experiences and collective care. 3008 At the Threshold of Learning: Visual Narratives of How Students Read Belonging and Possibility in Makerspaces Marijel (Maggie) Melo, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, melo1@ad.unc.edu Abstract: This study presents findings from a photovoice-inspired study of 24 first-time users across three university makerspaces. Participants created photo-and-caption storyboards documenting their initial impressions, revealing three interpretive frames: sections  within the makerspace were perceived as 'for me,' 'not for me,' and 'could be for me.' These frames emerged not from interpersonal interaction but from environmental design cues, including tool visibility, signage, and spatial organization. Findings highlight the role of passive guidance in supporting or discouraging entry, and call for treating spatial design as a core component of equitable pedagogy.

Research has shown that first-time users often feel like intruders when they arrive at a makerspace (Melo & Rodney, 2023), and the conditions that produce this feeling are frequently embedded in the space itself before any interaction with staff occurs. Students often decide whether to enter within seconds of arrival, making these early threshold moments critical in determining whether learning begins or ends before it starts. In these first encounters, first-time users rely on visible cues such as signage, layout, tools, and overall atmosphere to interpret whether the space is meant for them, whether they belong, and whether they can succeed there. These rapid, embodied assessments are not incidental to learning; they constitute a form of environmental reading through which students negotiate access, identity, and possibility before any formal instruction takes place. Despite growing investment in makerspaces as sites of equitable STEM learning, relatively little attention has been paid to what happens at the entry point and how spatial design shapes these consequential first judgments. This study represents the third and final phase of a multi-year project investigating how first-time users experience makerspaces at the threshold. The overarching research question guiding this project examined how and why firsttime users pause or stop e ntirely at the makerspace threshold rather than entering. Each phase builds upon and responds to the one before it. The first phase centered on makerspace administrators' perspectives, exploring what defining features constitute a traditional makerspace and, in other words, how a makerspace achieves its legibility as an environment. Administrators were asked to describe what they see, hear, smell, and feel within these spaces; their responses both distilled the fundamental characteristics of makerspaces and directly informed the design of the second phase. Drawing on those insights, the second phase constructed two virtual makerspace environments: a baseline space and a redesigned version developed in response to students' real-time reactions captured through think-aloud reporting. As students navigated both environments and narrated their experiences, they consistently preferred the redesigned space, one featuring clear signage, displays of student work, and comfortable seating that communicated invitation rather than intimidation (Melo & Rodney, 2023).  The third and final phase move d into operational campus makerspaces to examine whether these preferences h eld in physical settings. Using photovoice methodology, this phase document ed the visual and narrative dimensions of first impressions across three sites.

Theoretical and methodological framework This study conceptualizes makerspaces as environments that actively communicate meaning through spatial and cultural signals, rather than as neutral settings for learning. Ahmed's (2006) work on orientations provides a foundation for understanding how learners arrive at new spaces with embodied expectations and emotions that shape their sense of what kinds of participation are available to them. A space oriented toward a particular kind of user produces disorientation in others before a single word is exchanged. Calabrese Barton and Tan's (2019) framework of rightful presence extends this by calling for learning environments that do not merely tolerate diverse participants but actively signal that they belong. Chatman's (2001) account of everyday informationseeking further illustrates how individuals interpret unfamiliar environments through small, ambient cues that either validate or constrain their engagement. Together, these frameworks position the threshold not as a neutral entry point but as a site where belonging and exclusion are continuously produced through design. 3009 Photovoice, the participatory visual method developed by Wang and Burris (1997), was selected because it preserves the immediacy of first impressions while positioning participants as the authoritative interpreters of their own experience. Originally developed for community health research, photovoice has since been adapted widely in educational and spatial inquiry to surface how individuals read and respond to their environments (Catalani & Minkler, 2010). In this study, participants used analog Instax  cameras to photograph what stood out, what felt inviting, and what felt discouraging, then paired each image with a reflective caption. Treating these photo-caption storyboards as cultural texts (Mitchell, 2011) allowed the research team to analyze not only w hat participants noticed but how the space was being read and by whom. This approach aligns with constructivist grounded theory (Charmaz, 2024) in its emphasis on meaning co-constructed between participant, environment, and researcher.

Twenty-four first-time users participated across three university makerspaces. The study employed a photovoiceinspired, participatory design approach centered on how students interpret space through visual and narrative meaning-making (Wang & Burris, 1997). Participants created photo-and-caption storyboards documenting their first impressions, guided by prompts such as: What stands out? What feels inviting? What feels discouraging? Images and captions were treated as visual narratives and analyzed using iterative thematic analysis. Coding was conducted collaboratively with ongoing comparison and refinement to support consistency and reliability across the dataset.

Across the three sites, participants interpreted the makerspace through three recurring frames: 'for me,' 'not for me,' and 'could be for me.' These frames emerged not from direct interaction with staff or peers, but from environmental cues alone, including how tools were displayed, whether signage felt welcoming or institutional, and whether the layout conveyed openness or gatekeeping. Spaces perceived as 'for me' featured clear wayfinding, visible and accessible materials, and an atmosphere that signaled permission to explore. Spaces coded as 'not for me' were characterized by ambiguity, clutter, and a sense that expertise was assumed rather thandeveloped. The 'could be for me' frame was notably associated with passive guidance: subtle design choices such as open floor plans, labeled tool stations, and sample projects on display that lowered the threshold for engagement without requiring interpersonal interaction. Together, these findings reveal that belonging is not simply felt; it is read, and it is read quickly.

These findings suggest that educators and makerspace practitioners should reconsider how learning environments are designed at the moment of entry. What is novel is that first-time users rely primarily on environmental cues, rather than interpersonal support, to decide whether to engage, highlighting the importance of passive guidance embedded in design. Clear signage, intuitive layouts, and familiar entry points support independent exploration, while ambiguity and clutter signal exclusion. This pattern aligns with Ahmed's (2006) account of orientations and disorientation: spaces that feel designed for someone else produce estrangement before a word is spoken. It also resonates with Calabrese Barton and Tan's (2019) framework of rightful presence, which call s for learning environments that actively signal who belongs rather thandefaulting to an unmarked norm. Passive guidance, as this study frames it, is one mechanism by which rightful presence can be architecturally applied. Learning begins at the threshold, where students make rapid decisions about whether a makerspace is 'for them,' guided not by instruction but by design. If more equitable participation is the goal, openness cannot be assumed; it must be intentionally desig ned, with belonging made visible, legible, and unmistakable from the very first glance. These findings call for a shift toward treating spatial design as a central component of pedagogy rather than a neutral backdrop for learning. A makerspace that looks l ike it is only for experts will function that way, regardless of who is invited.

## Acknowledgments

This material is based upon work supported by the National Science Foundation under Award No.

those of the author(s) and do not necessarily reflect 3011 The Instructional Design Process for Youth Ensemble Devising Lisa M. Siciliano, University of Illinois Chicago, lsicil2@uic.edu Abstract: While models exist for stages of devising in professional theatre, studies of what the process of devising looks like for youth in informal learning environments are limited. In these spaces, students create original theatre together with the guidance of a teaching artist. This study focuses on three cases of instructional design processes developed by four teaching artists. Findings illustrate a conceptual framework for the instructional design of ensemble devising. Devising is a method of creating original theatre where ensemble members work together to develop, refine, and perform a brand-new show (Oddey, 1994). While models exist for stages of devising in professional theatre (Mermikides & Smart, 2010), studies  of what the process of devising looks like for youth in informal learning spaces—such as summer camps —are limited. In these spaces, students devise theatre together with the guidance of a teaching artist (TA): an educator who structures and facilitates a n artistic process and performance. The current research focuses on how TAs navigate the complex design and implementation processes entailed in engaging a group of young people in creating a piece of devised theatre. It contributes to the growing learning sciences literature on ensemble learning in the arts (Ćosić, 2024; Hollett et al., 2022; Leander et al., 2023, Vogelstein, 2020).

The present research conceptualizes the instructional design of theatrical TAs as a socioculturally situated practice that evolves over the course of the instructional process. Though TAs’ initial instructional designs can be viewed as consisting of a "repertoire of examples, images, understandings, and actions…" (Schön, 1983, p. 138) developed from prior experiences, each new instantiation of devising is always situated in the specific space, time, and structural context of the group. Thus, the design process of TAs reflects what they draw upon from prior experiences and belief s in interaction with what participants bring to the situation and the contextual constraints of the setting. The research reported herein focuses on three cases of instructional design processes developed by four TAs with respect to their planned instructional designs and how those designs were adapted to specific contextual constraints.

## Context and methods

Three youth ensemble devising summer camp programs served as the context for three case studies of the TAs charged with designing and implementing these theatre experiences. The summer camps were in  three cities located in different areas of the United States. The first case focuses on Belle, the instructor for a two-week highschool-aged program in the Southeastern US. In the second case, Jennifer guided a one-week program for students ages 10 to 14 in a different Southeastern city. The third case was co-taught by Peter and Lynn who held a weeklong devising process for 9-to-11-year-old students in the Pacific Northwest. Names of TAs are pseudonyms. Data sources informing the identification of the design processes and adaptations  for each case include:

1) hour-long semi-structured interviews with the TAs before, half-way, immediately after, and one month after

their camps concluded, 2) instructional artifacts created by the TAs (e.g. emails, lesson plans, worksheets, etc.),

3) daily ethnographic field notes, and 4) daily audio-recorded informal interviews with the TAs. First cycle

elemental coding methods (Salda ña, 2021) included descriptive and process coding to determine what activities and accompanying actions the TAs had planned for the ensemble. In vivo coding was utilized to track when TAs spoke about their designs in terms of things they "usually," "always," or "often" did. Analytic memos examine d TAs’ rationale regarding their initial designs. Several phases of the instructional design process emerged through second cycle focused and thematic coding analyses.

## Findings & Analysis

The findings indicate similarity across cases in conceptualizing  the instructional design process of ensemble devising as comprising four phases. Figure 1 depicts the four phases: Getting to Know the Ensemble, Engaging in Inquiry and D ecision Making, Building the S how, and P erforming the S how. With the exception of the performance phase, there was substantial variation across the cases in how the TAs planned to sequence the phases and how they planned for participant engagement in each phase. As well, in each case the arts organization sponsoring each of the devising camp experiences dictate d the topic  of the devising: a mash-up of The Little Prince and David Bowie's music  for Case 1; an adaptation of a myth, story, or legend for Case 2; and a hero’s 3012 journey for Case 3. Belle and Jennifer worked with the preselected topic s however the Case 3 TAs (Peter and Lynn) chose to ignore the topical constraint in favor of having their students determine their own topic on the first day of the devising camp.

Generally speaking, each of the cases situated the Getting to Know the Ensemble phase towards the beginning of the devising process – with Case 1 starting the phase before the program began.  Belle (Case 1)

## contacted the youth participants and asked them to send

videos of themselves so she could begin to get a sense of who her students were. In all three cases, the TAs planned for the initial days of each of the camp programs to feature community building activities (e.g. developing ensemble agreements) and exploratory activities (e.g. theatre games and group performance tasks).

Plans for t he Inquiry and Decision Making phase differed across the cases. Peter and Lynn (Case 3) planned to wait until the ensemble members gathered before having students perform the activities in this phase. On Day 1, they planned on showing a genre slideshow and supporting the students in both picking a topic and making foundational artistic decisions about the show (e.g. setting, characters, and general plot).  For Case 3, this phase was a primary vehicle for ensemble devising. In contrast, the other two  TAs did substantial p arts of this phase prior to meeting the students. Belle engaged in the bulk of this phase on her own,  exploring source material ahead of time (e.g. reading the book, watching a Claymation film, listening to musical selections). Likewise Jennifer developed source material for her students ahead of time, researching the Greek mythical creature, Scylla. Additionally, she began engaging in inquiry thinking of questions she wanted to know the answer to but  ultimately planned on asking the students about on the first day. Prior to meeting the youth ensemble members, Jennifer made foundational artistic decisions for the show, including tentatively framing the play with a meeting between two well-known Greek characters-Odysseus and Circe.

The phase Building the Show i s where the TAs in Case 1 and 2 primari ly situated ensemble devising. Belle planned for students to build the show through their work determining blocking, having them create what she called, physical metaphors and working with a skeleton script she had developed based on her pre-camp work. Jennifer planned for students to build the show by developing lines to say (and then typing them in a document), working on blocking, and making technical elements throughout the week. In Case 3, Lynn planned to write the script based on student contributions  from the first two days’ inquiry activities. However, Peter and Lynn also planned on having the students revise Lynn’s script draft before moving on to blocking the show as a group. These case studies provide a conceptual framework for the instructional design of ensemble devising. Findings illustrate how different components from the first three phases are taken up at different times as well as who performs which component in the phases. Each of the cases differs as to what the TA does on their own before the youth ensemble members convene and what they do once the youth are present. Additionally, the cases differ as to what parts of ensemble devising the youth ensemble members are tasked with accomplishing. For learning scientists who study ensemble learning, this paper provides an account of how TAs structure an ensemble artistic creation process and performance, illustrating the importance of TAs instructional planning as a key factor in collective learning  processes. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate how in youth ensemble devising contexts, TAs not only structure the learning process but their participation in the artistic process itself is consequential. This research serves as a basis for exploring whether and how the differences in where and the extent of student involvement in the various phases of the instructional process of ensemble devising matter for how students perceive the experience especially with respect to agency and ownership of the perf ormance. 3014 Interest Alignment in Peer Feedback Predicts Changes in Student Interest and Self-Efficacy Liwei Chen, University of Pittsburgh, liwei.chen@pitt.edu Christian Schunn, University of Pittsburgh, schunn@pitt.edu Abstract: This study examined whether alignment between students' pre-existing interests and peer presentations they reviewed predicted changes in psychology interest and self-efficacy (N=242). Students reviewed two randomly-assigned peer presentations on academic papers. Topic interest alignment with reviewed presentations significantly predicted increased psychology interest, while application interest alignment predicted enhanced self-efficacy. Alignment with students' own presentation topics showed no effects. Findings suggest reviewing peer work engages different learning mechanisms than presenting, with implications for peer feedback design.

Interest in educational contexts is a psychological state characterized by positive emotions, sustained curiosity, and active engagement that influences attention, persistence, and academic motivation (Hidi & Renninger, 2006).

When students demonstrate heightened interest, they typically show increased motivation to pursue and engage with related learning opportunities, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of academic engagement (Meece et al., 1990). Beyond its individual effects, interest has a social dimension, with studies documenting the contagious nature of interests within peer groups (Hazari et al., 2017). One context where such contagion might occur is peer feedback. Students providing open-ended feedback to classroom peers supports student outcomes (Er et al., 2021), activates student engagement, and deepens understanding of course content (Noroozi et al., 2023). Recent metaanalyses confirm that peer feedback positively influences motivation and self-efficacy (Lu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2021), yet the specific conditions under which these benefits emerge remain unclear. One underexplored factor is the alignment between students' existing interests and the content within the peer work that they review. Students enter courses with varied interests in specific topics and applications. S elfefficacy can be developed through mastery experiences  (Bandura, 1997), and students as reviewers may have such experiences when the reviewed content is familiar. Hidi and Renninger’s (2006) four-phase model of interest development suggests that broader interests candevelop from situational interest moments. This study e xamines whether the match between students' pre-existing interests and the presentations they review in a peer feedback activity is associated with changes in their levels of interest and self-efficacy with the course discipline. This study was conducted in an undergraduate developmental psychology course (N =242) in the US. This study was approved by the  university’s Institutional Review Board. Students completed pre-recorded presentations on academic papers. Each student selected one paper from a course-provided bank to present on and was randomly assigned to review two peers' presentations through the Peerceptiv online platform. Research has demonstrated that reviewing recorded presentations of journal articles related to a course can enhance students' content knowledge, self-efficacy, and attitudes toward scientific literature engagement (Kiselyov & Schunn, 2024).

## Measures

Topical and application interest alignment At the semester start, students indicated all course topics (12 items, e.g., cognitive development) and applications (13 items, e.g., clinical applications) that were particularly interesting to them. W e calculated each student’s average pre-course interest in the topics and applications covered in the two presentations they reviewed, creating measures of topic interest alignment and application interest alignment (each on a 0–1 scale). Psychology interest, self-efficacy, and identity During the first and final weeks of the semester, students completed measures of interest in psychology (5 items, α = 0.82), self-efficacy in psychology (6 items, α = 0.77), and psychology disciplinary identity (4 items, α = 0.90), adapted from validated instruments (Blatt et al., 2020). All items used a 4-point Likert scale. 3015 Using multiple regression analyses, we examined whether interest alignment between students' pre-existing interests and the presentations they reviewed predicted changes in their psychology interest, psychology self-efficacy, and psychology disciplinary identity, controlling for baseline levels. Interest alignment with reviewed presentations Students' topic interest alignment with the presentations they reviewed significantly predicted post-course interest in psychology (β =.14, SE =.09, p =.015, R² = 0.43, Figure 1 Left), controlling for pre-course interest. Students who reviewed presentations on topics they found interesting showed greater overall interest in psychology. Similarly, students' application interest alignment with reviewed presentations predicted post-course self-efficacy (β =.13, SE =.09, p =.046, R² = 0.27, Figure 1 Right), controlling for baseline. No significant effects were found for disciplinary identity (ps >.20).

Figure 1 Post-Course Outcomes by Interest Alignment in Reviewed Presentations. Plotted Values Reflect Residualized Outcomes after Removing Variance Associated with Baseline Measures. Interest alignment with presented papers In contrast, the match between students' interests and the paper they chose to present on showed no significant effects on any outcome, controlling for baseline levels (all ps >.08). This suggests that choosing to present on an interesting topic does not predict motivational changes, perhaps because interest was generally high. This study examined whether alignment between students' pre-existing interests and the presentations they review in peer feedback activities predicts changes in their interest and self-efficacy. The findings reveal an important asymmetry: while students' i nterest alignment with presentations they reviewed predicted learning outcomes, alignment with the paper they presented did not. This difference does not stem from restricted interest range in students' own presentation topics —interest distributions show similar means and variability across contexts. Instead, reviewing others' work may engage students differently than presenting one's own material. Reviewing requires critically engaging with others' interpretations and arguments, potentially prompting deepe r cognitive processing than preparing one's own presentation on familiar material. These findings have practical implications for peer feedback design in large courses. Instructors might strategically match reviewers to presentations based on expressed interests to enhance both engagement and learning outcomes. The distinction between to pic interest (predicting overall interest gains) and application interest (predicting self-efficacy gains) suggests different mechanisms: intellectual curiosity may sustain disciplinary engagement, while seeing practical relevance may build confidence in ability to apply knowledge.

## Limitations and future directions

While students were randomly assigned as reviewers to presentations, interest alignment was also influenced by the number of applications and topic interests they had, so strict causal claims cannot yet be made. Understanding whether interest alignment influences learning through enhanced feedback quality or via other mechanisms (such as increased time on task or deeper cognitive engagement) remains an important question for future analysis. Investigating whether these effects replicate across different disciplines and course structures would also strengthen our understanding of when and how interest alignment in peer review matters for learning. 3016 Bandura, A. 3017 Rivulet: A Framework and Tools for Fetching Pedagogically Generative Scientific Datasets Michelle H. Wilkerson, Berkeley School of Education, California, USA, mwilkers@berkeley.edu Adelmo Eloy, Universidade de Sao Paulo, Brazil and Teachers College, Columbia University, New York, USA, adelmo@fablearn.net Helen L. Fitzmaurice, Berkeley School of Education, California, USA, hfitzmaurice@berkeley.edu Abstract: Rivulet is a framework and collection of Python Jupyter notebooks for  fetching pedagogically generative scientific datasets. They provide executable templates for  accessing, filtering, and evaluating data from public databases using Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and expert insights regarding quantitative features of scientific interest. Our primary goal is to support educators and curriculum designers finding data that support meaningful statistical and scientific engagement through relevance to both students and to the domain.

## Motivation

The promise of “Goldilocks data” (Rubin, 2019), data that is not too big nor too small but just right for learners, has captured the imagination of educators. The continued use of classic datasets such as Old Faithful Geyser eruptions (Shaughnessy & Pfannkuch, 2002) or the “100 Cats” dataset in (Konold et al., 2007) highlight s how conceptually rich data can inspire meaningful statistical questions (e.g., “How faithful is Old Faithful?”). But their repeated use also highlights how difficult finding such generative datasets can be. At the same time, educators and researchers are calling for more up-to-date, relevant, and authentic datasets for students (NASEM, 2023; Rosenberg et al., 2020; Weiland & Williams, 2023). There are  calls for submission and guidelines (Krishnamurthi et al., n.d.) for building curated lists for identifying educational datasets (e.g., DASL, n.d.; SAS Data Depot, n.d.). However, static datasets cannot be easily updated or tailored to students’ or curricular needs. A more flexible approach introduces teachers or students to Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to make queries to livedatabases through code or specially-formatted URLs (Fergusson & Wild, 2021; Israel-Fishelson, Moon, Tabak, et al., 2024; Walker et al., 2024), but it is difficult to ensure that these data offer the resolution and robustness needed for rich statistical questions. And, there are ongoing challenges in finding data that can support connections between data and context (Penuel et al., 2025; Sagrans et al., 2022). The [Toolname] Project seeks to merge the flexibility of APIs with ways to ensure that these datasets are robust enough to support key statistical and topical learning goals. To work toward this balance, we are building Python notebook utilities, developed with input from domain experts, that allow users to identify relevant constraints (e.g. places or times of interest), and download robust datasets that illustrate generative patterns within those constraints. These interactive documents integrate customiz able API calls to robust  database systems, a series of Python methods to filter and evaluate fetched data for key  patterns, and discussion of how the fetched data address statistical and curricular learning goals, and explanatory text and instructive comments throughout. Design principles Our project draws from the learning sciences, statistics education, and data science education to inform the design of tools for fetching educational datasets. Specifically, we emphasize three key design principles. First, we support relevance and relationship building to establish the value of data as a meaningful tool for investigation. Rivulet notebooks demonstrate how queries can be tailored to specific geographies, time periods, events, or comparisons. We encourage and model that such datasets be paired with news stories, local hands-on investigations, or other sources of information that allow students to learn more detail about focal patterns in data. Second, we support the statistical generativity of a dataset to demonstrate patterns that are conducive to statistical analysis. Often, though large quantities of data are available for a given system, the specific indicators that are most likely to exhibit relevant patterns or make clear connections to content explorations can be more difficult to find, or may not be collected at a resolution that is conducive to analysis (e.g., monthly averages versus hourly samples). Rivulet utilities pre-emptively scandatasets for desired characteristics (such as the presence of high-leverage indicators, strong expected “signal” patterns as identified by  experts, high data resolution, and/or patterns of variability and comparative measures across groups that are sufficient for meaningful analysis). Third, we support the disciplinary generativity of a dataset, identifying what are the key patterns and related disciplinary concepts that can be examined in depth related to the data available through a given API, and what indicators and quantitative characteristics are necessary to unpack that specific idea. We consult with experts 3018 regarding what are “signature patterns” that clearly illustrate key disciplinary ideas,  support users in reviewing subsets of data to determine whether those patterns are evident and can be meaningfully analyzed, and identify corresponding statistical questions that can motivate investigations of those patterns. These principles are integrated and communicated through computational notebooks, a type of interactive document that mixes executable and editable code with rich text. Because the code presented is editable, users can customize their queries (Hüsing, et al., 2024). The design takes advantage of this flexibility to instruct users on how to tailor queries to access datasets that are relevant, and then to help users filter their results to identify datasets that have appropriate resolution, variability, and/or differe nces to warrant deeper analysis. An example: Sourcing pedagogically useful air quality data with AQS.ipynb The Air Quality Index (AQI) is important, but simply demonstrating that AQI goes up or down over time does not highlight how data can lend new insights. The AQS notebook was developed with a consulting scientist whose area of specialty involved neighborhood-scale air quality and guides users to fetch  datasets that allow for deeper engagement with air quality, related environmental and atmospheric science, and social impacts. The U. S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Air Quality System or “AQS” is a longitudinal database of air quality data collected by U. S. agencies that has been evaluated and verified for accuracy. In Part I of the AQS notebook, users are instructed on how to acquire an API, connect to the AQS  service, and query the status of the service to make sure it is online and able to provide requested data. Next, users identify a bounding box using latitude and longitude coordinates that defines a geographic region from which data should be fetched. They also identify a “target date,” which will serve as the center of a time interval of interest. The default date is June 6, 2023, when several large cities across United States experienced historically high levels of air pollution from a complex of wildfires in Canada. Users are encouraged to edit the date to make sense for their context. Once users have successfully connected to the API and defined their preferred settings, the notebook offers several query templates focused on particular scientific or statistical learning goals. These include:

(1) Investigating Pollutants. Exploring the dynamics of air pollutants can motivate investigations of the

underlying chemical and behavioral complexity of air pollution. For example, ozone (O3) often demonstrates a daily cyclical variation in concentration as a secondary pollutant that is generated when other pollutants interact with heat and light. In contrast, particulate matter levels (PM) rise after events that release particles into the air. The notebook models a query that identifies air quality monitors within the specified location and time range that report both Ozone (O3) and particulate matter (PM2.5) levels at high resolution, so that differences can be identified in the data. Users can edit the code to specify other pollutants, though this combination often yields dramatic differences in pattern that can support robust hypothesis generation (“Why does Ozone go up and down while PM follows a different pattern?” or “Why did PM rise more than Ozone during the wildfire?”) and examination of primary versus secondary air pollution and other key atmospheric chemistry concepts.

(2) Exploring Differences in Air Quality. Air quality can vary dramatically across even close geographic

neighbors, often due to a complex combination of geographic features, weather patterns, human behaviors, zoning and development, and other social and scientific causes. The AQS notebook allows users to specify whether they are interested in composite AQI or a specific pollutant for a given region. They are then given a list of monitoring sites within the region that report these values at least daily, ordered by concentration so that data that demonstrate stark differences can be identified and fetched for comparison and investigation.

(3) Unpacking AQI. The Air Quality Index is a composite index that tracks six main pollutants –ground

level ozone, particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide levels. The reported AQI reflects only the maximally hazar dous pollutant concentration at a given time; this may be different (e.g. Ozone versus PM2.5) within the same day. The AQS notebook identifies monitoring sites within the specified day and time that report as many of the AQI-constituent pollutants as possible. Once a site is selected, it fetches the dataset and calculates  the corresponding hourly AQI, supporting investigations into the composite measure (“Is the air really equally healthy if two sites that report the same AQI? Why or why not?”). Accessing Rivulet notebooks and next steps Rivulet notebooks are available for free under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International (CC BY-NC 4.0) License and can be accessed at https://github.com/CalCoRE/rivulet-utils. The notebooks are undergoing iterative development as we consult with expert advisors and as they are used as a part of active curriculum development. In addition to national and internationally-focused notebooks on air quality, we are developing notebooks focused on water quality using the United States Geological Survey’s Water Quality Exchange or WQX API, and weather data using the U. S. National Weather Service API. We look forward to learning what might be other areas of need or opportunity for this work, and to invit ing collaboration. 3019 Arnold, P., Bargagliotti, A., Franklin, C., & Gould, R. (2022). 3020 Empathy and Agency in Sociotechnical Engineering Design Vanessa Svihla, Madalyn Wilson-Fetrow, Stephen Secules vsvihla@unm.edu, mefetrow144@unm.edu, secules@unm.edu University of New Mexico Abstract: T echnically-focused undergraduate engineering p rograms inadequately prepare students for the complexity of designing solutions to sociotechnical problems. By supporting students to frame problems grounded in their everyday experiences set in places they are from, we investigate how they use their agency to make consequential decisions about both problem and solution. Interaction and discourse analysis show how an ideation approach helped students expand design problem spaces empathize with varied stakeholders. Scholars have motivated the importance of empathy by documenting ways designers’ end products are impacted by whom they empathize with—or not —and how (Sewell, 1992). Empathy is important but perhaps particularly challenging for engineers (Hess, 2024; Strobel et al., 2013; Walther et al., 2020). Methods that promote empathy during ideation can emphasize the experience of a single individual or group, narrowing the problem space and leading to less creative ideas (Gray et al., 2015). In this way, there is a tension between creativity and empathy in the ideation process. An ideation technique, the Wrong Theory Protocol (WTP) helps designers overcome this tension (Svihla & Kachelmeier, 2022). The WTP asks designers to concisely define the problem and name stakeholder needs, then playfully generate harmful and humiliating ideas before generating beneficial ideas. When compared to a similar approach—generating silly and impossible ideas —generating humiliating ideas reveals an advantage, as student designers who did so were significantly more likely to produce ideas that were jointly creative and empathetic (Svihla & Kachelmeier, 2022). T he capacity to design with empathy is by no means a guaranteed outcome of engineering programs, especially given the commonplace foregrounding of technical aspects (Kirn & Benson, 2018; Leydens et al., 2014).  We argue that instruction should support students to use their funds of knowledge in their learning processes (Verdín et al., 2024). One way to accomplish this is through querencia, a Spanish word that expands typical conceptions of place-based learning by emphasizing responsibility to, love of, and belonging to place (Ault Jr, 2008). Placing design problems within specific and familiar contexts may provide ways for students to bring their funds of knowledge to bear in the problem framing process; as such, it may be easier for students to use their agency to make consequential decisions about how they frame problems. Agency can be understood in design and learning as distributed, dynamic, and shared with other humans and nonhumans (Schön, 1983). The act of making consequential decisions about the problem frame is termed framing agency and involves making choices that change the problem frame  (Svihla et al., 2021). We consider how ideation can support and reveal students’ agency. While studies suggest there are benefits to using WTP, less is known about how  designers negotiate this process, an understanding of which could shed light on this phenomenon. To guide our work, we sought to investigate the following research questions: (1) How might a playful WTP ideation activity support students to expand their understanding of the problem space, stakeholders and their needs? (2) In what ways might students use their agency in this process? We examine how WTP supported particular forms of discursive engagement. Participants included first-year students enrolled in an integrative engineering design course (N=13 in three teams) at a southwest ern US Hispanic-serving R1 university. Instructors formed teams  of four or five. The class included 10 Latiné/Hispanic students, one Native student, two Black students, and two Asian students  and two women. The course included two design challenges, the first of which focused on water resilience in New Mexico. We supported students to identify issues related to water access in the  communities with which they had connections or experiences, thus building on t heir querencia and funds of knowledge. After initial framing, students engaged in the WTP: they concisely framed the problem, came up with harmful and humiliating ideas, then generated beneficial ideas. The teams refined their beneficial ideas, developed and tested prototypes, and finalized their design solutions. We video and audio recorded each consenting team as they engaged in the WTP. Data also include artifacts of students’ work. We analyzed video records and transcripts using interaction analysis as a way into the data (Ault Jr, 2008; Moll et al., 1992), then analyzed talk using the framing agency toolkit, a discourse analytic approach to examine agency in design talk (Jordan & Henderson, 1995). 3021 After initially exploring many potential problems related to water resilience in New Mexico, teams framed the problems they wished to solve. Team 1 identified  the problem as lacking an “effective system to divert flooding away from communities” and Team 3 as “lack of clean water within low-income communities and tribes.” Neither reflected a particular engineering discipline, and both display people-orientation in describing rural and low-income communities and tribal Reservations.  Their problem frames reflect querencia (Ault Jr, 2008) in that the problems are not only sited in place s familiar to the students, but they draw upon their firsthand knowledge of, care/concern for, and sense of responsibility to this place. During WTP, both teams immediately and playfully discussed harmful ideas, bringing  humiliation in somewhat later. For instance, Evan shared a playful idea: using untreated runoff from flooding to make a waterpark, an idea that is anatopic given the dry conditions of the high desert environment Evan and his teammates are familiar with. Proposing ideas that misfit the place suggests the team had taken up the notion of querencia and using their local knowledge. The students more easily proposed harmful ideas (which has more technical, productoriented aspects to it) than humiliating ones (a purely human experience), which parallels research showing students tend to arrive at technical solutions before considering human-centered values and care (Walther et al., 2020). Students who haven’t yet tried to conceive of the people involved in their problem space struggle to expand to human-centered reasoning. Looking for someone centrally involved to humiliate is a subtle / backwards way to expand this dimension.

Both teams displayed talk characteristic of framing agency, as they shared agency over their ideas (using the first-person plural pronoun “we”) and used modal verbs showing possibility (e.g., “could” “gonna”). These discourse markers are characteristic of framing agency (Svihla et al., 2021). This type of design talk is tentative and the speaker invites co-designers into the problem frame by including others in their idea (“e.g., “We could”). Teams displayed expanded agency and enjoyed the serious and intentional but simultaneously ludic and rebellious nature of the activity. They framed their problems in specific ways throughout the activity, making clear choices about the boundaries of the problem, even when being playful. Through what is in effect reverse psychology, the WTP makes its reque sts in ways that push thinking in desired dimensions while not actually demanding or explicitly suggesting the desired dimension.

For their final design, team 1 developed a system of canals and pumps that would divert water from Ruidoso to a nearby lake on the reservation of the Mescalero Apache tribe, avoiding dangerous and disruptive locations while benefiting wildlife and droughts. They recognized needing to obtrain permission from the tribe and divert water away from homes. Team 3’s final design was a system to remove uranium from the water used by the Navajo Nation. They created a solution that was portable  and for individual household use, identifying some residents’ limited infrastructure access. This included placing filters in community spaces to support unsheltered residents. The design was simple to operate and enabled safe dispos al of contaminants (preventing accidental build-up in people). The design addressed the context  of Navajo Nation and its spread-out nature. Concerns about build-up reflect their WTP ideas where there was no choice but to drink contaminated water. While more work is needed in other design contexts to understand how WTP functions, our analysis provides backing for using WTP. With no additional prompting, students generated multiple ideas, shifting their attention away from getting to the “right” answer —a common cultural expectation of school —and instead considering solutions as well as ideas related to the problem space, resulting in a more expansive understanding of the design problem. In both teams, the WTP process helped r emind the students of the various people who might be impacted by the problem, in turn, triggering actual empathy rather than telling students to empathize. As we prepare engineering students to meet the design challenges of the future, we need them to take ownership, to have agency, but we alsoneed to guide them away from some known tendencies—towards product-orientation, towards single solution anchoring, towards lack of questioning of positioning in systems of power. By allowing playfulness, the WTP takes one possible approach at creating the conditions for productive humancentered, sociotechnical reasoning. By asking students to get it “wrong” it candrive creative and empathetic ideation. Implications of this work include aiming for a balance of requesting students to stay on task, to genuinely push themselves into uncomfortable territory, but to also reason for themselves. Based on our insights, we also plan to more clearly support reflective practice following WTP, by asking students to evaluate the ways  antibeneficent reasoning was productive. 3022 Ault Jr, C. R. 3023 Designing a Table-Top Roleplaying Game for Understanding Learning Theories Matthew Duvall, Xinyue Cui, Joo Hyun Lee, Qiao Lin, Xinyu Liu, Jiawen Lu, Jiaxin Xu mduv@upenn.edu, cxinyue@upenn.edu, lee0@upenn.edu, linqiao@upenn.edu, xinyu15@upenn.edu, jiawlu@upenn.edu, jiaxinx@upenn.edu University of Pennsylvania – Graduate School of Education Abstract: This paper describes the development of The Learning Game, a tabletop roleplaying game designed to help master’s students in education better understand learning theories and the theorists behind them. Over the course of a semester, a team of six master’s  students and one faculty member collaboratively designed and play tested the game  with other students at their university. While the prototype was well-received, the process and product provided further evidence for the barriers to game-based learning in university settings. At a private graduate school of education in the northeastern United States, students take a class on the foundations of teaching and learning. One of the major assignments in that class is a learning theories matrix. Students work together to describe the  major tenets of foundational learning theories like behaviorism, constructivism, and sociocultural theory.

While it is important for education students to understand these theories, it can be difficult to evaluate if they are engaging with this assignment to  build knowledge. The advent of generative AI tools, like ChatGPT, make it even harder to disentangle what students understand and whether they can apply the theoretical mindset to real-world contexts.

Given this, our research team undertook a game design project to create an alternative way for students to collaboratively build their understanding of these theories. This paper describes our design process, the resulting game, and how this experience provided another example of the advantages and barriers to game-based learning in university settings.

## Theoretical perspectives

Lester et al. (2023) reviewed seventeen articles and identified affordances and constraints of game-based learning for university settings. Educators viewed games as collaborative, engaging, and easy to use. On the other hand, the lack of time for game dev elopment, issues with classroom settings and constraints, and lack of empirical evidence for GBL benefits were constraints that teachers reported. Our team was interested in redesigning the Learning Theories Matrix assignment with the goal of creating an experience that encompassed these affordances, while also inviting the game players to engage in knowledge-building. Our work draws from sociocultural theories of learning, tracing back to Vygotsky. Key sociocultural elements for this project include the use of signs/symbols for learning, the social nature of learning with other humans, and the importance of context (Lee et al., 2017; Pinkard et al., 2025). Because the context we are working in is a university, we drew from the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) for developing our game. This framework proposes that instructional activities can fall on a range – passive, active, constructive, or interactive. Chi and colleagues point out that the description of an activity is not enough to determine where it falls. Rather, it is necessary to observe the activity in practice. We also incorporated “dialogic teaching” (Alexander, 2008) to focus on ways to make classroom discussions more effective. These included students providing ideas for others to build on, asking open-ended questions, responding thoughtfully, and challenging others’ ideas respectfully. This is not unlike good role playing for games such as Dungeons & Dragons or the like. The design of the game drew from Gee’s (2005) principles of good learning in games and the MechanicsDynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) framework (Hunicke et al., 2004). Gee argued that good games empower learners, provide well-designed opportunities for learning, and offer opportunities to extend understanding. Gee further argued that formal education often missed opportunities to provide these experiences to learners, while game designers included these elements without any special training in learning theories. The MDA framework describes how the rules (mechanics) and implementation of those rules (dynamics) result in a specific player experience (aesthetics). This framework can be used to both design and evaluate games. We focused on aesthetics such as Narrative Game as drama and Fellowship Game as social framework to guide our design of mechanics and dynamics to help us achieve that style of game.

3024 The research team was made up of seven researchers (a lecturer and six master’s students) from the graduate school of education at a large private university in the northeastern United States.  The team met weekly during the spring semester After reviewing the relevant frameworks and playing a rough prototype designed by the lecturer, each team member designed and developed iterative refinements or reimaginings of the game. As a group, we played the games and then determined which elements were working well and carried those over to future iterations. Finally, the last week of the semester we did two play-testing sessions of the game with seven to eight participants in each, made up of other master’s students who had taken the foundations class but had not been part of the game design process.

The learning game 1.0 The Learning Game 1.0 is a semi-structured narrative roleplaying game for 3 to 6 players. Players are randomly assigned roles, including game master. The game master goes through a series of guided choices to set up the context, such as type of learning (e.g. kindergarten, workplace training, non-school museum learning), number of learners, income level (low, average, high), and population density. The game master also decides the learning topic and the country where the learning takes place. Two players are required to take on the role of their learning theorist, while others become learners, teachers, or other stakeholders. Then the players describe the learning context through the perspective of their role, with the game master guiding the discussion. Overall, feedback from the play sessions was favorable, but there were some suggestions for improvement related to the mechanics and dynamics, such as giving the game master more responsibility or having multiple discussion rounds. For the research team, t he game development process was engaging and productive, and contributed to our own better understanding of learning theories and the complexities of learning in the world around us. At the same time, we acknowledged that the process was time-consuming and resulted in a prototype that still needs further development to be classroom ready.

This design process raised some questions for us, as alluded to in the work of Lester et al. (2023). Chief among them is the tension between a formal educational setting and a game. In his foundational paper, Gee (2005) made a similar argument: education is not an ideal environment for taking advantage of the benefits of games. For example, a D&D campaign can take days, weeks, or even longer. But for our narrative roleplaying game, we have a two-hour class period to play. There is also the issue of scoring or grading this. How will we know if this works at least as well as the current activity we have in the class? One way is to evaluate the activity based on ICAP, but that still does not necessarily tell the effectiveness of an activity, but rather the potential for better learning. To summarize, this project left us with some questions, including whether a game designed specifically for education (a subset of games designed for learning) can be compared to games developed for entertainment. The nature of educational systems requires consideration of many factors that go against key features of what makes games good for learning. Indeed, Gee (2024) himself stated that his original article was intended to point out this discrepancy. We still believe that designing games, as either instr uctors or students, is an effective way to improve and display one’s own understanding of concepts. We also believe that playing such games may be an effective way for students to learn about topics, provided the games are well-designed and theoretically s ound. But it is not clear if these approaches are “better” than any other approach, or even what better would mean. It is also not clear if a game designed to be effective for learning in a formal educational context could also be a successful game outside  of that context. Games for education, to our current understanding, are their own specialized subcategory.

Based on the feedback and our observations from the play testing sessions, we are going to refine some of the game mechanics to better achieve our desired aesthetics, particularly the Narrative elements. We are also working on ways to speed the game up, without losing the goal of collective knowledge-building about learning theorists and theories. We plan to use the game as part of our instruction in the future, with observations, surveys, and interviews to understand if the students find it useful and whether it achieves our overall goals of being engaging, interactive, and beneficial for learning.
