Acta Psychologica, 253, 104705. 3026 Speculative Storytelling and Genai as Tools for Imagining More Just Futures Elizabeth Starks, University of Washington Bothell, eestarks@uw.edu Carrie Tzou, Northwestern University, carrietehli.tzou@northwestern.edu Veronica McGowan, University of Washington Bothell, vmcgowan@uw.edu Symone Gyles, University of California Irvine, sgyles@uci.edu Bryan White, University of Washington Bothell, bdwhite@uw.edu Abstract: T his study asks what opportunities speculative storytelling practice provided for examination of overlapping systems of power and subsequent biases perceived through AI image generation during an undergraduate STEM course for preservice educators. Initial systemic biases, and socioecological issues.

Just and equitable framings of STEM teaching and learning call for a broadening of what and whose ways of knowing (and toward what ends) count in these spaces to include the expansive ways in which humans and morethan-humans have contributed to constructing our material and digital worlds (Vossoughi & Vakil, 2018). Critical speculative design is a justice-centered approach that engages learners in complex systems thinking and modeling both critique the infrastructure and design of their own communities, and to engage in criticality of racialized and historicized decision-making that have created unjust landscape patterns at scale. Learning to recognize powered decision-making enables learners to see how their neighborhoods are part of the designed world. To build resilience, agency, and hope in learners, this act of criticality is coupled with collective speculative re-imaginings when redesigned through community visions (Dunne & Raby, 2013; Escobar, 2018). Speculative storytelling is a form of speculative design and pedagogy that recognizes the need for new pathways and imaginings to guide more just futures and support s feelings of agency and hope, especially for STEM-related learners in the Anthropocene (Tomin & Collis, 2023). Speculative fiction–one type of speculative storytelling–includes genres like science fiction and futurism, using imaginative scenarios to encourage future thinking, building capacities for considering the long-term implications of cur rent trends and decisions, and considering the ethical implications of decisions across time scales. Overall, speculative pedagogies aim to prepare students for a future that is dynamic, uncertain, and constantly evolving by engaging in intellectual modeling and simulations not only across time, but also across heterogeneous worlds. In this work, we describe the analysis of a speculative storytelling project in an undergraduate science course for preservice teachers. In particular, we analyze how the use of  an AI image generator in this  context can support students in developing connections between computer science content, systemic biases in algorithms, and socio-ecological issues in our designed world.

## Context, methods, and data analysis

teachers” course, designed to take the place of science content courses typically required for entry into teacher certification programs. In t he course we analyze here, students engaged in the learning and investigating of technology and engineering ethics (exploring AI and CS content critically toward justice, sovereignty, and equity) and gender-inclusive biology (exploring how life sciences may be taught in equitable and inclusive ways through gender expansive teaching). Driving design principles for the course are described elsewhere (authors, 2025) and included weaving STEM content knowledge and practices with critical data engagements, centering familial and cultural ways of knowing, and engaging in ethical decision-making. While these courses have undergone three co-design cycles (Cobb, et al, 2003), data for this study come from the Fall 2024 iteration of the course. We took a frame of critical socio-technical literacy as an approach to equity through the design of the course: the practice of learning to read the designed world for these patterns to situate and re-imagine these spaces for equity, justice, and health (McGowan, et al, 2020). The project we analyze here comes from the speculative storytelling project that served as the final project from this course. Data sources for this study include classroom artifacts such as the 18 students’ written stories, story presentations, and final reflections on their projects. Our design leadership team coded artifacts for themes (Miles, Huberman, & Saldaña, 2019) and then used grounded theory to make sense of emerging patterns across data sets (Strauss & Corbin, 1994). 3027 Speculative storywork design Through our iterative design, we found that imagining robust, more just futures could be a daunting task for students. To facilitate this imagining, we integrated speculative fiction reading and practices related to class content throughout the course (Imashara, et al, 2015; Jones, & Melo, 2021). To build from a shared world, the class collaboratively agreed on the time, place, and conditions of a future setting where they would set stories that imagine a more just future. For example, students selected bet ween a near or far future time scale and a local or global place, among other parameters. In small groups, students composed a shared story that took place in this future world, and then individually wrote a story from the perspective of a character they created as a part of that world. These different scales allowed students to explore aspects of intersectional identities and how social, technological, and ecological factors impact people in myriad possibilities. Students were given the option to generate images of their own characters using an AI image generator. Generating imagery of their characters not only personalized and illuminated the students’ visions of the future, but also offered an opportunity to peek into the “black box” of tools used to create these illuminations and recognize any biases they had examined in class. Through the course, students  engaged in hands-on technology activities, data engagements, and discussions around how image recognition and generative AI work, how systemic biases can be encoded in these data models (Benjamin, 2019), and the impact of these technologies on lived lives. Through these engagements, they began to recognize what types of decisions were being made by the algorithm when representing people of different genders, skin tones and their depicted societal roles, while also making sense of the types of data the model was likely provided. In the individual writing project, all but one student used an AI image generator like Microsoft Co-Pilot or ChatGPT to generate an image of their character. After presenting their stories, students reflected on the process of using these image generators to develop images of the characters they developed in their stories. Table 1 shows representative examples of students’ reflections. Table 1 Preservice Education Students’ Reflections on AI-Generated Images

## Initial results from character image generation

Student 1 The AI-generated image of He mostly aligned with my vision, but it also made me think about biases in technology. I didn’t specify He’s race or skin color, yet the AI generated a character with darker skin, likely reflecting stereotypes about poverty in the data it was trained on. Student 2 I searched up rich hijabi business woman and there were no results. Student 3 When it comes to using the AI generator I felt extremely lucky. This is because I am white and did not struggle with getting an image that represented me. It made me sad to hear about my classmates experiencing trouble just trying to view a character of color. Student 4 At some point I included the phrase “feminine features” for my character and it gave me a person only wearing a bra with no shirt or they would have a shirt but their bra would be showing. In these examples, we see students reflected on specific character biases, what factors in the training data may have led to them, and how they respond as designers. Specifically, students noticed unwanted sexualization of their characters, and clear biases including colorism. Through students’ reflection on generating characters in their group and individual  writing project and their in-class story presentations, we found that students made deep connections between science, engineering, and technology concepts, systemic biases, and socioecological issues. By engaging students with disciplinary content within historicized contexts, they were prepared to critically interpret the images they generated, making connections to data models and considering implications of their own use of these tools. As they told stories for more just futures, we saw students building resilience in worlds that may not be designed for them, imagining how they could build something different.

Educators lack consistent guidance and preparation for engaging with AI ethically in their schools (Doss et al, 2025). As technological tools advance and are integrated into educational settings, strong socio-critical digital literacy is important for future educators to make ethical decisions for their students and their own teaching practices. Speculative fiction writing and critical analysis of image generation uniquely allow students to consider how these i ntersecting STEM concepts affect and are affected by design decisions, and how they in turn affect the socio-ecological world.

3029 Conjecture Mapping as a Tool for Transdisciplinary Research Collaboration Heather Killen, Institute for Learning Sciences, hkillen@buffalo.edu Camden Miller, School of Architecture and Planning, camdenmi@buffalo.edu Ari Hock, Institute for Learning Sciences, arihock@buffalo.edu Christopher Hoadley, Institute for Learning Sciences, isls@tophe.net Lauren Fischer, School of Architecture and Planning, lf44@buffalo.edu University at Buffalo Abstract: Conjecture mapping (CM) to  support collaboration across disciplines remains underexplored. Grounded in boundary crossing theory, this study examines the introduction of CM in a transdisciplinary project involving learning scientists and urban planners. Using autoethnographic methods we investigate how the process of CM facilitated academic discourse and collaborative project design. We find CM supported transdisciplinarity, boundary practices, and the attributes of the team, such as a willingness to explore new knowledge spaces together. Our project team includes three learning sciences (LS) researchers and two faculty from a school of architecture and planning who all recognize that the integration of different disciplinary perspectives can lead to understanding concrete issues in innovative ways (Hirsch Hadorn et al., 2008). Conjecture mapping (CM) is a method for articulating theoretical and design conjectures in complex learning environments (Sandoval, 2014). CM has been widely used in education research to refine theory (e.g., Campbell, et. al., 2019), design technology (e.g., Gamrat & Zimmerman, 2021), and develop pedagogy (e.g., Magana, 2024). Recently, conjecture maps have also been explored as boundary objects to support interdisciplinary collaboration. A boundary object is “both plastic enough to adapt to local needs and constraints of the several parties employing them, yet robust enough to maintain a common identity across sites.” (Star & Griesemer, 1989, p. 393). While the conjecture map itself can be a boundary object, the proce ss of creating and refining a conjecture map may be a boundary practice, insofar as it coordinates joint work “that bring[s] together participants from different domains for ongoing engagement” (Penuel et al., 2015, p. 190).

Within architecture and planning research, emerging studies highlight the promise of CM. Wijesooriya et al. (2020) uses CM to develop and refine  a pedagogical model that integrate s biophilic design into an environmentally sustainable design studio course, focused on individual learning outcomes. De Blust et al. (2022) applies CM retrospectively to analyze and refine participatory studios for professional planners, emphasizing group learning outcomes. These examples suggest CM can help architecture and planning researchers organize complex design processes and foster collaborative learning. Here we describe how CM supported our multidisciplinary academic team in developing a research plan to explore a community-wide learning agenda in the context of transportation infrastructure reform. We answer the research question: How did conjecture mapping support academic discourse across a multidisciplinary research team as they developed a transdisciplinary study?

## Context and methodology

We report on our pilot effort to design community workshops within a transportation planning context. Our team’s design artifacts were first annotated for instances of boundary crossing by the first author, drawing on Akkerman and Bakker (2011) and  inductive coding (Saldaña, 2016) to create an initial codebook. This codebook was used to analyze individual narrative reflections on the role of CM in the design process, gathered from team members after the conclusion of the workshops. Individuals drafted their reflections based on analytic memos and member recollections of the project’s design processes. The first author independently coded these narratives, the second author coded a subset using the initial codebook alongside inductive coding, and the two rese archers compared and reconciled coding differences to identify prominent themes. Our analysis indicates that the value of the CM process for our transdisciplinary group was grounded in three ways. First, team members report that CM strongly supported transdisciplinary collaboration by clarifying project priorities, surfacing theoretica l connections, and focusing collaborative efforts, enabling the team to align 3030 outcomes and processes across disciplinary boundaries. A planning team member contrasted CM with prior experience in which transdisciplinary teams often relied on a “divide and conquer approach to research tasks.” She recalled this approach failed to produce transdisciplinary outcomes. In contrast, CM offered “substantive insights” into project development, giving her early confidence that the team would successfully “work together through an integrative project implementation.” As the project progressed, CM continued to serve as a clarifying tool. A planning team member described CM as enabling “a more clear pathway toward analyzing workshop activities.” Similarly, a LS team member valued the conjecture map giving the group “buy-in and clarity.” When she perceived a part of the project was beginning to exceed its original scope, she reported that having the option to “return to the conjecture map to emphasize what had originally been focused on” gave her confidence to challenge the new direction.

Second, developing a conjecture map was a boundary practice, helping researchers bridge disciplinary divides, foster a shared language, mitigate tensions, and strengthen collaborative confidence. Team members reported that the process surfaced differences in vocabulary, terminology, and theoretical perspectives, enabling CM to “guide team conversations” towards a shared discourse. Team members were required to articulate previously implicit disciplinary perspectives. This clarified contrasting meanings, preventing the team from “talking past each other” and instead having discourse “strengthened and clarified.” As one of the planning team members reflected, “I’ve come [throughout my career] to appreciate the amount of effort required to have clear conversations about what we are doing, and why, to research collaborators in the academy (fellow academics) and in the community.” Reflections also revealed that CM alleviated preexisting concerns among LS team members while fostering positive affect across the group. One LS researcher characterized the process of CM as a “release valve” as the team worked to “organize all of our ambitions and try to make sense of how they might (or might not) fit together.” Another LS team member noted that CM could “surface tensions before they took root,” addressing her initial worry that planning members might hold “very different ideas about what communityengaged work should look like [given] their own lenses and expertise” and uncertainty about how “that additional layer might change things [i.e. the care taken toward community interactions].” Finally, CM fostered a shared understanding by alleviating concerns, surfacing tensions early, and inspiring confidence in collaborative sensemaking across disciplinary boundaries. A planning team member described how “collectively, we started to work through conjuncture mapping,” characterizing it as a “journey of collaborative sensemaking-with interdisciplinary voices and perspectives which I found quite inspiring.” An LS team member similarly noted how CM revealed that the team held “shared commitments  to a participatory research ethos, [that included] working toward equity in both the process and outcome of our research.” Our team familiarity and comfort with CM’s core processes, a shared ethos toward community-based scholarship, and shared personal stances positioning team members as learners willing to explore new knowledge spaces together. Reflecting on learning mechanisms at boundaries (Akkerman and Bakker, 2011), CM supported identification of the shared values shaping the team’s collective inquiry, legitimated coexistence of disciplinary perspectives, and enabled sensemaking across practices. CM also structured coordination of project design, requiring joint, in-person meetings that fostered communicative connection. The conjecture map served as a method for refocusing project goals when activities began to overreach, helping team members understand how interests and expertise aligned, or could be broadened, to frameworks and ideas from outside their home discipline. CM’s effectiveness as a boundary practice was amplified by the team’s familiarity with iterative design processes, a shared ethos toward community-based scholarship, and personal stances positioning team members as learners, attributes aligned closely with CM’s core principles. Team members also demonstrated a willingness to revisit prior knowledge and engage in “productive struggle,” which CM structured into collaborative sensemaking. This synergy between tool and team underscores that while CM offers powe rful affordances, success may depend on complementary commitments by members. As a boundary practice, CM enabled the research  team to move beyond coordination toward genuine integration of perspectives, a hallmark of transdisciplinary work. CM not only clarified project priorities and surfaced theoretical connections but also fostered a shared language, mitigated tensions, and strengthened collaborative confidence. Implications for the learning sciences include the need to explore CM’s role in other transdisciplinary contexts, particularly in community-engaged research. Future work s hould examine how CM might be adapted to support transformation at boundaries, and whether its affordances scale in larger, more heterogeneous teams.

## Acknowledgments

We gratefully acknowledge funding and staffing support from the U niversity at Buffalo’s Institute for Learning Sciences and the University at Buffalo’s Rudy Bruner Center for Urban Excellence.  We also thank students Grace Wiseman and Jason Myrick for their support of this project. 3032 From Acronym to Practice: How Brazilian Teachers Reimagine STEAM in Public Education Franciele Gomes, Paola S. Ricci, Walter Akio Goya, Rita Junqueira de Camargo, Simone Kubric Lederman franciele@catalisador.org.br, paola@catalisador.org.br, akio@catalisador.org.br, rita@catalisador.org.br, simone@catalisador.org.br Instituto Catalisador Abstract: This study maps 222 teacher-led STEAM projects across 23 Brazilian states to understand how educators contextualize the approach in public middle schools. Findings reveal a culturally grounded “tropicalized” STEAM that fosters student authorship and belon ging, while exposing gaps in technology use and systemic barriers to scaling innovation. This research underscores the potential of culturally grounded practices while identifying systemic barriers to scaling innovation in Brazil.

In recent years, Brazilian public education has focused on middle school (grades 6–9) as a critical stage for student engagement (Todos pela Educação, 2025). This study, a partnership between Itaú Social and Instituto Catalisador, explores how STEAM can co ntribute to the development of students in their intellectual, social, and cultural dimensions.

With the research question "What forms of STEAM implementation are present in middle school public education (grades 6–9) in Brazil?", the project had as core objectives to: (1) identify how STEAM practices are being implemented in the Brazilian educational reality, (2) demystify STEAM by showing viability of such practices in different contexts, and (3) highlight evidence that these practices bring significant results for students. The theoretical framing draws on the Project Zero Maker Empowerment framework (Clapp et al., 2017), which emphasizes student agency and the creation of authentic artifacts as central to meaningful learning. Within this framework, STEAM is not just interdis ciplinary integration, but a pedagogical approach that fosters maker-centered dispositions like design sensitivity, collaboration, and iterative thinking. Moving beyond descriptive terms, this study analytically examines how participation, engagement and authorship (Sawyer, 2022) are fostered through STEAM practices which are contextualized to local Brazilian realities.  The project mapped 121 STEAM initiatives implemented in the middle school level across Brazil, revealing how the approach takes multiple shapes in diverse regional contexts. Findings suggest that Brazilian educators employ STEAM as a means to foster student engagement, authorship, collaboration, and a sense of belonging, particularly in vulnerable settings. As part of the initiative, a portfolio showcasing STEAM projects from all regions was organized and published. The insights generated from the portfolio may be especially relevant in full-time schools, a growing public policy movement in Brazil, aligned with the paradigm of Integral Education, a conception that transcends extended school hours to emphasize the whole development of students in their intellectual, physical, emotional, social, cultural, and ethical dimensions (Centro de Referências em Educação Integral, 2025) The project followed a multi-stage design (Table 1) involving the definition of STEAM with six specialists (Déborah De Mari, Leo Burd, Lilian Bacich, Luciano Meira, Paulo Blikstein, Susan Klimczak), a national mapping via questionnaires (254 responses were collected, yielding 222 valid responses after data cleaning and the focus of the final report analysis was the 121 projects implemented in middle school level), and qualitative interviews with the nine most "inspiring projects".

## Key findings and discussion

The analysis revealed a diverse mosaic of innovative practices, reinforcing the idea of a culturally grounded STEAM adapted to Brazilian realities. STEAM was reinterpreted to encompass broader meanings: Science included ecology and local contexts; Arts extended to Humanities and Social Sciences; Engineering emphasized construction and problem-solving; and Mathematics offered logical and quantitative grounding. Interdisciplinarity emerged as a defining feature, with 42.1% of projects integrating two disciplines —most often Technology with Engineering or Technology with Arts.

The analysis of the results showed that student engagement was highest when learners acted as creative agents. The practice of constructing artifacts ("mão na massa") was present in 67.8% of middle school projects. While only 26.4% explicitly mentioned ter ritory, successful cases like Aprendizado com as Galinhas  (PI) demonstrate how applying quadratic roots to the construction of a chicken coop makes learning meaningful through local cultural practices. Despite strong potential, the mapping revealed systemi c challenges that threaten the implementation and sustainability of STEAM practices across Brazil. The most frequent obstacles were limited infrastructure and resources (21.6%), unstable financing (16.2%), and low digital literacy and connectivity (13.5%). Other barriers included resistance to innovation (12.2%) within school communities and time constraints (11.3%), such as insufficient planning and scheduling conflicts with traditional classes. The mapping revealed a potent mosaic of innovative educational practices, reinforcing our thesis that a contextualized and culturally grounded, STEAM approach  can create opportunities for teenagers in middle school to reconnect with school and engage in meaningful learning. This mosaic is largely driven by the creativity, commitment, and agency of individual teachers, who have been key to fostering these innovative and context-responsive practices. However, for these opportunities to expand and reach more students, it is necessary to move beyond isolated efforts. The structural challenges identified —such as lack of infrastructure, unstable financing, and the need for rigorous teacher training—demand systemic solutions. By prioritizing investment in integrated public policies that sustain and strengthen these practices, Brazil can ensure that STEAM becomes an integral and effective part of its national public education curriculum. 3035 Anchoring Computing in Social Studies Through Co-Designed Concept-Rich Artifacts Adelmo Eloy, Universidade de São Paulo (Brazil), Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, Columbia University (USA), adelmo.eloy@usp.br Nathan Rabinovitch, Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, Columbia University (USA), nathan.rabinovitch@tltlab.org Walter Akio Goya, Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, Columbia University (USA), akio@fablearn.net Paulo Blikstein, Transformative Learning Technologies Lab, Columbia University (USA), Instituto Tecnológico de Monterrey (México), paulob@tc.columbia.edu Abstract: Brazil’s new computing standards call for meaningful integration across subjects, yet practical models remain scarce in K-12 social studies. We report on a three-year co-design partnership with History and Geography teachers in which interdisciplinary unit s were organized around concept-rich computational artifacts. Across four units-alternative regionalization maps, local weather stations, revolt graphs, and expanded medieval timelines-these artifacts functioned as representational anchors that kept co mputing in service of disciplinary inquiry.

Brazil’s new national computing standards encourage teachers to integrate computing across subjects (Brasil, 2022), yet practical pathways remain limited. While K –12 computing integration has expanded, most implementations still center on STEM disciplines,  with far less attention to social studies (Yeni et al., 2024). Scholars have noted epistemic tensions in integrating computing with the humanities, especially between interpretive, contested inquiry and more formalized computing activity, and called for a pproaches that respect these different ways of knowing (Güven & Gulbahar, 2020; Santo et al., 2023, 2024).

To address this gap, we take a constructionist approach to computing integration in social studies building on Proctor et al.’s (2020) pillar of material intelligence —computers as flexible representational media through which learners reorganize and express ideas (diSessa, 2000) —and co-designed curricular units with middle-school History and Geography teachers. A common feature across units was a tangible or manipulable digital computational artifact, co-planned with teachers and anticipated to connect powerful disciplinary ideas with computing practices. Since activities developed around these objects, our analysis foregrounds material intelligence by focusing on these concept-rich artifacts. They supported new ways of thinking not only about social studies content but also about what learning in this domain could look like (echoing Papert’s “objects-tothink-with” (1980)).  In particular, we ask: How do these artifacts anchor the integration of computing into middleschool history and geography, supporting both disciplinary reasoning and computing practices? This study is part of a three-year research–practice partnership with the Department of Education of a mid-sized city in Northeastern Brazil aimed at integrating computing into other subjects under the new national standards (Eloy et al., 2025). We focused on middle-school History and Geography areas (here treated as social studies) with comparatively fewer examples of computing integration in K –12 classrooms. Across three cohorts, the program involved 6 teachers in Year 1, 11 in Year 2, and 21 in Year 3. The professional development program followed a co-design approach (Penuel et al., 2007) organized into two yearly cycles: in Cycle 1, teachers engaged with introductory computing activities designed by the research team and tested them in their classrooms; in Cycle 2, teachers collaboratively selected disciplinary topics, brainstormed connections to computing, and co-designed and piloted early versions of interdisciplinary activities. We conducted a design analysis of four interdisciplinary units specified for Year 3. Teachers in Years 1–2 co-designed the units and task sequences, defining social studies  goals, validating digital tools, and iterating activity sequences. In Year 3, participating teachers were introduced to these units and supported in selecting and adapting at least one to local needs. Using unit lesson plans and PD documentation (e.g., co-design notes, slides, and design rationales), we analyzed the student-constructed artifacts specified in each unit. For each artifact, we identified the intended disciplinary ideas and computing practices and mapped the planned task sequence designed to support them. In this poster, due to space limitations, we report documented affordances and design intentions rather than classroom outcomes.

3036 We identified four manipulable digital artifacts specified in the units, each linking a core social studies  idea to a fitting computing practice through its representational medium. Figure 1 Sample Co-Designed Artifacts in History and Geography Lessons: (a) Regionalization of the Americas based on the most Popular Sport and HDI; (b) Prototype for a Local Weather Station; (c)Sub-Graph of Regency Revolts with a focus on Slavery and Death Attributes; (d) Expanded Medieval Timelines, Highlighting the Persas, Inca, and Gana Empires in Parallel.

a) Alternative Regionalizations of the Americas (PlayData Scratch extension; Fernandez et al., 2023).

Interactive maps to rethink the standard North– Central–South division using social, economic, or environmental data. Students create new maps grouping the Americas by chosen criteria (e.g., HDI, sports), justifying their choices, foregrounding evidence-based regionalization through data selection and iteration.

b) Local Weather Station (GoGo Board; Sipitakiat et al., 2004). DIY station for collecting local humidity

and temperature data. Students build and deploy the station, collect field data, and compare local readings with external sources, linking microclimate concepts to input/output design, calibration, data cleaning, and plotting.

c) Graphs of Regency Revolts (Obsidian). Networks of revolts showing causes, leaders, and outcomes

across 19th-century Brazil. Students identify patterns in a revolt graph and enrich it with new attributes (e.g., leader gender, lesser-known revolts, weapons), linking comparative historical reasoning tonetwork

d) Reimagined Medieval Timelines (Landbot). Expanded “Middle Ages” timeline, including African,

Asian, and American societies, shared through a chatbot. Students research non-European societies and program the chatbot to present alternative accounts, linking re-periodization and sourcing to information architecture and branching logic.

Our analysis suggests that concept-rich computational artifacts can anchor computing in social studies by aligning representational media with disciplinary aims. In contrast to widely adopted platform-based approaches in Brazil (Reis, 2025), these designs position computing as representational work in service of social  studies inquiry, echoing calls to locate computing in more diverse spaces of learning (Wilkerson et al., 2020). Early teacher feedback suggests a low floor for meaningful participation and strong potential for adaptation across topics and grade levels.

Since here we report design intentions rather than classroom outcomes, our next step is to study enactments to trace how students take up these artifacts in practice. We also aim to investigate what teachers carry forward from co-design as they adapt and extend the units over time, to extend prior work on teacher professional growth (Eloy et al., 2025) and refine the professional  development model to better support teacher agency in integrating computing. More broadly, we argue that constructionism can productively inform pedagogical designs in which computing supports disciplinary inquiry.

## Acknowledgments

We thank the teachers and students who participated in this program, as well as the Limmat Foundation for its generous financial support. We also thank Leah Rosenbaum for her thoughtful comments on the manuscript. 3038 Bridging the Disconnect: Relational Ontologies and the Situated Nature of Computational Thinking Rohini Thapa, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, rthapa@umassd.edu Ezra Gouvea, Rethink Learning Labs, ezra.gouvea@rethinklearning.com Shakhnoza Kayumova, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, skayumova@umassd.edu Chandra Orrill, Rethink Learning Labs, chandra.orrill@rethinklearning.com Ramprasad Balasubramanian, University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, r.bala@umassd.edu Abstract: Computational thinking (CT) is often framed as a universal cognitive skill, yet this view often can overlook the lived realities of learning. This paper advances a relational ontology of CT, positioning learning as emerging through relationships among people, tools, values, and contexts. We propose four dimensions, identity, ethics and affect, community, and embodiment, and illustrate them through classroom practice, highlighting implications for designing more inclusive and meaningful CT experiences. Since Wing’s (2006) influential call to view computational thinking (CT) as a “universally applicable attitude and skill set,” CT has become central in STEM education (Grover & Pea, 2013; Lee et al., 2011). Often framed as generalizable problem-solving skills, such as abstraction, decomposition, pattern recognition, and algorithmic thinking, CT appears adaptable across disciplines. However, this framing can render it decontextualized, treating it as purely cognitive and detached from identity, ethics, and care (Denning, 2017). To move beyond procedural problem solving, CT must be understood as a deeply human activity. Learning sciences research emphasizes that knowledge is situated and relational, shaped by participation, tools, and identities (Greeno, 1998; Lave & Wenger, 1991). Critical computing scholars further argue that equity in computer science involves addressing power, values, and purpose, not just access (Scott et al., 2015; Vakil, 2018).

This paper responds by framing CT through an ontological lens, viewing learning as emerging from relationships among people, technologies, and the world. Drawing on sociocultural and posthumanist perspectives (Barad, 2007; Gutiérrez, 2017), we reconceptual ize CT as relational sense-making where ethics, identity, and material engagement are intertwined. We propose four overlapping dimensions of relational CT, identity, ethics and affect, community, and embodiment, to inform more inclusive and meaningful learning design. Relational ontology in learning A relational ontology challenges the view that knowledge resides within individuals, instead framing knowing as emerging through participation in collective practices and interactions with the material world (Holland et al., 1998; Nasir et al., 2006). From  this perspective, CT is not a mental routine but a set of relationships among learners, technologies, and cultural tools.

Posthumanist and Indigenous perspectives extend this view by emphasizing the inseparability of cognition, emotion, and ethics, with learning occurring through entanglements among human and nonhuman actors (Bang et al., 2011; Barad, 2007). As Gutiérrez (2017) and Radford (2021) suggest, education is an ethical event, meaning computational reasoning is shaped by learners’ values, care, and responsibilities in their interactions with others and technology.

Reframing computational thinking CT as identity work Learners’ identities shape how they engage with computing. When CT connects to cultural knowledge, artistic expression, or everyday practices, it fosters belonging and expands who sees themselves as a computational thinker (Kafai et al., 2014).

CT as ethical and affective practice Computational reasoning always carries ethical and emotional dimensions. Empathy, curiosity, and care guide how learners define problems and imagine solutions (Sohr et al., 2023; Vakil, 2018).  A relational framing invites 3039 educators to position emotion  not as  a distraction from logic, but as  a way of attending to fairness and responsibility, recognizing that algorithms reflect human choices and values. CT as community and culture Computational thinking develops most powerfully in community, where learners negotiate meaning and build shared norms through collaboration. In integrated coding and science projects, students’ discussions and disagreements become part of their computation al work (Dickes et al., 2020). When connected to community issues, such as environmental monitoring or storytelling, CT becomes a form of civic and cultural participation (Tzou et al., 2019).

CT as embodied and material Computational thinking extends beyond code to include gesture, movement, and material creation, connecting abstract ideas to physical experience (Huang & Looi, 2021; Sengupta  et al., 2018). It lives not only in digital systems but also in bodies, tools, and spaces where ideas are made visible. Illustrative example: Designing for fairness in the classroom In an elementary classroom, students design a system to distribute limited supplies after a storm. Working in groups, they plan how a robot might deliver packages and debate what counts as “fair.” Some propose equal distribution, while others prioritize elders and families with infants. When their algorithm fails, they physically trace routes, act out movements, and debug through talk and gesture, making the process both social and embodied.

This moment illustrates relational computational thinking. Students engage in decomposition and iteration, yet their reasoning is inseparable from ethical reflection and collective negotiation. Fairness becomes something enacted within a community, shaped by care, dialogue, and material interaction. As Vakil (2018), Sohr et al. (2023), and Sengupta et al. (2018) suggest, these entanglements show that computational learning is not purely technical but relational and situated.

## Implications for design and pedagogy

Designing for relational CT requires rethinking computational competence and how learning environments connect problems, tools, and communities (Gutiérrez, 2017; Nasir et al., 2006). CT becomes meaningful when rooted in contexts that matter to students, enabling authentic inquiry (Tzou et al., 2019). Affirming students’ identities is central, as cultural knowledge and community narratives position computing as self-expression (Kafai et al., 2014; Scott et al., 2015). Collaboration supports shared meaningmaking (Dickes et al., 2020; Lave & Wenger, 1991).  Relational CT also foregrounds ethics and emotion, highlighting that algorithms are moral as well as logical artifacts (Sohr et al., 2023; Vakil, 2018). Integrating digital, physical, and embodied modes supports creativity and conceptual depth (Huang & Looi, 2021; Sengupta et al., 2018).

Professional learning should model these principles, supporting teachers in culturally and ethically responsive design (Gutiérrez, 2017; Radford, 2021). Assessment must move beyond speed and accuracy to value collaboration, creativity, reflection, and care.

Reimagining computational thinking (CT) through a relational ontology invites a shift from viewing it as isolated cognitive skills to understanding it as a social practice emerging through relationships among ideas, identities, materials, and values. Rather than separating computing from ethical and cultural contexts, this perspective frames learning as participation in interconnected communities of people, technologies, and practices. It highlights that inclusion is not simply about access, but depends on how knowledge is defined, whose experiences are valued, and what purposes computation serves.

By challenging assumptions of neutrality, a relational view recognizes that algorithms and design reflect human intentions and responsibilities. In doing so, it positions learners not only as problem solvers, but as ethical actors engaged in shaping the worlds they inhabit through computational practices. In the end, a relational ontology reminds us that computational thinking is not only about constructing efficient algorithms or elegant abstractions. It is also about constructing relationships, between people and ideas, between logic and empathy, between human creativity and technological possibility. When learners experience CT as relational, they engage in the ethical and communal work of imagining a more connected world, one where computing becomes a means of caring for, understanding, and shaping the s hared realities we inhabit. 3040 Bang, M., Marin, A., & Medin, D. ## Perspectives on Co-Design for Equity: What it Means to Work with

a Community Katherine Walters, James Madison University, L5PGRS@jmu.edu Abstract: The purpose of this study was to explore how learning designers describe the process of working with a community, and what that reveals about their assumptions about co-design. Interviews with three designers engaged in equity-focused community-based projects involving learning designers from different nationalities, institutional roles, and positionalities relative to the communities they collaborated with were analyzed using discourse analysis. Findings reveal that designers’ conceptions of co-design are shaped by this  positionality, their values, and the socio-cultural dynamics of each project.

Co-design in educational contexts refers to collaborative efforts made between researchers and practitioners to address educational problems of practice through design (Gomez et al., 2018). Much of the research on co-design has focused on researchers from institutions of higher education collaborating with K-12 teachers to develop and study designs (e.g., tools, curricula) aligned with the specific needs of teachers  and their students (Gomez et al., 2018). Co-design is widely recognized as a promising approach for advancing equity in K-12 education, with research showing its potential to enhance student learning, engagement, and agency (Dahlstrom-Hakki et al., 2025). This study explores how researchers perceive and frame the co-design process when engaging with communities to design learning experiences outside of formal educational contexts. The purpose of this study was to explore how learning designers describe the process of working with a community, and what that reveals about their underlying assumptions about co-design. The two research questions guiding this study were,

• How do learning designers’ descriptions of co-design projects reflect their understanding of co-design?

• How does this understanding relate to their values, the goals of the project, and the interactions and roles

embedded in the project?

This study use d discourse analysis to examine how three learning designers described co-design projects that involved collaborating with communities to design and sustain diverse learning experiences and to address issues of social justice. Discourse analysis was selected as a methodology because it provides a situated, context-focused way of understanding the meaning made through language  (Tsindos, 2023). In discourse analysis, the researcher connects the themes and patterns within the text to both the social contexts (i.e., here, the projects) of the text and their chosen theoretical lens (Tsindos, 2023). For this study, I framed my analysis with a socio-cultural perspective on learning design.

## Participants and data collection

Each participant was interviewed about their project as part of a broader, multiple-case research study focused on how learning designers attend to issues of social justice (see Walters & Kopcha, 2025), and were selected for this study due to their emphasis on co-designing with communities. Participants included a tenured administrator at a Canadian institution, a clinical faculty member at  an institution in northeast Africa, and a tenure-track faculty member at  a US institution. Their projects included designing, respectively, a non-credit course with an Indigenous tribe, a community of practice led by scholars in the Global South, and a variety of technologyenhanced experiences for rural libraries to offer to their patrons.  Data included an  approximately 1-hour Zoom interview with each participant.

## Data analysis

Each interview was transcribed and then structurally coded in NVivo. Structural codes were used to organize the interview data by concepts  related to the theoretical framework: values, goals, interactions, and roles.  Once organized, the coded data were analyzed using Gee’s (2014) discourse analysis framework. Gee (2014) identified seven building tasks of discourse, including significance, practices, identities, relationships, politics, connections, and sign systems and knowledge. These tasks represent the different ways language constructs meaning.  Each coded section of text was analyzed for these building tasks with a focus on how the language enacted these tasks 3042 in relation to the structural code. This analysis was captured in tables, which were then analyzed within and across codes to create findings for each interview.

Co-design project #1 In this co-design project, a group of higher education researchers worked with an Indigenous community to codesign a non-credit-bearing, professional learning course. The participant in this study was a non-Indigenous researcher and administrator. Overall, the analysis of their interview revealed a centering of Indigenous authority and an intentional contextualization of the need for this authority. Language such as “that’s a no-go” and “there’s no choice” when discussing Indigenous protocols for participation in the project highlighted the authority of the Indigenous people to set the expectations and boundaries. Throughout the interview, the participant provided contextual information that helped situate challenges within a broader narrative of power dynamics, while also acknowledging the oppression and exploitation that educational institutions have enacted in Indigenous communities. This socio-cultural context continually included by the participant served to re-frame challenges in the project as something non-Indigenous team members could act on by developing a better understanding of who they were working with.  Indigenous representation on the project was not a given, but something to work for/towards by engaging with the community on their terms. Co-design project #2 In this co-design project, a small group of globally distribu ted learning designers in higher education worked together to establish an open community of practice focused on inclusive online learning. This resulted in several designs, including resource repositories, workshops, webinars, and a conference. The participant in this study was a key organizer  of the group located in northeast Africa.  Using language such as “everybody” and “everyone” when identifying needs revealed that the participant assumed they understood the community's broader needs. At the same time, they also described collecting and implementing feedback, describing this iterative process as allowing the project to “morph into whatever people needed” (Interview).  This “morphing” language also indicated that this participant understood the project's goal and direction to ultimately be in the hands of the community of participants. These language choices indicate a collective identity. In this context, co-design was not only about collaboration but also about shared ownership and expertise. Co-design project #3 This co-design project involved a partnership between higher education researchers and rural libraries to design and implement technology-enhanced experiences for library patrons. The participant in this study was a higher education researcher on the team located in the southwest US. Importantly, this researcher positioned themselves as an outsider to the field of librarianship. The discourse analysis highlighted the impact of the insider/outsider dynamic on knowledge building in the co-design process. Key to this dynamic was building understanding, which required building relationships. The participant emphasized that when you are working with a community you are an outsider of,  you need to “work with an insider ” to “learn the language ” (Interview). In other words, the participant recognized that understanding the design from the community’s perspective was critical to the project's success. In this perspective, relationships and knowledge  sharing are connected—you cannot access one without the other. However, just because a researcher desires a relationship that supports knowledge sharing does not mean they get to access it; as the participant explained, “Not everyone wants to be included in the conversation that you’re starting” (Interview). Therefore, not only are relationships and understanding key to this perspective on co-design, but also participants' agency.

The findings from this study are useful for preparing researchers to engage in co-design work. Co-design requires a deep understanding of context—including how the community you are working with has experienced academic institutions and researchers, as wel l as how your own identities and values may shape the design process. It also involves rethinking assumptions about how knowledge is shared in partnerships and recognizing that not every community will want to participate in co-design. This work goes beyond building respectful relationships and moves toward a commitment to epistemic justice.  Also, d ifferences in how labor was distributed among codesigners across  projects raise questions about what it means to co-design for equity in terms of who carries responsibility and how roles are negotiated in practice.  Designing for equity does not  necessarily mean equal participation in every task; it means being thoughtful about who carries what kind of labor and ensuring that the process itself reflects the values it aims to uphold.

3044 Agentic Synthesis in Professional Development: How Teachers Recontextualize Knowledge by Creating Mini-courses for Peer Teacher Learning?

Aya Isaac, Jianwei Zhang aisaac@albany.edu, jzhang1@albany.edu University at Albany, State University of New York Abstract: This study examines how teachers learn  through designing mini-courses for peers on a collaborative online platform. Grounded in theories of Knowledge Building and teacher agentic s ynthesis, it conceptualizes teacher learning as recontextualization of personal, professional, and contextual knowledge into instructional designs. Using qualitative case-study The preliminary findings show that teachers learning emerg ed through contextually situated goals, problems of practice, and iterative design.

Existing professional development programs for teachers often feature content delivery by external experts, limiting teachers’ creative input. To support classroom innovation and improvement, the field needs to create participatory teacher learning environments that encourage teachers’ agency for working on innovative learning designs drawing upon personal experiences and distributed expertise (Günal-Aggül et al., 2024). Although teacher design work is widely recognized as professionally meaningful, less is known about how teachers learn when they create professional development resources in open, networked environments. This study addresses that gap by examining how teachers’ knowledge and learning became visible in their design of mini-courses on t he Knowledge Network for Innovation in Learning and Teaching (KNILT) platform, with attention to how they drew on prior experience, professional commitments, local contexts, and interaction with peers.  KNILT is a design-based research project implemented in an online teacher education program. The participating educators are inservice teachers, college instructors, technologists and designers, librarians, and other professionals. They create mini-courses to support teacher learning in high-need areas. Initial designs of the mini-courses were reviewed by peer teachers for feedback. Refined mini-courses are shared on KNILT for broader peer teacher learning. In the context of KNILT, we have been investigate how teachers build public knowledge in the form of minicourses for peer teacher learning  the current study analyzes the following questions: What types of personal, professional, and contextual knowledge do teachers build on their design work? How do teachers recontextualize these knowledge sources in the process of design? And how is teacher agency expressed through the instructional choices teachers make in their designs?

This study draws from Knowledge Building (KB) principles and a gentic synthesis to understand how teachers recontextualize knowledge through professional learning (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 20 22). KB aims to nurture knowledge-creation practices among learners, who collaboratively build  knowledge for community advancement. This study focuses on three  out of twelve  KB principles: Epistemic Agency, Real Ideas, and Community Knowledge, aligned with teachers’ design activities.  Agentic synthesis (Marshall & Horn, 2025) explains the knowledge reservoirs teachers draw from, running parallel to and intersecting with KB. It describes how teachers actively integrate, interpret, and transform resources rather than simply adopting them. In minicourse design, teachers recontextualize accessible information into usable knowledge for learners, with recontextualization manifesting agency and sense-making that intersect with KB’s epistemic agency.  KB and agentic synthesis thus represent two sides of teacher professional development: KB emphasizes epistemic agency in knowledge creation; Agentic Synthesis emphasizes agency in resource transformation and contextualization.

## Method

This qualitative case study (Yin, 2014) focused on two teachers (Sarah and Scarlet)  who designed mini-courses as part of their course work in an online graduate education program. Each mini-courses includes 3-5 learning units to address an authentic knowledge need among teachers, moving from pedagogical principles (know-what, know-why) to practice (know-how in classroom context).

The data included the two teachers’ mini-courses, portfolios that documented their design process, postproject reflections, and peers’ comments on their design ideas and drafts  (Cresswell & Guetterman, 2019). Although inductive coding was initially planned,  however, the researcher’s background prompted deductive 3045 coding using KB principles and agentic synthesis (Saladana, 2021). Accordingly, the researcher deductively coded each unit in the mini-courses as the unit of analysis and coded the paragraphs of the reflections and peer feedback as the unit of analysis  (Miles et al., 2020). Coded excerpts  where then analyzed  and lead to the study themes,

figure 1. Codes traced how teachers referenced knowledge sources, adapted ideas, and expressed agency through

design decisions, reflections, and peer interactions. Analysis examined knowledge reorganization across artifacts and interactions, making visible how learning emerged through iterative design and recontextualization of personal and community knowledge.

The findings reveal five interconnected themes in Figure 1, depicting teacher learning as an iterative, agentic process of recontextualization rather than rote uptake of prescribed ideas. Teachers synthesize personal knowledge, organized professional reper toires, peer feedback, and situated problems of practice to redesign learning, transforming these elements into shareable mini-courses that reflect contextual goals and epistemic agency.

Figure 1

## Thematic Findings Diagram

Through designing mini-courses on the KNILT p latform, teachers demonstrated  the dual process of epistemic agency  for KB and r econtextualization of k nowledge as they anchored designs in contextually situated goals, organized knowledge around recognizable problems of practice (RQ1), synthesized personal and professional knowledge, and iteratively recontextualized ideas through reflection and peer feedback  (RQ2). This design work extended professional development by showing how teachers actively constructed learning as authors of PD resources rather than passive consumers  (RQ3). Contributing agentic synthesis and KB  as interconnected frameworks for understanding teacher learning through iterative knowledge construction and recontextualization across contexts.

As limitations, this study only analyzed a small sample of the KNILT minicourses. In the next phase, we will further expand the analysis and produce deeper analysis of teachers’ professional design and knowledge-building efforts that lead to the minicourse creation.

SAGE 3047 Interdisciplinary Concepts and Language: Energy in Physics and Chemistry Kevin Lenton, Vanier College, lentonk@vaniercollege.qc.ca Sean Hughes, John Abbott College, sean.hughes@johnabbott.qc.ca Michael Dugdale, John Abbott College, michael.dugdale@johnabbott.qc.ca Elizabeth Charles, Dawson College, echarles@dawsoncollege.qc.ca Abstract: This poster presents design-based research by a practitioner-led team examining a simulation-based intervention in a college science course. The intervention supported small group cognitive reconciliation and conceptual integration. Discourse analysis showed students navigating negative potential energy (NPE) across physics and chemistry, demonstrating a sensemaking trajectory marked by shifts in terminology. However, students’ language misuse indicated reliance on intuitive reasoning, influenced by simulation scaffolding that made a noncanonical interpretation particularly salient.

Interdisciplinary instruction integrates knowledge from two or more fields  (Klein, 1998; You, 2017) and is increasingly central to curriculum reform  (Markauskaite et al., 2024). In Quebec,  two-year college s cience programs now reflect this objective through the competencies of an integrative course, yet the broader program structures remain siloed and discipline bound. Associated challenges include designing instruction to overcome the difficulties students face in understanding cross-cutting concepts  –– e.g., concepts of force, energy and equilibrium, (Nagel & Lindsey, 2015; Haskell et al., 2022). This poster reports on a practitioner-led intervention where cross-disciplinarity was examined in the context of a physics-chemistry instructional unit. Cognitive reconciliation and conceptual integration involve bidirectional reasoning across  disciplinary boundaries (Gouvea et al., 2013). The goal is not  replacement, but the development of a coherent understanding of each discipline’s epistemic framing of a concept and how it is represented in other disciplines (Holley, 2009). Instructional solutions promoting these forms of reasoning often use analogies (Borda et al., 2022) and other comparative methods to help students refine and integrate disciplinary ideas into a coherent conceptual framework (Dreyfus et al., 2014a). Science education  has explored paired tasks linking atomic interactions to analogous scenarios – e.g., a skateboarder descending a hill  –– to help students transfer their understanding of potential energy (PE) to other contexts (Borda et al., 2022; Dreyfus et al., 2014 b). Results show that students struggle to transfer the idea of PE in gravitational fields directly to chemical bonds (Lindsey, 2014). Reconciling energy concepts across physics and chemistry, particularly negative potential energy (NPE), remains challenging (Dreyfus et al., 2014a, 2015; Nagel & Lindsey, 2015).  This study investigates how a designed intervention supported the development of students’ ability to engage in conceptual integration of PE concepts across the two disciplines and what this tells us about the cognitive reconciliation process. This design-based research (DBR; Anderson & Shattuck, 2012) is led by practitioners working within a ResearchPractice Partnership (RPP)  team, working at the college-level, in Quebec, Canada. The intervention was implemented as part of a Chemistry course (students having taken a pre-requisite high school physics course) with students working in groups of four or less. Data collected included audio recordings of the six groups  and the written worksheets. This analysis selected Group 2 (pseudonyms: Matthew, James, Sally, and Adam), based on their level of sense-making, confirmed by the observer’s fieldnotes. All participants provided formal consent. The 80-minute intervention utilized paired PhET simulations  (PhET Interactive Simulations, n.d.). The chemistry simulation modeled atomic interactions using a Lennard-Jones potential energy surface as a function of internuclear distance. To provide an analogical anchor, the physics simulation  featured a visually  similar Ushaped track where potential energy was represented as vertical height. This pairing allowed students to map macroscale "height" onto the microscale "energy well" to visualize PE.  The intervention was therefore designed to help address differences in disciplinary interpretations of chemical bonding. Chemists often describe chemical bonds as a result of attractive and repulsive forces (strength) between interacting atoms, and express bond energy as positive quantities reflecting the energy required to break these associations (Flowers et al., 2019). In contrast, 3048 physicists may describe chemical bond formation as a lowering of potential energy (stability), and by convention express this energy as a negative value (Ling et al. 2016). For learners, understanding that these interpretations describe exactly the same phenomenon can be conceptually challenging. Thus, we looked for the use of these terms in analyzing student artifacts and in group discussion transcripts. Similar to other research, we observed that students rel ied on familiar physics concepts, which operated at the macroscale, to interpret microscale chemical representations (Dreyfus et al., 2014 b; Borda et al., 2022). W hen grappling with the meaning of bond energy, the group used physics terminology, prompted from the intervention, to explain NPE in the chemical bonding context – Matthew: The atom has used more energy than needed to reach the equilibrium point and the height of epsilon”. By using the word height, the students applied  physics jargon normally associated with gravitational PE (mgh) to appropriately explain the energy required to break the chemical bond in the chemical context.  They were also capable of resolving sign conventions related to energy, as highlighted in Matthew’s statement: “since we’re going below the reference height, that’s why we’re going into the negative”. Meanwhile, Sally displayed bidirectional reasoning, linking the chemistry to the physics simulation: “... pretty much like the Y axis of both is just potential energy”. After exploring the minimum PE p osition in the  chemistry simulation  (the intervention), the group attempted to explain the ‘depth’ of the PE graph and its relationship to chemical bonding. Earlier in the discussion, James referenced bond strength but after some reflection, self-corrected by drawing upon the physics concept: “Yeah, just stability. It’s not strength ”. Both Adam and Sally agree d, with the latter  elaborating further: “Yeah, I'm pretty sure like the less potential energy the more  stable it is. If I’m not making it up i t is about stability not strength”. Working through the activity prompted the  group to disentangle these concepts, a conceptual conflation recognized by Zohar and Levy (2019). Interestingly, this discussion arose spontaneously; it was not prompted by the designed activity.

Despite having resolved strength and stability, Matthew later conflated force and energy to explain why atoms separate if too close: “The initial repulsion energy between the two atoms is greater than the overall attraction energy.”  This misuse of energy and force language  revealed that students were relying on intuitive reasoning, mirroring findings of prior studies  (Nagel et al., 2015). The focus on repulsion appears linked to the simulation scaffolding, which made the repulsive response particularly salient. processes involving analogical reasoning and collaborative discourse exchanges. Recognizing the similarities and differences between the two contexts, the limits of the analogical comparison  showed that ‘height’ could not be used literally when applied to the chemistry context. Instead, the mgh framework is needed to establish a relative energy conception based on reference height – a similar feature to other studies (e.g., Nagel & Lindsey, 201 5). Furthermore, students made connections clarifying the role of NPE in both contexts, most notably its role in explaining the nature of a chemical bond – also seen in Dreyfus et al. (2014). Notably, the intervention initiates a willingness among group members to experiment with the language of both disciplines to construct a common understanding of NPE across both contexts  (physics and chemistry). Statements such as ‘repulsion energy’ are canonically incorrect, yet they may demonstrate an effort by the students to achieve a measure of conceptual integration  using language from both disciplines, which future work can inform. Recognizing the limitations of study,  specifically our small sample, future exploration will also include more data and a reiteration of the implementation.

Working within the practitioner-led RPP highlighted the value of a collaborative model in which practitioners engage with research tools and methodologies while  maintaining the contextual authenticity of classroom practice. Discussions among the authors were instrumental in revealing epistemic differences between fields and fostering a meta-level of reflection. Through this process, practitioners became increasingly attuned to disciplinary distinctions, enabling the team to interpret student challenges with  greater nuance. This enhanced understanding of interdisciplinary boundaries directly informs instructional practice, with practitioners noting that the formative insights gained through this reflective RPP engagement is shaping their current teaching. 3049 Anderson, T., & Shattuck, J. 3050 Comparing Layered and Non-Layered LLM-Generated Feedback: Effects on Learning Gains and Learner Perceptions Jie Cao, The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, jiecao@unc.edu Chloe Qianhui Zhao, Carnegie Mellon University, cqzhao@cmu.edu Jionghao Lin, The University of Hong Kong, jionghao@hku.hk Kenneth R. Koedinger, Carnegie Mellon University, koedinger@cmu.edu Abstract: This study investigated how layered versus non-layered large language model – generated feedback influences learning gains across task types and learner perceptions  through an experimental design. Results indicated that non-layered feedback produced greater learning gains on multiple-choice questions, while no significant difference for open-ended tasks. However, learners receiving layered feedback reported a stronger sense of connection with the feedback provider, although perceived acceptance did not differ. Feedback has been regarded as a cornerstone of learning, as it supports knowledge construction, sustains motivation, and fosters self-regulated learning (Hattie & Timperley, 2007). However, the impact of feedback is not uniform; its effectiveness is shaped by contextual features and the content and structure of the feedback (Vander et al., 2015; Wisniewski et al., 2020).  Some studies underscore that elaborated feedback that offers not only the correct answer but also interpretive explanations and strategic advice helps learning (Butler et al., 2013; Swart et al., 2019; Vander et al., 2015; Wisniewski et al., 2020). Yet, immediate provision of correct answers may inadvertently discourage cognitive effort, as learners might focus on reproducing the solution rather than actively engaging with the task (Kulhavy, 1977). Emerging perspectives from learner-centered feedback theory argue that feedback should move beyond the transmission of information to actively foster  emotional engagement  and learner agency (Ryan et al., 2021) and put the emphasis on prompting students’ independence to find the correct answer rather thandelivering it directly. Guided by these insights, the present study introduces a dynamic layered feedback framework that integrates the strengths of learner-centered and elaborated feedback. In this design, the first layer provides encouragement, autonomy, and actionable suggestions, without disclosing the correct answer. If learners continue to struggle, a second layer then supplies elaborated feedback that includes the explicit solution, explanation, and improvement tips. Moreover, delivering such dynamic feedback at scale poses challenges for human educators. The recent advancement of large language models (LLMs) offers new opportunities to generate adaptive, personalized feedback that mimics human-like support. While stud ies have begun to explore LLM-generated feedback (e.g., Cao et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025), little is known about how layered versus non-layered LLM feedback (only elaborated feedback) affects learning across different task types, or how learners perceive these feedback designs in terms of emotional connection and acceptance.  Therefore, we propose two research questions: RQ1. How do layered and non-layered feedback influence students’ learning gain across different task types? RQ2. How do students perceive layered and non-layered feedback in terms of connection and acceptance?

## Participants

Participants were 215 U.S. university students (109 female; Mage = 32) who were randomly assigned to either the layered feedback condition (n = 105) or the non-layered feedback condition (n = 110). This study received approval from the Carnegie  Mellon University Institutional Review Board. Complete pre-and post-test, and process data were collected from all participants, and 199 valid survey responses were obtained. Measurement Perceived acceptance We adapted two items from Strijbos et al. (2010)  to assess learners’ willingness to accept feedback, using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree; Cronbach’s α =.86). Perceived connection Based on Ryan et al. (2021), we developed three items to assess learners’ perceived emotional connection with the feedback source. Responses were rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = disagree to 5 = agree), and the scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach’s α =.80). Learning gain Learning gain was calculated by subtracting the pre-test scores from the post-test scores. Pre-and post-tests contained 16 items (20 points total), including 14 multiple-choice and 2 open-ended questions. 3051 The open-ended responses were scored using an LLM-as-a-judge approach (GPT-5), which showed high agreement with human ratings (𝑟𝑟 =.86 and.94 for 10% responses).

## Research procedure

Participants were randomly assigned to a group. After completing a 10-minute pre-test, participants engaged in independent learning-by-doing activities consisting of eight multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and five openended questions. During these activities, the experimental group received layered feedback, while the control group received non-layered feedback. All feedback is generated by GPT-5. This phase lasted approximately 20– 40 minutes, depending on individual progress.  The learning materials are about the Multimedia Principle, which constitutes a chapter of a graduate-level course. Afterward, learners completed an identical post-test and a self-report questionnaire on their learning experience and demographic information. As shown in Figure 1, independent-samples t-test show that a significant difference was found for the MCQs performance, t(213) = 2.21, p =.028, d = 0.30, indicating that students who received non-layered feedback (M = 1.17, SD = 1.93) achieved higher gains than those who received layered feedback (M = 0.56, SD = 2.12). In contrast, no significant difference was observed for open-ended que stions, t(213) = 1.27, p =.205 >.5. For learners’ perceptions, independent-sample t-tests showed that participants in the layered feedback condition reported significantly higher perceived connection with the feedback system (M = 3.43) than those in the non-layered feedback condition (M = 2.87), t(182.9) = –3.93, p <.001, d = 0.56. In contrast, no significant difference was found in perceived acceptance, t(195.7) = –1.03, p =.306. Figure 1 Comparison of Layered and Non-layered Feedback on Learning Gains across Task Types A significant difference emerged in MCQs: students receiving non-layered feedback showed greater learning gains than those receiving layered feedback. This suggests that for structured MCQs, feedback that provides correct answers and explanations immediately may better support rapid error correction and knowledge consolidation. One possible explanation is that MCQs mainly assess recall and comprehension and provide limited opportunities for open reasoning; thus, delaying the correct answer may simply postpone confirmation rather than promote deeper cognitive processing (Haataja et al., 2023). For open-ended tasks requiring reasoning and reflection, layered feedback did not reduce performance, suggesting that delayed correctness may still support cognitive engagement in more generative learning contexts. However, layered feedback also did not outperform non-layered feedback, possibly because the additional guidance increased learners’ cognitive load and required more effort and revision time  (Taxipulati et al., 2021). Despite lower MCQ performance, students receiving layered feedback reported a significantly stronger perceived connection with the feedback provider. The layered format (beginning with encouragement and actionable guidance) may have made the system appear more attentive and supportive. However, perceived acceptance did not differ significantly between conditions, suggesting that while layering enhances emotional connection, it may not influence perceptions of feedback usefulness.  Future research should examine the long-term effects of layered feedback across different subjects, given the short-term nature of the current study. Analyzing learners’ interaction logs and submission data could also clarify how feedback informs subsequent revisions.
