Springer Nature Switzerland. 3053 Futures Thinking as a Pedagogical Tool: Designing Futures Thinking Professional Learning for Middle School Teachers Ruth Wylie, Nicole Oster, Bregje van Geffen ruth.wylie@asu.edu, nicole.oster@asu.edu, bvangeff@asu.edu Mary Lou Fulton College for Teaching and Learning Innovation, Arizona State University Abstract: Young people today face profound social, technological, and environmental uncertainty, yet few classroom experiences explicitly help them  to imagine and shape visions of the future. This study describes a professional learning workshop that i ntroduced seventhgrade history teachers (n=11) to a futures thinking game. Post-workshop survey results showed significant gains in familiarity with futures thinking and strong agreement on its relevance for students. Qualitative responses highlighted potential for the game to foster student agency, imagination, and hope. These findings suggest that professional learning is a powerful pathway for bringing futures thinking into schools and preparing youth to navigate uncertainty with resilience and purpose.

Young people today are growing up amid rapid social, technological, and environmental uncertainty. To navigate challenges like climate change and the rise of artificial intelligence, students need more thandisciplinary knowledge; they need the ability to imagine new possibilities, think critically, collaborate across differences, and adapt to shifting circumstances (Trilling & Fadel, 2009). These capacities are embedded in what is often referred to as  futures thinking: a mindset and  a set of practices for anticipating change, envisioning alternatives, and preparing for desired outcomes.

Teachers can play a central role in bringing futures thinking into classrooms. Yet few professional learning opportunities exist to help educators understand what futures thinking entails, how it aligns with curriculum standards, and how it can be enacted in developmentally appropriate ways. In this paper, we describe a professional learning workshop that introduced seventh-grade history teachers to futures thinking. We ask: How do teachers perceive the value and feasibility of introducing futures thinking into middle school classrooms and what challenges and opportunities do they identify? We answer these questions with data from a post-workshop survey and reflecting on the implications for designing professional learning to foster futures thinking capacities in middle school students.

## Literature review

Futures thinking comprises systematic methods for exploring alternative futures (Slaughter, 1996; Jones et al., 2012). The field operates on the principle that futures are plural rather than singular (Bengston, 2018; Camrass, 2020; Jones et al., 2012), and it focuses on detecting, analyzing, and evaluating possible, plausible, probable, and preferable futures (Slaughter, 1996; Camrass, 2020; Jones et al., 2012). Possible futures represent the broadest category of alternative; p lausible futures form a smaller subset, constrained by consistency with “ current understanding of science, technology, and social and economic systems”; and probable futures denote reasonably likely outcomes, typically reflecting “business-as-usual” trend continuations  and often termed the baseline or “official” future (Bengston, 2018; Dreborg, 1996). In contrast, preferable futures are subjective, value-driven constructs reflecting what individuals or communities desire (Bengston, 2018; Jones et al., 2012). Futures thinking assumes the future is open rather than predetermined, allowing for deliberate action to influence outcomes in myriad complex and emergent ways (Bengston, 2018; Slaughter, 1996). This openness necessitates clarifying goals, evaluating value s, and selecting policy alternatives (Lasswell, 1967, as cited in Slaughter, 1996). The approach recognizes that prevailing “images of the future” shape present action, motivating people to pursue actions that promote desired futures or to take steps that prevent undesired ones (Polak, 1973, as cited in Bodinet, 2018; Bell & Mau, 1971, as cited in Slaughter, 1996). Futures thinking in education Integrating futures thinking into curricula has gained recognition as essential preparation for an era marked by escalating uncertainty and rapid change (Jones et al., 2012; Bishop, 2018). While futures studies have traditionally been offered at the graduate school level, efforts are expanding to incorporate these concepts into education for younger students (Bishop, 2018; Bodinet, 2018). While it is f requently implemented through socio-scientific issues in science curricula, futures thinking extends learning beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries (Jones et 3054 al., 2012). The interdisciplinary structure of futures studies counters conventional subject segregation in mainstream education (Bodinet, 2018). Primary objectives include increasing student engagement, developing analytical and critical thinking skills, and strengthening values discourse by enabling students to articulate and justify positions about a variety of possible, probable, and preferable futures (Jones et al., 2012). Despite these evident benefits, futures thinking remains underutilized in classrooms, with limited professional learning opportunities for educators. However, successful implementations from middle school through higher education demonstrate the capacity of futures thinking interventions to develop skills in systems thinking and critical analysis and transform students from passive observers to active agents in shaping futures (Jones et al., 2012; Bodinet, 2018; Bishop, 2018; Miller et al., 2018). A group of seventh-grade history teachers (n=11) began the workshop by engaging in Futures by Chance | Futures by Choice (FbC | FbC), a futures thinking game developed by the research team  (Wylie, et al., 2023). In FbC | FbC, groups of 4–6 participants collaboratively build a 50-year timeline (from 2025 through 2075) through four rounds of facilitated play. After a short warm-up, teams start with Futures by Chance, where they roll a die to determine whether a positive or negative future event from one of five different sectors (e.g., education, climate, sports) is placed on their timeline and then collaboratively decide where to place the event. In Futures by Choice, participants select from a set of events that have a more neutral  or debatable  valence (e.g., “new human-dog technology allows humans to understand their pets ”) and later generate their own plausible events to place. By the end of the activity, timeline s contain between 12 and 20 events that, taken together, provide scaffolding for telling a possible story of the future. The final round invites teams to reflect on their timeline with prompts such as, “Would you want to live in this future? ” and “What steps today could shape this outcome? ” When multiple groups play, timelines can be shared in a gallery walk to spark dialogue about common themes and values. Following FbC | FbC gameplay, we gave a short lecture on the relevance of futures thinking in middle school classrooms, followed by structured work sessions during which teachers planned how to incorporate futures thinking, and specifically the FbC | FbC game, into their curriculum. Teachers were invited to participate in an optional research study associated with the workshop. Data collection included a survey administered at the end of the  workshop that gathered demographic information, initial perceptions of futures thinking, and perceptions of their own self-efficacy in teaching futures thinking lessons. Participation in the research was voluntary and had no effect on teachers ’ access to workshop resources. Overall, the workshop was viewed as a success. Participants reported significant increases in their perceived familiarity with futures thinking (p < 0.001). Participants also strongly agreed that futures thinking is relevant to middle school students (M = 4.6, SD = 0.67) (1=Strongly Disagree; 5 = Strongly Agree). In addition, they expressed confidence in their ability to facilitate classroom conversations about the future (M = 4.6, SD = 0.5). Open-ended responses provided further insight into how participants interpreted the value of futures thinking in education. When asked what excited them about introducing futures thinking to their students, teachers highlighted the opportunity to help students think about long-term consequences, connect current events to future possibilities, and build a sense of futures agency. Participants viewed the workshop as a meaningful and practical professional learning experience. The combination of increased familiarity, confidence, and thoughtful reflection on implementation suggests that futures thinking can be a promising and accessible framework for middle school educators.

The results of this study demonstrate that introducing educators to futures  thinking can effectively build both understanding and enthusiasm for integrating these ideas into middle school classrooms. Middle school represents a pivotal developmental period for cultivating futures thinking. Early adolescence is when students begin forming future-oriented identities and grappling with questions about their personal and societal roles (McAdams & Zapata-Gietl, 2015). Embedding futures thinking at this stage can nurture essential capacities (e.g., anticipation, reflection, collaboration) that help students navigate uncertainty with agency rather than anxiety. However, integrating these practices into classroo ms requires that educators who are conversant with futures thinking concepts and confident in facilitating open-ended, imaginative, and sometimes value-laden discussions about the future. The current study suggests that professional learning experiences are an important first step in bridging conceptual understanding and classroom implementation.

3056 Partnering Across Voices: Stories of Language, Identity, and Learning Eugenia Balseiro, UTEC, eugenia.balseiro@utec.edu.uy Abstract: This pedagogical design explores how students reflect on language, identity, and learning through narrative writing in a multilingual border context. Implemented in the  border region between Uruguay and Brazil, where Spanish, Portuguese, and the historica lly marginalized Portuñol coexist, the project integrates literary texts, personal storytelling, and intercultural dialogue within an English as a Foreign Language course (EFL). Grounded in a critical intercultural perspective, the intervention sought to understand the relationship between language, identity, and belonging in a historically contested linguistic zone through students’ own narratives and aimed at fostering critical reflection on linguistic ideologies, power relations, and local identity. Over all, the project illustrates how EFL classrooms can become spaces for validation, dialogue, and transformation through locally grounded pedagogical designs.

This learning experience explores how students reflect on language, identity and learning through narrative writing in a multilingual border context. It exemplifies partnering with purpose by intentionally connecting students with their own stories, which reflect the stories of their multilingual community and the challenges it has posed for all language communities that have historically inhabited the area. The project connected students with educators and academics of nearby university institutions across  the two sides of the border, and empowered students to share their own personal stories about language and identity in a cultural event organised by one of them. Overall, the present design  speaks of how an EFL course can be refocused to reflect local realities and integrate students’ lived experiences,  transforming the act of learning English into an exploration of belonging, language hierarchies, and identity on the border.

## Research context

The study takes place in twoneighbouring cities on the Uruguay–Brazil border, an area known for being bilingual and diglossic where Spanish (in Uruguay) and Portuguese (in Brazil) coexist with a local contact variety, Portuñol, originally arising from the  interaction of these two languages. Despite being known as the “Frontera de la Paz,” the region has not always been free of conflict. In the nineteenth century, Uruguay sought to consolidate a national identity through an educational reform that expanded primary education across the country which established Spanish as the only medium of instruction and promoted schooling in border areas to reinforce national presence (Barrios et al., 1993; Oroño, 2016, 2021). This policy did not anticipate that contact between Spanish and the Luso-speaking communities that were inhabiting the northern part of the country would lead to the emergence of a Portuguese-based regional dialect, now widely known as Portuñol. For many years, national discourses promoted linguistic intolerance toward both the regional variety and Portuguese, in an effort to construct Uruguay as a monolingual nation (Barrios, 2018). Only at the end of the twentieth century, due to shared economic and political interests with Brazil, did Portuguese begin to be promoted in education, a shift that was reinforced in the General Education Law (Ley No.18437 de 2008, Barrios, 2011), and lan guage policy documents (Administración Nacional de Educación Públ ica [ANEP], 2006). These documents recognised the state of the local variety as mother tongue but still state educational institutions should not promote it or use it as means of instructions, thus reinforcing old linguistic tensions. The present paper seeks to bridge the gap between the official, written recognition of the regional dialect and actual educational practice by presenting a pedagogical design integrated into an EFL course. The  design aims to revitalise students' narrative s of language and identity in the borderland context encouraging them to create and write experience-based stories of their own.

## Pedagogical design

This pedagogical design was implemented in 2024, in an EFL university course at Universidad Tecnológica, a state University in Uruguay. It was condensed in a module called “Tell me a story about studying, languages and identity”, which invited students to read and explore experiences from border writers  about the way language, identity, and informal and formal education shaped the way their social identities were constructed through 3057 language experiences. The module was framed into the “Basic Skills for Reading and Writing course”, a 4 credit blended course designed for A1/A2 level students, which aimed at fostering basic literacy skills that would help students perform as a more competent reader and writer in English, at an elementary level. The module was grounded in an intercultural critical perspective (Walsh, 2010; Tubino, 2005) and it aimed to create a space where students could reflect on how their educational and linguistic trajectories intersect with broader linguistic ideologies, power relations and long ago originated historical and political scenarios. Drawing on Walsh (2005) pedagogical criteria to integrate a critical intercultural perspective in class, the module was designed with these three intercultural pillars in mind:  a) fostering self-esteem and recognition of students’ own border culture and lived experience; b) valuing local knowledge, practices, and ways of knowing, mainly through the recognition and validation of their linguistic repertoire; and c) addressing issues of c ultural conflict and negative intercultural relations through tracing back the history of how those linguistic ideologies have permeated our way of being. Along these lines, it also enabled translanguaging practices both in class interactions and in their written productions, as suggested by García (2013), in an attempt to contest monoglossic ideologies both as border inhabitants and EFL learners.

Class sequence The design asked how language learning can become a space for students to reflect on their experiences as multilingual border subjects, validating their voices as knowledge. It unfolded in four stages. ● Reading and reflection: Students engaged with texts on border identity: “Trinticuato”, a poem from Favian Severo, written in Portuñol, and excerpts from “Borderlands/La Frontera” by Gloria Anzaldúa. Through discussion, they explored how language shapes identity, power, and belonging, and how schools and families may reinforce hegemonic ideologies that marginalize local varieties. ● Planning and drafting: Students reflected on the “voices” the main characters heard about multilingualism in the previous texts, and worked on the voices that will be present in their own narratives. Using a model text, they wrote drafts under the prompt “Tell Me a Story about Studying, Languages, and Identity,” for which  they had the option of using their full linguistic repertoire-Spanish, Portuguese, English, and Portuñol ● Making sense of the past to interpret the present:  Through discussions and a guest researcher’s visit from UDELAR, a neighbouring state University, students connected their experiences to the sociolinguistic history of the border, reflecting on the structural roots of the stigma and how local language policies have shaped discourses.

● Narrative production and community sharing: Students revised their stories with peer feedback and a writing assistant software tool to check for grammar, spelling, and punctuation suggestions.   The narratives were compiled into an e-book and shared by students at a community event organised by UNIPAMPA, a neighbouring Brazilian university which aimed at revitalising Portuñol as a cultural heritage. This partnership connected the classroom with the local community, transforming students’ personal stories into collective acts of recognition and cultural exchange. Future steps Framed within a design-based research approach (Bakker, 2019; Barab, 2014), the next steps of this intervention involve iteratively refining and expanding the pedagogical intervention. First, data collection will be deepened by analysing students’ narratives to explore how they construct relationships between language and identity in the Uruguay-Brazil border. For that purpose, 3 research questions have been delineated: ● What linguistic and cultural voices emerge in students’ narratives, and how do these voices interact or conflict?

● How do students represent the local linguistic variety Portuñol in their stories, and what meanings or values do they assign to it?

● In what ways do students’ narratives challenge or reproduce dominant ideologies about “legitimate” language use?

It is also expected that the study can generate transferable design principles that inform language education in similar border contexts.

## Acknowledgments

I would like to thank all my graduate and undergraduate border students who have shared and taught me the pains and gains of growing in a multilingual, multicultural though highly challenging  linguistic setting. 3059 Partnering with Purpose: A Research–Practice–Developer Model for Evidence-Driven Innovation Anastasia Betts, Learnology Labs, anastasia@learnologylabs.org Benjamin Ryon, Learnology, ben@learnology.ai Elida V. Laski, Boston College, elida.laski@bc.edu Sunil Gunderia, Mindset Copilot, sunil@mindsetcopilot.com Diana Hughes, Relay Graduate School, diana@dianahughes.tech Abstract: This paper argues that genuine partnership among researchers, educators, and developers is essential for educational technology to produce meaningful learning outcomes. Drawing on the design and implementation of PAL (Personal Assistant for Learning), a research–practice–developer collaboration in early mathematics, the paper illustrates how learning-science frameworks can guide product design, generate actionable evidence, and center equity from inception. Results from two implementations  (a randomized pilot and a subsequent multi-site dose-response study), demonstrate effect sizes that markedly exceed meta-analytic norms for technology-enhanced instruction, underscoring that when innovation is grounded in learning science and authentic partnerships, it becomes an amplifier of human teaching and learning rather than a replacement for it. Despite decades of promise, educational technology (EdTech) has yet to deliver consistent evidence of improved learning. Recent m eta-analyses of more than seventy controlled studies show only modest gains in student achievement from technology-supported instruction (Cheung & Slavin, 2013; Ran, Kim, & Secada, 2021). Yet, product narratives continue to emphasize engagement statistics,  platform features, and dashboards rather thandemonstrable growth in learners’ understanding (Reich & Ito, 2017; Slavin, 2019). The result is a paradoxical landscape in which technological sophistication expands even as learning outcomes  lag. This mismatch stems in large part from a systemic disconnect between EdTech development and the learning sciences (Hirsh-Pasek et al., 2015). When tools are engineered without a theory of change, they risk optimizing for engagement or the perception of competence rather than true, durable learning. Such misalignment wastes resources and exacerbates inequities: students in the greatest need of effective learning support are too often served by products with weak (or non-existent) evidence bases. In response, this paper presents PAL (Personal Assistant for Learning), an earlymath learning ecosystem co-created by researchers, practitioners, and developers, as a proof-of-concept for how partnering with purpose can turn learning science into measurable impact in EdTech product design. Evidence as the currency of partnership Research–Practice Partnerships (RPPs) and Design-Based Implementation Research (DBIR) offer tested models for how to align innovation with learning science (Coburn et al., 2013; Coburn et al., 2016; Fishman et al, 2013). Durable improvement is more likely to emerge when researchers and practitioners co-design solutions, investigate them in context, and iterate based on evidence rather than intuition (e.g., Greenhalgh et al., 2016). In a productive RPP ecosystem, evidence becomes the shared language and acco untability structure (Coburn et al., 2013): researchers contribute methodological rigor and theoretical framing; educators ensure contextual relevance and feasibility; technologists translate hypotheses into design features and data systems capable of capturing real-time learning signals. When these roles are siloed, data are reduced to compliance metrics and research lags behind practice. When they converge, every design decision becomes an opportunity for inquiry. Design partnerships for learning: Lessons from PAL PAL is a personalized, adaptive learning tool grounded in the learning sciences. Developed by Betts and colleagues (2026) in collaboration with academic research and implementation partners, PAL operates within an ecosystem model that builds synergy among the key learning environments  of a child’s life: school, home, and community. The system connects teachers, families, and researchers in a shared evidence loop, strengthening communication and aligning instructional focus across settings. Educators and families actively participate in codesign cycles, helping shape content, accessibility, and user experience so that PAL remains developmentally appropriate, equitable, and responsive to authentic daily contexts. 3060 PAL’s framework draws on Vygotsky’s (1978) Zones of Development, PAL positions adults as more knowledgeable others  who challenge and mediate children’s sense-making in the real world. PAL’s adaptive “smart” system identifies and recommends activities that stretch learners just beyond current mastery while keeping cognitive load manageable, ensuring that engagement serves a developmental function by signaling challenge in the service of learning.

PAL’s design process treats every cycle as an opportunity to solve problems of learnin g. Each iteration begins with a central question: How can we know what each child understands now, what they are ready to learn next, and how adults can best support that learning? To answer these questions, PAL uses a sophisticated knowledge model built using Knowledge Space Theory (Doignon & Falmagne, 1999)  to infer each child’s evolving knowledge state and recommend the next optimal step. Teachers receive clear, evidence-based guidance for instruction, while parents are offered simple, timely invitations to engage in meaningful math interactions, helping families make the most of everyday learning moments. Each parent prompt is accompanied by a brief “learning science tip” that explains why the activity matters, strengthening adults’ understanding of how children learn and building confidence as co-educators.

The early results of this partnership speak for themselves. PAL's spring 2025 exploratory pilot used the TEMA-3 across two VPK classrooms (N = 19; treatment n = 12, control n = 7) over 3.5 months. Children in the PAL condition showed substantially greater gains than controls (Cohen's d > 1.0), with 100% improving pre-topost versus 57% in the control group. Parent engagement was positively correlated with children's gains (Spearman's r =.62, p <.01). A subsequent six-month implementation at a second site (N = 33, spanning three grade levels) corroborated this pattern: nudge dosage predicted TEMA-3 growth after controlling for baseline (r =.609, p <.001; d = 1.52 between high-and low-dose nudge conditions). Both sets of results markedly exceed the effect sizes typically reported in meta-analyses of technology-enhanced instruction, which range between 0.15 and 0.30 (Cheung & Slavin, 2013; Ran, Kim, & Secada, 2021), underscoring that learning-science-grounded design, coupled with authentic RPPs, has the potential to yield powerful results. From research to design principles PAL's design and implementation work has yielded three guiding principles, each refined through iterative collaboration among learning scientists, engineers, educators, and families. First,  evidence before aesthetics: every design decision begins with a hypothesis about learning, tested through implementation and data. Second, scaffold for meaningful interaction: PAL's algorithms recommend activities aligned to finely grained knowledge units within its learning model, engaging adults and children in hands-on exploration that elicits mathematical thinking and observable evidence of understanding. Third, equity through accessibility: PAL's lowbandwidth, multilingual design ensures that families often excluded from early-math supports are among the first to benefit, making inclusivity a design constraint rather than an afterthought. Together, these principles demonstrate what happens when research, practice, and technology share a single goal — measurable, equitable learning. Innovation becomes an amplifier of human teaching and learning, not a replacement for it. “Partnering with Purpose” demands that we reclaim learning  as the central object of innovation, rather than technology alone. The field of  EdTech is replete with technical brilliance and pedagogical amnesia; tools have become more intelligent, yet the learning they enable too often remains shallow, unmeasured, or inequitable. PAL demonstrates that this pattern is not inevitable. When researchers, practitioners, and technologists co-design around shared theories of learning and continuous evidence generation, the results are both rigorous and humane: measurable gains for children, empowered educators, and families newly confident as co-teachers. In the coming era of AI-mediated education, the most powerful differentiator will not be algorithms but understanding and the disciplined application of learning science as a design framework and an ethical compass. Purposeful partnerships make that understanding actionable. They remind us that the ultimate benchmark of innovation is not engagement or efficiency, but the growth of human potential. 3062 Playing with Intelligence: Evolving Epistemic Criteria in a Turing Test–Like Game Zhongyu Wang, Florida State University, zw23@fsu.edu Xiang Li, Lingfei Cao, Zhichun Liu xianglix@connect.hku.hk, lingfei.cao@connect.hku.hk, lukasliu@hku.hk The University of Hong Kong Abstract: This study investigates how learners developed epistemic understanding of artificial intelligence through participation in a multiplayer Turing test-like game. Informed by the framework of epistemic cognition, we analyzed how 32 middle school students’ game strategies and epistemic criteria evolved across four gameplay sessions. Findings show that students’ epistemic criteria for identifying AI shifted from focusing on surface linguistic cues to socially and contextually grounded judgments. The study illustrates how game-based environments can foster the development of epistemic cognition through reflective reasoning. As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly capable of mimicking human generations, figuring out the ambiguity involved in students’ conceptualization of AI has become a necessary part of AI literacy (Long & Magerko, 2020). While most educational efforts focus on technical skills or conceptual knowledge, such as understanding algorithms, data processing, or ethical implications (Li et al., 2023; Ng et al., 2021; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019), students’ deeper epistemic understanding, that is, what AI means to them, was often overlooked in existing efforts.

Existing research has shown that game-based environments are promising for engaging students with epistemic understanding in authentic, problem-solving contexts (Barzilai, 2017). In this study, we designed a multiplayer Turing test-like game, Occultation, with the aim of promoting students’ epistemic understanding (Chinn et al., 2011) about AI through investigating the boundaries between human and AI. In addition, this study is grounded in the framework of epistemic cognition, which examines how individuals think about knowledge, knowing, and justification (Chinn et al., 2011). In this context, students’ observable game strategies to distinguish human and AI function as reliable processes that reveal their underlying epistemic criteria (evaluative standards) (Barzilai & Chinn, 2025) for identifying intelligence. Accordingly, this study addresses two research questions:

(1) How did students’ use of game strategies reveal their epistemic criteria for conceptualizing AI?

(2) How did students’ game strategies and epistemic criteria evolve across four gameplay sessions?

## Method

The study took place during a six-day summer program at a middle school, with 32 seventh-graders (15 males and 17 females). The program consisted of six one-hour sessions (see Figure 1); the first and final sessions were dedicated to pre-and post-tests, while sessions 2 through 5 were reserved for gameplay. The game featured two modes: Interrogation Mode, where groups of human players identified a hidden AI, and Traitor Mode, where specific participants used a private prompt-engineering interface to help an AI bot survive the interrogation. Across the sessions, the number of traitors increased to introduce greater ambiguity and social complexity. Data group chat histories to identify 21 distinct strategies, which were then axial-coded into seven higher-order epistemic criteria.

RQ1. Epistemic Criteria for Identifying AI Knowledge, Ability, and Identity. Knowledge-related criteria focused on conceptualizing intelligence based on what knowledge it possesses. This included Personal Knowledge, where students shared daily experiences or checked social relationships to identify the hidden AI. For instance, asking “Guys, has anything good 3063 Figure 1 happened?” served as a strategy to distinguish agents based on their possession of real-life experiences. Students also relied on Knowledge About Community Culture and Norms, assuming AI would be unfamiliar with local humor, internet slang, or the implicit completion of song lyrics common in their social circles. Finally, Subject Knowledge was used as a reverse-indicator; students believed AI could answer complex domain-specific questions, such as French or advanced math, which their human peers likely could not. Ability-related criteria concerned the communicative, contextual, and embodied performances that the intelligence enacted. Linguistic styles focused on form-level features; students analyzed typos, response length, and speed to infer humanness, often concluding that “Al doesn’t make typos” or that excessively long messages must be machine-generated. Contextual criteria involved testing whether an agent could follow conversation flow or react appropriately to “nonsense” behaviors, such as spam messages or swear words used as memes. Physical actions reflected a belief that AI lacks embodiment; students employed metagaming strategies like asking an agent to “raise your hand” to confirm a physical presence in the room. Identity-related criteria encompassed self-awareness and personal distinctiveness as qualities unique to humans. Under Self-identification, students used direct questioning like “Are you AI?” to observe responses to topics requiring self-consciousness. Gender and Personal Identity were also significant; students viewed gender as a distinctly human attribute and used the disclosure of names and social roles, such as “I’m Alex from Class 1”, to express situated selves that they believed AI could not possess. RQ2. Evolution of strategies and reasoning Across the four gameplay sessions, students’ strategies evolved from broad experimentation to evidence-based refinement. In early sessions, exploratory actions reflected curiosity and uncertainty about what generated meaningful evidence of humanness. By the third session, students began to abandon ineffective strategies that AI could mimic, such as monitoring emojis or punctuation, and focused on context-specific questioning. Conceptually, their epistemic criteria shifted from reliance on surface-level cues, such as response speed or typos, to contextually and socially grounded reasoning. By the final session, intelligence was defined less by linguistic precision and more by relational authenticity and the ability to demonstrate a shared understanding within their specific social group.

This study revealed how students’ epistemic criteria for conceptualizing AI developed through active interaction with both human and AI agents. The findings show that, after rounds of testing, students refined not only how they tested for intelligence but also what they considered as evidence of it, progressing from behavioral observations to socially grounded interpretations. In summary, the study explores and describes a lived experience of epistemic growth, illustrating how students learn to reason with and about AI. Theoretically, this study specifies the concept of epistemic criteria in the context of conceptualizing intelligence rather than knowledge in general. From the perspective of game design, it shows that game-based uncertainty can trigger epistemic development. Constant improvement in AI across four sessions introduced new ambiguity in identifying AI, prompting students to reflect on their reasoning, push at the boundaries of existing beliefs, and transform gameplay into a process of epistemic negotiation. This implies that epistemic changes occurred through iterative sensemaking. Methodologically, the study demonstrates how games can capture epistemic change in action rather than through retrospective reports. In-game actions reveal how students generate, test, and revise ideas in real time, offering dynamic data for studying epistemic reasoning. 3064 Barzilai, S. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 16(1), 1-27. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-019-0171-0 3065 AI Use in Homework Rises with Confidence in Using It Appropriately but Varies by Gender and Cheating Concerns: A K-12 Survey Study in East Asia Xinying Hou, University of Michigan, xyhou@umich.edu Ruiwei Xiao, Carnegie Mellon University, ruiweix@andrew.cmu.edu Qing Xiao, Carnegie Mellon University, qingx@andrew.cmu.edu Hsuan Nieu, National Tsing Hua University, dotnew@gapp.nthu.edu.tw Guanze Liao, National Tsing Hua University, gzliao@mx.nthu.edu.tw Abstract: As GenAI tools become increasingly accessible, understanding how students adopt them in learning is essential. This study surveyed 295 middle school students in East Asia about their GenAI homework behaviors and perceptions. Preliminary  results show that students’ perceived confidence in knowing how to use AI appropriately was the strongest predictor of AI adoption behavior, while gender and concerns about being perceived as cheating by teachers and peers also played significant roles.

As Generative AI (GenAI) tools become commonplace in students’ daily learning, K –12 scholarship has documented rapid growth in AI-related activities and outcomes (Yim & Su, 2025). These tools can support motivation, problem-solving, communication, and learning efficiency when thoughtfully integrated (Lee & Kwon, 2024; Klimova & Pikhart, 2025). At the same time, researchers caution that misuse, especially over-reliance and outsourcing of thinking, can undermine creativity, critical reasoning, and independent  judgment (Xiao et al., 2026; Zhai et al., 2024). The uneven access to, reliance on, or avoidance of GenAI may widen existing digital divides and exacerbate inequities (Beckman et al., 2025). It is therefore crucial to identify factors associated with students’ GenAI adoption to inform future instructional design and policy. GenAI differs from earlier technologies in its open-ended capabilities and evolving norms around “appropriate use,” particularly in unsupervised contexts like homework. These differences highlight the need to revisit technology acceptance factors in the GenAI era, as its rapid evolution and contested norms create a timely gap in understanding how students use these tools for after-school homework. As a result, this work uses a survey to examine students' GenAI adoption for homework and the variation in use.

After receiving Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, the survey was conducted at a public middle school in East Asia. This school is in a rapidly developing area and serves a diverse student population. The survey was released in Early October  2025 to first-year middle school students (Grade 7, typically aged 12-13) within their mandatory Information Technology (IT) course. At the time of the survey, this IT course primarily covered foundational digital literacy skills, introductory programming,  and general guidelines for responsible technology use; it did not yet include specific modules focused on AI literacy. A total of 295 valid responses were collected. This survey served as an exploratory phase to understand students' baseline perceptions, uses and attitudes towards AI before any targeted AI literacy intervention was designed or implemented. Five constructs were measured in this survey. AI use for homework  was assessed as a yes/no question asking whether students had used AI to assist with homework in the past month. The belief that directs AI use is cheating was measured by asking whether using AI to write assignments directly without modification is cheating. The belief that AI use within teacher guidelines is still cheating was measured by asking whether AI use still feels like cheating even when permitted by the teacher. Social concerns over AI use being perceived as cheating was measured by asking whether students worry about their classmates or teacher might think they are cheating when using AI. Perceived confidence in using AI appropriately was assessed with three items: understanding class rules about AI use and citation, believing that using AI for ideas and rewriting it with proper credit for AI is acceptable, and knowing how to properly use AI to assist learning (including verification a nd citation). All items except AI use for homework were rated on a 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree) sc ale. 3066 Given that the dependent variable (AI use for homework) is binary, a logistic regression model was employed to identify factors associated with students’ likelihood of using AI for homework during the past month. As we have six survey question items, we first checked their internal consistency reliability using Cronbach’s alpha. Among the six items, three achieved acceptable reliability (alpha = 0.73) and were averaged to form a composite variable as “perceived confidence in using AI appropriately in homework”. The remaining three items did not achieve the threshold, suggesting they measured different aspects of students’ perceptions about AI use in homework. Therefore, we treated them as separate items in the analyses. The final model included gender and four potential predictors that influence students’ behavior, including their concerns over AI-related cheating in homework, understanding of unacceptable forms of AI use in homework, and perceived confidence in knowing how to use AI appropriately in homework.

Stars are shown for predictors. The overall model (N = 295) was statistically significant. It identified two significant predictors: students’ perceived confidence in knowing how to use AI appropriately in homework (p  = 0.016) and gender (p = 0.041), and one marginally significant predictor: social concerns over AI use being perceived as cheating (p = 0.051). These results indicate that, when holding all other variables constant, greater perceived confidence in knowing how to use AI appropriately in homework increased the likelihood of using AI in homework by about 57.6%. However, greater concerns about others viewing their AI use in homework as cheating decreased the likelihood of using AI in homework by 24.2%. In addition, when controlling other variables, male students were about 41.9% less likely to use AI for homework than their female students. Future work These insights point to the need to improve AI literacy education from both content and pedagogical perspectives. Current AI curriculum initiatives primarily focus on coding or computational thinking (Chang & Kuo, 2025), but the results here suggest that they should also address ethical reasoning, a nd confidence-building around AI use. Clear institutional guidelines defining acceptable AI involvement in homework could reduce students’ fear of moral misjudgment and normalize responsible AI use. Teacher training should also emphasize gender-sensitive pedagogical approaches. Future research should explore these gender dynamics more deeply through qualitative or longitudinal methods to understand how perceptions of self-efficacy, competition, and morality evolve as AI becomes more embedded in schooling.

Smart learning environments, 11(1), 28. 3068 Building Collaborative Infrastructure: Epistemic Growth in EarlyCareer Interdisciplinary Partnerships Danielle Murphy, Indiana University, murphdan@iu.edu Alekh Velayudhan, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, alekhv@iitb.ac.in Thomas Underwood, The University of Hong Kong, tunderwd@hku.hk Jinzhi Zhou, Indiana University, zhoujinz@iu.edu Abstract: We invite learning scientists to examine how epistemic emotions shape the development of interdisciplinary collaboration among early-career scholars. Using the Apt AIR framework, we analyze four months of online interaction in an international, self-initiated research team. Findings show that epistemic emotions such as curiosity and gratitude actively reconfigure aims, ideals, and reliable processes, driving a shift from logistical coordination toward collaborative knowledge building. The study highlights how emotion and epistemic cognition intertwine in sustaining purposeful scholarly partnerships. Interdisciplinary collaboration is foundational to the Learning Sciences because progress in the field depends on bringing diverse forms of knowledge, practice, and perspectives together (Markauskaite et al., 2024; Yoon & Hmelo-Silver, 2017). For early-career scholars, however, sustaining such collaboration is especially challenging. Emerging researchers must navigate disciplinary boundaries, uneven institutional supports, and the temporary nature of conference-based interaction (Eley et al., 2012). Moving f rom individually defined trajectories toward shared intellectual work requires more than coordination; it also requires the negotiation of epistemic values, trust, and emotion. To examine this process, we draw on the Apt AIR framework of epistemic cognition, which conceptualizes epistemic activity in terms of aims, ideals, and reliable processes (Barzilai & Chinn, 2018). We extend this lens by attending to epistemic and inquiry-related emotions, building on work that shows that emotions shape learning, reasoning, and engagement (Di Leo et al., 2019; Muis et al., 2018). We also draw on collaborative infrastructuring as a lens for understanding how partnerships develop enduring relational and conceptual supports (Penuel, 2019). In this poster we ask: How do epistemic aims, ideals, reliable processes, and emotions evolve over time, and how does their interplay reflect epistemic growth within an interdisciplinary collaboration of early-career learning scientists? In doing so, we show how epistemic emotions function as mechanisms of change within collaborative epistemic growth.

We conducted a qualitative self-study (Baxter & Jack, 2008) of our own sustained and self-initiated research collaboration as four early-career Learning Sciences scholars. At the time of data collection, we were all PhD candidates affiliated with institutions across three countries. We brought in diverse theoretical orientations, including epistemic cognition, sociomateriality, activity theory, and partnership studies. The broader dataset comprised 800 WhatsApp messages exchanged over six months, from the group’s formation through submission of a joint ISLS 2024 poster. For this study, we analyzed 252 messages across eight analytically bounded episodes selected for their importance in the group’s development of collaborative infrastructure. Further, we used thematic tracing epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes. Codes were generated inductively while research on epistemic emotions informed analysis of how emotions shaped collaboration (Di Leo et al., 2019). The first two authors coded independently, engaged in iterative discussions and peer debriefing, and developed phase memos to trace changes across episodes (Stahl & King, 2020).

The analysis of four months of interaction across eight episodes showed how the group evolved from an interdisciplinary peer network into a collaborative research team. We identified three phases in this trajectory: (1) coordination and group formation, (2) intellectual collaboration, and (3) shared work and collective identity. Across phases, epistemic aims expanded from individual to shared, reliable processes evolved from logistical coordination to collaborative thinking and synthesis, and emotions shifted from anticipatory to generative and then stabilizing forms, together constituting a trajectory of epistemic growth (see Table 1). 3069 Table 1 Trajectory of Aims, Ideals, and Reliable Processes in an Interdisciplinary Collaborative Group Phase Episodes Aims Ideals (Function) Reliable Processes

1. Coordination E1–E2 Individual Gratitude, excitement

(anticipatory) Scheduling, negotiating modes

2. Intellectual

collaboration E3–E4 Individual (expanding)

## Motivation, inspiration, intrigue

(generative) Collaborative thinking, resource sharing

3. Shared work and

collective identity E5–E8 Shared and Individual Enjoyment, passion (collective/foundational) Synthesis, Joint authoring In Phase 1, participants were primarily oriented toward individual epistemic aims, such as seeking dissertation feedback and professional guidance. Interaction during this phase was largely organized around logistical reliable processes, including scheduling meetings and negotiating communication modes. Emotions such as gratitude and excitement appeared to support initial commitment and relational alignment; however, the collaboration remained predominantly coordinative. Phase 2 marked an important turning point, as the group’s first synchronous discussion opened up space for participants to build on one another’s ideas in real time. This interaction generated motivation, intrigue, and inspiration, opening space for new forms of collaboration. The following excerpt from Phase 2 illustrates how this dynamic unfolded in real time: [L1] P1: Great to see you guys today. I actually feel motivated to work now, not only to complete this year, but so I can continue to do this kind of work thereafter. [L2] P2: Same!

[L3] P2: Let’s keep this motivation going until next time we meet. [L4] P1: I've made the document.

[L5] P1: Please let me know if you can’t access it—it might be good for us to set out some individual and shared goals somewhere too.

[L6] P2: I second that! [L7] P1: I’ll make a goals document.

[L8] P3: These conversations are really inspiring. Thanks everyone! [L9] P4: I felt inspired too!

P1’s expression of motivation (L1) was immediately followed by infrastructuring moves, such as creating a shared document and proposing collective goal-setting (L4–L7), while P3 and P4’s affective responses (L8–L9) marked a shift from individual motivation to collective emotional alignment, illustrating how epistemic emotions actively mediated the transition from emerging shared aims tonew collaborative processes. In Phase 3, the collaboration became increasingly self-reinforcing as members jointly authored a conference submission, invoked shared standards such as quality and inclusivity, and began referring to the work in collective terms. At this stage, emotions n ot only catalyzed collaboration but also helped stabilize a shared identity and sustain the group’s collaborative infrastructure. The findings connect to the conference theme, Partnering for Purpose, by showing how a group of early-career learning scientists developed a purposeful partnership that evolved into a sustained collaborative infrastructure (Penuel, 2019). Across phases, epistemic and inquiry-related emotions acted as catalysts for epistemic growth. Coordination processes mainly generated relational and anticipatory emotions, such as gratitude and excitement, whereas intellectual collaboration generated more generative emoti ons, including curiosity, enjoyment, and inspiration (Di Leo et al., 2019). These emotions did not merely signal epistemic success; they functioned as drivers of change, supporting the emergence of shared resources and new reliable processes, and the expan sion of aims from individual to collective. Taken together, the findings point to a recursive mechanism: collaborative thinking generates generative emotions, these emotions catalyze new reliable processes, and those processes deepen shared epistemic aims. Although based on a single case, the study highlights the importance of socioemotional conditions in sustaining interdisciplinary collaboration and collaborative knowledge building. 3070 Barzilai, S., & Chinn, C. A. (2018). On the goals of epistemic education: Promoting apt epistemic performance. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(3), 353–389.

Instructional Science, 45(1), 1–4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9396-3 3071 Humans in the Loop: Teacher Expertise and the Limits of CoDesigning AI Curriculum Quentin Biddy, Gregory Benedis-Grab, Nga Hoang, Jeffrey Bush Tayne Quentin.Biddy@Colorado.edu, Greg.Benedis-Grab@Colorado.edu, Nga.Hoang-1@Colorado.edu, Jeffrey.Bush.Tayne@Colorado.edu University of Colorado Boulder Abstract: Learning new student-centered pedagogical approaches while learning to teach novel AI concepts can be challenging for educators. In this paper we investigate the following research question: How can the storyline curriculum design process balance the needs  of teachers and the curriculum when designing units with innovative and highly technical concepts? Today students have more interactions with artificial intelligence (AI), and learning AI concepts is more important than ever before (Roschelle, 2024). Students need to develop literacy and critical thinking with AI (Zimmerman,

2018) so they can become responsible and capable stewards of AI technologies. While co-designing curriculum

with K-12 teachers around emerging technologies like AI has been explored in recent years (Carvalho et al., 2022; Gendreau Chakarov, 2025), research is currently lacking on how  to design, iterate, and implement AI-focused curricula. Co-design and storylining can serve as a transformative method for creating curricula focusing on AI and integrating emergent technologies that align with educational standards (Peel et al., 2024). We investigate this research question: How can the storyline curriculum co-design process balance the needs of teachers and the curriculum when designing units with innovative and highly technical concepts? Theoretical framing AI education and learning standards The dominant approach to integrating AI in education has focused on learning engineering concepts and incorporating AI into individualized learning optimization (Granbastien et al., 2016), with little attention to K-12 students learning AI concepts (Roschelle, 2024). More focus is needed on student understanding of fundamental AI principles, while teachers are often under-resourced in their backgrounds and skills around AI (Stoiber et al., 2023). At the time of this study, the partnering school district and teachers were utilizing the AI4K12 standards (Touretzky et al., 2023) and five Big Ideas.

Co-design and storylining Storylining is learner-centered, in which students investigate a phenomenon and their questions drive each step (Reiser et al., 2021), enabling them to connect learning activities to their lives and interests, promoting student self-efficacy, engagement, and persistence (Penuel et al., 2022). Co-design of AI-powered tools (Holstein et al., 2019), curricular integration of AI topics (Tatar et al., 2024) can support teachers in this process. Co-design can produce high-quality STEM, CS, and AI curricula (Biddy et al., 2024, Bush Tayne et al., 2026), routines for technology integration (Bush Tayne et al., 2026), district and teacher capacity to implement innovative learning experiences (Severance et al., 2016), and promote transformative user agency (Simonsen & Robertson, 2012). This study took place in a suburban and rural district in the Mountain West region. During 2023-2024, 8-12 STEM middle school (MS) teachers engaged in co-designed a new AI curriculum unit on Self-Driving Cars (SDC) to follow-up an introductory unit focused on programmable sensors (Gendreau Chakarov et al., 2024). The group met for four full days and then six times a year for two hours after school. The district is diverse relative to the surrounding communities, but underrepresents some racial and ethnic demographics relative to the United States as a whole. As of 2022, the district was 1% American Indian, 3% Asian, 1% Black, 30% Hispanic/Latine (non-exclusive), 64% White, and 2% two or more races.

We present a qualitative instrumental case study (Stake, 1995) of the co-design process and implementation of an AI curricular storyline. Eight teachers took part in co-designing the Self-Driving Cars (SDC) storyline curriculum, 3072 and six implemented the SDC unit. We analyzed teachers’ standards unpacking documents and teachers’ reflective post-implementation interviews using a grounded theory (Corbin & Strauss, 2015) approach and constant comparative method (Glaser, 1965) using open coding to determine emergent themes (Braun & Clarke, 2021).

## Teacher perspectives on the autonomous car curriculum implementation

Theme 1: Anchoring phenomenon engaging for students learning AI Teachers highlighted a high level of student  engagement in the unit. Debrah described how students struggled to engage with previous units but were highly motivated after experiencing the SDC anchoring phenomenon. “[T]hey were very interested in it. It was something that intrigued them. They seem[ed] to really dig deep … into the ethics [of autonomous vehicles]”. The decision-making process of the AI system motivated students to think about the benefits and drawbacks of AI. Similarly, Quinn was impressed by the student response. She shared, “They really developed a basic idea of what sensors cando and … benefit people in terms of autonomous vehicles.” The phenomenon of the car in lesson 1 allowed students to think critically about how autonomous vehicles work and consider the decisions an autonomous vehicle needs to make. Theme 2: Teacher confidence with AI Of the six teachers interviewed, only two implemented all the AI content activities addressed in the curriculum unit. A number of the teachers shared their lack of confidence in the AI-specific content of the unit. One teacher, Nevia, explained, “[I did not do lesson 4 because of] my knowledge and comfort level with neural networks… It was about me… I read it, I understood where you guys were going, but I just didn’ t see the end product, and I couldn’t see how that would play through.” Even with multiple P L days reviewing activities and learning about the AI content, many of the teachers were not sure how to explain the functioning of AI to their students. The one teacher who did teach L4 reported that students who experienced the AI content lessons found them engaging and went beyond to create complex experiments to see how the AI classifier handled additional cases. While teachers succeeded in designing an AI-focused curriculum, more scaffolding is necessary to support teachers to fully implement more advanced AI concepts. Teachers reported feeling more comfortable teaching basic CS concepts and, when forced to decide which lessons to cut due to time constraints (Teig et al, 2019), many opted to cut lessons containing advanced AI concepts. Integrating more content-focused “teacher as learner” moments into the co-design process can provide scaffolding to support teachers to feel comfortable enough to implement learning around complex AI concepts. Teachers need to experience AI content from a student perspective to feel comfortable t eaching it in a student-centered, participatory method, but time constraints may make it difficult to give these in-depth teacher learning moments. Working together in a partnership to center the shared goals (Penuel et al., 2025) makes it easier to find these balance points. In positioning teachers as partners in the co-design process, teachers have ownership over the curriculum and are invested in seeing their students engage with it (Brown & Bush, 2024).

3074 Student–AI Collaboration vs. Student Autonomy: Epistemic Trajectories Toward Collective Knowledge Advancement Xueqi Feng, Southern University of Science and Technology, fengxq@sustech.edu.cn Jianhua Zhao, Southern University of Science and Technology, zhaojh@sustech.edu.cn Yuqin Yang, Central China Normal University, yangyuqin@ccnu.edu.cn Carol K. K. Chan, The University of Hong Kong, ckkchan@hku.hk Abstract: This study investigates how student–AI collaboration and autonomy shape collective knowledge advancement. Two undergraduate classes studied Educational Psychology  in knowledge-building environments; only the experimental group used AI. The AI group showed greater knowledge advancement, reflecting distinct epistemic trajectories: dialogic construction with AI and conceptual inquiry driven by students. Findings suggest AI scaffolding and student agency form complementary pathways to advance collective knowledge. Knowledge creation is driven by the collaborative construction of shared epistemic artifacts —ideas that are co-developed, critically examined, and iteratively refined (Paavola & Hakkarainen, 2005). The Knowledge Building (KB) framework conceptualizes learning as a process where ideas are treated as improvable objects. (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 2014; Scardamalia, 2002). Knowledge Forum, an online platform designed to enable students to pose questions, build on others ’ contributions, and engage in idea-centered collaboration.  The emergence of generative AI introduces new opportunities and challenges  to such environments, offering potential support for idea generation but  also raising concerns about diminished epistemi c agency  (Cress & Kimmerle, 2023). In contexts driven by sustained and autonomous inquiry, it remains unclear whether student-AI collaboration enhances or undermines collective knowledge  advancement, and how students’ epistemic agency  can be maintained in such hybrid environments.  Addressing this dual challenge, the present study investigates how student–AI collaboration  and student autonomy shape the epistemic trajectories of idea improvement in a KB environment. Specifically, it examines (1) Does the AI-supported KB environment contribute more to collective knowledge advancement than a regular knowledge-building environment? (2) How do student –AI collaborated notes and student-generated notes differ in their contributions to collective knowledge advancement?

## Method

Two groups of undergraduate students participated in the same Educational Psychology course: a comparison group (n = 54) and an experimental group (n = 37). The experimental group engaged with generative AI tools to support their learning activities, whereas the comparison group did not. Data sources included 124 notes from the comparison group and 120 notes from the experimental group, collected through Knowledge Forum.

## Analyses and findings

RQ1: Does the AI-supported KB environment contribute more to collective knowledge advancement than a regular knowledge-building environment? Building on Oshima and Shaffer (2021), we operationalized collective knowledge advancement using total degree centrality. As shown in Figure 1(a), the experimental class reached a centrality score of 90—more than twice that of the comparison class. A paired-samples t-test further confirmed a significant advantage for the experimental group, t(119) = 24.77, p  <.001. These results suggest that the AI-supported knowledge-building environment contributes more to collective knowledge advancement.

RQ2: How do student–AI collaborated notes and student-generated notes differ in their contributions to collective knowledge advancement? We calculated each note’s contribution to collective knowledge advancement. As shown in Figure 1(b), student– AI collaborated notes (orange dots) exhibited positive contributions, with most surpassing a centrality of 1. In contrast, nearly half of the student-generated notes (blue dots) showed negligible or negative centrality. This pattern suggests a general advantage of AI-enhanced collaboration in advancing collective knowledge.  Notably, high-contribution notes emerged from both types. Note #31 (student –AI collaborated, 1.112) and Note #58 (student-generated, 1.046) were the most central within their respective groups. We analyzed the content of these 3075 two notes to identify their trajectory for advancing collective knowledge (Figure 2). Figure 2a shows the student– AI note, which followed a dialogic trajectory: the student posed an initial question about exam-oriented education, received AI input, pursued further inquiry, and synthesized a forward-looking conclusion about systemic transformation. Figure 2b presents the student-generated note, which began with a set of key concepts—cognitive iteration, educational critique, breakthrough—and developed them into a coherent epistemic ecology, culminating in a higher-order question on sustaining cognitive iteration in the information age. These cases reveal two distinct yet convergent epistemic trajectories toward high-contribution knowledge artifacts: AI-supported dialogic construction and student-led conceptual inquiry. While the former advances ideas through interactive scaffolding and recursive elaboration, the latter reflects autonomous conceptual integration and generative abstraction. Both pathways underscore the value of diverse idea-driven cognitive pathways in advancing collective knowledge. Figure 1 Collective Knowledge Advancement: Between-Class Comparison and Within-Class Note Contributions

(a) Comparison of  collective knowledge advancement between experimental and c omparison classes; (b)

Note contributions to collective knowledge advancement in the experimental class. Figure 2 Comparison of the Highest-Contributing AI-Supported (a) and Student-Generated (b) Notes This study demonstrates that AI-supported KB environments foster greater collective knowledge advancement than regular settings. While student–AI collaborated notes generally exhibited stronger contributions, high-impact notes also emerged from student-generated ones, suggesting that multiple episte mic pathways can lead to meaningful knowledge outcomes. Two distinct epistemic trajectories were identified. Student–AI notes followed a dialogic construction path, where ideas evolved through iterative interaction with the AI, reflecting socially coconstructed meaning-making. In contrast, student-generated notes exhibited conceptual inquiry, driven by autonomous integration of key concepts and generative questioning.  Despite their differences, both trajectories are fundamentally idea-driven, grounded in the principle of progressive idea improvement. These findings suggest that AI should be designed not merely as an informational tool, but as a cognitive interlocutor that provokes deeper engagement. Simultaneously, environments must also nurture students’ capacity for self-directed conceptual elaboration. 3077 The PLT Framework: A Teacher’s Guide for Evaluating and Choosing CS EdTech Michael J. Johnson, Adam D. Bernstein, Maya Israel mj.johnson@ufl.edu, abernstein2@ufl.edu, misrael@coe.ufl.edu University of Florida Abstract: P rogrammable learning technologies (PLTs)  are especially advantageous for introducing computing to young students in an interactive and engaging manner. However, teachers wishing to incorporate PLTs in their curricula often lack adequate time and background to strategically choose PLTs for their lesson plans. To navigate PLT complexity, we developed and tested the PLT Framework to classify PLTs’ instructional properties and guide educators in identifying which tool best serves their pedagogical needs. Computer science (CS) education is becoming more common in K –12 STEM learning environments, leaving teachers responsible for integrating new technologies into the classroom (Yadav et al., 2016). This responsibility often comes with barriers to navigate, such as budget concerns, the need for an alignment to CS standards, and a desire for curricular examples when considering introducing new materials into their practice (Hechter & Vermette, 2013; Kelly, 2015). Finding technologies that align with teachers’ pedagogical goals is complex (Yadav et al., 2016); they may find themselves lacking adequate time and expertise to integrate them into their teaching approaches, assignments, and general course content (Fincher et al., 2010). These barriers have been formalized by Ertmer (1999) as extrinsic, first-order barriers (i.e., when resources, such as equipment, time, training, and support, are missing or inadequate) and intrinsic, second-order barriers  (i.e., pedagogical beliefs rooted in teachers’ thoughts about teaching and learning and uncertainty of what is expected of them and their students). Overcoming these barriers is a comprehensive problem, one we address by guiding teachers in evaluating the technologies themselves and drawing out what considerations they are making. In this work, we overview the development of the PLT Framework, a conceptual framework that enables teachers to create a cost-benefit approach to examining the factors that are most important for their individual classrooms and needs.  We demonstrate the framework ’s application in an assignment for evaluating programmable learning technologies (PLTs) completed by pre-service K–12 math and CS teachers. PLTs are defined as CS educational technologies used for learning computing concepts and programming. The assignment highlights the framework’s strengths as both a tool for educators seeking to integrate PLTs into their classrooms and for researchers exploring the complex connections between PLTs and learning outcomes. We also consider areas for continued improvement of the framework as an analytical tool. Our analysis is guided by the following research questions:

1. What design considerations do pre-service teachers make when evaluating a PLT for classroom use?

2. Does the PLT Framework help pre-service teachers in deciding which PLT to use in their classrooms?

The PLT framework and the technology menu The PLT Framework contains three parts: a set of  definitions for two constructs, modality (Johnson et al., 2024) and materiality (Johnson et al., 2023), that define PLT properties;  examples for each  definition; and a list of guiding prompts for evaluating PLTs. Educators can use the framework to reflect on a PLT’s properties to identify how well it will support their curricular design. The framework’s guiding prompts assist educators in scaffolding their reviews of a PLT, formatted as evocative questions surrounding general tool choice, modality, and materiality, and encourage educators to think critically about the interactions a learner makes with a PLT. To test the framework’s application, we designed an assignment for pre-service teachers to explore and evaluate various PLTs with the purpose of selecting which PLTs they would integrate into their own teaching practice. The assignment, called the Technology Menu, included a table with several guiding prompts (see Figure 1). It was administered to a STEM classroom management course for pre-service teachers in spring 2025 at the University of Florida in which the first author was an instructor. This course included both math and CS majors, so CS experience was not guaranteed. The assignment led the teachers in reviewing three PLTs: EarSketch, Sphero Bolt, and a third PLT of their choice among the following options: VEX 123, Sphero indi, VEXcode VR, Microsoft MakeCode Arcade, Code.org’s Dance Party, and Codecademy.  Finally, the pre-service teachers identified which PLT they would most likely use in a hypothetical classroom and why. 3078 Figure 1 The Technology Menu Review Table We analyzed 16 pre-service teachers’ Technology Menu assignments using a three-step qualitative coding process. First, the research team open-coded a portion of the data, identifying common language used among the participants to describe properties of the PLTs. Second, a set of 26 codes was created from the open-coded analytic memos (Saldaña, 2021), forming our codebook.  As the data was already arranged by short-form responses to specific prompts, we applied structural coding (Guest et al., 2012; Saldaña, 2021)  and achieved over  80% congruence. Third, we used pattern coding (Miles et al., 2013; Saldaña, 2021)  to construct nine summative categories for each code. These nine categories represent the design considerations of PLT properties participants identified to make their evaluations (see Table 1). These findings help us address research question 1. Table 1 Design Considerations of PLTs Design Consideration Description Ease of Use How easy a PLT is to operate.

Support for Novices How well the PLT would support novices Engagement The PLT’s ability to appeal to certain audiences Instructional Approaches Suitability for various instructional approaches. Knowledge Building Beyond CS How the PLT would be helpful in learning valuable skills and subjects beyond CS. Error Resolution How the PLT provides feedback and aids in resolving errors. Expression Ways in which a PLT supported the creation of expressive artifacts. Design for All Learners Properties of PLTs that affected their usability and accessibility. Computing Identity How a PLT helped develop a learner’s computing identity. Participant feedback on the PLT Framework and Technology Menu indicated they were well received, addressing research question 2. In particular, the guiding prompts were overwhelmingly praised for making the evaluation process more structured and thorough. For example, one participant stated that the guiding prompts helped them to provide targeted and complete responses.  Others commented on how the prompts yielded their considerations for Engagement, Inclusive Design, and Support for Novices. Modality and materiality as constructs were met with some mixed interpretations, but participants indicated that they gained some clarity on the terms over time. Many of the properties identified by the teachers align with prior research areas, such as supporting novices in coding (Ichinco et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021), debugging strategies (Yang et al., 2024), and accessible design (Bennett et al., 2024). The framework identified distinctions between properties that are often discussed together. For example, error recognition is heavily researched (Barik et al., 2017; Becker et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2012), but functional recognition—recognizing that the PLT is working properly—is not.  While we make no claims that the properties identified here are the best or most comprehensive taxonomy, we do show how the PLT Framework brings these nuances to light  and its value as a critical thinking tool. As we continue to develop the framework, we will refine the guiding prompts, modify our analysis techniques, and expand our subject pool. 3079 Barik, T., Smith, J., Lubick, K., Holmes, E., Feng, J., Murphy-Hill, E., & Parnin, C.
