## Measuring Physics Teacher Instructional Changes in the Context of

a Responsive Professional Development Maggie S. Mahmood, Hamideh Talafian maggiesm@illinois.edu, talafian@illinois.edu University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Abstract: Addressing the challenge of measuring the impacts of science teacher professional development on teachers’ practice, we present an instructional audit  tool that measures how physics teachers reallocate between instructional activities, how this aligns with their goals, and the to what they attribute shifts. The tool comprises a retrospective syllabus audit, self-rankings, and qualitative responses. Pilot results from 23 teachers  showed instructional change  was positively correlated with teachers’ perceptions of progress toward science education reform goals.

To determine whether responsive teacher professional development (PD) (Inouye & Gunshenan 2024; Talafian et al., 2025) can promote durable, instructional change requires a methodologically creative solution since in this flexible approach, teachers ’ practices become increasingly customized.  This paper describes a methodology for measuring shifts in teachers’ instructional time allocation consisting of (1) retrospective lesson plan and syllabus audits; (2) retrospective self-ratings of self-efficacy and instructional emphasis; and (3) qualitative responses about the mechanisms by which the changes oc curred. To justify our methodology of using changes in instructional time-allocation as a barometer for understanding teachers’ instructional change, we look to two relevant frameworks: Opportunities to learn (OTL), the notion that quality educational opportunities are correlated with students’ academic outcomes (for popularization of framework, see Smithson et al., 1995; see Greeno & Gresalfi, 2008; Perry et al., 2024  for more recent use), and time on task, the study of content exposure as a variable on student learning outcomes (Fredrick & Walberg, 1980). The methodology proposed in this paper focuses on measuring unit-level changes in student exposure  to quality  science reform-minded activities and groupings. In turn, this paper asks: Are high measures of instructional change in the group positively correlated with teacher perceptions of the impact of this change toward science education reform-goals?

The study context  is the Illinois Physics and Secondary School s partnership program  (IPaSS), a high school physics teacher community of practice consisting of ~100 hours of responsively facilitated PD per year for a fouryear term. All teachers are provided access to university-level physics instructional materials and class sets of a multi-sensor lab device, yet the messaging of the PD is complete flexibility in implementation of these resources. Out of fifty returning teachers, 23 submitted complete responses to all sections of our survey tool. Development of Instructional Modality Time-Allocation Audit Tool (IMTAAT) The Instructional Modality Time-Allocation Audit Tool (IMTAAT) measures shifts in the time teachers allocate to different instructional practices in a single instructional unit (here, the momentum unit in high school physics). We chose to focus on the modality of instructional activity – defined as how the content is presented – as opposed to teacher emphasis on disciplinary content or learning goals for three reasons.  First, there exists significant variance in content emphasis in this (and all) physics unit(s) by course level and school. Second, for reasons similar to those cited by Cunningham et al (2009) we believe the modality of instruction can be a more realistic indicator of teacher value shifts with respect to the philosophical tenets of modern science education reform (such as responsive, student-centered classroom culture) than emphasis on specific physics concepts in any given unit. Third, this choice can allow the tool to be adapted to any scientific discipline, or other fields. The IMTAAT consists of three parts: (1) Syllabus / lesson plan audits (2) Retrospective Likert rankings of self-confidence and instructional self-efficacy; and (3) Qualitative responses  soliciting teachers’ characterization of their instructional changes and perceived mechanisms of those changes. The syllabus audit is a simple but powerful responsive table  in Excel where  teachers can log instructional activities (labs, problem solving, full class instruction, projects, and assessments), which generates a responsive dropdown for subcategories (e.g., open-ended labs) and the time allocated to each. First, using lesson plans and syllabi that are 3081 already an administrative requirement in most teaching roles, teachers retroactively input the activities from their pre-IPaSS plans and current ones into the spreadsheet. Second, teachers answer retrospective Likert-style survey questions (Moore & Tananis, 2009; Pratt et al., 2000) about shifts in their self-confidence and instructional selfefficacy in the instructional unit. The final section is a qualitativ e reflection on unit changes in open response format. Our results focus on the relationship between the first and second sections. First, the pre and post  percentage of total minutes in the  momentum unit allocated to each sub-category of instruction was calculated for each teacher. Means and standard errors on these values were computed  to detect any large-scale trends in the 23-teacher pool. The second phase of analysis included the calculation of absolute values of percentage shift in each subcategory (e.g., labs, problem-solving, assessment, whole class instruction and other). Calculating absolute values is useful here because some pre-post shifts were in the positive direction and some in the negative direction, so a simple sum meant that teachers who had (for example) reallocated all their direct instructional time to labs could show a net zero change. Instead, to get a raw sense of the magnitude of each teacher ’s instructional change, the sum of absolute values of percentage shifts in each subcategory was calculated and ranked. We call this numerical representation  the Absolute Value of Instructional Time Reallocation (AVITRe). We justify our use of absolute change in this measure, as opposed to favoring a priori certain types of change, due to our orientation as a responsive PD program: I f we make our measurement tool sensitive to unconventional or unfamiliar patterns of instructional change, we can learn something new about how instructional reform plays out in different contexts.

Considering five large instructional categories  on the IMTAAT  (labs, problem solving, full class instruction, projects, and assessments) a paired t-test (N=23) detected an increase in the percentage of total instructional time in the momentum unit that teachers allocated to labs  (pre: M = 21, SD = 13.5; post: M  = 28.9,  SD = 16.1; t = 3.6, p =.001), and a significant decreases in direct instruction (lecturing) (pre: M = 18, SD = 13.3; post: M = 12.1, SD = 11.8; t = 3.8, p =.001). In part 2 of the IMTAAT, teachers who reported large shifts in their perceived ability to promote science education reform goals such as student-centered instruction, student engagement in science practice, and deeper student learning, were more likely to have a large AVITRe score indicating absolute amount of instructional change (ρs = 0.44 with p = 0.03665). This calculation, while providing some face-validity to the AVITRe metric, demonstrated that in general, teachers in the community feel that their instructional changes align with science education reform goals (the focus of the self-report retrospective Likert questions). Q ualitative responses indicated that specific changes they made (e.g., greater number  of labs, less direct instruction, more opportunities for students to work in groups) resulted in what they viewed as higher-quality science instruction. Quantifying and visualizing shifts in instructional activity time-allocation can be a powerful way to represent impacts of a teacher PD intervention when triangulated with other qualitative metrics such as observations, interviews, and qualitative survey responses. A broad focus on time-allocation to instructional modalities can be useful when PD programs take a more flexible approach to teacher implementation. Our results demonstrated that teachers’ absolute instructional shifts per  the AVITRe were  correlated with their perceived progress toward science education reform goals. Imagining another community with different PD goals, (or one wherein instructional change is imposed rather than organically integrated), we could imagine teachers with high AVITRe rankings but lower self-efficacy with respect to their progress toward science education reform goals. More work is needed to consider the usefulness of the AVITRe score for assessing teacher comparative change within a community, and how it can be leveraged as a tool to identify big shifts to later investigate the mechanisms by which they occur.  Our initial results  from the pilot IMTAAT  suggest a link between certain teacher-held instructional reform goals to specific kinds of activity-level instructional shifts in teacher practice. Although it is not shocking, it should be noted that teachers who identified success with student-led instruction increased group collaborative problem-solving activities and/or reduced direct instruction, and that teachers who found success with inculcating deep conceptual learning increased the amount of time spent on open-ended labs. These associations indicate that it could be important in future work on teacher professional learning and change to include data at the level of instructional modality time-allocation, as it could reveal progress toward these broader science education reform goals.  Finally, early data suggests comparison of teachers’ AVITRe shifts in the years before entering a PD program to AVITRe shifts during a PD program as a promising future method for PD program impact evaluation.

## Acknowledgements

This project is supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) grant, DRL 201088. We thank the participating teachers for their invaluable contributions, members of the research team, Eric Kuo, Morten Lundsgaard, and Tim Stelzer for their support of this work, and the anonymous reviewers who provided insights and expertise that assisted in the strengthening of the paper. 3083 Equity Goals as Mediators of Teacher Learning in Curricular Customization Jason Y. Buell, Yang Zhang, Etta Pope, Brian J. Reiser jason.buell@northwestern.edu, yang.zhang2@northwestern.edu, ettapope2029@u.northwestern.edu, reiser@northwestern.edu Northwestern University Abstract: Curricular customization is one potential approach for teachers to be able to use reform-oriented, high-quality curricular resources while still adapting for their own context and students. While curricular customization is often presented as beneficial fo r students, it is also potentially productive for teacher learning. This paper presents the case of two professional learning communities engaged in curricular customization but with two different equity goals. We illustrate in these cases how the different equity goals ultimately mediated how teachers interacted with their curricular materials, with one group engaging in fine-grained analysis of participation structures within lessons and another staying at a wi der-grained analysis of how content builds across lessons. These cases illustrate how equity goals are not simply an important consideration for students, but also potentially for teacher learning. Curriculum-based professional learning (CBPL) is an approach to teacher professional learning that is anchored on using high quality instructional materials (HQIM) as a catalyst for teacher learning. By grounding professional learning in the context of HQIM, CBPL provides a way for teachers to make sense of abstract principles using concrete examples and learn with materials from their everyday instructional contexts (Short & Hirsh, 2023). While CBPL is a promising approach to teacher learning (Smith et al., 2022), one potential pitfall is that teachers only engage with superficial features of implementation rather than the deeper principles instantiated in the materials (Davis et al., 2016; McNeill et al., 2018). From our own experiences facilitating CBPL, we see one possible reason for this pitfall is due to how teachers and professional learning facilitators may construct and negotiate participation frameworks where teachers take on a sensemaking role focused on how best to implement materials with fidelity. Teachers often see their role in CBPL as learning about and using HQIM. A potential re-framing for teachers’ professional learning (Webster-Wright, 2009) may be through focusing CBPL on curricular customization (Gerard et al., 2022; McNeill et al., 2026). Rather than seeing their role as learning to use HQIM, teachers can instead see their role as finding ways to best leverage and customize HQIM for their particular educational contexts. However, the mere presence of curricular materials does not facilit ate learning, it is the interactions with the tool that matter for learning (Werstsch, 1998). Thus it is important to study not just what teachers are interacting with, but how they interact with the curricular materials to understand the kinds of learning opportunities that CBPL affords. In this paper, we present findings from a research project that focuses on curricular customization. We ask, “How do equity goals mediate interactions with curricular materials during customization?” Data from this study come from the third year of data collection from the NSF-funded Customize research project.

The study took place in partnership with middle school science teachers in a K-8 school district in the United States. The focus of this paper is on two 8th grade teacher-led professional learning communities (PLCs) that met throughout the school year in order to customize the OpenSciEd curriculum (OSE; OpenSciEd Middle School Developers Consortium, 2022). Researchers worked with PLC leaders to provide resources to work through a customization cycle (McNeill et al., 2026). All PLC meetings were led by teachers. The first PLC, based at Central Middle School, was led by Shirley and was attended by two other science teachers, Brenda and Carl. The second PLC, based at Pine Middle School, was led by Jane and attended by one other science teacher, Sandra, as well as a special education teacher, Wendy, and an English-language support specialist, Travis. Both teacher-leaders were the most experienced teachers in their PLCs, had taught for over 15 years, and had participated in researcher-led PLCs the year before. All of the teachers had prior experience teaching with OSE except for Travis. All of them attended the OSE PL and each group customized two units during the school year. All names and locations are pseudonyms. For analysis, researchers transcribed videos and worked together on creating a structured memo template for each meeting that contained guiding questions focusing on how teachers interacted with the curricular 3084 resources, their customizations, and their learning about equity, teaching, and the curriculum. We used the structured memos to identify the areas of the curricular materials that teachers identified problems with and what kinds of customizations they made and met to discuss themes across the memos.

We find that PLCs identified different areas of the curriculum to customize based on their equity goals. When we examine how the teachers interacted with the curriculum, we see differences in the grain size each team chose to work on and in the customizations they created. Pine, in aiming to customize the curriculum so students, especially emerging multilingual learners (EMLs), see their ideas driving their learning, kept the overall scope and sequence of the lessons intact, changing participation structures to invite more students’ sharing. Central, focusing on relevance, added or substituted entire lessons, spending little time customizing existing lessons. For both schools, we discuss only one of their customization cycles for clarity, however, we observed consistent patterns for both PLCs across both of their cycles.

The teachers at Pine Middle School focused on wanting students to feel comfortable with sharing out and on having multiple modalities for expressing their thinking and zeroed in on participation structures for their customizations. After looking at student  data and speaking about their goals, the Pine teachers looked at a list of common areas for customization provided by researchers. Sandra states, “I like hovering around discourse and interaction strategies and adding support within the existing lessons, like turn and talk, quick writes, maybe a quick draw.” The teachers talk through different interaction strategies that they can add and do not attempt to change the structure of flow of the overall unit. For example, they add more structure to the shareout  of an initial model so that students have more opportunities to talk about what patterns they have in common. Pine teachers approached customization by going through each of the slides of a lesson and finding ways to give students more opportunities to participate. Most frequently, they gave students more opportunities to work through their ideas in smaller groups or individually, such as by adding turn and talks, opportunities to draw, or by having students share in small groups before turning to the whole group. They also added more structured opportunities for sharing, such as stand up, pair up, and share so that students had a chance to share with students not from their table.

While Pine teachers kept the overall activity structure of the curriculum intact, focusing on the participation structures of the lessons, Central teachers primarily focused on substituting or adding entire activities while keeping existing lessons largely intact. At Central Middle School, they articulated their goal as increasing relevance for better participation and sensemaking. In their work in PLCs, they focused on attending to students' questions and curiosities. Central teachers, in thinking about student experiences, were trying to attend strongly to students’ questions and their engagement with their learning. Their major customizations for each unit involved inserting or changing a new activity, with a new phenomenon. In this customization, teachers were responding to students’ questions about how genetic inheritance works in humans. In their second PLC of this unit’s customization cycle, the teachers wanted to find a place to talk about humans. Unlike Pine teachers, they did not go through the unit slide by slide. Instead they focused on the overall flow of the unit by identifying key learning ideas at each lesson. Shirley states, “I feel like I want to go back and take a look before putting it in between [lesson] six and seven. What is happening in five and six? What do we need to emphasize leading up to that? So that when we do bring in these new activities or this new lesson, that it makes sense in the flow.” The teachers then proceed to discuss the main idea of each lesson. Their discussion was at a much broader level than Pine thinking about the entire arc of the unit without ever diving into the details of any single lesson. For each PLC, we observed different kinds of interactions with the curricular materials. Pine teachers had an equity goal that focused on equitable participation and thus took a fine-grained approach where they went through each slide of every lesson in or der to focus on the participation structures within each daily activity. Central teachers had an equity goal that focused on students’ experiences and they focused on students’ questions and relevant phenomena. They took a broader approach and stayed at the lesson level to try to insert phenomena that addressed students’ questions and still fit within the content progression of the unit. In both PLC groups, teachers formulated an equity goal and customized their curriculum to better meet these goals. However, the kind of goal mediated how teachers interacted with the curriculum. We think this finding is important as how teachers interact with the curriculum can ultimately afford what they learn about and with the curriculum. Researchers and facilitators of p rofessional learning can be aware and anticipate how teachers will likely interact with materials given their equity goal and find ways to help teachers to move from both fine-grained and broader interactions to ensure learning at multiple scales.

3086 “It’s Not Just a Hurricane”: How A Cajun Teacher’s Fugitive Space Informs Her Climate Change Pedagogy Ayça K. Fackler, The University of Missouri, facklera@missouri.edu Clausell Mathis, Michigan State University, mathisc8@msu.edu Abstract: As climate change reshapes the Gulf of Mexico, teachers from coastal Louisiana are navigating what it means to teach climate change in science classrooms amid loss and uncertainty. This case study focuses on an elementary teacher from a Cajun community, a climate refugee from South Louisiana, who participated in a place-based climate change education project and co-taught fourth-grade lessons on climate-induced water issues. Using the lenses of fugitivity and teacher identity, we examine how she reflected on her relationship to place, community, and teaching after repeated hurricanes. Through interviews, observations, and dialogues, we unpack her pedagogical stance as an act of refusal, resisting deficit framings of her community and instead positioning lived experiences as sensemaking resources. Findings reveal how lived experiences informed her sense of self and desire to cultivate belonging and hope for students. This study highlights how fugitive, place-affirming pedagogies nurture resilience and contextualized science sensemaking.

Major issue addressed While recent scholarship in climate change education has emphasized the importance of strengthening  teachers’ content knowledge, pedagogical practices, and self-efficacy for teaching about climate change (e.g., Leve et al., 2023; Shea et al., 2016), less attention has been given to teachers who live and teach in communities directly experiencing climate disruption.  For teachers who are themselves climate refugees, displacement survivors, or residents of environmentally fragile regions, teaching climate change is not only a disciplinary and pedagogical act but also a deeply emotional, ethical, and existential endeavor (Vossoughi et al., 2016). This study addresses this gap by centering the lived experiences  (Avraamidou, 2019)  and fugitive pedagogies (Givens, 2021a) of teachers whose professional and personal lives are intertwined with the realities of environmental, social, and cultural disruptions due to climate change. Specifically, it examines how a Cajun elementary teacher, Ms. Zehra, from South Louisiana, herself displaced by hurricanes, draws upon her identity, lived experiences, and local knowledge to reimagine climate change education as an act of refusal, care, and place-affirmation. This study asks: How do Ms. Zehra’s fugitive space and teacher identity inform how she enacts and reimagines climate change pedagogy?

Theoretical approach Fugitivity The concept of fugitivity describes the subversive, identity-affirming acts through which Black people have pursued knowledge and liberation under oppressive systems that sought to deny their intellectual and human capacities (Givens, 2021b; Harney & Moten, 2013). Fugitive pedagogies represent practices of refusal, including refusal of erasure, silencing, dismissal, and compliance with dominant narratives that constrain what and whose knowledge counts in schools.  Fugitivity offers a powerful way to understand how teachers in climate-impacted regions resist deficit framings of their communities and reimagine teaching as an act of survival, care, and belonging.

Science teacher identity In this study, science teacher identity is conceptualized as an evolving, contextually situated construct that reflects how teachers understand and represent themselves in relation to their teaching, their communities, and the sociopolitical conditions tha t shape both (Avraamidou, 2014). Following Gee’s (2000) framework, Ms. Zehra’s identity can be understood through intertwined lenses of discourse, institutional, and affinity identities. She continuously negotiates who she is as a science teacher within institutional constraints that often depolit icize climate education, while aligning herself with community-based, place-affirming practices of knowing. This study examines how fugitivity and science teacher identity intersect to shape a justice-oriented science teaching practice that challenges dominant deficit-oriented discourses and affirms the epistemologies of place and lived experience. 3087 Methodological approach This case study (Merriam, 2009) e plored how a Cajun teacher enacted fugitive pedagogy while teachin g climate change in coastal Louisiana. This design illuminated how Ms. Zehra’s acts of resistance and care honored lived experiences amid pressures to depoliticize and decontextualize science. Data sources included classroom observations, interviews, and reflective dialogues. Data were analyzed thematically through a three-round inductive coding process (Braun & Clarke, 2006), informed by the lenses of fugitivity and teacher identity. In the first round, open coding was conducted using twelve sensitizing codes derived from the dat a, while remaining attentive to emergent subcodes. In the second round, related codes were grouped into themes to capture the complexity of Ms. Zehra’s practices, namely, Climate Change Pedagogy as Resilience and Care, Situated Identity, Loss, and Belonging in Teaching Climate Change, and Complexities and Possibilities of Teaching Climate Change. The third round involved theoretical interpretation, mapping these themes onto the intersection of fugitivity and teacher identity to illuminate how Ms. Zehra ’s narratives constituted an act of pedagogical survival and imagination within the sociopolitical and ecological precarity of coastal Louisiana.

## Major Findings

Due to space limitations, we provide a condensed summary of Theme 3. Theme 3: Complexities and possibilities of teaching climate change Theme 3 highlights the tension between the possibilities of hope and the complexities of teaching about climate change within economically and socially constrained contexts. For Ms. Zehra, teaching climate change involves helping students recognize their own capacity to act while acknowledging the limits imposed by structural inequities. Her optimism emerges through small, tangible actions: “They can make small changes. Maybe not littering, keeping an eye on the news, and speaking up.” These hopeful acts, what she calls “small changes,” represent potential agency and environmental stewardship.  Ms. Zehra cultivates an accessible sense of agency, encouraging them to “have a better appreciation for their home.” Ms. Zehra also highlights the tension of teaching climate change in economies tied to its causes:  “Our economy is very reliant upon the same company that caused the issue in the first place.” Her statement reveals the tension of teaching climate justice where livelihoods depend on extraction.  As she explains, “If your dad works on the oil rig, the same people who are feeding you are the same people dredging the canal s, causing more erosion.” In these words, Ms. Zehra names the structural entanglements that make critique risky and action complicated. Recognizing that “no one here has enough money to make a real change. If they’re paying you, you’re able to feed your kids. T hat’s a mentality for people  here. Are we supposed to do that  [critique]?”, she situates her pedagogy within constrained community agenc y. Holding both tension and possibility, Ms. Zehra’s teaching embodies a fugitive stance amid survival and sustainability. education involves navigating the intertwined realities of livelihood, land, and survival. Through acts of resilience and care, Ms. Zehra reframed climate pedagogy as a community-centered practice that linked disciplinary knowledge to moral responsibility and local observation, foregrounding students’ lived experiences as legitimate sites of inquiry. Her situated identity positioned climate change teaching as an affective and cultural endeavor that grappled with grief, belonging, and the erosion of land and language while reclaiming beauty and pride in place. At the same time, her navigation of economic exploitation and systemic contradictions exposed the tensions of teaching climate justice in communities dependent on extractive industries. Yet within these constraints, small acts of hope shaped her climate pedagogy, nurturing students’ agency and stewardship. Findings position climate pedagogy as emoti onal, relational, and justice-driven. This study urges shifting from self-efficacy and content mastery models to approaches that honor teachers’ lived experiences, identit ies, and emotional labor in climate change education.

3089 Connecting Global Competencies to Local Contexts: How Egyptian Teachers Interpret 21st-Century Learning Christine Tewfik, University of Toronto, c.tewfik@mail.utoronto.ca Doha Sayed, University of Toronto, doha.sayed@mail.utoronto.ca James Slotta, University of Toronto, jim.slotta@utoronto.ca Abstract: This paper examines the integration of 21st-century competencies in non-Western educational settings, where teachers in non-hegemonic cultures respond to calls for Western pedagogies with limited professional development. It highlights the need for support  that enables culturally responsive transformation of teaching practices while preserving local values and addressing contextual challenges. Conducted within the Critical Action Learning Exchange (CALE), an international community of critical educators (Ca rvalho et al., 2021), the study explores how teachers navigate these complexities.

This study reports on a formative intervention involving Egyptian public-school teachers working to integrate 21st-century competencies aligned with the Education 2.0 policy. This national shift moves from rote learning toward student-centered, competency-based pedagogies. We examine how teachers enact these competencies in ways that honor local cultural values while navigating a professional development model informed by a Western university. To avoid cultural imperialism, defined as disproportionate ideological influence (Mains, 2009), we adopted a critical practitioner inquiry approach (Cochran-Smith & Lytle, 2009). This positions teachers as knowledge producers rather than passive recipients. As a professional learning community (PLC), participants used an "inquiry-as-stance" to design culturally grounded lesson plans within the Critical Action Learning Exchange (CALE) project (Carvalho et al., 2021).

## Theoretical framework

The study is grounded in two primary traditions. First, Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) posits that human activity is rooted in evolving historical and social contexts. CHAT-informed interventions prioritize sociocultural norms and support "expansive learning cycles" to transform collective practices (Sannino et al., 2016). It provides a lens to analyze power dynamics and overcome systemic contradictions. Second, we utilize Critical Action Learning (CAL), which draws on Freirean 'conscientização ' (Freire, 1970). This approach empowers students as transformative agents through critical reflection, critical motivation, and critical action (Watts et al., 2011), viewing social structures as changeable rather than inevitable. This project investigated a Cairo-based PLC over three months. Eight participants from public, private, and Egyptian Japanese Schools engaged in online workshops and classroom implementation. Developed within the broader context of the CALE project, we sup ported teachers with a Web-based community, customized for use by teachers using WhatsApp in the course of their daily practice as well as scheduled online Zoom meetings. Teacher participants were engaged in a formative intervention professional development to examine their practices through the lens of practitioners' inquiry methodology, which positions practitioners as drivers of social and educational change and intends to develop the inquiry-as-stance mindset (Cochran-Smith & Lytle, 2009, p. 121). Practitioners in this study were guided to problematize their current practices, interrogating the different ways knowledge and practice are constructed, examined, and used. This allowed them to critically generate knowledge that helps them to change the status quo in their own learning environments. Inquiry-as-stance is perceived as a means of changing school cultures (Cochran-Smith and Lytle, 1999), emphasizing the collective nature of this stance as opposed to one’s individual stance. This collective element was important for this study: No single teacher was able to find a solution for the issues and dilemmas that were being addressed in the CALE curriculum.

The formative intervention included two phases: a workshop phase and an implementation phase. The workshop phase included four 3-hour sessions, conducted online. A pre-survey and the engagement in various critical discussions served as the double-stimulation artifacts prescribed by the Formative Intervention critically use the concepts introduced in the 4 workshop sessions to create teaching and learning models that are 3090 culturally relevant and contextual to their own and their students’ experiences. The goal of this w orkshop phase is for teachers to design their own curricular and/or extracurricular lesson plans using the frameworks and approaches presented during the workshops. The implementation phase was the second phase of this professional development opportunity. In this phase, participating teachers implemented their designs in their own classrooms/schools. Teachers received ongoing mentoring and peer feedback during this phase. We understand that innovative pedagogies go through different iterative phases to enhance the teaching and learning experience for teachers and students. For this purpose, participants continued to have follow-up sessions with a CALE mentor during and after the implementation of their designs.

Guided by participatory methods and "inquiry-as-stance" (Cochran-Smith & Lytle, 1999), teachers used the CALE model and peer feedback to redesign curricula via WhatsApp and Zoom. Data from surveys, workshops, and interviews were examined via thematic analysis to answer the central research question: How do Egyptian teachers, teaching the national curricula, understand and integrate 21st-century competencies in their classrooms?

Using CHAT, we conceptualized the subject as both individual educators and the collective PLC, while the object was authentic competency integration. Tools included the CALE framework and digital platforms. We applied rules (curricular mandates and cultural norms), community (colleagues and leadership), and division of labor (professional roles) as analytical lenses to identify tensions shaping practice. as rules mediating the interpretation of CALE. A central tension emerged between "rules" (time constraints and coverage) and the "object" (competency integration). While some teachers treated competencies as superficial "add-ons," others resolved this by redesigning tools into locally relevant units. Those with deeper understanding designed extended units that fostered authentic student engagement, where as others used superficial activities without meaningful skill development.

Crucially, teacher readiness depended on school context and prior training. We categorized participants into three groups: ● Developing: Experienced strong tensions and lacked professional development, hindering implementation.

● Intermediate: Showed partial alignment but lacked conceptual clarity. ● Proficient: Primarily in Egyptian Japanese Schools; benefited from coherent community support and sustained learning for authentic enactment.

The limited workshop duration was a challenge, particularly for "developing" teachers who required more time to grasp 21st-century frameworks. While 3-hour sessions worked for proficient educators, they were insufficient for those with minimal exposure. Future programs should assess teacher readiness levels beforehand to provide diversified, tailored support that accommodates varying levels of awareness regarding competency-based education.

New Directions for Child and Adolescent Development, 2011(134), 43–57. https://doi.org/10.1002/cd.310 3092 Designing for Epistemic Fluency and Local Scientific Identity: Insights from a Community-Engaged Course-Based Research Experience Adam Papendieck, Abigail Granath, Jennifer Rudgers apapendieck@unm.edu, absgranath@unm.edu, jrudgers@unm.edu University of New Mexico Abstract: We report early findings from design-based implementation research on a novel community-engaged course-based research experience at the University of New Mexico. The course engages early undergraduates in interdisciplinary research with Tribal and communit y partners to address environmental challenges. Results from a mixed methods analysis of endof-course surveys, interviews, and artifacts show how boundary objects and arts-based practices mediated progress in the development of epistemic fluencies and local scientific identities. Authentic community engagement in academic science matters. Scientific practice in culturally and disciplinarily heterogeneous contexts requires attunement and responsiveness to the epistemological and axiological traditions that organize different communities of knowing. Despite successful models, persistent challenges remain. Community-engaged researchers report that engagement in science is often difficult (Mason et al., 2013), undervalued (Teufel-Shone, 2011), and even counterproductive when tokenistic or reinforcing of deficit views (Philip et al., 2013). Rather than only asking whether  engagement is possible or beneficial, we must investigate how it succeeds or fails, and what impacts it has on different participants. It is only by better understanding situated conditions and processes of engagement that we candesign infrastructures and practices that meaningfully involve communities in producing relevant and useful science.

Course-Based Research Experiences (CBREs) have become prevalent and valued contexts for science learning in higher education, especially at the undergraduate level in Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) (Auchincloss et al., 2014; Papendieck and Clarke, 2024). As CBREs proliferate across university curricula, they offer potentially transformative and broadly scalable settings for developing and assessing new approaches to community-engaged learning and scientific collaboration between universities and communities. This study summarizes early findings on learning processes and outcomes from the spring 2025 pilot iteration of the Resilience Solutions Incubator (RSI), a novel Community-engaged Course-based Research Experience (C-CBRE) at the University of New Mexico designed to (1) cultivate scientists capable of navigating diverse epistemologies, and (2) position them within community-engaged research networks. The RSI brings together undergraduates, faculty, and community partners to co-design research addressing environmental challenges such as water contamination and climate resilience in a southwestern state. RSI treats science as both a technical and cultural practice, and an endeavor accountable to communities, histories, and places. The pilot year iteration of the RSI was initiated per two explicit design conjectures (Sandoval, 2014) related to epistemic fluency (Bang and Medin, 2010; Cajete, 2000; Markauskaite and Goodyear, 2017) and local scientific identity (Semkin et al., 2017; Vareles et al., 2012). First, we conjectured that RSI participants would develop epistemic fluency  by navigating and integrating diverse knowledge traditions through collaborative engagement with boundary objects (Akkerman and Bakker, 2011; Star and Griesemer, 1989) that are meaningful across social contexts. Activities like hybrid scientific poster/in fographic assignments and cross-cultural science communication lectures should prompt learners to translate between university and community perspectives, designerly and scientific reasoning, and Western and Indigenous knowledge systems. This should foster  learning through dialogue, empathic reasoning, and epistemic games.  Second, RSI participants would develop l ocal scientific identity by engaging research questions grounded in local ecological and social contexts, including collaborative research on local mine bioremediation and creative reflection in the local salience of research. Such a design should facilitate identity work, allowing learners to explore and explicitly link scientific and local cultural identities.

## Method

A formal mixed-methods (Teddlie & Tashakkori, 2009) design-based implementation research (DBIR; Penuel and Fishman, 2012) approach was used to examine student learning in the pilot semester of the RSI course. The study triangulated quantitative and qualitative data to understand how students developed research skills, scientific 3093 confidence, and community-oriented perspectives through participation in a community-engaged, interdisciplinary course-based research experience. Data sources included post-course surveys, semi-structured interviews, and course artifacts. Ten of eleven students completed a modified Undergraduate Research Student Self-Assessment (URSSA; Weston & Laursen, 2015), which measured perceived gains in research skills and selfefficacy. Two additional validated survey instruments –the Predictors of Scientific Civic E ngagement (PSCE; Alam et al., 2023) and the Place Attachment Index (PAI; Williams & Vaske, 2003) --captured orientation to community and place. Two students and one teaching assistant participated in semistructured interviews (30–120 minutes) after the course that explored learning experiences and learning processes, and focused on the role that elements of course design played in promoting learning outcomes of interests. Data analysis involved descriptive statistics for survey items and thematic coding of interviews to document how specific course structures, assignments, and interactions supported learning across boundaries of discipline and culture. Analytic memos and data displays (Miles and Huberman, 1994) integrated findings across sources to identify patterns in outcomes and mechanisms of learning for subsequent theory building and design refinement. Students reported gains in scientific competence, civic orientation, and– to a lesser extent –place-based identification. URSSA measures suggest growth in scientific thinking and practice, with the highest mean gains in “Figuring out the next step in a resea rch project” (M = 4.70) and “Understanding the relevance of research to my coursework” (M = 4.60). Gains were similarly strong for “Preparing a scientific poster” (M = 4.80), “Making oral presentations” (M = 4.40), and “Defending an argument when asked questions” (M = 4.30). Personal and identity-related URSSA items revealed similar development. Students reported substantial gains in “Confidence in my ability to do well in future science courses” (M = 4.50) and “Taking greater care in conducting procedures in the lab or field” (M = 4.50), underscoring the growth of both research competence and conscientiousness. Artand design-based strategies, such as creating hybrid poster-infographics, mediated these learning gains by giving students multimodal means to organize and communicate their findings, helping them make progress in terms of both procedural research skills, articulating knowledge in public and interdisciplinary settings, and beginning to identify as a capable scientist. One first-year student summarized this shift: “Before I started the class, scientific research seemed like this alien world. Now, it feels like I can actually do this.” Evidence from the PSCE supported the RSI’s second design conjecture on integrated local scientific identity. Students rated “I value the importance of using my science skills to improve life in my community” highest (M = 4.70), followed by “I am confident  in my ability to use my science skills to make a difference in a community” and “I plan to become involved in my community using my science skills” (both M = 3.80). Boundary objects such as reflective poems mediated this civic orientation by connecting pe rsonal identity with ecological and social responsibility. One student reflected, “It showed me how important it is for research to start in a place where you’re trying to identify a community issue and then base all of your science off of that.” Connection to place was evident, but relatively less strong. On the PAI, “Being at this place says a lot about who I am” (M = 3.11) received the highest rating, while “I identify strongly with this place” (M = 2.44) was lowest, suggesting a developing sense of local identification. “The things I do at this place I would enjoy doing just as much at a similar site” (M = 3.22) suggested partial substitutability, an expected result for students early in their studies, who grew up outside of the region, and who were new to local issues. Student reflections contextualized these numbers: “I learned a lot about the specifics of the Pueblo of Laguna and the Jackpile Mine. I had never known about it before.” Another student noted, “Being in this program made me think about how I’m connected tonew Mexico—the land and the people who’ve lived here before me.”

## Significance

CBREs are effective but relatively novel and complex learning environments that are expanding in university curricula. This study provides insights into if and how they can be designed using principles of community engagement and place-based learning to reframe undergraduate research as a relational and ethical practice rather than solely a technical one. In the case of the RSI, by combining narrative, art, and local ecological inquiry, RSI positioned science as a practice of care that connects knowledge pr oduction with social and environmental accountability. Findings suggest that the course design fostered both technical and civic dimensions of scientific learning. Qualitative analyses of participant perceptions of learning processes and mechanisms —which w ill be presented in greater depth in the full presentation—indicate that future iterations of the course should deepen local engagement through field-based collaboration, use of creative boundary objects (e.g., poems, infographics), and science communicati on to strengthen relational accountability and local commitment. Specific design recommendations will be elaborated for exploration and refinement in discussion. 3094 Akkerman, S. F., & Bakker, A. (2011). Boundary crossing and boundary objects. Review of Educational Research, 81(2), 132–169.

3095 Partnering with different Communities in STEAM learning: Culturally Responsive E-Textile Learning for Expression Zhuoyun Joy Cai, Xintian Tu-Shea, Naomi Thompson zhuoyunc@buffalo.edu, tuxintian@gmail.com, naomitho@buffalo.edu University at Buffalo Abstract: Guided by design-based research and the conjecture map approach, this study applied a culturally responsive approach to  STEAM activities across two communities. In an  African American community, children engaged in culturally grounded conversations that informed artifacts expressing pride and identity. In an  Asian American community, children’s designs reflected cultural expression grounded in family memories. Findings suggest that adapting conjecture maps can support cultural expression and inclusive STEAM experiences. Recent scholarship emphasizes incorporating culturally responsive pedagogy into STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics) education. These approaches are often enacted through construction kits such as e-textiles, which position cultural resources as integral to the technological exploration process and enhance students’ learning and design processes (Peppler & Thompson, 2024; Searle & Kafai, 2015). As Wohlwend and Peppler (2017) observe, such material engagements link tools and techniques to valued knowledge and heritage, allowing stories and meanings to emerge through making. These experiences enhance non-dominant learners’ STEM engagement by connecting circuitry and design with personal and cultural narratives (e.g., TofelGrehl et al., 2017).  Despite the potential of culturally responsive pedagogy with e-textile tools, research often overlooks learners’ prior experiences, families, and community cultural resources (Bush, 2020; Roque et al., 2021). Addressing this gap requires aligning design with local values, children lived experiences and personal narratives. Therefore, building on culturally relevant and sustaining pedagogies (Ladson-Billings, 1995; Paris & Alim, 2017), this study aims to address the following research questions:1) How were the learning designs through conjecture maps adapted to consider the partner community’s cultural values and ways of knowing?  2) In what ways did students’ e-textile creations reflect their personal, familial, and cultural values and experiences? From 2023 to 2025, we partnered with two community organizations in the Northeastern U.S., First Maple Church (FMC) in an African American community and Riverside Club (RC) in an Asian American community, engaging students in STEAM workshop through culturally responsive pedagogy (Fig. 1). Using  conjecture mapping approach (Lee, 2018; Sandoval, 2014) within Design-Based Research  (Collins, 1992), we explored diverse community in relation to th eir cultural values and  histories. We used conjecture mapping as a retrospective analytic tool to iteratively refine our design in response to issues identified in Year 1 and to strengthen collaborations in Year 2. Both workshops consisted of four sessions over four days. We collected second-year data from both sites. We video-recorded all activities, then applied Interaction Analysis (Jordan & Henderson,

1995) and Derry et al.’s (2010) framework. We selected one case from each community (see Table 1) to show

how design adaptations supported students’ creations and cultural expression through making. Figure 1                                                                         Table 1 Partnership with Two Research Sites                            Demographic Information and Artifacts of Participants Based on reflections from Year 1 at both sites, we continuously modified and adapted  the design conjectures (embodiment and mediating processes) while retaining the high-level conjecture and theoretical conjectures in our conjecture map to better align with cultural values, histories, and cognitive styles of students (see Fig. 2). At the African American site, we incorporated quilt patches as the central mode of expression to reflect the site’s cultural-historical connection to sewing practices that supported both community service and its global mission work. At the Asian community site, we adapted the embodiment process to learners’ developmental levels and 3096 made the mediating process flexible to support children’s exploration through co-construction. We use two cases to show how the se adjustments created space for culturally meaningful artifacts and strengthened children’s creativity in design.

Case 1: First Maple Church (FMC) — Cultural artifacts through learning (Mark) To better align with FMC’s culturally relevant resources, we modified four elements of the embodiment process by adding fabric for patchwork and incorporating media on fabric history to support identity exploration (see Fig. 2). These changes created space for students to make circuit-based e-textile artifacts on fabrics of their choice and to express their stories. We select ed Mark, a 9-year-old boy, to show how this revised design  supported his expression in practice.  Mark’s learning evolved across lessons and culminated in an unfinished but meaningful artifact. In the first session, after being introduced to African American quilting history through video clips, Mark engaged with the history of enslaved people and quilting, showing historical awareness through discussions on language and representation. On Day 4, Mark created a fabric "freedom" flag with a blue background and a yellow star. He placed the power holder on the star and the LED in the sky, drawing on the historical meanings of “freedom” discussed in the first lesson (see Fig. 3). His artifact shows how the revised design conjecture supported storytelling by connecting personal and cultural experience to African American heritage and linking past and present, thereby fostering identity development through culturally responsive STEAM activity. Case 2: Riverside Club (RC) — From “cultural” to "personal and meaningful” (Adrain) The second case comes from RC, where we worked with a younger age group (participants ages 5– 7). To better align with their developmental characteristics and emerging cultural memories, we adapted the embodiment process by using story-based activities and simplified materials, such as larger bulb light s. We also revised the mediating process  by acknowledging observed children’s fragmented memories, encouraging exploratory attempts such as scribbling, and restructuring tasks and participation formats. We chose Adrian, a 6-year-old boy, to show how these adjustments supported more personally meaningful artifacts (e.g., self-portraits) and enhanced children’s confidence in the design process. Adrian first struggled to generate ideas when teachers invited students to design artifacts that reflected who they were but was inspired by Pokémon after a discussion about their favorite animations (see Fig. 3). He chose Pikachu because both he and his father l iked this character, and choosing Pikachu reminded him of his love for his dad. Adrian placed a red light on Pikachu’s mouth, saying it symbolized a police siren, which represen ted his dream of “saving the world.” This moment highlights how age-appropriate design enabled second-generation children to express identity through e-textiles by weaving together intercultural experiences, popular culture, family relationships, and aspirations into meaningful designs. Figure 2                                                                                                Figure 3 Revision of the Conjecture Map in the Two Research Sites                                Mark and Adrian’s E-Textile Works Prior work on culturally relevant pedagogy (Ladson-Billings, 1995) and culturally sustaining pedagogy (Paris & Alim, 2017) highlights the importance of linking instruction to learners’ cultural repertoires. This study extends this vision into STEAM learnin g by adapting designs to community contexts and children’s cultural resources. Our study reveals the need for future design that: (1) reimagining conjecture maps to align with partner communities' cultural identity-affirming design; (2) integrating material and personal cultural resources to coconstruct agency for underrepresented learners; and (3) recognizing students’ developmental limits and support developmentally appropriate practices. We hope this work inspires scholars and educators to design community-based culturally responsive pedagogy to better support nondominant students in STEAM learning, benefiting both their STEM learning and humanistic development.

3098 Pre-Service Teachers’ Perceptions of Environment-Focused Mathematics Tasks: Lessons from a Partnership with Local Scientists Tracy E. Dobie, Bailey N. Ondricek, Lynne Zummo tracy.dobie@utah.edu, bailey.ondricek@utah.edu, lynne.zummo@utah.edu University of Utah Abstract: Given the rapidly changing environmental conditions affecting communities globally, environmental education  must be integrated into K-12 schooling. Through partnerships with local environmental scientists, we  developed elementary mathematics tasks that engage students in authentic sensemaking related to environmental issues. We use a multiple case study design to consider pre-service teachers' perceptions of the tasks and propose design conjectures that can inform the design of tasks that are perceived as beneficial and usable. In a time of pressing environmental problems, it is critical that environmental issues be taken up meaningfully in K-12 education (Morales-Doyle, 2017). However, enacting lessons that center student sensemaking of complex environmental issues can be a challenge for teachers  given concerns such as time constraints and the politization of such issues (Blank, 2013; Nation & Feldman, 2021). These concerns can be exacerbated for pre-service teachers (PSTs), who must also navigate socialization into the teaching profession and pressures to conform  (Bloomfield, 2010; Zeichner & Gore, 1990). Our team of teacher educators partnered with environmental scientists to create a set of environment-focused K-12 mathematics and science tasks  that are locally relevant, center student sensemaking, and feel approachable for PSTs. This poster focuses on the elementary mathematics tasks, exploring the following research questions: What features of environmentally based mathematics tasks support pre-service teachers’ perceptions of the benefits and feasibility of using such tasks in their future classrooms? What challenges do pre-service teachers identify related to utilizing environment-focused math tasks in their future classrooms? Conceptual grounding Research in science education has demonstrated the value of using phenomena—observable situations or events — to ground science learning (e.g., Windschitl et al., 2008). R elevant phenomena c an engage students in the sensemaking and explanatory practices sought in modern  science and math  standards (National Governors Association Center for Best Practices & Council of Chief State School Officers, 2010; Passmore et al., 2014). Environmental phenomena,  or naturally occurring observable situations connected to issues of environmental quality, can provide rich  contexts for STEM learning  (e.g., Gürbüz & Çalik, 2021). P articularly impactful are local phenomena that offer deep engagement with meaningful issues (Aguirre et al., 2019; Lee & Grapin, 2022) and work toward environmental justice (Skovsmose, 2023). In designing novel learning experiences around local environmental phenomena, this study builds on learning sciences research that has advocated for integrating place and civic participation in science learni ng (e.g., Birmingham & Calabrese Barton, 2014)  and engaging students with local sociopolitical and socioscientific issues (e.g., Morales-Doyle, 2017; Zeidler et al., 2019). At the same time, there are a range of documented challenges when  teachers use environment-focused tasks and tasks that center student sensemaking, such as teacher anxiety and lack of confidence (Meylani, 2025), fear of  letting go of control and students experiencing frustration (Dobie et al., 2025), and concerns about controversy (Nation & Feldman, 2021). In mathematics, PSTs  have struggled with having sufficient knowledge to meaningfully integrate environmental topics into math curriculum; needing time and support to work with and reflect on such tasks, develop relevant  pedagogical strategies and  content knowledge, and address both mathematics and societal issues in conjunction, emphasizing action steps and ways to assume responsibility (Kanandjebo, 2024; Steffensen & Kasari, 2023; Su et al., 2023). Our research team partner ed with environmental scientists to identify locally relevant environmental issues that could be made accessible to K-12 students. Partners shared details of their work that we used to  design tasks aligning with state standards; tasks were then shared with the partners to get feedback. The elementary math tasks 3099 focused on the work of Dr. Alexandra Ponette -González, whose lab researches the role of trees in reducing air pollution (e.g., Ellis et. al., 2023). We developed three tasks: a kindergarten task introducing the idea  of trees as a barrier to air pollution that involves math concepts related to counting and comparison, a first/second grade task where students hypothesize about what tree types are best for blocking air pollution and then collect and represent survey data describing classmates’ hypotheses, and a fourth/fifth grade task in which  students approximate the area of different leaves and determine  the amount of particulate matter each leaf type might collect. Tasks were reviewed by three groups of 6 PSTs in an elementary math methods class at a large university in the Mountain West United States  (N=18). After small group discussions and a whole class review, each PST completed a written exit ticket to reflect on what was novel or interesting to them about the task they reviewed, benefits and challenges they would anticipate from using the task, and whether (and why) they would be likely to use the task. A udio recordings of small and whole group discussions  were collected. Through a multiple case study (Yin, 2009), we identified  themes across groups and contrasts in perceptions of the tasks. Two team members reviewed all data and engaged in inductive coding (Miles et al., 2014) to identify patterns in two primary areas: PSTs’ perceived benefits and challenges of using the tasks in their future classrooms. We coded all written exit ticket data and compared emergent findings with content on each group’s poster. We then listened to each audio recording to identify quotes that exemplify each theme, as well as any new themes that emerged. We identified three themes across the data analyzed. First, i ncluding novel and complex science content in tasks posed a challenge for PSTs while also contributing to perceptions of rich integration.  At least one PST  in each group mentioned integration as a benefit of the tasks. At the same time, all six PSTs  in the grade 4/5 group grappled with the novelty of the science content integrated in the task, as the idea of leaves collecting particulate matter from the air was a new topic for them. One PST wrote, “It seemed confusing to me and I think that it would make my students confused as well.”  PSTs’ comments suggest that a lack of familiarity with the environmental topic played a role in their  assumption that the task would be too complex for students.  Second, PSTs perceived tasks as being authentic and locally relevant, and having high potential for student engagement and applicability. Again, at least one PST  in each group mentioned the real-world aspect of the task  being engaging for students, with all six  PSTs in the grade 1 /2 group attending to the local relevance of the task and perceived impact on students. One PST wrote, "This is a task that I think would leave students being so aware of the trees in their communities and which ones block the most pollution. It's an activity that wouldn't just stay in the classroom but would influence their world view!” Third, PSTs perceived tasks as empowering students to take action and make change in their communities.  At least one PST  in each group identified the value of this empowerment, with all six PSTs in the kindergarten group noting this theme. For example, one PST wrote, “The benefit of using this task is that students will be able to see how they are capable of making change even if [they’re] small.” We connected the three themes above with aspects of the tasks that likely supporte d or worked against perceptions of the tasks as beneficial and usable. From these analyses, we propose three design conjectures: First, increased novelty or complexity of science content necessitates additional time for  PSTs to unpack that content to enhance perceived task usability. While content integration was perceived as meaningful and rich—a valuable finding, given that teachers often have little time in their schedules for science teaching (Blank, 2013)— additional time to dig into the science content likely would have helped PSTs gain access to the task. Second, i ncluding investigation of both issues and solutions in environment-based math tasks makes potentially controversial topics more accessible and likely to be used in the classroom.  No PSTs expressed concerns about the tasks being too controversial or getting backlash from parents—concern s that were voiced about other tasks explored in this class and have been discussed in prior research (e.g., Nation & Feldman, 2021). Given PSTs’ emphasis on potential for community impact and  empowerment, we propose that considering solutions can support PSTs’ perceptions of the usability of environment-focused math tasks—aligning with the notion of “constructive hope” that is necessary for dealing with complex environmental challenges (e.g., Ojala, 2023). Third, t o support potential for student empowerment, include advocacy-focused action steps. Only the kindergarten task included an option for students to explicitly advocate for change by talking with someone in a position of power, and the theme of empowerment came up most in that group. Thus, we propose that including an opportunity for students to advocate to an external stakeholder has the potential to enhance PSTs’ perspectives of the tasks as supporting student empowerment. We recognize that this data comes from a limited sample of PSTs, and that PSTs reviewed the tasks but did not implement them or participate in the tasks as students. A second iteration of this work recently took place to address these issues and test our proposed design conjectures. We are particularly grateful to Dr. Alexandra Ponette-González and her lab for their sharing their work with us. 3101 Middle School Teacher Conceptual Change of Culturally Responsive Pedagogy Through Teaching Computer Science: A

## Longitudinal Case Study

Gillian Bausch, University of Texas at El Paso, xbausch@utep.edu Abstract: This study investigate s how a middle school teacher developed understandings of and practice in  culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP) to teach computer science (CS). Grounded in conceptual change theory, this study explores a teacher’s CRP pedagogical development through evolving definitions and their enactments. The findings reveal how a teacher reflected on and refined pre-existing notions of CRP and beliefs about “who belongs to CS”, gradually transforming them into more expert-like knowledge and practice. Computer science education is shifting from a focus on technical skills toward critical literacy, which is essential for modern life. To address historic inequities, educators have turned to equity-oriented approaches like CRP to empower students as agents of change. However, a critical gap remains: there is insufficient empirical investigation into how teachers internalize and implement CRP within their CS classrooms (Hwang et al., 2023). The foundation of this study is a multi-year professional learning project funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF), which aimed to build middle school teachers’ capacity for teaching Computer Science (CS) by engaging students with diverse backgrounds in creating apps for social good (Ni et al., 2021). In this paper, I aim to address two research questions:

• How did the teacher develop a conceptual understanding of CRP to teach CS?

• How did the teacher’s pedagogical enactment of CRP evolve across years in diverse CS classrooms?

## Theoretical framework and related work

Culturally responsive pedagogy (CRP) acknowledges and leverages students’ cultural assets and identities to cultivate meaningful learning experiences and support student success.  CRP has gained prominence in CS education because it can effectively reach traditionally marginalized populations, which has led tonew efforts toward broadening participation in CS (Madkin et al., 2020; Scott et al., 2015).  Many CS education scholars and organizations have conducted research studies and developed guidance and frameworks for teachers to effectively implement CRP in teaching CS  (Leonard and Sent ance, 2021; Scott et al., 2013, 2015). While frameworks like Culturally Responsive-Sustaining Computer Science Education (CRS-CSE) provide normative pillars for classroom implementation  (Kapor Center, 2021), there is a critical gap in empirical research to understand  the internal journey that teachers undergo to process CRP concepts. This study addresses this gap by applying a dual conceptual change lens. First, by applying diSessa’s Knowledge-in-Pieces lens (diSessa, 1988, 1993, 2014), this study moves beyond seeing teacher’s development as a single theory-shift, instead interpreting it as the gradual, context-sensitive organization of fragmented p-prims—intuitive knowledge elements derived from personal intuitive knowledge (i.e., life experience, professional identity). P-prims can help map how the discrete pieces of understanding eventually coalesce into coordination classes — a large, complex, and systematic collection of knowledge represented in learners’ mental schema (diSessa, 1993), which provides teachers  with the systematic fluency required to adapt a pedagogy across diverse classroom contexts. However, pedagogical growth in CRP is not merely a technical reorganization of knowledge; it is deeply embedded in social and structural dimensions. To account for this, I integrate Philip’s Ideology-in-Pieces (2011) framework to scrutinize the naturalized axioms that underpin teacher ’s sense-making. These axioms represent socially-derived, taken-for-granted assumptions—such as deep-seated beliefs about "who belongs in CS” that can either catalyze or constrain a teacher's pedagogical evolution. By combining these dual lenses, the study provides a more nuanced narrative of a teacher’s conceptual change trajectory of their CRP concept development  in teaching CS. In addition to examining teachers ’ p-prims in the development of CRP concepts, I also investigate the impact of teacher’s socially derived natural axioms (e.g., stereotypes and assumptions) about their students’ cultures on the formation of their  own concepts. Combining both physical p-prims and socially derived natural axioms provides a more comprehensive picture of the role of pre-existing beliefs and cultural assumptions in teacher’s conceptual change.

## Method

3102 This study is situated within a 5-year Research-Practitioner Partnership (RPP) involving two universities and three urban school districts. The project  hosted professional development (PD) workshops and professional learning communities (PLC) to support middle school teachers in developing a sustainable, CRP-embedded computer science and digital literacy (CSDL) curriculum centered on mobile app development for community good. The participant, Jen, is a white technology teacher with 25 years of experience but no prior formal training in CS or CRP. Over four years of participation, she implemented the curriculum with over 400 students in a district serving high populations of underrepresented minorities and students with special needs. To capture Jen's four-year CRP pedagogical trajectory, we collected: (1)  Verbatim end-of-year interviews; (2) Meeting notes from semi-structured researcher-teacher one-on-one sessions; and (3) Teacher reflections from PD and PLC meetings. Data were analyzed using narrative analysis (Lieblich et al., 1998) to first map the complete spectrum of Jen ’s CS integration over time. I also extracted specific CRP applications, which were coded through dual conceptual change lenses, as discussed above. The trajectory of conceptual change Jen’s four-year development reveals a three-phase evolution of CRP, transitioning from a baseline necessity for contextual relevance to a sophisticated commitment to cultural awareness. Initially, her practice was activated by a gender equity p-prim derived from her  former professional identity as a female engineer, which led her to challenge the male-dominated representation of programmers. By Year 3, she demonstrated emerging coordination class fluency through her  technology class “ Inventor and Invention” unit, where she leveraged student cultural assets to drive engagement. By Year 4, Jen demonstrated the formation of a coordination class bt restructuring the curriculum to address representation gaps identified by her students. This shift represents a move from reactive, crisis-driven interventions toward proactive, student-led critical reflection on the societal impact of CS.

Navigating axioms and deficit ideologies Despite Jen’s growth in pedagogical enactment, the I deology-in-Pieces lens highlights the persistence of deep-seated naturalized axioms. While she successfully modified her curriculum to be more inclusive, her underlying belief system continued to harbor deficit ideologies. In Year 2, Jen attributed unequal student out comes to socioeconomic factors and home environments, such as  whether parents read to students, rather than systemic barriers or curriculum design. These axioms remained largely unchallenged throughout the study, suggesting that CRP conceptions are discrete, adaptable elements that do not always change in unison. In general, the findings suggest that developing CRP competence is a non-linear process of restructuring knowledge fragments within the CS context. While Jen achieved systematic fluency in curriculum modification, her persistent biases underscore that well-intentioned te achers can implement equity-oriented tools while maintaining problematic social assumptions. For the Learning Sciences, this indicates that professional development must move beyond prescriptive pillars to explicitly target the cognitive elements of common sense and naturalized axioms that educators bring to the classroom. Collectively, this study provides a roadmap for fostering the nuanced, expert-like CRP knowledge necessary to empower marginalized students as agents of social change.

In conclusion, this study applied two distinguished conceptual change theories to understand a teacher ’s CRP conceptual change through participation in a PD program and implementing CRP to teach CS. By applying Knowledge-in-Pieces and Ideology-in-Pieces frameworks, this study maps the non-linear trajectory of a teacher’s CRP development within a CS context. Empirically, the findings demonstrate how teachers can flexibly refine fragmented knowledge into “expert-like” pedagogical enactments. Theoretically, the study reveals that while instructional practices may evolve, deep-rooted naturalized axioms and deficit biases can persist even in well-intentioned educators. These insights provide a critical roadmap for designing CRP-focused CS  professional development that moves beyond technical  curriculum implementation to explicitly challenge the underlying deficit belief systems that can persist in well-intentioned CS educator. 3103 diSessa, A.A.
