Sustainability, 14(21), Article 14549. https://doi.org/10.3390/su142114549 3128 Seeds in the Soil: Conceptualizing Urban Gardens as Educational Technologies Colin Hennessy Elliott, Drexel University, ch3457@drexel.edu Christopher G. Wright, Drexel University, cgw57@drexel.edu Abstract: To make conceptual room  for designing for and researching learning in urban agricultural spaces in Philadelphia, we argue for the conceptualizing urban gardens – in all their plurality – as educational technologies themselves. To explicate the conceptualization, we depict garden infrastructures – social, material, and cultural – and their alignment to a larger theorization of education technology. Considering urban gardens as educational technologies in Philadelphia offers a window into  their possibilities as keystones in learning pathways for children, youth, and adults across the city.

Grounding Community gardens and farms are important learning spaces for communities to develop place-based knowledges and relations. They also offer cross-cultural challenges and opportunities in even defining what gardens are and their applications to STEM learning (i.e., Bang, 2016b). Bang (2016a) points out that the inability to know about the plants and animals we interact with in our lives, is a fundamental result of the displacing nature of settler colonialism and the commodifying of land, waters, flora, and fauna. Urban gardens, therefore, pr esent opportunities to develop spaces to re-place community knowledges of – and relationship to -- the lands, water, and living organisms they live amongst (Hect & Nelson, 2022). They can be powerful learning spaces for learning about community and culture  (Penniman, 2018; Bang, 2016b) and dreaming about a more just future.  In this poster we use the city of Philadelphia to conceptualize the possibilities for learning urban gardens offer. In the United States, school gardens have been used for a long time as tools for experimental education and investigations  (Subramaniam, 2002). Since the 1990s, school gardens across the country have waxed and waned in importance (Blair, 2009). Yet now,  school and other less formal learning spaces, are awash in digital educational technologies that, seemingly, idealize individual learning (i.e., Waters, 2020) or police learners’ behavior (i.e., Robinson, 2021). Currently, technology industrialists are marketing so-called Artificial Intelligence tools as useful learning technologies in K-12 learning institutions and beyond. In solidarity with scholars calling for a luddite praxis to critique the seemingly inevitability of AI in schools (i.e., Logan 2024)  we argue for the conceptualizing urban gardens – in all their plurality – as educational technologies: tools for learning and teaching about one’s relation to the lands, waters, flora and fauna. Further, we believe in their potential as places and spaces for joyful transgressions in dreaming a more just, relational, future (Vossoughi, et al., 2023). According to the City of Philadelphia’s first urban agricultural plan (Philadelphia, 2023), urban farms and gardens provide opportunities for people to engage in the food system and beautification of their city on lands that are not their own. In this way, urban gardens and farms are inherently in tension with larger hegemonic notions of property and individual prosperity. They produce spatial imaginaries (Jenkins, 2021) that often resist the oppressive structures of city developments and provide foundations for liberatory material practices. Framing them as educational technologies offers conceptual space to understand and design with their liberatory praxis. Spatial productions and educational technologies Spatial imaginaries are how socio-spatial relations are collectively understood through perception and experience—people's discursive and performative practices within a given space shape these relations (Jenkins, 2021; Mann & Dudek, 2024). Building from scholarship within geography, a spatial imaginary framework considers how societal beliefs on race, class, and gender are reflected in the organization and control of physical spaces (Jenkins, 2021). Spatial  imaginaries conceptualizations often produce material impacts through policy and/or distribution of resources.  Urban gardens, in defiance of the imagined geographies of urban spaces that are often structured by oppression and discrimination (Jenkins, 2021; Lipman, 2018), often rely on speculative nature of spatial imaginaries. Scholarship in spatial imaginaries contends that spaces are not inert, neutral, or ahistorical (Hawthorne, 2019; McKittrick, 2006). Spatial imaginaries challenge us to theorize and problematize the dominant spatial narratives that dictate how we view “urban” and “gardens” within the larger educational enterprise (Jenkins, 2021; Mann & Dudek, 2024). In producing such  spatial imaginaries, urban gardens are products of complex infrastructures (i.e., soil, access to water, labor, plants from elsewhere); they are a technology. Drawing 3129 on scholarship in STS (i.e., Benjamin, 2018; Star, 1990; Winner, 1989) we articulate that urban gardens are “technologies” in their social construction as products and producers of spatial imaginaries in urban landscapes. Since Winner (1989) asked “ do artifacts have politics ?” using the case of Robert Moses intentionally racist design of highways in New York, scholars have theorized the socio political nature of technologie s. Benjamin (2018), for example, argues that in shaping our social and material experiences in the world, “race itself is a kind of technology” which “operates as a tool of vision and division” (p. 38). In this way, technologies shape the powered relations of who uses them and how  (Star, 1990). For  example, anti-Black racism is encoded into many of our digital technologies (Benjamin, 2018) perpetuating injustices at the interactional and structural levels. Educational technologies – although often undertheorized with a taken-for-granted view of technology (Oliver, 2013) --  are products of large social and material infrastructures, including the ethical nature of their applications (Januszewski & Molenda, 2008). They are also products and producers of stories we tell about learning and technology. Visions of how people learn (i.e., input-output behaviorist perspective on learning) are less visible  but deeply important  parts of the infrastructures of educational technologies (Watters, 2020). Therefore, conceptualizing urban gardens as educational technologies challenges us to articulate the underlying visions of how people learn in them and the social and material infrastructures that they both produce and are products of.  As Bang (2016b) articulates, depending on their form, function, and local cultural practices, gardens have the potential  to shape powerful learning experiences. This moves us from seeing them as merely contexts for ecological learning to being  tools for developing social, cultural, and environmental relations with our communities of humans and non-humans.

## Conceptual framework: Urban farms and gardens as educational technologies

Urban agriculture (gardens & farms) refers to a wide array of places and organizations, even within the city limits of Philadelphia. In Philadelphia, by some counts there are 193 community gardens, 38 school gardens, and 71 community farms.  Their spaces vary from small lots to complex spaces across neighborhoods. Some are organized as, first and foremost, community spaces (i.e., Norris Square Neighborhood Project) that celebrate cultural heritage. Others are organized as a series of single plots that local  community members can apply to receive opportunity to take care of (i.e., Summer-Winter Garden). Others are farms developed on vacant lots with the goals to both support local community members in participating in land-based practices and feeding the local community (i.e., Santuary Farm). Others are organized around a particular way to grow food like through permaculture practices (i.e.,  Fernhill Food Forest). What holds these different forms and functions  together are the prevailing activities of growing food and other plants in relation with and for community. Each of these types of community urban gardens are different shades of the garden as educational technology: tools and infrastructures used to support learning. Each has undergirding infrastructures of social organization, lands, histories, and material & machines that make them what they are (Winner, 1989). They are spatial productions that shape how people who engage with them see their relations in the broader world. And each are loci of community dreaming (Benjamin, 2024) where communities can both become more in tune with the seasonal nature of food, of living, and of the lands and waters around them. In Philadelphia – a majority Black & Brown city – each of the example gardens we share above  offer a re-placing and re-membering of what the land can be, in relation to cultural heritage, especially for Black and Brown people (Penniman, 2021; Penniman, 2018). In other words, they are grounds for developing what Germinaro (2025) calls Black Spatial Storylines. For example, the Norris Square Neighborhood Project, which has been around since 1972 as a site for community and youth programming, ha s developed its programming, artwork, and even gardens as homages to the Puerto Ricandiaspora that incorporates so many from the surrounding community. This offers a spatial storyline about who belongs in that neighborhood and how their histories of gardening and food can be represented. As technologies producing different spatial imaginaries, urban gardens have pedagogical possibilities towards more liberatory environmental education (Hecht & Nelson, 2023; Bang 2016). They are tools for dreaming  about and developing community (see Norris Square Neighborhood Project) and infrastructures that we, as STEM educators, can learn from.

## Implications

Conceptualizing urban gardens as educational technologies opens up a possibility for further depicting the impact they have as intergenerational learning spaces  that center joy, the work of community garden organizers, and imagining gardens’ role in developing more just futures that unroot settler colonial logics and legacies  through spatial and community relations. They offer an entry point into what Vossoughi et al. (2023) articulate as relationality within and across humans, place, and more than human relations.  Further, it offers educators and educational researchers conceptual seeding to grow learning spaces through co-designing with leaders and organizers of community gardens and farms. 3131 AI as a Lesson Planning Thought Partner: A Design-Based Pilot with Preservice Elementary Teachers Gianna Shields, San José State University, gianna.shields@sjsu.edu Abstract: This design-based pilot study investigated how a group of elementary pre-service teachers used Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a thought partner in a teaching practicum seminar. They learned about an AI-Mediated Teaching Framework in 3 sessions and used it  to design a sequence of three 45-to-50-minute AI-Mediated standards-aligned lessons. Mixed methods drew on anonymous pre/post surveys (pre n=9, post=6, unpaired). Quantitatively, agreement among the respondents increased across all items (i.e., confidence, equity planning, bias awareness), with all preservice teachers agreeing that AI has a positive role in K-12 education. discussed.

In response to the growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in TK-12 education, I redesigned a first semester seminar around the AI-Mediated Teaching Framework (Shields, 2025). By using AI as a thought partner, preservice teachers use reflective cycles to design inclusive, differentiated lessons for diverse learners in their classrooms. This paper reports design-based evidence from that redesign, examining pre-post shifts and how the framework influenced preservice teachers’ lesson planning practices. Preparing preservice teachers to design rigorous, inclusive lessons that focus on higher-order thinking can be a challenge. Design in this case refers to design-based research (DBR), which highlights the importance of iterative refinement, and attention to c omplex learning situations (Brown, 1992; Cobb et al., 2003; Design-Based Research Collective, 2003). Building on social design principles that focus on equity, historicity, and participant agency (Guti érrez & Ragoff, 2003; Gutiérrez, 2008; Jurow & Shea, 2015), this study piloted how first semester preservice teachers leveraged an AI-Mediated Teaching Framework to plan 3 consecutive lessons in a 5-week intensive seminar. Preservice teachers were encouraged to use one of the AI programs that was modeled in cl ass (ChatGPT, Gemini, MagicSchool) as a planning partner, not a curriculum generator, while documenting prompts, adaptations and reflections. These AI programs were chosen because many of the students in the course had engaged with these programs prior and had some working knowledge of how to use them. This paper asks: (1) How does an AI-mediated teaching framework that embeds social design principles affect preservice Grades K-5 teachers' knowledge of AI, self-confidence, ethical awareness, and equity orientation? (2) How does an AI-mediated teaching framework influence preservice Grades K-5 teachers' ability to plan and develop lesson plans? AI Mediated Teaching Framework Figure 1 AI-Mediated Teaching Framework Figure 1 shows the AI-Mediated Teaching Framework used in this pilot. The framework positions AI as a thought partner for lesson planning by centering pedagogical content knowledge, learner agency and access, applied AI fluency, and ethical/reflexive practice. It guided both the intervention design and the analysis of how preservice teachers used, revised, and evaluated AI-generated outputs. 3132 The study This design-based pilot took place in a 5-week summer practicum seminar in an elementary credential program at a public university in the United States. During the final week of the course, preservice teachers engaged in three class sessions focused on the  AI-Mediated Teaching Framework, guided use of AI tools, and independent planning of a three-lesson sequence. Participants were invited to use tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or MagicSchool as planning partners and to document their prompts, outputs, revisi ons, and reflections. The data included anonymous pre/post surveys from consenting participants (pre n =9, post n=6), lesson plans, and written reflections. Survey items asked about self-reported understanding of AI, confidence integrating AI into lesson planning, awareness of bias, troubleshooting, equitable access planning, and beliefs about AI in K– 12 education. Qualitative data were thematically analyzed across reflections and lesson artifacts with attention to patterns in how preservice teachers used AI, what they accepted or revised, and how they described the role of AI in planning. Because this was a small pilot with anonymous unpaired surveys and a brief intervention, findings are interpreted as descriptive design-based evidence rather than generalizable effects. Three themes emerged across the survey patterns, reflections, and lesson artifacts. AI appeared to support pedagogical structuring and alignment. Across reflections, preservice teachers described using AI to help organize lesson flow, clarify standards alignment, draft checks for understanding, and generate possible exit tickets or sentence frames. Several noted that AI was more useful when prompts were narrow and specific than when they asked for a full lesson. Rather than producing ready-to-teach instruction, AI often functioned as a starting point for planning decisions. Descriptively, survey agreement increased across all items, with the largest gains in confidence integrating AI and planning for equitable access. Preservice teachers used AI to broaden equity-oriented access and supports, particularly through multilingual scaffolds, multiple representations, and differentiated options. In lesson artifacts, candidates incorporated AI-generated suggestions such as sentence frames, visual supports, and culturally connected examples, but they also reported needing to revise these ideas to make them more locally relevant, developmentally appropriate, and feasible within a 45–50 minute lesson. These patterns suggest that AI may help surface access-oriented possibilities, while the teacher remains responsible for selecting and contextualizing them. The most consistent pattern across the lesson plans was adaptation rather thandirect acceptance of AI outputs. Most AI-generated suggestions were revised before being included in lesson plans, indicating that participants were not simply outsourcing planning. Instead, they engaged in a process of accepting, adapting, and rejecting outputs based on pacing, fit, originality, and student needs. Reflections also showed that participants became more attentive to source verification, bias, and representational gaps. At the same time, understanding of training data and algorithmic bias remained less developed than other areas, suggesting that conceptual AI literacy requires more explicit instructional attention.

These findings also surfaced three tensions relevant to teacher education. AI often generated too much content, requiring trimming and simplification. Some preservice teachers worried that AI could flatten teacher creativity or voice. Others found that AI outputs still required careful checking for bias, credibility, and developmental appropriateness. Together, these tensions point to the importance of framing AI as a provisional design partner rather than an authoritative instructional source. This study contributes early design-based evidence that preservice teachers can learn to use AI as a lesson-planning thought partner while retaining pedagogical agency and equity-oriented judgment. The central design insight is that AI appeared most useful when embedded in a routine that began with PCK and used AI for specific, verifiable subtasks rather than full lesson generation. Under these conditions, preservice teachers used AI to support alignment, scaffolding, and brainstorming while continuing to m ake substantive professional decisions about what to keep, revise, or reject. The findings also suggest that teacher education should not treat AI fluency as solely a technical skill. Candidates need opportunities to examine how AI systems work, where bias enters outputs, and how ethical judgment shapes classroom use. In this pilot, confidence and openness appeared to increase more readily thandeeper understanding of training data and algorithmic bias. That gap is important for future design. This study is limited by the small sample, anonymous unpaired surveys, short duration, and reliance on self-report and course-based artifacts. For the Learning Sciences, the contribution is not a claim that AI improves lesson planning in general, but a design-based account of how AI can be positioned to support teacher learning without displacing teacher judgment.

## Acknowledgments

I am extremely grateful to Ferdie Rivera and Sandra Zuniga Ruiz for their generous mentorship and support. 3134 Community Learning Agendas: Aligning Community Knowledge and Collective Inquiry to Address Societal Challenges Heather Killen, Institute for Learning Sciences, hkillen@buffalo.edu Ari Hock, Institute for Learning Sciences, arihock@buffalo.edu Christopher Hoadley, Institute for Learning Sciences, isls@tophe.net Camden Miller, School of Architecture and Planning, camdenmi@buffalo.edu Lauren Fischer, School of Architecture and Planning, lf44@buffalo.edu University at Buffalo Abstract: The most pressing societal challenges cannot be solved in isolation. We introduce community learning agendas as a conceptual and practical tool for aligning and orienting local knowledge and collective inquiry toward solutions. Drawing upon literature in e ducation, organizational science, and public policy research, we define community learning agendas as evolving sets of ideas about whoneeds to learn what to address issues of mutual concern. Developing community learning agendas The most urgent challenges reverberate across global systems, yet their impacts are often felt most acutely at the local level. Together with our community partners in the Northeast of the United States, we ask how a locally instantiated challenge around transportation infrastructure might be met in ways that strengthen solidarities among existing residents, rather than provoking fear and political polarization. We introduce community learning agendas as a tool for aligning and orienting local knowledge and collective inquiry. Drawing on literature in education, planning, organizational science, and public policy, we define a community learning agenda as an evolving set of ideas held by community members about whoneeds to learn what to identify and address issues of mutual concern.  Rather than a static document or artifact, we conceptualize learning agendas as a dynamic process, created and contested through participatory structures. Societal challenges and why they are hard to solve Societal challenges extend beyond individual learners to encompass the complexities of human cultures and the ecological systems we inhabit. This orientation (e.g., Nasir et al., 2020), positions education researchers alongside urban planners, policymakers, and others working to reorganize society for wellbeing, social justice, and planetary survival. Within urban planning, Rittel & Webber (1973) coined the term “wicked problems” to capture the inherent intractability of these kinds of challenges: They are complex, political, and often ambiguously formulated, lacking a clear definition and refusing any kind of definitive solution (e.g., poverty, the rise of authoritarianism, and the climate crisis.). Planning and public policy scholars have recognized the need to address these challenges through learning, though there are varying ideas about the right unit of analysis to theorize and study this kind of learning (e.g., von Schönfeld et al., 2020). Education researchers have formulated related efforts under the guises of problem-based learning (Barrows, 1986), challenge-based learning (Leijon et al., 2022), and place-based education (Sobel, 2004). While these efforts often mobilize students using the existing infrastructures of schooling, meaningfully addressing wicked problems requires learning that spans across ages, disciplines, institutions, and sectors. We need to extend the locus of learning from students and schools to communities writ large. This involves new mechanisms.

The concept of a learning agenda and why it is helpful Community learning agendas help address wicked problems in two key ways: by aligning actors and by orienting collective inquiry around partially overlapping conceptions of the wicked problem. To develop this framing, we draw on psychological research that demonstrates how articulating learning agendas facilitates alignment in classroom settings. We then extend these insights to studies of coalitional alignment across activity systems. We also integrate perspectives from education, organizational science, and policy to understand how learning agendas can be a useful tool for collective inquiry.

Learning agendas as a tool for alignment Learning agendas can help address societal challenges by aligning the goals and activities of diverse actors. In educational psychology the term “learning agenda” was popularized in studies of classroom contexts to measure correlations between learning goals and outcomes. This emphasis on alignment is equally critical beyond the 3135 classroom. Wicked problems require outcomes that benefit society as a whole and demand coordination among people, institutions, and resources. Achieving this coordination requires alignment in how joint work is organized. While Senko et al. (2013) conceptualize alignment as a dyadic relationship between teacher and student, learning scientists are increasingly considering the infrastructuring work needed to create alignment within and across communities (Berger & Hayden, 2025; Engeström et al., 2025). Learning agendas as a guide for collective inquiry Learning agendas can also orient collective inquiry. Scardamalia and Bereiter’s (1991, 1994) concept of knowledge-building communities illustrates this principle in education. Their emphasis on collective questionasking offers a model for conceptualizing community learning agendas: dynamic, evolving sets of ideas (rather than static documents) that guide joint inquiry. Organizational learning research reinforces this focus on inquiry. Argyris and Schön (1978), Greenwood, Argyris, and  Schön (1995), and Brown & Duguid (1991) show that learning in organizations is tied to shifts in practice and underlying assumptions. Learning agendas in this context target systemic change, prompting revisions in mental models, strategies, and norms, rather than surface-level skills. By prioritizing questions that challenge structural assumptions, learning agendas become catalysts for organizational adaptation and innovation.

Zooming out, policy contexts demonstrate how learning agendas can institutionalize learning processes and collective inquiry at scale. In the U.S., the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 mandated “learning agendas” for 24 federal agencies. These agendas were framed as strategic plans for identifying priority questions and systematically addressing evidence-building needs (Newcomer, Olejniczak & Hart, 2022) with agencies implementing learning agendas through structured steps. Understanding from the field of policy development underscores how learning agendas can formalize inquiry and coordination within complex systems, offering lessons for community-based applications. Taken together, these traditions converge on a shared insight; learning agendas are not static lists of topics but dynamic tools for aligning actors and orienting inquiry toward collective community learning.

Operationalizing community learning agendas Learning agendas may be contested, as community members often hold differing views about each other’s knowledge needs and capabilities relative to a particular issue. Moreover, some important societal challenges do not correspond neatly to a single community, but span multiple communities, or may even require the formation of new communities. For this reason, a community learning agenda should continuously evolve through dynamic participation structures. Agendas may emerge spontaneously as people collaborate on shared problems; or they may emerge from deliberate, facilitated processes aimed at assessing current knowledge needs. The Corridors of Community Learning project is our early effort to support the formation of a community learning agenda. The project includes a series of community workshops designed to surface local knowledge related to residents’ neighborhoods and the adjacent highways that have shaped the area’s past, present, and future. We work with residents to help guide inquiry around a central question: What transportation planning decisions should be made regarding two highways bisecting the city? This highly contentious question has been fiercely debated among politicians and local activists, leaving residents questioning the benefits and drawbacks of various possibilities. Analysis indicates that although participants hold differing ideas, they continually seek to understand each other’s perspectives through dialogue and creative collaboration. Moreover, participants identify perspectives that are missing from the conversation and seek to include those  in their ongoing inquiry. The process of building a community learning agenda can help to surface and align local knowledge, catalyzing collective solutions to shared challenges. With our emphasis on community learning agendas, we encourage learning scientists to consider learning beyond the scale of individuals or institutions, to that of the broader community engaged in a societal challenge. When setting learning agendas, it is important to work with a broad set of stakeholders and create a space for shared inquiry, collective goal setting, and capacity building. In other words, rather than institutionalizing a private “regime of learning,” learning agendas should help communities learn to “become public” (Biesta, 2012) by convening local concerns, translating these concerns into publicly accessible endeavors, and then developing the shared knowledge base to address them. Fortunately, learning scientists are well-positioned to facilitate this work. We acknowledge that many within the learning sciences community are already engaged in similar efforts to help communities learn to overcome challenges as they work towards justice and vitality. With this in mind, we hope that by articulating our understanding of a community learning agenda, we might begin to establish a learning agenda within the discipline, to better understand how learning scientists could learn to more effectively engage in this important community-based work. 3136 Argyris, C., & Schon, D. We also thank students Grace Wiseman and Jason Myrick for their support of the workshops. 3137 Feeling like a Scientist, Engineer, and Computer Scientist: Exploring Students’ Disciplinary Identity in an Integrated STEM+C Curriculum Namrata Srivastava, Vanderbilt University, namrata.srivastava@vanderbilt.edu Gabriella Anton, Digital Promise Global, ganton@digitalpromise.org Shruti Jain, Vanderbilt University, shruti.jain@vanderbilt.edu Clayton Cohn, Vanderbilt University, clayton.a.cohn@vanderbilt.edu Umesh Timalsina, Vanderbilt University, umesh.timalsina@vanderbilt.edu Naveeduddin Mohammed, Vanderbilt University, naveeduddin.mohammed@vanderbilt.edu Jennifer Chiu, University of Virginia, jlc4dz@virginia.edu Gautam Biswas, Vanderbilt University, gautam.biswas@vanderbilt.edu Abstract: Integrating computational thinking (CT) into STEM curricula can engage students in authentic, interdisciplinary practices. Yet little is known about whether students perceive themselves as members of these disciplinary communities. This study examines middle school students’ disciplinary identity within a three-week integrated STEM+C Earth  Science curriculum. Analysis of reflection surveys revealed that most students identified with at least one disciplinary role, most often as engineers or comput er scientists, while fewer felt like scientists.

Integrated STEM+C curricula engage students in authentic, interdisciplinary practices that mirror modern scientific and engineering work (Weintrop et al., 2016; Basu et al., 2022). However, doing  authentic interdisciplinary work does not always mean students feel like  authentic members of those disciplines (Archer et al., 2010; Aslan et al., 2024). This distinction between doing and being is critical: students’ developing identities shape their motivation, persistence, and sense of belonging in STEM (Carlone & Johnson, 2007). Carlone and Johnson’s science identity framework comprises competence (scientific knowledge), performance  (enacting scientific practices), and recognition  (being acknowledged as a “science person”). In computing, Kong and Lai

(2022) proposed a parallel framework of engagement, imagination, and affiliation. Yet, existing frameworks have

largely addressed science and computing identities in isolation, leaving the integrated identity work required by STEM+C curricula relatively underexplored. This study addresses that gap by identifying specific curricular experiences that transform “doing” into “being” in an interdisciplinary STEM+C context.

## Instructional context

The SPICE curriculum is a computer-supported, three-week project-based unit (15 lessons, 60– 70 min each) in which students redesign an urban schoolyard to minimize water runoff. It integrates Earth science concepts, NGSS engineering design practices, and computational thinking (CT), with computational modeling bridging science and engineering (McElhaney et al., 2020). Students cycle through three roles: scientists  (Lessons 2–5: building conceptual runoff models), computer scientists  (Lessons 7–10: building rule-based computational models in a Domain-Specific Modeling Language on NetsBlox), and engineers (Lessons 1, 11–13: designing and optimizing a schoolyard solution).

We implemented the curriculum with 104 sixth-grade students (51% male, 49% female; 67% White, 14% Black/African American, 11% Asian, 8% Hispanic/Latino) across four classrooms in an urban public middle school in the southeastern United States, taught by two experienced science teachers. The study was conducted in February 2025 and approved by the Vanderbilt University Institutional Review Board. Upon completing the curriculum, students responded to an anonymous post-survey with three 5-point Likert items (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree): I felt like I was a scientist / engineer / computer scientist while doing the SPICE project. Open-ended prompts followed, asking students to describe when and why they felt this way. We computed descriptive statistics for each Likert item and categorized students into high-identity (ratings greater than and equal to 4) and low-identity (ratings less than 2) groups, then examined identity combination patterns across scientist (S), engineer (E), and computer scientist (C) roles. Open-ended responses were analyzed using iterative in vivo  coding (Saldaña, 2014) into five practice categories: modeling, design, 3138 programming, research, and general curricular structures. Inter-rater reliability on a 20% subset yielded near-perfect agreement (κ = 0.93, SD = 0.11).

## Quantitative analysis

We found that students reported the strongest identity alignment with engineers (M = 3.65, SD = 1.20) and computer scientists (M = 3.56, SD = 1.26), while scientists were weakest (M = 2.94, SD = 1.25). Majorities identified strongly as engineers (63.5%) and computer scientists (67.3%), but only 37.5% did so as scientists, with an equal 37.5% reporting low scientist identity.

Table 1 shows identity combination patterns. Nearly one-third (31.7%) identified with all three roles (SEC); 25% with engineer and computer scientist only (EC). Scientist identity was rarely expressed alone. Only 9.6% did not identify with any role, and 15.4% showed a science-only low-identity pattern. ## Qualitative findings

Open-ended responses revealed distinct identity-practice associations across the three disciplines. Science identity was linked to diverse practices: modeling (23%), programming (11%), research (10%), and design (10%), suggesting an interdisciplinary view of science beyond traditional K –12 activities. Engineering identity centered on design (32%) and modeling (31%), with programming (19%) also prominent, reflecting students’ perception of engineering as authentic problem-solving. Computer science identity was most strongly tied to coding (39%) and computer use (18%) which is a narrower, practice-centric view relative to the other two disciplines.

Our findings extend prior work on disciplinary identity in STEM+C contexts (Aslan et al., 2024; Carlone & Johnson, 2007) by revealing how students perceived their participation across disciplines. Most students identified with at least one disciplinary role, and many identified with multiple roles, suggesting the integrated design supported recognition of the interdisciplinary nature of real-world problem-solving. However, students identified most strongly as engineers and computer scientists; scientist ide ntification was notably weaker. Design and programming components were likely more salient as markers of disciplinary participation, while scientific inquiry practices may have been less visibly framed as authentic science. We hypothesize students may be developing more expansive views of science, extending beyond traditional K –12 norms. Qualitatively, science identity drew the most varied, interdisciplinary connections, while computer science identity was anchored narrowly in coding and computer use. The use of a DSML within the block-based environment may have blurred the boundary between computational modeling and authentic scientific work (Hutchins et al., 2020), supporting broader science identity connections. Several limitations should be noted. First,  the use of single-item Likert prompts to measure identity is a recognized constraint; richer instruments could better capture the competence, performance, and recognition dimensions of the frameworks used here. Second, framing the prompt around "science" broadly may have introduced ambiguity, as students' responses could have differed had they been asked about specific sub-disciplines (e.g., Earth science, biology). Finally, qualitative coding was primarily organized around curricular activity structures; deeper analysis theorizing how specific activities shape identity dimensions remains an important direction for future research. Overall, this study offers promising evidence that integrated STEM+C experiences can support students' sense of belonging across multiple disciplines which is a meaningful step toward more inclusive STEM education.

Gaeun Lee, Rabia Ibtasar, Joseph E. Michaelis glee94@uic.edu, ribtas2@uic.edu, jmich@uic.edu University of Illinois Chicago Abstract: Value interventions may support broader participation in CS by relating how each student’s personal interest may intersect with computing. We conducted a quasi-experimental study to understand how value-based homework prompts impact the way students engage with a social robotics program. We conducted thematic analysis on student homework responses and found that if value-based prompts are prompted towards problem solving, students relate CS more deeply to their personal experiences of designing and coding social robots. Prior work has shown that students often view Computer Science (CS) as boring, isolating, and disconnected from students’ personal interests (Goode et al., 2018).  A wide range of CS curricula is aimed at introducing younger learners to computational thinking (CT) and CS concepts (Costa Junior et al., 2024; Grover et al., 2015), however, it doesn’t necessarily address student’s personal interests. This issue may contribute to and perpetuate narrow views of CS where students perceive it solely as working on computers and writing code (Armoni, 2016). To address these limited perceptions of CS, there should be an extension of student perceptions toward broader social context and values (Liao, 2022). Even programs that don’t use computers like CS Unplugged found that students described CS as being limited to “fixing technical problems” (Taub et al., 2012). Value interventions (Hulleman et al., 2020) are strategies that intentionally communicate why a subject is relevant to learners and help connect their learning to personal and/or societal values. Value interventions in the form of writing activities can increase the reflection on personal relevance of the learning materials (Hecht et al., 2019). Therefore, we implemented a value intervention in a curriculum, MyTurn, designed to engage students in CT and CS through problem-based activities (Ibtasar et al., 2023; Ibtasar et al., 2025). The students complete a sequence of pre-coding activities that supports students' CT learning process, then build and code their social robots. As our prior work routinely found that students did not connect their own project work with social value of CS emphasized in the program (Ibtasar et al., 2025), we introduced value-based homework prompts so students can reflect on problem-solving in CS with their family or communities.  We ask the following research question: How do value based homework prompts impact the way students engage with the MyTurn Social Robotics curriculum?

## Method

A four-week classroom study was conducted with 32 sixth-grade students attending a Midwest private school. Study participants were recruited from two sections taught by the same teacher who had previous experience with the curriculum. Of the 32 participants, 25 students (male=11, female=14) returned consent forms and were included in the data analysis forming Treatment (n=10) and Control (n= 15) sections. Students worked in pairs, with 8 groups for each section. Students identified as White, with four students identifying as multiracial. During the study we provided value-based homework prompts to treatment and control sections (See Table 1). Table 1 Intro Homework and Ending Homework Questions Given to Students Section Intro Homework Question Ending Homework Q1 Ending Homework Q2 Treatment When you go home, share what you have learned about social robots with your family/community member. Write down ONE way in which that family member thinks a social robot could help them solve a problem in their lives.

Discuss with your family/ community members your designs for the social robot.

Write down the problem you tried to solve.

Discuss with your family/ community members and write down what other problems you would want to solve with a social robot in the future.

Control When you go home, share what you have learned about social robots with your family/community member. Write down ONE reaction or idea that your family member had about social robots.

Discuss with your family/ community members your ideas for the social robot.

Write down these ideas.

Discuss with your family/ community member and write down what other ideas you have for a social robot in the future.

3141 To analyze the impact of the value-intervention, two researchers examined student created robot interactions and compared these to homework responses for alignment between the student designs and their homework responses. We then conducted a Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022) on students’ homework responses beginning with a process of open semantic coding that were collaboratively refined through multiple rounds of discussion, comparing interpretations and resolving discrepancies until reaching a shared understanding of the data. There were a total of 5 codes including: robots functional problem (RFP), personal probl em solving (PPS), emotional support (ES), societal problem solving (SPS), Family member feelings (FF). Finally, themes were iteratively proposed and refined by all three researchers until consensus was reached. The Thematic Analysis revealed two key themes.  In Theme 1, we found that students in the treatment group seemed to describe specific and personal problem-solving scenarios while those in the control described generic conceptualizations of social robots. For the intro homework, all students in the treatment group described specific problem-solving situations. For PPS, P5 shared “My mom and dad said they would love to have a social robot that could organize mail and sort clothes” For SPS, P4 said “can help the world out in a unique way because people could one day always relax and they could have personal assistance.” In contrast, control group students shared generic perspectives that social robots were “cool” (P21, P24, P30), “love the idea” (P22), “odd and weird” (P29) or “meany” (P30). The ending homework showed differences in how students expressed problem-solving perspectives. The treatment group continued discussing problem solving, but some students narrowed their focus on RFP. P15 said “A problem I had to solve is seeing how to connect things together and seeing how to activate the robot.” In the control group, students who initially gave generic or emotional descriptions began referencing specific personal problem-solving (PPS) in responses. This suggests that treatment group students may have been able to reflect more precisely on the challenges they encountered during the design process because they began by taking on more specific problem-solving perspectives. Responses for both sections showed students’ take on a societal problem-solving perspective when prompted to consider future problems or ideas. For example, P3 (treatment) wrote, “A robot that is like a dog that helps people not be lonely”  and P24 (control) shared, “In the future when the social robot is more advanced it can help fix things around the city.” Figure 1 Examples of Theme 2: Connection between Students’ Project Ideas and Ending Homework Q1 In Theme 2, we found students in the treatment group, but not the control group, made connections between their homework reflections and their own project work. Ending Homework Q1 responses that were submitted after students completed the  curriculum showed that students in the  treatment section consistently grounded their reflections of problem-solving to their own social robots project work whereas control group students referred to abstract and hypothetical scenarios (see Figure  1). We found that  all students from the treatment section referred to their projects in their Homework 2– 1 reflection. In contrast, while students in the control group also discussed problem solving, their responses were not related to the robots they had designed. In summary, both groups developed a problem-solving view of CS through the curriculum. However, the value-based prompts in the treatment group helped students connect problem-solving with their own social robot projects. These prompts encouraged more focused reflection and helped students relate CS concepts more deeply to their personal design and coding experiences. For future CS education, we should consider value-based interventions around problem solving to help students better connect learning material  to their own lives. 3142 Armoni, M. (2016). ## Acknowledgments

This work was supported by Spencer Foundation Rapid Response Bridge Funding and NSF  #2342099. 3143 Movers and Shakers: Immigrant Mothers as Architects of Language Education and Community Change Jackson Gzehoviak, Flora Zempleni jgzehoviak@g.ucla.edu, fzempleni@g.ucla.edu UCLA Abstract: Scholarship has not attended much to how immigrant women learn new languages. We argue that the complex everyday constraints on immigrant women’s everyday agency throw in sharp relief moments when they insist on their own agendas for learning. We analyze ethnographic data of an ESL class we taught at a U.S. immigrant services center, exploring how immigrant mothers assert their needs and wants for curriculum, altering top-down educational power dynamics and transforming the learning environment. With the rise of xenophobic state violence against immigrant communities across the United States, there has been renewed interest in how schools and education can best support immigrant students. However, most of this focus has been on K-12 students, with  significantly less attention being paid to adult learners. However it is important to note that, shaped by their families’ needs, immigrant mothers pursue their own educational careers in a number of fields. In this paper, we focus on the experiences of a  group of immigrant mothers in an English language class. They articulate their reasons for taking English as directly linked tonew forms of participation in social settings and cultivating belonging for themselves and their families as a form of social action (Goodwin & Goodwin, 2004). Further, how the mothers participate in their learning environment shapes the learning environment itself. We focus specifically on moments when students drew upon their agency and pushed back against our curricular design,  instead advocating for instruction that they felt would better support themselves, their peers, and their families.

Theoretical framing Researchers have established peer-based learning and cooperative learning techniques as pinnacles of practice in English as a Second Language (ESL) classrooms (Liang, Mohan, & Early, 1998). Collaboration between learners helps build the social practice of learning as the co-construction of knowledge, promoting higher-order thinking among learners (Zhou, 2021). Research shows how a collaborative orientation to learning English as a new language helps boost student confidence as they find themselves able to participate and help out their peers (Jin et al., 2022). We use this theoretical approach to teaching and learning in the field of ESL to highlight how motherstudents take up various social roles and collaborate throughout our classes. Mothers with more familiarity with written texts in English help their peers with decoding and phonics. Others, with more facility with spoken English, help suggest words for their peers. Others, with more experience in English language classes, push for instruction that they think will better help their peers. We also draw on research of learning environments that highlight the joint activity that teachers and students accomplish together in educational settings (Vossoughi et al., 2021). We interlace this framework onto our work with adult immigrant mothers to bring to the fore the many ways that we (the authors and our students) play off of one another discursively to offer suggestions for how to implement learning activities. We draw on this theoretical framework to situate the collaborative learning practices (between the students, us, and each other) that we see as essential in fostering a learning environment where we can understand what learning the mothers wish to center. The learning sciences has a long history of taking up questions of power dynamics in learning environments, such as in Fred Erickson’s (2006) “side by side” approach to collaboration. In our classroom, we sought to replicate a similar model and followed the mothers’ agentic moves every class (and between classes), which had ripple effects on the iterative process of (re)designing curriculum. We show how the students step into their own agency by offering suggestions for instruction, design, and curriculum, as collaborators and class co-designers. The data we use in this analysis includes audio recordings and field notes of English class; interviews with students; messages from the class’s WhatsApp group; lesson plans; a “living” slide deck from each class, where suggestions, questions, and work done by the students were recorded; and classroom artifacts (such as stories written by the students). We conduct a micro-analysis of interactions in the class, looking specifically at 3144 moments when students pushed back against our curricular design and instead advocated for the type of Englishlanguage instruction that they saw as essential to their own futures. This is put in conversation with classroom discourse analysis (e.g. Rymes,  2016), whereby we analyze how hegemonic discourses and ideologies around language, (im)migration, and belonging shaped what the students felt they and their peers should learn.

## Setting and participants

The English language class at the center of this study takes place at an immigrant resource center in a large city in Southern California in the U.S. The class was born out of a desire by a small group of Latina immigrant mothers to have access to an English class that is built to fit within their work and family schedules. The two authors of the paper, as volunteers at the resource center, offered to co-design and co-teach the class and have been doing so since mid-2024. In acknowledgement of the caregiving responsibilities of the mothers who requested the class, the center offers the English class concurrently with a free childcare program. Our analysis suggests that immigrant adult women take up numerous social roles that are rooted in collaboration with one another and with us (their teachers). Their learning is intimately linked to collaboration, their perceived need to acquire certain linguistic forms, and asserting their own educational agency.

1. The class’s students’ learning was rooted in traditions of collaboration. The mothers come from

cultural traditions of collective meaning-making – from the highlands of Guatemala to the Caribbean coastal regions of Colombia. Their learning is inextricably bound up in these social practices. In one session, we asked mothers to describe their hobbies using new targeted vocabulary about activities and pastimes. One mother said she liked to listen to music and dance, and she pantomimed putting on headphones  and bopping her head, and then dancing to cumbias she likes. Another mother with less skill in speaking English clearly understood what the first had said. She took in the full semiotic packaging presented by the first woman and responded by asking her in Spanish what kinds of dancing she liked to do. Though not speaking in the target language, the second mother demonstrated linguistic skill and collaboration by extending the first mother’s ideas. Taking up this moment as a pedagogical opportunity, we wrote down the conversation in our living slide deck, translating what the second mother had said into English. Through this we engaged the women’s collaborative talk toward an emergent learning product – a mentor text that we then used as sample dialogues for practicing reading and speaking with other pairs of mother-students.

2. Mothers expressed what we are calling language learning ideologies, or beliefs on how they and their

peers would best be able to learn English. They advocated for the pedagogical approaches that they saw as best, as a way to  show care for their peers and friends. For example, one student, Pilar, repeatedly asked for more corrections in the class. She later described in an interview that she saw corrective feedback as an act of care, as this would help the other women learn English and help them avoid situations where they may be made fun of for making mistakes.

3. The mothers in our class are more than just caregivers and wives. They are learners in their own right.

During each class, new anecdotes ar ose from different participants about times when they wanted to share something in English but couldn’t. For example, one mom thought she heard a few white boys talking badly about her while she was working at her cleaning job at a nearby college. She wante d to learn how to react to them in English, and how to understand what they were saying. She also wanted to learn more vocabulary about cleaning in general so that she could advocate for better working conditions and ultimately find a better cleaning job. The mothers offered suggestions for how she might respond to these boys, and they validated her with similar anecdotes in different settings. The mother expressed her desire to learn as a part of her own educational steadfastness. In a world where her actions are severely restricted by bordering regimes, she was able to make her own choices about how to spend her time toward a future of her own design. We offer these analyses in a spirit of ongoing dialogue and sense-making. Educational research must take note of the complex dynamics that arise when adult immigrant women, themselves responsible for caring for their communities, assert their agency in classroom settings. They offer powerful lessons about how learning environments might best be organized for their educational success. As learners, they find ways to collaborate intrasententially, translanguaging between English, Spanish, and K’iche’ to offer  support and validation to one another, and our own pedagogical instincts help us to document these interactions to provide fruitful lessons in English. Our classroom is one that respects and responds to the changing needs of these students each class session as well. We continue to carry these lessons into the future as we keep iterating new designs for learning and teaching that support the dignity of immigrant mothers. 3145 Goodwin, C., & Goodwin, M.H. (2004). 3146 Co-Designing a Work-Integrated Learning Pathway: Building Equitable Access to Medical Imaging Careers Sohee Linda Lee, Pepperdine University, linda.lee@pepperdine.edu Anna Badua, University of Southern California, abadua@usc.edu Abstract: This poster presents the co-design and iterative refinement of a 12-week, work-integrated learning pathway preparing underrepresented learners for medical imaging careers. Developed through a partnership between a nonprofit workforce organization and a medical imaging company, the program integrates e-learning, virtual instruction, and clinical rotations. Grounded in Design-Based Implementation Research and situated learning, findings across four cohorts highlight the importance of authentic workplace participation, structured mentorship, and co-design for mutual benefit.

Healthcare systems in the United States face persistent shortages of skilled imaging technologists, driven by rising demand for diagnostic procedures and an aging workforce (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024; American Society of Radiologic Technologists, 2023). Individuals from historically underrepresented populations continue to encounter barriers to affordable, work-based training in allied health, as traditional models often require significant tuition and unpaid clinical hours (Betancourt et al., 2003; Carnevale & Smith, 2018). To address these challenges, a nonprofit workforce organization and a leading medical imaging company formed a cross-sector partnership to co-design a 12-week, paid “earn-and-learn” pathway integrating classroom instruction, e-learning, and supervised clinical rotations.

This effort is grounded in Design-Based Implementation Research (DBIR), which addresses persistent problems of practice through iterative, collaborative design and capacity building (Fishman et al., 2013), and situated learning theory, which frames learning as legitimate participation in a community of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Together, these frameworks position the workplace as a primary learning site where professional identity develops through authentic participation. The partnership identified three design priorities: (1) expand access for underrepresented learners through an earn-and-learn structure, (2) ensure instruction reflects authentic workplace practice, and (3) build capacity for sustained collaboration. Philanthropic funding from the industry partner removed cost barriers by providing paid rotations, certification-exam coverage, and tuition-free participation.

Program design and co-design process The program prepares participants for three entry-level roles in medical imaging—Patient Service Representative (PSR), DXA Technician, and MRI Technologist Aide —through sequential rotations blending asynchronous e-learning, synchronous virtual instruction,  and guided clinical practice. This structure reflects a flipped, apprenticeship-based model: learners review materials independently, engage in facilitated sessions, then apply knowledge in clinical settings (Collins et al., 1991; Herrington & Oliver, 2000). Admissions criteria were co-designed to emphasize potential rather than prior credentialing, using skills assessments and behavioral interviews evaluating communication, reliability, and problem-solving that demonstrate the deliberate design decision t o broaden the candidate pool beyond those with existing healthcare credentials. Mentorship was embedded throughout all rotations. Preceptors modeled professional standards while providing real-time feedback, and site supervisors documented the program participants’ progress through structured scorecards and progress reports. The decis ion to embed mentorship directly within clinical workflows was driven by situated learning principles: mentoring relationships scaffold legitimate peripheral participation, enabling learners to gradually assume greater responsibility within the community of practice (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Weekly coordination meetings among site mentors, clinical managers, and program staff ensured alignment between learning objectives and site-level expectations. The co-design process followed DBIR’s four principles (Fishman et al., 2013) where stakeholders iteratively reviewed labor-market data, regulatory standards, and learner feedback in collaborative workshops. Industry partners contributed domain expertise on compliance and clinical operations, while the nonprofit provided learner-support infrastructure and inclusive recruitment pipelines. Each design cycle concluded with joint reflection sessions analyzing student outcomes and site observations, informing adj ustments to rotation schedules, onboarding procedures, and mentorship structures across subsequent cohorts. 3147 exposure to authentic clinical environments produced measurable growth. For instance, clinical progress reports indicated over 90% of learners achieved full competency in all required skills by program end. Learners attributed their readiness to sustained hands-on practice rather than e-learning alone, suggesting the design decision to center clinical rotations as the primary learning site was effective. Second, structured mentorship and proactive coordination were central to retention. Regular check-ins provided timely intervention for attendance or performance concerns, contributing to a 92% program-completion rate at the time of this report. Survey data  revealed learners valued the consistent presence of a mentor and reflective dialogue with instructors, reinforcing the theoretical expectation that guided participation supports identity development (Lave & Wenger, 1991).

Third, iterative co-design surfaced ongoing tensions between instructional standardization and site-specific adaptation. Sites varied in patient volume, technology, and supervisory capacity. Regular debriefs were crucial to implement rapid adjustments as needed, demonstrating the importance of flexible yet coherent systems across diverse clinical contexts. Three design principles emerged: (a) center authentic workplace participation; learning was most effective when embedded in real imaging workflows rather  than simulated settings (Billett, 2011); (b) embed structured mentorship and reflection: integrating mentorship into clinical rotations scaffolded development and supported retention; and (c) co-design for mutual organizational benefit: sustained collaboration yielded designs meeting both equity and operational goals through transparent communication and shared data systems.

## Topics for poster discussion

The poster will feature a visual overview of the program’s design-iteration cycle, including a diagram mapping design decisions to DBIR principles and a summary table of cohort outcomes across the four implementation cycles. We invite discussion on strategies for balancing standardization with site-level adaptation in distributed work-integrated programs, the role of co-design in sustaining cross-sector partnerships, and methods for evaluating equity-focused workforce pathways in allied health and related fields. 3148 Mapping Generative AI Policies in U.S. Universities through LLMAssisted Content Analysis Wei Wang, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, wwang93@vols.utk.edu Qi Sun, University at Albany, State University of New York, qsun5@albany.edu Abstract: This poster reports a content analysis of institutional generative AI policies across the top 100 U.S. universities. Using a locally hosted LLM-assisted coding workflow and human adjudication, we mapped policy orientation, integrity provisions, disclosure rules, pedagogy, ethics, and implementation authority. Findings show cautious maturity: policies are mostly balanced and integrity-driven, while guidance for permitted pedagogical use, disclosure practices, and tool specificity remains uneven. Generative AI has pushed universities to reconcile academic integrity with new forms of learning, writing, research, and instructional support (Ping et al., 2025). Recent sector guidance calls for transparent, humancentered, and pedagogically meaningful AI governance, yet institutional documents remain uneven in tone, specificity, and enforceability (EDUCAUSE, 2024; Holmes & Miao, 2023; McDonald et al., 2024). This study maps how leading U.S. universities frame GenAI use and asks: (1) How do U.S. universities orient their institutional GenAI policies? (2) How do these policies operationalize academic integrity, disclosure, and pedagogical adaptation?

We conducted a structured content analysis of official GenAI policies from the 2025 U.S. News top 100 universities. Each institutional corpus consolidated centrally endorsed guidance related to teaching, assessment, research, student conduct, or responsible technology use. Policies published or updated during 2024-2025 were cleaned into plain text while preserving headings and source metadata. A locally hosted LLM environment was used to assist quote-anchored extraction and structured labeling. The model produced JSON outputs for ten analytic dimensions: purpose and scope, permitted uses, prohibited uses, disclosure and citation, accountability and enforcement, pedagogical integration, ethical and equity considerations, tone and orientation, implementation authority, and tool specificity. Labels used a 0-2 scale (0 = absent, 1 = weak, 2 = strong) plus an overall orientation classification (restrictive, balanced, or permissive). Human coders reviewed and adjudicated the outputs, with 15-20% of the corpus dual coded to support interpretive consistency.

RQ1: Policy framing and orientation Institutional policies most strongly emphasize purpose and scope, prohibited uses, ethical responsibility, and implementation authority. In contrast, permitted uses and tool specificity receive lower emphasis, suggesting that universities often explain why GenAI must be governed but provide less operational detail about how students and instructors may use specific tools in coursework or research. Across coded statements, 60.8% were balanced, 32.0% restrictive, and 7.2% permissive, indicating conditional acceptance rather than broad endorsement.

Table 1 Mean Policy Strength across Ten Analytic Dimensions Dimension M Dimension M Purpose and scope 1.51 Accountability and enforcement 1.04 Prohibited uses 1.21 Disclosure and citation 1.04 Ethical and equity considerations 1.21 Pedagogical integration 1.04 3149 Tone and orientation 1.20 Tools specificity 1.00 Implementation authority 1.12 Permitted uses 0.95 Note. Coded strength ranges from 0 = absent to 2 = strong. N = 136 policy units from 100 universities. RQ2: Integrity, disclosure, and pedagogy Academic integrity remains the most explicit policy anchor. Prohibited-use clauses are overwhelmingly restrictive, while accountability statements frequently connect misuse to instructor discretion, academic conduct procedures, or institutional offices. Disclosure and citation, however, are usually framed as balanced: universities increasingly require or encourage acknowledgment of AI assistance, but few provide detailed templates or discipline-specific standards. Pedagogical integration shows the greatest openness, with many policies encouraging critical AI literacy, instructor guidance, and reflective classroom experimentation. Table 2 Tone across Integrity, Disclosure, and Pedagogical Dimensions Dimension Mean Restrictive Balanced Permissive Prohibited uses 1.21 95.7% 3.3% 1.1% Accountability and enforcement 1.04 64.0% 34.9% 1.2% Disclosure and citation 1.04 5.1% 94.9% 0.0% Pedagogical integration 1.04 7.9% 64.5% 27.6% Illustrative excerpts show this asymmetry. Integrity-oriented policies prohibit confidential data sharing or submission of AI-generated work as one's own. Disclosure clauses ask students to acknowledge AI involvement in methods, citations, or acknowledgments. Pedagogical clauses use a more developmental tone, encouraging instructors to build students' critical judgment and workforce readiness. Together, the findings show a sector moving beyond blanket prohibition but still privileging risk management over detailed pedagogical design.

The policy landscape suggests cautious maturity. Universities have largely accepted that GenAI cannot be addressed through prohibition alone, but their guidance still centers academic integrity, accountability, and responsible use more than instructional innovation. This pattern aligns with calls to redesign assessment and clarify expectations rather than rely primarily on detection or punitive control (Luo, 2024; QAA, 2023). Three implications follow. First, institutions need dynamic disclosure standards that identify when AI use must be cited, acknowledged, or described methodologically. Second, faculty development should translate broad principles into course-level examples, including acceptable collaboration with AI tools, prohibited shortcuts, and reflective student documentation. Third, governance should connect central policy authority with departmental discretion so that common ethical principles can be adapted to disciplinary assessment norms. Across one hundred leading U.S. universities, GenAI governance is becoming more balanced but remains unevenly operationalized. Policies increasingly recognize AI as part of contemporary academic work, yet they provide stronger guardrails for misconduct than supports for transparent, equitable, and pedagogically productive use. Future work should extend this corpus longitudinally and examine how instructors and students interpret these policies in practice.

International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 32(3), 527-563. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00270-2 3151 Studios of Joy: Teachers Reimagining the Pedagogical Possibilities of their Elementary Classrooms Sarah Jaewon Lee, Camille Ungco-Santos, Jessica Thompson Sjlee25@uw.edu, cungco@uw.edu, jjthomps@uw.edu University of Washington Abstract: Recent research suggests emotion, specifically designing for joy, supports  teachers in learning how to co-create justice-oriented, dignity-affirming educational environments.

Using four principles from the pedagogies of joy framework, this paper explores a group of novice teachers who engaged in a professional development model (Studio Days) to co-design for social justice. Through this lens, we saw how one studio focused on positioning culture, families, and communities as rightfully belonging inspired another teacher to host another studio on recognizing that power, historicities, and futures matter. This second studio  then inspired a fellow teacher to try out a lesson on disability justice in her kindergarten class. These in parallel, and how these pedagogies can lead to expansive pathways for different teachers to learn how to enact justice oriented, dignity-affirming curriculum in their classrooms.

## Motivation

Emotions are often ignored in educational contexts (Boler, 1999), and especially teacher learning settings where there is more of an emphasis on pedagogical and content knowledge, classroom management, and assessment. Among the many emotions that teachers experience,  it is especially important to attend to joy because of its potential to support learning environments to be dignity affirming (i.e. welcoming whole people and their diversity of backgrounds, expertise, and cultural knowledge;  Espinoza et al., 2020; Scipio et al., 2025)). In this paper, we build off Scipio et al. (2025)’s pedagogies of joy framework to explore the complexity of joy as it diffuses through a community of teachers into their classrooms with their students.  This paper asks how are pedagogies of joy enacted within teaching learning (specifically, a studio model), and how does joy spread in expansive directions into teachers’ classrooms?

## Theoretical framework

In this paper we argue that supporting joy is an act of social justice in teacher education. In their review on social justice in teacher education, Hossenini et al. (2025)  commented on how teachers often struggle with  "navigating the risk of reproducing inequity;… coping with vulnerability; and struggling to practice social justice education within the current system." (p. 16). More recent research has suggested that focusing on joy can be a solution to addressing these feelings of risk, fear, vulnerability, discomfort, and uncertainty involved in trying to enact social justice-oriented curriculum. The pedagogies of joy (POY) framework offers four lenses for both designing for and following joy. Attending to affective entanglements  means paying attention to opportunities for learners to experience laughter, witness, connection, belonging, and other feelings that shape the learning activity. Switching roles means intentionally disrupting traditional power dynamics and encouraging learners to step into leadership positions they may often be denied. Cultivating third space (Gutiérrez, 2008) means co-creating hybridity between learners, teachers, and researchers so that multiple cultural repertoires are welcomed and honored in the learning environment. (Co)dreaming to enact  means to follow the learners’ lead in imagining new and expansive possibilities and future trajectories of the collective learning activity. The next section will describe how analysis was conducted through these four lenses across multiple professional learning events to show how both teachers and students engaged in joyful learning.

In [PROJECT NAME], we provided professional development (PD) for teachers in  the form of 1:1 coaching sessions, monthly Zoom meetings to host critical friends’ groups of each other’s practice, quarterly convenings, and individual lesson observations with follow up feedback. This paper focuses on Studios, which was a new addition in the 24-25 school year of the project. Our studios were  an all-day job-embedded PD hosted in one of our teachers’ elementary classroom. Similar to Lesson Study (Lewis et al., 2006), Studios supported improvement of teaching through cycles, with the goal being to improve a particular lesson with the support of researchers and teacher colleagues. Host teachers and researchers met before the Studio Day to co-design lessons. On the day of 3152 the Studios, teachers and researchers co-taught two portions of a lesson to the same group of children, debriefed between the lessons, then adapted pedagogical approaches tailored to that particular group of children.  We focus on one “chain” of PD events that features three teachers: Susy (4th/5th grade, studio host), Dhara (2nd, studio host), Helena (K, classroom observation).

The data analyzed for this paper included: Swivl recordings of the PD events, researcher field notes, exit tickets from the events, and Zoom recordings of exit interviews with the teachers.  Videos and transcripts were content logged (Derry et al., 2010)  then compiled into an excel sheet for deductive coding (Corbin & Strauss,

1990) based on the four principles of pedagogies of joy and the justice-oriented commitments of our project. This

coding process revealed the prevalence of joy in the process of teachers learning to co-design justice-oriented curriculum, as described in the next section.

Across one “chain” of events (Susy’s studio, a convening, Dhara’s studio, and a classroom observation in Helena’s classroom), we noticed an overall pattern that j oyful social justice  was a collective rather than an individual endeavor. By analyzing professional learning sessions through the four POY lenses, this section provides examples of how each lens as a design principle  was enacted and how teachers learned to co-design dignity affirming learning environments. W e argue that POY lenses allowed for teach ers to specifically learn how to incorporate social justice into their teaching, which our literature review showed can be quite difficult to implement. These three teachers focused on  two justice-oriented commitments that our  project introduced: positioning culture, families, & communities as rightfully belonging (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020), and recognizing that power, historicity, & futures matter (Agarwal & Sengupta-Irving, 2019). By studying how our teachers enact justice and joy, this section aims to  show how teachers help researchers co-theorize a more coherent and expansive  definition of social justice-oriented teaching. First, Susy hosted a studio where she  incorporated family stories into  a lesson on stars, the moon, and seasons  (POY: cultivating third space). This idea was the shared out at a convening, and Dhara then incorporated family stories into a unit on structures and materials. During her lesson, she also added a wonder walk to consider not only how the students’ favorite structures are build and cared for, but also how the school is breaking down and needs attention (POY: attending to affective entanglement). Helena, who attended Dhara’s studio, incorporated the wonder walk idea when teaching her kindergarteners about disability justice: She asked them to take notes on how their school’s playground is accessible (or not) for friends with disabilities, and to design a more accessible playground (See Figure 1; POY: switching roles + co-dreaming to enact).  These four data points tell a story of how pedagogies of joy (POY) guided the teachers toward learning how to support  dignity-affirming learning environments. These four moments analyzed through the POY lenses show how collaboratively designing justiceoriented science curriculum can be a joyful, dignity affirming process for both teachers and students.  Together these teacher s felt empowered and encouraged to design for joyful social justice through a collaborative and expansive process. Without POY and the PASTEL social justice commitments, the teachers reported that they may have had many “missed opportunities” to support dignity-affirming learning (Community Meeting, 2026). Figure 1 Examples of Helena’s Students’ Playground Observations (Left) and Design (Right) Worksheet

## Significance

The teachers highlighted in this paper represents just one example of a pathway for joyful teacher-student learning through research-practice partnerships. This concrete example contributes to the literature on teacher learning specifically by showing how teachers can learn to co-design justice-oriented, dignity affirming science lessons in elementary contexts. This paper also contributes to research on emotion in the learning sciences by showing how pedagogies of joy can be seen and designed for at both the teacher and student level.
