Science Education, sce.21983. https://doi.org/10.1002/sce.21983 3154 Negotiating Power Through Interactions: A Focus on Discourse in RPPs Taryn Williams, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Patricia Fuentes Acevedo tarynmw@uci.edu, ckimmerl@uci.edu, r.santagata@uci.edu, pcfuente@uci.edu University of California, Irvine Abstract: Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) aim to disrupt power hierarchies between participants. However, little is known about how in-the-moment discursive moves impact power. This study conceptualizes how power is negotiated through interaction by analyzing conversations among stakeholders in the context of an RPP centering instructional improvement in mathematics. An integrated framework was developed and applied to conversation transcripts. Findings indicate that RPP members enacted discursive moves tonegotiate and share power, supporting the expression of teacher voice. Research-practice partnerships (RPPs) aim to disrupt traditional power hierarchies between researchers and practitioners by creating structures that deliberately disrupt power dynamics in traditionally hierarchical settings such as professional development (PD) (Farrell et al., 2019). Little is known, however, about how in-the-moment interactions impact power distribution. This study aims to fill this gap by analyzing discourse in co-design meetings between researchers, teachers, and administrators centered  on mathematics instructional improvement. We ask: How do RPP members negotiate power through conversational interaction?

## Theoretical framework

We draw on Ekström and Stevanovic (2023)’s definition of power as the “transformative capacities of social agents in virtue of their social relationships.” (p. 01) Power is (1) conditioned by social structures and institutions and (2) negotiated through interaction. In this study we focus on interactions by investigating discursive moves.

## Context

This study was conducted in the context of a larger RPP focused on instructional improvement in mathematics in two local Title-1 elementary schools. A Math Leadership Team (MLT) was created where researchers, teachers, and administrators came together monthly to co-create PD. The MLT was designed to disrupt traditional power dynamics by inviting teachers to be a part of the conversation about how the PD was crafted and implemented for their colleagues. This study focused on one school and involved four university researchers (one senior, three junior), four teachers, one school principal, and occasionally two county-level administrators. Data Data included transcripts of 15 audio-recorded MLT meetings (range: 15-73 minutes) during a two-year period.

## Analytic method

We applied a codebook capturing discursive moves (Nguyen et al., 2026) that was developed in the context of a study of curriculum co-design. We focused on understanding power sharing by documenting speakers’ roles and moves they enacted. If, for example, t eachers took on directive discursive moves (see Table 1), that could be evidence that they felt empowered in these settings. We first applied the codebook to a subsample of data (year 1 meetings at one school). Once we reached satisfactory intercoder reliability, we coded the entire dataset. Child codes focus on the specific discursive moves, whereas parent codes highlight their implications for power negotiation.

Table 1 Power Negotiation Codebook (adapted from Nguyen et al., 2026) Parent Code Definition Child Codes 3155 Directive Discourse moves that serve to provide feedback or examples regarding something that has been said. validate, suggest, give examples Facilitative Discourse moves that serve to support facilitation of the conversation by summarizing or acknowledging what has been said, or by bringing more people into the conversation summarize, acknowledge, check task progress, call on

## participants, invite all to share

Reflective Discourse moves that contribute to the conversation by supporting dialogue that has already been shared

## up participants’ ideas for group

Participatory Discourse moves that relate to sharing new ideas or responding to other people’s ideas with agreement, disagreement, or request for clarification share ideas, react, ask for clarification Preliminary findings indicate that RPP members enacted various discursive moves—such as teachers questioning their administrator or the research team—tonegotiate and share power, supporting the expression of teacher voice. An example of both a facilitative and directive discourse move follows. Facilitative example: Researcher invites teachers to share their perspectives At the start of one of the first meetings of the project, the senior researcher began with the following question: Researcher: “We're open to thinking about it also in different ways … We were wondering, we know some things about this already, but we wanted to ask you, if you have particular goals, things that you're hoping for in relation to mathematics, teaching, and learning at [school] both in the long term, and then by the end of the school year?” In this example, the researcher began the conversation by eliciting from the teachers how they would like to spend their time during staff meetings. This is significant, as PD is often top-down with administrators or district personnel planning how the tim e is going to be spent (Kennedy, 2019). This creates a noticeable power shift by allowing teachers to have voice in the decision-making process. Directive example: Teacher exercising power through discourse Following the researcher’s invitation for teachers to share their perspectives, one teacher comments that she feels she benefits most from seeing how her colleagues teach: Teacher A: “I've learned best like I've had trainings where I sit through…  I've had … the experience of like, trying it out myself. But I really feel like … it's so powerful when you get to see someone teaching it with live kids. So it'd be really cool if  we can somehow; we could go to your guys' [other teachers’] class.” In this example, Teacher A is making a directive move where she shares what she would like to see happen. In response to the researcher’s request above, Teacher A takes the opportunity to answer the question and suggest something that would be beneficial for her. This suggests a shift in power dynamics, as decisions are no longer made solely by administrators or researchers, as is customary in traditional PD settings (Kennedy, 2019). This teacher is taking advantage of the opportunity afforded by the researchers’ invitation to share by requesting something that is important to her.

Infrastructure that promotes teacher voice—such as the MLT in this study—is essential to disrupt traditional hierarchies that elevate researchers over practitioners and administrators over teachers. However, infrastructure alone cannot alter power dynamics; administrators and researchers must also make discursive moves that actively share power. In this study, in-the-moment interactions determined how power manifested; researchers and administrators used both explicit and subtle discourse to amplify teacher voice. Future directions include further refining the framework and applying it to the entire data corpus. 3156 Ekström, M., and Stevanovic, M. (2023). 3157 Beyond Tools: Aesthetic Encounters in Maker-Integrated University Classrooms Anna Zi Lin, Yumiko Murai, Mitra Nikimaleki anna_lin_3@sfu.ca, ymurai@sfu.ca, mitra_nikimaleki@sfu.ca Simon Fraser University Abstract: This exploratory study explores how university instructors integrate making into their teaching through the lens of aesthetic encounters and sociomaterial theory. Four themes arose: designing for sensory engagement, material-meaning coupling, participatory visibility, and contextual dynamics. The findings highlight how instructors intentionally design sensory, material, and spatial conditions that facilitate embodied learning, creativity, and reflection in maker-integrated higher education classrooms.

With the rise of makerspaces in postsecondary institutions, new resources and opportunities have emerged for instructors seeking to integrate hands-on and project-based learning into their curricula. While existing studies often emphasize tangible engagement and technological innovation, less attention has been given to the sensory, material, and affective relationships that emerge through making (Vossoughi et al., 2016), particularly regarding how instructors perceive and interpret these experiences in higher education contexts. Such sensory, material, and affective relations are essential for learning because they connect thoughts, values, feelings, senses, and actions that help to shape tacit knowledge that can hardly be achieved by purely verbal or repre sentational instructions (Paavola et al., 2004). In times of uncertainty and change (e.g., environmental instability, political and economic challenges), it becomes important to learn beyond immediate applications or predictable outcomes to explore sensory and material relations that can spark imagination, reflection, and creative possibilities. Makerspace and hands-on, project-based learning embody the principles of maker-centered and constructionist pedagogies, which perceive learning as an experiential and embodied process of constructing knowledge through tinkering and making in collaborative and interdisciplinary environments (Peppler et al., 2016). We argue that aesthetic encounters are moments when sensory, material, and affective experiences shape our understanding and imagination, which play an important role in fostering authentic and creative learning that focuses beyond technical mastery or functionality (Dewey, 2005; Greene, 2013; Papert, 1980). Rooted in the philosophical tradition of aesthetics and originally stemming from the Greek αἰσθητικός ("sensory perception") (Guyer, 2014), aesthetic encounters mean not just the "beauty” but "related to perception, sensation, imagination, and their connection to knowledge, understanding, and emotional responses to the world" (Clapp & Jimenez, 2016, p. 483). This study adopts the sociomateriality concept, a concept that inspired by posthumanism, feminist new materialism, and post-structuralist philosophy that highlights the nonlinear and more-than-human models of learning (Psaros, 2022), to perceive aesthetic encounters as relational moments that do not exist in a person or an object, but emerge in the intra-action among bodies, artifacts, and environments (Barad, 2007). From this perspective, learning happened to transcend the dichotomies  of human-as-subject and material-as-object, engaging with the constant flux of matter, spaces, uncertainties, and tensions in sense-making (Renlund et al., 2023; Bennett, 2010). Building on earlier work that explored university instructors’ aesthetic experiences during maker-centered professional development works hops (Lin  & Murai, 202 5), this study extends the inquiry to instructors’ own pedagogical reflections on integrating making into higher-education classrooms. Aesthetic encounters require mindful attention and slowing down to notice the often invisible qualities in social and educational contexts (Marini, 2020). This exploratory study aims to understand how aesthetic encounters are perceived and enacted to enrich pedagogical design in postsecondary contexts. The research question in this study is: how are aesthetic encounters manifested in university instructors’ reflections on the sensory, material, and spatial dimensions of maker-integrated classrooms? We analyzed five semi-structured interviews with university instructors from publishing, history, labour studies, design, and physics at a Canadian university. Each interview took approximately 45 to 60 minutes and included questions about instructors' course contexts, pedagogical goals, perceptions of materials and tools, sensory and spatial considerations, classroom challenges, and reflections on assessment and student engagement. We used reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2012) that combined inductive coding, which captured emergent meanings from instructors’ own language, with deductive attention to concepts from aesthetic encounters and 3158 sociomaterial theory (Renlund et al., 2023; Clapp & Jimenez, 2016; Barad, 2007), particularly moments of disruption, sensory awareness, and shifts in perceptions as instructors engaged with materials and environments. Four interrelated themes illustrate how aesthetic encounters appeared in instructors' reflections. Sensory engagement Instructors across disciplines framed sensory experiences (e.g., weight, resistance, sound, and motion) ground the theory. One instructor pointed out that the sensations and feelings, such as tinkering with the pulling big drawers full of lead, cranking a proofing press that takes some muscle, before ending the session with smiles and giggles at having made a print in one sitting, make knowledge stick and carry forward. Another instructor also pointed out that physics is a contact sport, learning activities  such as banging carts into each other to help students see conservation laws in motion, could prime perception and make abstract ideas approachable, memorable, and motivating. Such viewpoints tune attention toward what materials and forces can afford and how activity plans would have explicit sensory goals, about what should be felt, resisted, or heard, that may support the conceptual learning goals of the class.

Material-meaning coupling Instructors mentioned that materials are not merely technical elements, but critical parts in meaning reconstruction and storytelling. Making and tinkering are filled with decisions with materials and how the meaning of artifacts changes with the structures and process. For example, one instructor noted that a student who laser-etched Rosie the Riveter on see-through biodegradable plastic, then used the essay to trace how the icon’s meaning represented across labor and gender politics with their created physical manifestations. One other instructor said that their class pushes the activity called "exploring the book as an object", an activity that asks publication design to read differently through felt materiality rather than flat digital design. Another teacher showed the limit of materials can facilitate semiotic value. When students cannot hollow a timber, they use clear acrylic and cover it with wood veneer which preserves the look but changes the structure and assembly. These examples show material choi ces shape audience interpretations and students' conceptual understandings. Participatory visibility Public displays, fairs, and peer reviews provided by the class made the learning accessible to others and support students to rethink about what they are capable of. Learning that allows public distribution shifts student ways of perceiving their work (not only to be reviewed and marked by their teachers), making in such a context become a social, audience-involved practice. One instructor mentioned that "for many, when the head of the college comes by…it feels kind of important." One instructor also identified that students through the process learned what ‘count,’ name intimidation, and are reassured, "don’t be intimidated…there's something here that all of you cando." In the participatory design opportunity, aesthetic encounters emerged when students’ work gathers meaning as others engage, question, and extend it.

Contextual dynamics Space and time arrangements and uncertainty were used by instructors pedagogically. Instructors noted their experiences of navigating unexpected conditions, such as long studio blocks that leave long buffered time for iteration, congested labs that promote  hybrid craft and digital activities, and outdoor sessions that made ambient conditions (e.g., rain, cold, sun) part of the learning atmosphere. Instructors transfer the uncertainties as pedagogy, one instructor tells their students, "if it fails, that's good, you will learn more." Adopting the aesthetic encounters lens, this study found that instructors' integration of making into higher education classrooms goes beyond just technology or tools; it focuses on creating sensory and affective moments while considering participatory and contextual design aspects. Teaching could become a process of learning through matter, space, and tension. Several implications for instructors seeking to integrate making can be drawn from these dimensions. Instructors might (1) intentionally design for specific sensory and affective experiences within activities, (2) document and justify material choices, (3) create opportunities for public sharing and dialogue around students’ work, and (4) plan for spatial and temporal flexibilities to support iterative and exploratory processes. F uture work should incorporate student perspectives, artifact analyses, and in‑situ observations to understand how aesthetic encounters unfold. 3159 Bennett, J. (2010). Thing-Power. ## Drawing as Translanguaging Method to Understand Collaboration

within a Mathematics Afterschool Program Aakriti Bisht, Alejandro G. Vargas, Alessandra Pantano, Sandra Simpkins, Guadalupe Rosas abisht1@uci.edu, agranad4@uci.edu, apantano@uci.edu, simpkins@uci.edu, grosas4@uci.edu University of California, Irvine Abstract: This study examines drawing as a translanguaging method within a culturally responsive mathematics afterschool program. Grounded in ethnographic methods, we investigate how drawing helps researchers understand students, their interactions, shared participation, and mathematical thinking. Drawing functions both as a communicative and an epistemic tool, making visible the subtle, often overlooked aspects of collaboration; for example, how students negotiate meaning, construct shared knowledge, and e xpress ideas through visual and multimodal forms. By extending translanguaging beyond linguistic expression, this study positions drawing as an informative way of representing data and meaning making in educational research. Findings suggest that drawing c aptures relational and cultural dimensions of learning that traditional methods may overlook, offering deeper insight into students’ diverse ways of knowing and doing.

Translanguaging is a theory of language that describes the linguistic, semiotic, and multimodal languaging practices people engage in to make sense of their worlds (Li, 2018a). These practices include what is traditionally considered language (e.g., words, speech) but also extend beyond it to encompass the various non-linguistic multimodal and semiotic meaning-making repertoires (e.g., visual arts, drawing) (García, 2009). Several scholars have provided guidance on using translanguaging as a method (Donley, 2022; Lee, 2022). Adopting a translanguaging stance also requires centering the epistemologies of marginalized communities, often rendered invisible by Western/colonial frameworks, to valorize diverse ways of representing data (Phyak, 2022).  Western cultures tend to prioritize alphabetic representational practices, particularly writing, which candevalue meaning-making practices involving modalities beyond speech (e.g., visual arts, drawing) (De Souza, 2016). Implementing visual arts, like drawings, in our methods “allow us to be specifically attentive of the small details of everyday life that present opportunities to ask big questions of small data” (Ndhlovu, 2018, p. 16). Although translanguaging has been widely studied, little attention has been given to how it can guide data collection and analysis. This paper extends translanguaging to include drawing as a visual and semiotic form of data representation, offering a simple yet powerful way to study learning and collaboration in education research. In learning settings with students from diverse cultural backgrounds, drawing serves as a powerful medium to connect and integrate multiple ways of knowing and understanding. It makes visible forms of thinking and collaboration that highlight relationships and shared meaning making. For instance, studies of Mexican-heritage and Indigenous-heritage children show fluid collaboration as a way of working together through shared de cision making without explicit instructions (Ruvalcaba & Rogoff, 2022) in contrasts with the more individualistic, turn-taking, or negotiated roles often seen in European American contexts. As a methodological tool, drawing captures the minute details of w orking together among students, which otherwise might have been overlooked. Drawing on data from a mathematics afterschool program, we argue that drawings capture relational and cultural dimensions of learning that traditional Data and analysis The data is drawn from an ethnographic study (Fall 2023 –Spring 2025) conducted in partnership with an after-school mathematics program for middle-school students at a university in Southern California. Across 20 observed sessions, data include detailed tex tual field notes along with observational drawings documenting student interactions, learning processes, and the broader classroom environment. Participants include middle-school students and undergraduate mentors. Author 1 (Aakriti) conducted participant observation and, in early phases, produced field notes followed by iterative analytic memos in both textual and visual (drawing) forms. These initial drawings in form of memo exposed limitations of text-based descriptions in capturing micro-level embodied details of collaboration, such as students’ postures (e.g., leaning in, or bending over shared work) and how this informs us about collaboration, revealing situated modes of engagement (Goodwin, 2000). Informed by these 3161 earlier analytic memos, subsequent observations increasingly foregrounded moment-to-moment interactional detail, with drawing integrated directly into field note practices. This shift enabled close attention to students’ posture, gaze, and gesture, helping in deeper noticing of how collaboration happened in diverse forms. The ongoing analytic memoing further supported the surfacing and articulation of these patterns around collaboration, strengthening both its interpretation and representation. The following theme illustrates how drawing, as a method of memo-ing that extended into field note taking, deepened the observational process and supported attention to participants’ minute actions within the program. Drawing offered a form of noticing beyond textual description; it encouraged slowness, embodied attentiveness, and a shift from capturing “what happened” to attending to “how people are, act, and respond.” As Causey (2017) argues, drawing foregrounds what is present rather than presumed. The theme below shows how collaboration emerges as students build on one another’s efforts, with drawings as field notes capturing and informing these moments by revealing subtle, embodied interactions through which students coordinate and inhabit the shared learning space.

Seeing relationships within the Mathematics Classroom During Day 2 of ethnographic observation, a student survey was being conducted, an annual data collection activity designed to gather insights into student’s mathematical experiences. Although students were instructed to complete the survey individually, the first author observed a girl, Cathy, filling out the form for her neighboring student, Daniel (see Figure 1). It appeared she had already completed her own survey, as she was copying primarily from her own responses onto his form. As I drew my daily field notes at the end of the day, to form a visual understanding, I attended closely to Cathy and Daniel’s interactions and their presence within the space, capturing not only their actions but also their ways of being. Daniel often appeared distracted, fidgeting with objects in his hands and showing minimal engagement with the survey, while Cathy, seemingly familiar with him, completed his form, occasionally pausing to ask clarifying questions. These observations were important, as translating them into drawings required attentiveness to their personalities, gestures, and relational dynamics within the visual narrative. Later the first author got to know that they were siblings. As the session led to the math activity, which involved the superimposition of tw o triangles projected on the screen, Daniel remarked, “It looks like a sandwich.” Cathy, still processing the image, asked him to explain, and Daniel replied, “It’s a sandwich, break it in half.” Cathy nodded and quickly sketched a sandwich on her whiteboard, adding a dividing line across it. Their exchange was interrupted when Daniel accidentally knocked a gadget off the table, prompting Cathy to scold him gently in Spanish, her facial expression revealing disappointment even without verbal comprehension. Through drawing as a method, these subtle yet significant details, the shifting gestures, gazes, and expressions became more visible. The act of sketching allowed me to trace how their sibling dynamic unfolded through moments of care, correction, and collaboration. Cathy emerged as a curious learner who fluidly moved between roles of sister and peer, while Daniel’s imaginative remark revealed his creative approach to mathematical reasoning. Drawing thus enabled a deeper noticing of how familial relationships shape participation and meaning making in learning environments.

Figure 1 Cathy and Daniel working on Survey form This study showcases how drawing, as a translanguaging method, informs educational research toward care centered and culturally responsive observation. By slowing down and engaging visually, the researcher was able to notice the fluid and relational nature  of the student's collaborative mathematical participation. Framing drawing through translanguaging sheds light on the importance of multimodal meaning making within educational research practice, expanding how learning and interaction can be understood and represented. 3162 Causey, A. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology, 81, Article 101438. 3163 Preserving Heritage: How Diaspora Children Engage with a Persian Language Learning App Shafagh Hadinezhad, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, shafagh2@illinois.edu Sourabh Garg, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, sourabh3@illinois.edu Sepideh Shahi, Seed Foundation, Sshahi@seedfnd.org Sharifa Sultana, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, sharifas@illinois.edu Abstract: Persian-speaking diaspora families face challenges in helping their children learn Persiandue to limited engaging resources. We introduce a gesture-based multimodal mobile app using culturally inspired pedagogy to make Persian reading interactive and meaningful.

Using a design-based research approach, we analyze video interviews to examine patterns of engagement of child-app interaction. Findings reveal three patterns: cross-linguistic mapping, gesture-based recall, and self-initiated engagement,  emphasizing the potential of culturally relevant multimodal learning to support heritage language learning. Persian-speaking families in diaspora wish for their children to learn Persian and connect with their cultural roots. However, most of today’s Persian learning resources struggle to address challenges specific to the Persian language structure and script. To address these challenges, we developed a mobile app featuring minigames that integrate audio, visuals, narratives, and hand gestures to strengthen letter recognition and recall by combining perceptual, motor, and contextual support. Literature on language learning indicates the benefits and promising potential of gesture-based and digital game-based learning for children (Chevalier et al., 2018; Alper et al., 2017; Hussein et al., 2019; Vasalou et al., 2017). This study examines the patterns of engagement emerging as the children of Persian-speaking families in the diaspora interact with multimodal games of this Persian learning mobile app.

## Theoretical framework

Effective learning can be supported through multimodal approaches that draw on various sensory modalities, including visual, auditory, and kinesthetic, which strengthen how learners process and understand information. Studies have shown that employing multimodal learning and multiple modes of representation, both verbal and non-verbal, can significantly enhance the learning experience (Cook, 2023). Mixed modality can make the learning process more effective as it engages different senses of children (Moreno & Mayer, 2007). Within multimodal approaches, gestures have been identified as an effective mode of learning in many educational contexts (Alibali & Nathan, 2012; Garg et al., 2025; Kita et al., 2017). Gesture-based pedagogy has proven a great deal of potential in STEM education and language learning in recent years (Alibali & Nathan, 2012; Goldin-Meadow, 2011; Kita et al., 2017). Guided by these frameworks, this study explores how gesture-based multimodal games can make learning Persian more fun, engaging and accessible. We utilize a design-based research approach and focus on qualitative methods, primarily analyzing video data from the check-in Zoom meetings with participants from the Persian-speaking community. Data is being collected through an 8– 12-week testing process, during which each child and their parent(s) participate in a video-recorded weekly one-hour session. We use a semi-structured interview to gather general feedback on the app and ask specific questions about gestures and different games.  For the app, the educational approach employed in its design is based on the method developed by Ali Sedaghaty (http://amookhayat.com/), which emphasizes simplifying the learning of Persian.  The app includes a progressive curriculum that covers vowels, letter-vowel combinations, sentence building, and reading comprehension (see Shahi et al., 2024). It comprises 18 games (e.g. Table 1) focusing on vocabulary expansion, learning the Persian alphabet, reading, and comprehension skills. By incorporating stories, characters, and themes from Iranian culture, the app fosters a sense of cultural connection and identity in young learners (see Hadinezhad et al., 2024). 3164 Table 1 Examples of the Games

(a) Letter Tracing

(b) Story Telling

(c) Letter Matching

(d) Scratch and Discover

and curiosity observed across participants, resulting in three emerging key patterns: Pattern 1: Cross-linguistic mapping We found that all the children demonstrated a connection between Persian and English by associating the gesture for the Persian letters with the English letters, for example, Persian letter بbe"), taught with Persian translation of rice (berenj), and they recalled the English letter R. In one instance, Sam and Sahel’s mother, Sahar (all pseudonyms), mentioned that “Sometimes they forget to connect the gesture to its associated letter and assigned word and instead associate the gesture with the English tr anslation of the word." While the app does not include English translations or prompts, which suggests that this connection was not externally facilitated but rather internally constructed, this indicates a transfer of phonological knowledge across languages, grounded in the embodied association of gesture and sound, where gesture acted as a mediator between both languages.

Pattern 2: Gesture recalls We showed the letters to the children and asked them if they recognized the letter, if not, we made the gesture and asked if they remembered it. When Augusta was shown a letter R (رhe failed to recognize it at first, but showing the gesture helped him to immediately remember the letter. This demonstrates retention of knowledge through gestures, where the embodied association was remembered, but the letter shape was not. This emphasizes the role of bodily activity in learning. Another participant, Ramtin, did not remember the letter, so the gesture was demonstrated. Although the gesture was remembered, its conceptual mapping shifted from Persian to English. These examples suggest semantic interference in bilingual learning, where a dominant language, English, overshadows retrieval in the heritage language, Persian (Paradis, 2001). This also indicates that gestures serve as embodied anchors, even when the verbal component changes. Pattern 3: Self-initiated engagement beyond the app We found that the app encouraged curiosity among young learners and extended their engagement beyond the digital environment. They applied their learning by identifying Persian letters in grocery lists, magazines, and even attempting to write their own nam es or recite Persian letters. For example, Negar, Ramtin, and Ladan’s mom mentioned that “They try to find different letters around the house in magazines and Persian books. So, activities are happening that show they are building interest in learning the language.” These voluntary behaviors demonstrate children’s extended learning process beyond the app use and reflect intrinsic motivation (Deci & Ryan, 1985). The digital games here are a tool for language instruction and  trigger autonomous learning behaviors, which is significant in the context of heritage language learning, and it highlights a shift from passive exposure to active use, a key step in language socialization. Children engaged in ways beyond screen-based interaction, such as using gestures to recall sounds, linking knowledge across Persian and English without prompting, and extending learning to daily life. While gestures encouraged curiosity and supported new knowledge, they were also influenced by the dominant language. The pedagogy combines cultural and linguistic needs, promoting both the preservation of minority languages such as Persian and the sustainability of cultural heritage. Preliminary results show a  promising reception. Future work should further investigate the individual and combined roles of these modalities while learning a language.

## Acknowledgments

This work was funded by The Grainger College of Engineering IDEA Institute at the University of Illinois UrbanaChampaign, Grant #: GIANT2024-04 and Grant #: GIANT2025-09. 3166 Cultivating Multilingual Youths’ Epistemic Agency and Science Identity Via Relational Re-Mediation in Science Garden Activities Samantha Salguera, Allison Burgos, Roxana Adriano, Kaela Reisch, Alexie Leauthaud sesalgue@ucsc.edu, aiburgos@ucsc.edu, radriano@ucsc.edu, kreisch@ucsc.edu, alexie@ucsc.edu University of California, Santa Cruz Samuel Severance, Northern Arizona University, samuel.severance@nau.edu Abstract: This 3-year study explores undergraduates’ efforts to support the science learning of multilingual learners (MLLs; age 7-12) from three Spanish-speaking families through ongoing home garden activities. This study found (1) family members’ initial positioning influenced MLLs’ epistemic agency; (2) undergraduates’ facilitation of science activities re-mediated systems of learning relationships to promote epistemic agency; and (3) MLLs developed nascent science identities, using science practices and ideas for their own purposes. Multilingual learners (MLLs), notably Spanish-speaking learners in the United States, often must navigate the dominance of individualistic and Western approaches in science that conflict with community-centric values (Herrera & Sánchez, 2022), impacting how these learners construct pathways and identities in STEM (Rincón et al., 2021). Positioning learners to have epistemic agency in their science learning—where they have meaningful authority over how to figure out phenomena and problems through the use of disciplinary practices (Stroupe, 2014)—can provide opportunities for learners to see their learning as relevant to their lives and communities (Carlone et al., 2021). This study examines Spanish-speaking undergraduates mentors’ efforts to engage MLLs (ages 7-12) in meaningful science learning via activities in families’ home gardens. This study asks: (a) How did undergraduate mentors’ ongoing visits and engagement with families  shape opportunities for MLLs’ epistemic agency in science learning? (b) What effect did undergraduate mentors’ facilitation of science activities have in orienting MLLs towards science, including developing identities as someone who does science? This study occurred between 2022 and 2025 and focused on three Spanish-speaking MLLs—“Arturo,” “Carlos,” and “Daniela” (all aliases)—and their families. Sources of data included entry and exit interviews across eight participating families (including focus families) and undergraduates’ fieldnotes and structured reflections from facilitating science garden activities during 31 family visits (ranging from 1-2.5 hours). Data analysis drew on sociocultural perspectives on the transformation of learning settings (Gutiérrez, 2008), as well as identity formation (Penuel & Wertsch, 1995). Researchers (including undergraduate mentors) developed analytic memos periodically (Saldaña, 2009), surfacing patterns of interest across participating families (e.g., parents’ roles, MLLs’ initiative, undergraduates’ relationships with families) which informed subsequent analyses. All data underwent rounds of inductive and deductive coding (Emerson et al., 2011), with codes including talk about goals, talk about learning, science practices, and guidance/support applied to reduce the data. If disagreements in coding occurred, researchers resolved the disagreement through group discussion and iteration of the coding scheme. Patterns that emerged from coding led to the derivation of  themes around identity development, agency, and relationships. Excerpts indexing these themes underwent further discourse analysis (Scollon, 2002), and formed the basis of evidence (or counter-evidence) for claims informing the study’s research questions. Families’ positioning during activities influenced MLLs’ initial epistemic agency How the parents/guardians of MLLs positioned themselves in relation to their child during science garden activities shaped MLLs’ opportunities for epistemic agency, particularly opportunities to use disciplinary practices to figure out phenomena and problems. In Arturo’s family, undergraduate mentors noted how his parents’ (over)involvement inhibited Arturo’s own agency in his science learning: “I have an inkling that [mother’s] presence may be a slight hindrance to his willingness to form individual curiosities and questions […]. He needs to struggle, to think things out, alone. Her answering all his questions […] doesn’t give his mind space to wander” (Fieldnotes, 3/2023). Undergraduates interpreted the parents’ actions, while well-intentioned, as limiting opportunities for Arturo to engage in asking questions, a fundamental science and engineering practice 3167 (NRC, 2012). In contrast, the positioning of Daniela’s family allowed her significant initial agency in shaping her own learning: “The dad would often come in and out of the session, supervising and adding any tips or words of advice. He would often encourage Daniela and her cousin to make their own decisions: for example, when Daniela didn’t know what seeds to plant, he said, ‘it was up to her to plant whatever she wanted’” (Fieldnotes, 2/2024). In essence, Daniela’s father sought to position Daniela to have authority over her learning, including how to engage in the practice of planning and carrying out an investigation (NRC, 2012). Together, these examples illustrate the importance of surfacing family positioning—whether domineering or more laissez-faire—to inform how to best work with families and promote more agentic forms of science learning. Undergraduates re-mediated systems of learning relationships for epistemic agency Over time, undergraduates forged learning relationships with MLLs while facilitating science garden activities in Spanish and English. Their approach employed a “light pedagogical touch” (DiGiacomo et al., 2016), providing support but always positioning MLLs to make consequential decisions. The insertion of this positioning served to “re-mediate” (Gutiérrez, 2008) the system of learning  relationships between parents/guardians and children, expanding them into a new form. After several undergraduate visits, Arturo’s learning relationship with his mother shifted from her directing his actions to his having more epistemic agency: “He has officially begun to take initiative! Arturo led all the questions today, [...] [Mother] is a little more in the backseat now; [...] It’s a bit more cooperative rather than ‘do what I say’” (Fieldnotes, 5/2023). With his mother adopting a new but still supportive stance, Arturo had space to take the lead in using science and engineering practices like asking questions  (NRC, 2012). In Carlos’s family, his mother’s early concerns about his abilities gave way to trusting undergraduates’ learning relationship with Carlos: “In my head, I was just like, ay, Carlos, do something else. But at the same time [...] even if it seems kind of s illy [...] if somebody's there to guide it and make it a learning experience [...] that taught me like, okay, you gotta just let him do his thing.” (Exit interview 7/2025). Rather than move to adjust her child's “silly” ideas, she recognized how the undergraduates’ approach could support him in productively owning his science learning. The re-mediation of learning relationships shown here positioned MLLs with more opportunities for epistemic agency while—importantly —still maintaining valued familial bonds and support. Epistemic agency supported MLLs in developing nascent science identities As MLLs continued to wield epistemic agency during science garden activities, some began to orient towards doing and using science for their own purposes, forming nascent science identities. For Carlos, his experiences encouraged him to continue using scie nce and engineering practices and ideas in new contexts. During a visit to a local Harvest Festival, undergraduates observed him—unprompted—sharing science ideas (i.e., communicating information; NRC, 2012) with others: “‘Do you know what element was produced during the Big Bang? Hydrogen! This element makes up almost everything,’ Carlos continued to walk up to vendors and other staff [...] telling them about some fun facts and found himself spreading some not-so-true information but was persistent nonetheless” (Fieldnotes, 10/2024). Furthermore, at a science fair organized by undergraduates for MLLs, Carlos chose an unfamiliar topic, physics, for his project and with measured support from undergraduates led the planning and carrying out of an investigation (NRC, 2012) around dropping an egg (Fieldnotes, 11/2024). In addition, undergraduates noted how some MLLs had begun to apply new knowledge from science garden activities to their own lives. For example, Arturo began “identify[ing] different types of plants /veggies at the grocery store [...] rather than just ‘green is yucky’” (Fieldnotes, 11/2023). This study provides insights into how to support Spanish-speaking MLLs in navigating science learning often at odds with commonly held community-centric values (Herrera & Sánchez, 2022; Rincón et al., 2021). Tangibly, this study highlights the importance of working with families to promote MLLs’ epistemic agency, particularly the potential of leveraging and expanding families’ learning relationships. While prior work has observed how family members can shape the epistemic agency of their children (Jung et al., 2023), this study demonstrates a means to “re-mediate” (Gutiérrez, 2008) learning relationships to support MLLs’ epistemic agency in science learning, through the purposeful introduction of a positioning that seeks “relational equity” (DiGiacomo et al.,

2016) during MLLs’ learning while keeping familial bonds and support focal. This study also shows the

importance of having MLLs —even within a setting as unique as a home garden—take the lead in using science and engineering practices, echoing other approaches to fostering epistemic agency (Ko & Krist, 2022; Stroupe, 2014). For others seeking to organize science learning that deeply involves families, this study points toneeded future work, such as how to extend gains in MLLs’ epistemic agency to other potential settings (e.g., schools and other out-of-school settings) and, more programmatically, how to scale up and sustain this study’s core approach of undergraduate mentors working with families in their homes to support MLLs’ science learning. 3168 Carlone, H. 3169 Paying Back the Cognitive Debt: Role of AI in Makerspace Learning Yuna L. Zhang, James D. Slotta yunalei.zhang@mail.utoronto.ca, jim.slotta@utoronto.ca OISE, University of Toronto Abstract: Generative AI has entered classrooms, raising urgent questions about learning in classrooms and other environments. While AI accelerates idea generation, it risks creating cognitive debt, which can be seen as borrowed knowledge that remains unintegrated into students' own understanding (Kosmyna et al., 2025). Building on cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) and epistemic debt (Bereiter, 2002), this poster introduces the notion of using AI as a tool to foster cognitive debt during embedded learning, while examining how AI-borrowed ideas transform into embodied understanding through critical thinking and making. The goal is to help learners develop an embodied, culturally grounded understanding by transforming AI-borrowed ideas.

Theoretical and pedagogical perspective Generative AI has already become part of how students learn, think, and generate ideas, raising questions about what happens when knowledge is borrowed but not fully earned. Drawing on Kosmyna et al.’s notion of cognitive debt as knowledge borrowed but not  earned, and on cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016), this study approaches such borrowing as a pedagogical condition that extends beyond a deficit view. We extend this through the notion of repayment, understood as the process by which AI-borrowed ideas are reworked through making and reflection into embodied and personally meaningful understanding. Situated in a makerspace context, this perspective highlights how ideas are not simply carried into practice, but are critically reshaped and grounded through active engagement with materials, tools, and making decisions. Rationale: Why material art and design?

This workshop focuses on material art and design, specifically in the form of Jewellery, a topic that is experienced every day and appreciated from an aesthetic stance, but often overlooked in terms of its artistic depth and meaning. In this study, we organize Jewellery as an educational domain through multiple dimensions, including cultural, aesthetic, material, historical, ideological, symbolic, and interdisciplinary (See Table 1). Table 1 Important Dimensions of Jewellery as an Educational Domain

## Dimensions Description Pedagogical Implications

Cultural Reflects rituals, identity, and meaning. Supports culturally responsive pedagogy. Aesthetic & Material Involves form, texture, and the sensory experience of making.

Promotes embodied understanding and material literacy through creative practice.

Historical Connects craft, technology, and design. Builds historical and material awareness. Ideological/ Symbolic Reflects power, gender, and values.

Enables critical pedagogy and reflection on representation and inequality.

Interdisciplinary Bridges art, science, math, and tech. Integrates making with STEM for inquiry. This depth allows us to examine how learning can be strengthened through embodied activity that engages borrowed knowledge. Jewellery connects directly to the body and identity (Astfalck, 2007), requiring sustained engagement with material, form, and meaning. Its interdisciplinary and deeply personal nature allows a form of critical making (Ratto, 2011), providing a strong curricular anchor for our study of AI-in-Making. Table 1 summarizes these dimensions and their pedagogical implications, showing how wea rable art mediates between personal experience and collective knowledge. This study focuses on Jewellery as an educational medium in which critical making, reflection, and meaning-making converge.

## Research questions

(1) How can jewellery making frame AI as a tool for exploration without reinforcing dependency?

(2) How can jewellery making serve as a transformation mechanism through which AI-borrowed ideas become

embodied understanding within the domain?

3170 This study adopts a Design-Based Research (DBR) approach (Sandoval, 2013), in which the design process serves as a form of inquiry into how learning unfolds. Data include AI interaction records (prompts and outputs), sketches, process images, artifacts, and reflective journals from a workshop with 8 novice participants. Figure 1 AI-in-Making Learning Path: From Borrowing to Knowledge Transformation/Ownership

## Research design

The two-week workshop (n=8) followed the model of Miles and Peck (2017) as shown in Figure 1 and unfolded across five phases. Borrowing Phase: Students generate designs with AI and annotate them in a “cognitive debt ledger” to mark borrowed knowledge, which is structured according to the five dimensions outlined in Table 1 and aggregated into a community knowledge base (Slotta, Quintana & Moher, 2018). Making Phase: Students construct prototypes through embodied learning, where materials resist and reshape intentions (Ingold, 2013), prompting reinterpretation and design change. Reflection Phase: Structured reflection is integrated through artist statements, critiques, journaling, and Narrative Framing (Rose, 2012), linking artifacts to personal or cultural stories. Exhibition Phase: The workshop concludes with an exhibition-as-curriculum (Pérez de Miles & Peck, 2017), where peers and community members provide feedback and collaborative dialogue. Transformation/Ownership: Across these phases, participants connect borrowed knowledge to material form through critical making and reflection, supporting more coherent and personally meaningful understanding. Three levels of transformation: Student A demonstrates transformation through material constraint and reflection. The shift from an idealized design to the locally available petals shows how material conditions reshape AI-borrowed ideas into contextually grounded and personally meaningful forms (See Figure 2a-d). Student B shows conceptual understanding, but limited transformation. AI-borrowed ideas are not fully tested through making. Student C remains at the level of execution, with no evidence of transformation. AI-generated designs were treated as final answers, reflecting a misunderstanding of AI’s role. Learning does not occur through AI outputs alone, but through material constraints that reshape ideas and are consolidated through reflection.  AI-borrowed knowledge is transformed through critical making.  The ideas are reworked through making and reflection under material constraints. Student A illustrates how this process supports entry into unfamiliar domains, providing process-based evidence of transformation. The value of AI lies in how ideas are materialized and transformed through critical making. Future work will examine how critical making connects personal experience, material practice, and shared knowledge Figure 2 Process: (a) AI-generated ideas, (b) Critical making, (c) Reflective notes and (d) Artifact.

Harvard Educational Review, 86(2),  206–232. https://doi.org/10.17763/0017-8055.86.2.206 3172 Learning with Water: Making Nature-Culture Relations by Attending to the Sound of Water Arjun Krishna, UCLA, arjunkrishna@ucla.edu Abstract: The natural world is an active learning environment and provides a discursive context in which humans make meaning with one another. One way to experience collective meaning making in this learning environment is through group forest walks by walking, stor ying, and mapping lands and waters which Marin et al. (2020) refer to as ‘learning on-the-move.’ This ongoing micro-ethnographic study uses video-based interaction analysis to understand the moment-to-moment unfolding of learning by paying attention to the  semiotic layering of talk and movement while on forest walks during the monsoon season. The preliminary findings demonstrate how water shapes learning processes and learning environments as participants attend to relations with water through shifts in the ir movements, bodies, and conversation in relation to water while on forest walks.

## Theoretical framework

This poster of an ongoing study analyzes participant-generated video data with the Siddi community in India to understand how water actively shapes learning as participants attend to relations with water by orienting their bodies, movements, and conversations while on group forest walks. Walking, or the starting and stopping of one’s feet, is a form of human mobility and a way to experience the world and build meaning in  place, through place, and with place (Ingold, 2004; Marin & Bang, 2018). While recent developments in the learning sciences place an emphasis on “learning on-the-move” (Marin et al., 2020) and embodiment (Goodwin, 2000), lands/waters and walking within educational settings are often historically saturated and tied to Western constructions of  humans as separate from nature (Marin, 2020, p. 282). Therefore, an important framing of the research design intentionally takes learning ‘on-the-move’ out of formal education spaces and into the everyday. Land education, as a theoretical grounding for this study, offers an opportunity to understand how learning activities can foreground Indigenous ways of knowing about the world. A major part of land education involves learning to ‘read’ lands and waters (Bruce et al., 2023) where knowledge and literacy about water is not limited to its physical properties, wetness, or molecular structure, as in science classrooms, but also the ways that water shapes sensory experiences, relationships to the natural world, and enables life. Soundscaping is the “intentional ‘planting,’ designing, or intervening in the landscape of sound” (Ahern, 2022, p. 1). Sonic landscapes in learning environments can shape the way that learners interact with one another and their environment, and comprises both verbal and non-verbal sound (Ahern & Frith, 2013; Brownwell, 2019). In this case, I understand the sonic landscape outside the classroom to be the way that water ‘soundscapes’ the learning environment for groups on forest walks, and the way that learners make relations with water by moving, conversing, and interacting with it.

My overarching research question is: How does water organize attention, storying, and movement for learning? My sub-questions are (a) How do participants learn to ‘read’ water (Bruce et al., 2023) while on-themove? (b) How do lands/waters guide attention in multiple and simultaneous ways (Rogoff & Correa- Chávez,

2005) while on forest walks? (c) How does water shape the way that Siddi members assemble stories of place

while on-the-move, and on repeated walks through the forest? Walking through land presents opportunities for the natural world to organize human attention and guide movement across multiple sensory dimensions. “Talk, gesture, and movement form a layering of semiotic resources that provide opportunities for the transformation of action and learning” (Marin & Bang, 2018, citing Goodwin, 2013; Melander, 2012). Movement directed by the sights and sounds of the natural world can best be understood by a continuous account of situated activity through video. Videos in this study are participant-generated in order to maximize agency. Members of the Siddi community are offered wearable cameras using a simple lanyard in order to minimize the camera obstructing primary walking activities. This was particularly important for three reasons: (1) it avoids a culture of surveillance and places agency in the hands of Siddi people to document their own walk, rather than the researcher taking videos of subjects; (2) it does not require Siddi people to actively record thei r walk, and the camera passively accompanies them while on their walk, freeing them to go about their walk with minimal interference; (3) cameras mounted in the center of the body de-privilege what Marin (2020) calls a bias towards ‘ocular’ forms of attention 3173 and instead privileges movements of the rest of the body. While this was an intentional choice, it also marks a departure from traditional forms of interaction analysis that rely on facial expressions, as the face is notably left out of this data collection method.

The ‘walkers’ are Siddi family members at least age 7 and able to simultaneously walk through the forest, wear a video camera, and carry conversation with other group members. Each walk was documented by at least two walkers, providing multiple subjective  perspectives from which to analyze body positioning, attentive responses to sound, and directional agency.

This paper analyzes four two-hour walks (eight hours of video in total) from the monsoon season. Videos from forest walks are content-logged and transcribed three-dimensionally (Mondada, 2016; Rymes, 2015) to include human action, speech, and the sonic landscape with sights and sounds of the natural world such as water, birds, wind, and trees. Birds chirping, the wind blowing, leaves ruffling, and water flowing are all ways that nature provides a discursive context for meaning making (Ingold, 2007, 2010; Ingold & Vergunst, 2008). Videos and respective transcripts are synchronized during each walk in order to observe simultaneous actions and events from multiple perspectives.

## Preliminary results and findings

Manoj (aliased) explains to me that his family has been living on two acres of land, transplanting paddy and foraging for food. While walking through the forest which is densely populated with cicadas and birds,  a nearby stream of water calls us to it and Manoj walks toward the sound of water as it gets louder. Listening closely for the sound of water as it becomes more intense, Manoj utters “hm” as he turns towards it (01:02), indicating a shift in his attention away from the birds and cicadas and toward the water. The camera swaying up and down (01:02-01:07) aligns with the sound of water ascending in loudness, providing bodily movement towards a sonic cue. As Manoj is crossing the stream (01:08), he tells me that he sees a deer in the distance and that h e now understands why deer frequent this place (because, he concludes, they drink water from the stream). Water plays a central role in organizing our movement and making sense of other observations related to deer and other species. However it is not know ledge about water’s properties; rather it is the sound produced by water flowing through land that organizes our attention and movement through the aural or the sonic. Bruce et al. (2023) refer to this as ‘reading water,’  and Manoj attends to his sonic landscape by reading the sound of water not as a static observation but as an embodied, on-the-move practice. ‘Reading’ implies that Manoj not only ‘hears’ the sound, but ‘listens’ for it, deriving meaning from the sounds that water offers. In this instance, the natural world is actively soundscaping (Ahern, 2022) Manoj’s learning environment, an experience that only arises in this situation because water is flowing throug h a creek as he is walking, to understand his landscape and imagine next steps. Attention and movement occur at the same time as conversation about water and the environment that surrounds it, such as other forms of life like the deer. As for Manoj’s (2.0) pause, Western cognitive frameworks often frame multi-sensory environments as a battleground of ‘competing stimuli’ requiring mental filtering (see critiques by Ingold, 2001; Correa -Chávez & Rogoff, 2009). This moment instead demonstrates a relational epi stemology where attention is a socially and ecologically situated practice (Bang et al., 2012). In an environment where the body is already embedded within systems of sound such as birds and cicadas, water offers an opportunity for the body to relate to it. Manoj stops, turns left, and initiates a new path towards water and brings this relationship back to his ecological reasoning about deer. This micro-analysis illustrates how the natural world provides an active, discursive context for meaningmaking. By attending to the sonic landscape, participants actively learn to ‘read water’ relationally, which fundamentally organizes their attention, physical movement, and storying of the land. Using participant-generated cameras on a lanyard to capture this ‘learning on the move’ highlights the profound ways that water shapes sensory experience and ecological relationships outside formal educational settings. 3174 Ahern, K. In Classroom discourse https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315775630 3175 Exploring Digital Learning Processes through Webcam-Based Eye Tracking: Development and Applications of SNUWET Siwon Sung, University of California, Irvine, siwons1@uci.edu Hyerin Ryu, University of Maryland, hyerin@umd.edu Juno Hwang, Seoul National University, wnsdh10@snu.ac.kr In Chull Jang, Seoul National University, icjang@snu.ac.kr Abstract: This paper introduces webcam-based eye tracking as a methodological alternative for exploring the multimodal nature of digital learning processes and presents Seoul National University Webcam-based Eye Tracking (SNUWET), a browser-based qualitative research suite. Two illustrative cases, one empirical study of multimodal meaning-making and one pedagogical application in pre-service teacher education, demonstrate webcam-based eye tracking's potential for moment-to-moment process tracing in authentic learning contexts, along with its methodological implications.

Digital platforms now generate extensive traces enabling large-scale analyses of learner engagement. While such datasets provide valuable insights into online behavior, they reveal little about how learning unfolds moment by moment as learners navigate and make decisions within complex digital environments (Baker et al., 2020; He & Cui, 2025). Capturing these processual dimensions requires methodological tools that can observe learning as it happens, with minimal intrusion. While process-tracing technology such as screen recording and keystroke logging reveal procedural aspects of learning (Séror, 2013), they primarily capture overt manual actions leaving opaque gaze behaviors that precede and guide those actions. Without gaze-level data, process-tracing research remains limited in gaining holistic understanding of learners’ multimodal engagement with the diverse resources that mediate learning in digital environments (Sung & Jang, 2024). Eye tracking has long been used in research across language processing (Godfroid, 2019; Michel et al., 2020), human– technology interaction (Korkmaz, 2026), and technology-mediated learning (Cappellini & Hsu, 2022). Despite its value, conventional laboratory-based systems are costly and limited to artificial settings, thereby constraining ecological validity and accessibility. Addressing these limitations, webcam-based eye tracking utilizes built-in webcams to unobtrusively capture gaze data across authentic learning environments—classrooms, homes, and informal spaces (Yang & Krajbich, 2021). This paper introduces webcam-based eye tracking as a methodological alternative for qualitatively exploring the micro-processes of digital learning. It presents SNUWET, a browser-based qualitative research suite that makes process tracing accessible to educators and researchers, and reports one empirical and one pedagogical use case illustrating its potential as an educational research suite.

SNUWET: A webcam-based eye tracking tool for educational research Developed by a research team in the Department of English Language Education at Seoul National University, SNUWET is a browser-based qualitative research suite for collecting multimodal data, including screen and audio recordings and eye-tracking data, across formal and informal learning environments. Grounded in a design-based implementation research (DBIR) approach, it examines the usability, validity, and educational affordances of webcam-based eye tracking in authentic contexts. Through iterative design  and research cycles across K –12, graduate, and teacher-education settings, the system was refined to ensure usability for both researchers and participants.

The interface features a two-stage pipeline consisting of a recording platform and a post-analysis tool. The recording webpage (snuwet.io) allows users to capture webcam, screen footage, and microphone audio, which are saved locally or to cloud storage. MediaPipe (Grishchenko et al., 2020) is used for face-landmark detection to monitor user positioning and gaze stability, generating multimodal datasets comprising user metadata, video, and audio. For post-analysis, a Python-based tool extracts and calibrates  gaze data and generates gaze-plot visualizations. L2CS-Net (Abdelrahman et al., 2023) is employed for yaw and pitch estimation, addressing the limitations of standard facial-landmark models in gaze estimation. These estimates are fitted to calibration videos using a regression model that accounts for individual webcam positioning and screen size, producing corrected gaze coordinates. The post-analysis tool operates in Google Colab, reflecting iterative design refinements from an initial standalone Python script to address operating-system constraints and support accessible, cloud-based use. The resulting interface enables researchers and educators to conduct learning analyses through an accessible, 3176 browser-based workflow, reflecting SNUWET’s broader commitment to expanding methodological access and participation in webcam-based eye tracking research.

Applying webcam-based eye tracking to learning and teaching contexts Case 1: Researching multimodal meaning-making in digital text comprehension Forty-four eighth-grade EFL (English as Foreign Language) students viewed three digital advertisements in a school computer lab while gaze data were collected via SNUWET, after which they responded to three comprehension questions designed to assess their interpretation of advertising intent. The 10 participants whose recordings yielded the highest gaze accuracy were subsequently selected for stimulated-recall interviews, in which they verbalized their thought processes while watching their own gaze-plot recordings. Drawing on multimodal discourse analysis, participants’ reading paths (Kress & Van Leeuwen, 2006) were examined through an iterative qualitative coding process applied to both data sources. One learner (Cecil) actively attended to slogans, facial images, and brand logos yet produced a literal rather than inferential reading of the advertisement (see Figure 1), whereas other learners focused primarily on visual elements with less attention to linguistic slogans, yet correctly inferred the intended meaning. These contrasting patterns demonstrate that visual attention to multimodal elements does not automatically translate into successful comprehension, but meaning-making involves active integration across semiotic modes. Crucially, these processes were only made visible through the real-time screen recording triangulated with gaze data and stimulated recall, illustrating how the method can be employed in classroom contexts to collect ecologically valid data on learning processes as they become increasingly mediated by digital technology.

Case 2: Pedagogical use in pre-service teacher education As part of a methods course at an English teacher education program in South Korea, 14 pre-service teachers participated in a two-hour learning analytics workshop using SNUWET. They were tasked with conducting a learning analytics where they recorded 20 minutes of online English learning activities of EFL learners, conducted stimulated recall interviews, and wrote an analytical report tracing how learners attended to multimodal cues and employed strategies in a digital learning environment, along with discussions of pedagogical implications. In one instance, a pre-service teacher identified a “text first, image second” strategy in reading an English webtoon, where the learner reread surrounding text for vocabulary inference before consulting images (see Figure 2). Suggesting the implications of guided vocabulary teaching using webtoon, the pre-service teacher acknowledged the analytical usefulness of the gaze data. By making visible the hidden processes of language learners’ interpretation of multimodal text, and with its accessibility and usability, SNUWET enables teachers to engage in evidence-based pedagogical reasoning about how to support language  learners in digital environments. With two empirical illustrations, this study presents SNUWET as both a research and pedagogical tool that enables ecologically valid qualitative exploration of learning processes in digital contexts. By incorporating gaze data, SNUWET enables a more holist ic understanding of learners’ moment-to-moment digital learning processes. Moreover, its accessibility and ease of use open new avenues for creative collaborations among researchers and practitioners. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that there is a trade-off between accuracy and ecological validity, suggesting that users strengthen interpretations through triangulation with complementary data sources, such as stimulated recall interviews, to achieve rigorous and contextually grounded research.
