## Acknowledgements

This work was funded by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF-2024S1A5A8026540). 3178 Artificial Revelation: How Artificial Intelligence Exposes the Indiscernibility of Learning Steven Zhao, Columbia University, sz3451@tc.columbia.edu Quincy Q. Wang, Simon Fraser University, quincy_wang@sfu.ca Paula MacDowell, University of Saskatchewan, paula.macdowell@usask.ca Abstract: This study reframes artificial intelligence (AI) in  education not as technological disruption but as a revelatory event. Drawing on Luhmann’s concept of autopoiesis, we argue that AI exposes pre-existing epistemological flaws in education’s operational logic. Education reproduces itself through self-referential proxies of performance and assessment that stand in for learning.  AI makes this substitution visible by collapsing the distinction between authentic and simulated learning, inviting us to re-think how learning is defined, verified and evaluated. The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated intense debate about its consequences for education. Concerns about academic integrity, authorship, cognitive offloading, automation, and the future of learning now shape much of the discourse. Educational responses generally take two directions. The first is control-oriented: revised integrity policies, AI-detection tools, and restrictions on use are introduced to limit plagiarism and misuse (Marsoof et al., 2023; Perkins, 2023). The second is pedagogical: institutions seek to develop AI literacy and promote ethical, informed use of AI in teaching and learning (Ng et al., 2021; Walter, 2024). Although these responses differ in emphasis, both tend to assume that AI introduces a new educational problem that must either be controlled or integrated. We  argue that AI reveals a longstanding institutional and philosophical problem that education has always contained but often overlooked. At issue is a fundamental epistemological limitation: private subjective states cannot be directly accessed between persons and can only be inferred through social communication (Buehler & Weisswange, 2020; Georgiev, 2020). Education, as an institution, must therefore assess what it cannot directly know: whether, and to what extent, a student has learned. This problem is not incidental. It is built into the structure of educational assessment, where learning  is inferred largely through examinations, writing, presentations, grades, and credentials as proxies for  learnedness. These artefacts make judgment possible, but they do so by standing in for what they cannot fully reveal. The emergence of AI makes this substitution newly visible. It exposes a constitutive indiscernibility at the core of education: the inability to reliably distinguish genuine learning from strategic performance or successful simulation.

## Theoretical framework: Autopoiesis in education

Our argument draws on the concept of autopoiesis, first developed by Maturana and Varela (1974) and later extended by Luhmann (1995) to social systems. In biological terms, autopoiesis describes a system that reproduces and maintains itself through its own operations. Luhmann adapts this concept to explain how institutions sustain themselves through recursive communication.  From this perspective, education is a self-referential communication system that organizes, evaluates, and reproduces communication about learning through institutionally recognized forms. Assignments, examinations, feedback, grades, and credentials are not just administrative tools. They are the communicative operations through which education constitutes itself as a system. This means that education does not access learning in any immediate sense. It produces the conditions under which learning becomes describable  and assessable within its own operational logic. What counts as learning is therefore inseparable from the forms through which education recognizes and appraises it. Over time, these forms come to function not simply as indicators of learning but as its operational definition.  Autopoiesis also implies operational closure. A system can respond to its environment, but it does so according to its own distinctions and criteria. In education, many important aspects of learning remain difficult to observe or measure, including personal struggle, partial understanding, creative insight, or even unnoticed cheating. As a result, education does not capture every dimension of learning. Instead, it relies on the kinds of evidence that its assessment system is designed to process.

The indiscernibility of learning Reliance on institutional proxies produces a structural epistemological problem: learning and the indicators used to represent it cannot be fully aligned. Because learning occurs internally, educational assessment must infer it from observable performances  such as essays, exam responses, and presentations. These artefacts provide 3179 evidence about learning, but they do not directly reveal it (Messick, 1995). Assignments may reflect genuine understanding, strategic compliance with expectations, or successful deception. Yet the institution must treat such outputs as meaningful evidence because its evaluative operations depend on visible and comparable performances. This co ndition creates a tension between education’s goal and its operational means. Although education aims for true understanding, it can only measure learning through obser vable assessments. Students face a dual challenge: acquiring knowledge and demonstrating it through clear performance. Performative success becomes consequential because institutional judgment depends on artefacts that can be recorded, evaluated, and graded. Historically, this limitation remained manageable because producing convincing academic work required substantial ef fort and competence. Even strategic performance often involved real engagement with the task. Institutional proxies streamlined education al evaluation by limiting evidence to observable artefacts, but this approach omits aspects of learning like tacit knowledge, intellectual challenge, and personal growth. Artificial intelligence as education’s revelatory event Educational assessment has long depended on a particular junction. First, it computes mostly static and empirical artefacts rather than holistic, longitudinal, or processual learning. Second, these artefacts are often produced asynchronously and at a dista nce. What generative AI disrupts  is the cost structure of exploitation. They can generate essays, explanations, summaries, and reflections that satisfy many conventional indicators of learnedness without requiring equivalent human understanding. AI produces outputs that look like evidence of learning while leaving their subjective source uncertain. Unlike tools such as search engines, calculators, or hyperlinks, LLMs generate variable responses through probabilistic processes across dynamic neural networks (Atil et al., 2024). This variability matters educationally because unpredictability and stylistic variation were previously treated as signs of human cognition or authorship. With generative AI, such signs are no longer reliable indicators of subjective engagement. The issue, then, is not only that students may use AI. It is that the institution cannot reliably discern when an output reflects understanding, strategic assistance, or machine generation. AI reveals are not simply the insufficiency of current policies or detection tools. It reveals that education lacks direct access to learnedness itself, but its institutional approximations. This does not mean education has failed in a moral sense. Rather, it has operated through a necessary but limited epistemic arrangement. AI exposes the fragility of conventional assessment  by making the production of substitutes faster, cheaper, and more convincing. The problem is therefore not exclusively technological. It is structural. Toward a process-visible model of learning If AI highlights the shortcomings of artefact-based assessment, simply increasing detection or control is insufficient. Instead, shifting to process-visible learning offers stronger evidence by making student progress observable through time, interaction, and revision.  Three directions follow.  First, assessment can foreground process-based evidence rather than final artefacts alone. Iterative drafts, reasoning traces, reflective commentary, annotated revisions, and records of decision-making make knowledge development more visible. These do not eliminate indiscernibility, but they reduce reliance on static end products.  Second, instructional design can focus on interaction-based learning activities. Observable learning is better demonstrated through dialogue, questioning, explanation, and collaboration rather than individual submissions. Activities like oral defense, peer than isolated outputs. Third, learning can be inferred more responsibly through developmental trajectories rather than one-time performances. Conceptual development across tasks, transfer between contexts, and evolving explanations over time offer stronger foundations for judgment than single artefacts assessed in isolation.  This proposed model does not solve the epistemological problem once and for all, it needs more research.

## Implications

AI raises a deeper question for the learning sciences: not only how learning happens, but how learning becomes observable. Instead of  treating AI solely as a challenge of misuse, integrity, or efficiency, we should also investigate the epistemological conditions under which education defines, verifies, and evaluates learning.  If educational systems have always relied on proxies, then the task is not to recover a pure access to learning. It is to develop better ways of making learning processes visible without confusing those processes with the artefacts that represent them. For the learning sciences, this means renewed attention to process, interaction, temporality, and the institutional conditions through which learning is rendered knowable.  AI, in this sense, is revelatory. It exposes the indiscernibility that education has long managed but rarely confronted directly. That exposure may be destabilizing, but it also creates an opportunity to rethink how learning is recognized and cultivated be yond inherited metrics.

International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 21(1), 15–29. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-024-00448-3 3181 Student Agency in Communities of Practice: Organizing a StudentLed Undergraduate Computing Conference Matilda Gaddi, Deepika Senthil, Kaitly Aguilar gaddi.mati@gmail.com, dsenthil@ucsd.edu, k4aguilar@ucsd.edu University of California, Sandiego Abstract: We examine student agency within communities of practice through a case study of a student-led undergraduate computing conference that we organized. Drawing on Wenger

(1999) and Klemenčič (2015), we analyze how designing a conference creates new forms of

legitimate peripheral participation while shifting organizers toward core community members. Over nine months, we facilitated 27 accepted projects, with 13 final presentations and ~100 attendees. We analyze participation patterns, learning outcomes, and tensions between agency and institutional constraints. To address our dual role as organizers and researchers, we ground our analysis in established theory and report descriptive outcomes alongside reflective accounts, illuminating the scope and limits of student agency in shaping their own learning communities. Our work shows that agency can be exercised not only through participation but through infrastructuring, with students building the spaces where learning happens. Undergraduate computing students often complete substantial independent work but lack accessible venues to present it, leaving a gap between coursework and participation in academic communities. While Lave and Wenger

(1991) describe learning as movement fr om peripheral to full participation, academic conferences often exclude

undergraduates from even peripheral access by demanding expertise and imposing formal gatekeeping. This leaves students without intermediate opportunities to practice professional comm unication or explore research pathways.

While Wenger (1999) conceptualizes learning as participation within existing communities, Klemenčič (2015), Cavagnetto (2020), and others expand this view to consider how students actively reshape learning environments themselves. Self-directed and self-regulated learning are key mechanisms through which such agency develops (Gupta et al., 2024). These perspectives suggest that students may not only join communities of practice but also construct new ones.

Student-led initiatives including peer-run conferences, hackathons, and learning communities, have been shown to support identity formation, peer learning, and professional skill development (Almeida et al., 2022). We position our conference as an instance  of student infrastructuring, where students create new participation pathways rather than navigating existing ones.

## Method: Conference design as community building

We conducted a case study of the conference we organized over nine months, analyzing both participant outcomes and our experiences as organizers. Given our dual role, we adopt a theory-informed reflective approach, using communities of practice and student  agency frameworks to interpret outcomes while reporting concrete participation data. Our conference design is inspired by academic conferences that the organizers themselves attended, as well as guidelines presented in Corpas et al. (2008). Our design followed three principles:

1. Communities of practice (Wenger, 1999): Create authentic yet accessible versions of academic practice

(paper writing, review, presentation) and foster shared repertoire and mutual engagement among students who might otherwise work in isolation.

2. Learning-by-teaching (Duran, 2017): Enable presenters to strengthen their knowledge through

explanations to peers.

3. Student agency  (Klemenčič, 2015): Position students as organizers and decision-makers rather than

recipients of predetermined structures, and faculty serving in advisory rather thandirective roles. We implemented a two-track system (emerging/established projects), a blind review process emphasizing constructive feedback, and checkpoint-based support. Faculty and graduate reviewers contributed to academic legitimacy. We defined our own evaluation crit eria, grounded in graduate level conference review criteria, but focused on feasibility and growth for the springtime application, then quality and complexity in the fall. Our hybrid structure allowed us to exercise agency and extend accessibility while remaining legible within existing academic norms. Our structure emphasized accountability through encouragement rather than enforcement. 3182

## Conference participants

We received 35 applications and accepted 27, with 13 final presentations. Attrition was highest before the first checkpoint, suggesting challenges in sustaining engagement over extended, self-directed work. Teams and established projects had substantially higher completion rates than sole applicants and emerging projects, indicating that prior structure and collaboration support persistence, consistent with theories of self-regulated learning (Gupta et al., 2024). Participants represented diverse disciplines and projects. Most had no prior experience with IEEE-style writing or formal technical communication, requiring them to translate their work into shared disciplinary forms, an instance of legitimate peripheral participation. Although the event feedback survey data was limited, observational and anecdotal evidence suggests that peer relatability played a key motivational role. Consistent with Nguyen et al. (2021), participants reported that seeing near-peer work made success feel attainable, supporting identity development within a community of practice. The conference also facilitated new interactions among students, faculty, and industry participants. We observed networking leading to research discussions, collaborations, and interest in future organizing. These outcomes suggest that the conference functioned as a boundary space, connecting otherwise separate communities.

While autonomy enabled participation, many students struggled with long-term commitment. Our checkpoint system provided scaffolding but may not have been sufficient for participants without prior experience in extended self-directed projects.

Table 1 Submission Progression by Team and Project Types Sole Applicants Teams Emerging Projects Established Projects Total Applied 27 8 26 9 35 Accepted 22 5 21 6 27 Finalist 9 4 8 5 13 Only 41% of sole applicants made it to final submissions compared to 80% of teams, and 38% of emerging projects compared to 83% of established projects. Student organizers As organizers, we experienced agency as practice, developing skills in coordination, decision-making, and adaptation under constraint. We alsoneeded to remain dedicated to the program, or risk leaving dozens of students with an unexpectedly vanished institution. Organizing required navigating institutional requirements while maintaining student ownership. We simultaneously held power, while having little control over participant engagement and persistence. We observed how agency operates within these existing power structures. Unexpected challenges including attrition and logistical issues required real-time adaptation, reinforcing learning through participation in authentic practices. Organizing functioned as legitimate peripheral participation in academic conference production, moving us toward more central roles. At the same time, our reliance on faculty reviewers and speakers highlights the limits of student autonomy. Institutional legitimacy, resources, and credibility remained partially external. We are planning the second iteration of this program, using these reflections, providing more structure through checkpoints, and connecting participants with mentors. Our case demonstrates that students can act as community architects, creating new structures for participation rather than only entering existing ones. This extends communities of practice theory by foregrounding infrastructuring as a form of agency. At the same time, our findings highlight constraints: balancing autonomy with support, sustaining participation, and navigating institutional dependencies. Student-led initiatives are most effective when they combine genuine decision-making power with enabling structures that support persistence. Lowering barriers to entry while maintaining authentic elements of practice creates meaningful learning opportunities for developing skills such as coordination, ambiguity tolerance, and adaptive problem-solving that are difficult to cultivate in traditional coursework. Future work should examine how to scaffold low-barrier-toentry long-term engagement in high-agency contexts and further theorize student-led initiatives as sites of learning within and beyond formal education. We encourage students to identify unmet needs within their communities and take initiative in addressing them through similar efforts. 3183 Almeida, J., and Daniel, A. D. Cambridge university press. 3184 “Why Should I Care Where My Chemicals Come From?”: DesignBased Research on Chemistry Graduate Students’ Systems Thinking Elizabeth L. Day, The University of Texas at El Paso, elday@utep.edu Abstract: Solutions to the climate crisis require a significant shift in professional training and practice of chemists. However, the proposed holistic, systems thinking approach is a complex performance and may conflict with narratives about what “is” and “is not” chemistry. To study how chemistry doctoral students may develop a sustainable worldview  through formal instructional support, a systems and sustainability course was designed with an ecofeminist lens and Mezirow’s Transformative Learning Theory. The unsuccessful hypothesis was that graduate-level chemists can generate holistic research problem definitions through a scaffolded set of modules to engage in systems thinking, values thinking, futures thinking, and strategic thinking.

Innovations for sustainability require chemists to have competency in the areas of green chemistry and systems thinking (Hurst et al., 2019; Mahaffy et al., 2019; Meadows, 2008). However, current policy prescriptions from international scientific and  professional chemistry societies add these competencies onto the undergraduate curriculum, with an overemphasis on introductory courses; the literature base has limited  evidence that these competencies can be developed through direct instruction (Bruce et al., 2023; Reynders et al., 2025; Talanquer, 2019).

Design problem The big challenge for implementing these innovative competencies for sustainability is a shift in perspective of the disciplinary nature of chemistry. Such concerns have been relegated (often by other academic chemists) to the realm of “not science” or framed as antithetical to scientific and economic progress; a systems-perspective of sustainability may not align well with a  discipline that was originally designed to extract, transform, and profit off the mass production of chemicals.  These ideas of “what chemistry is” stems from social reproduction. By focusing on the epistemic framing within this  social reproduction, formal instruction can engineered to facilitate how graduate students  develop the boundaries  of “chemistry research problems” to incorporate sustainability. This project explores the question: How does formal instruction on systems thinking influence the development of research projects (problem definitions) and systems thinking in chemistry graduate students?

## Theoretical framework

To challenge doctoral students’ conceptualization of what “is” science, this design uses both an ecofeminist lens of sustainability and a theory of change based on Mezirow’s Transformative Learning Theory. An intersectional, non-essentialist ecofeminist framing would challenge th e rigid dualism and artificial separations (Gaard, 2011; Kings, 2017)  and the notion of hierarchies  as a natural consequence, a position taken in the canonical text (Meadows, 2008). This design positions ecofeminism as a point-of-view to serve as a disorienting  dilemma that prompts critical reflection, as described by Mezirow’s Transformative Learning Theory  (Mezirow, 1997). This theory of change connects to the socialization and education of graduate students, who are adults seeking instrumental and normative forms of learning within a particular discipline. Methodological approach A course on systems thinking is used to probe the theorized formal stage in the graduate student  socialization theory. The methodology is a design-based research approach. Figure 2 reflect s the first implementation in the iterative process, illustrated as  a conjecture map (Sandoval, 2014)  to understand how treating formal instruction as a community of practice (CoP) (Lave & Wenger, 1991) within the disorienting ecofeminist framing allows for the emergence of different ways of thinking (see Figure 1). This would position the instructor as a provocatuer or facilitator to promote self-direction in the transformation of graduate students’ frame of reference, within which a habit of mind that emerge from a particular point-of-view (Mezirow, 1997). Course and conjecture design 3185 The course was inspired by the “ways of thinking” framework (Dalal et al., 2021), which paired the use of systems thinking with other forms of thinking useful to considering the logic(s) underpinning a system’s structure and function. By rearranging these ways of thinking into a progressive set of modules and adding driving questions to form the “design architecture” of the course. These four modules are connected to the overall Engineering Practice of Defining Problems  (Day et al., 2024; McFall-Boegeman et al., 2025; National Research Council, 2012)  to explore the graduate student par ticipant’s research context in a holistic way.  In each multi-week module, the course readings and discussion are oriented towards addressing the driving questions associated with each type of thinking (part of the Design Embodiment in Figure 1). The implementation of the ecofeminist lens is in the selection of readings to serve as a provocation.

Figure 1 Design Conjecture Map for Course Components In order to  develop systems thinking, participants in the systems course are engaged in democratic towards two major course assignments: a research problem pitch in which the graduate student conceptualizes their research as a system problem  and the first, initial draft of their introductory dissertation chapter in the Engineering Practice of Defining Problems  (Day et al., 2024).  Peer feedback on both of these deliverables facilitates the negotiation mechanism of this course as a community of practice (CoP). T he immediate outcome for participants was theorized to be a more sophisticated and holistic problem definition.

## Key findings

The initial implementation was a 3-credit graduate course that met twice weekly. Enrollment included 24 graduate students from chemistry, biochemistry, science education (with a chemistry background), and environmental science & engineering. The amount and complexity of reading did not match well with the reading practice of the students. While some early discussions pertaining to values thinking were productive, the discussion structure did not serve as a CoP for a mediating process. This  values discussion is best summarized as noted in the title: “why should I care where my chemicals come from?” The disconnect between sustainability and science was apparent. The initial design included embodiment structures to promote democratic discussions about the assigned STS readings (which were intended to provoke and facilitate an ecofeminist reframing). This discursive structure was theorized to provide for the development of the course CoP as a mediating structure—this failed to materialize in part due to the challenging STS material and mismatch  with doctoral students’ reading practices.  The task and discursive structures of the design revealed a strong orientation towards the framing provided by the doctoral advisor. The design requires serious revision before the next implementation to provide more structure and accountability in the participant structures.

3187 Positioning AI in Teacher Education: Comparing a Designerly Stance with an Instructional Assistance Stance Anna Eunji Kim, Pennsylvania State University, aek5559@psu.edu Suyoung Park, Pennsylvania State University, smp7073@psu.edu Seunghoon Han, University of Northern Iowa, seunghoon.han@uni.edu Amy Voss Farris, Pennsylvania State University, amy@psu.edu Abstract: We examine two contexts of preservice teachers’ (PSTs’) engagement with artificial intelligence (AI) tools. In one c ase, PSTs generated lesson plan s using large language model s and wrote critical reflections about the process and product. In the second case, PSTs designed and trained a machine learning tool for analyzing sound. The findings illustrate  affordances of framing AI in ways that highlight the role of interaction between humans and machines in a process of design and critique.

Teaching is an endeavor in iterative and dialectical design  (Clark et al., 2024; Schön, 1987). Teache rs face innumerable ill-structured opportunities for design every day––constantly eliciting learners’ ideas and responding to them with moves that are highly dependent on immediate circumstances and for which there are often many solution paths. As  artificial intelligence (AI) continues to reshape education and the work of teaching, teacher education faces new demands in  preparing educators to meaningfully engage with and  critically interpret AI technologies. This rapid rise in prominence of AI poses an urgent question for teacher education: How should educators position AI in teaching and learning? Some approaches emphasize using AI as a teachers’ assistant or peer in designing and evaluating instruction or assessments, while others emphasize AI-integrated, technologyenhanced opportunities in learning and design, as well as critical understanding of the underlying mechanisms that make AI possible, and the ways those mechanisms lead to bias and error. Recent studies in teacher education have explored AI as both a pedagogical assistant that supports instructional design (Lo, 2023; Vanden Berg & du Plessis, 2023; Wen & Wen, 2024) and within content relevant to literacies with AI, including algorithms, data, and bias (Celik, 2023; Farris & Kim, 2022). While emerging research emphasizes AI literacy for teachers, much less is known about how preservice teachers’ perceptions and sense of agency differ when AI is framed in these contrasting ways. This study compares two cases in which preservice teachers engaged with AI from distinct framings and task designs. In a social studies methods course, preservice teachers used ChatGPT to create lesson plans on historical topics and wrote critical reflections on the process  and product. Secondly, in an introductory physics course for educators, preservice teachers used Google Teachable Machine to train a model distinguishing sounds by pitch, loudness, and timbre, then reflected on their design of model and its performance. Both contexts required learners to engage with AI, but each positioned it differently: as a curricular assistant (ChatGPT, GPT-4o) and as a designable, trainable  system (Teachable Machine). We draw on students’ written work to explore how the preservice teachers construct ed the meanings of AI and how this positioning shapes their affective and ethicsoriented responses. We do not treat these cases as a controlled comparison; rather we juxtapose them as contrasting illustrations to surface how different task designs and AI positionings shape the kinds of engagement that emerge. We aim to answer: (1) How do preservice teachers position AI differently a cross these contexts? (2) What emotions and forms of agency are evident when preservice teachers engage with AI as an instructional “assistant” versus as an environment for iterative design?

## Context and methods

This exploratory qualitative study draws on written reflections from 44 preservice teachers across two courses at a large U.S. research university. In a social studies methods course (n = 22), participants used ChatGPT to develop standards-aligned history lesson plans and critically reflected on the  process and product. In an introductory physics course (n = 22), participants trained Google Teachable Machine models to classify sounds, then reflected on their learning. Both sessions included brief AI concept presentations before hands-on engagement. Both tasks took place within one class period (approximately 75 minutes). Drawing on methods of reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2019), we a nalyzed the written products produced by the two groups of preservice teachers. In this poster, we focus on themes of emotional tone, ethical stance, and descriptions of agency. Analysis proceeded in three iterative stages: (1) identifying language 3188 that positioned AI  as a tool for thinking “with” or as a tool for thinking “for”, (2) cross-context comparison of affective and ethical meanings, and (3) theme development. Theme 1. AI as assistant: Efficiency and ethical ambivalence Preservice teachers in social studies education expressed mixed emotions toward the large language model ChatGPT, oscillating between fascination, guilt, and professional anxiety. Many admired its speed—“it was jarring how quickly AI could generate something that takes me four years to learn”—yet described the experience as “a blessing and a curse,” “helpful but dangerous,” or “felt like cheating.” They questioned what remained of a teacher’s creativity when “anyone can make a lesson if they know how to use ChatGPT.” Such reflections show that efficiency evoked both admiration and moral unease. Still, some recognized its value as “a good jumping-off point” or “creative boost when used in moderation.” Overall, participants framed ChatGPT as an impressive but morally ambiguous assistant—useful only when bounded by human judgment and ethical reflection. Theme 2. AI as trainable system: From abstraction to real-world contexts Before the activity, many preservice teachers  associated AI solely with text-based tools like ChatGPT. After training sound-classification models, they described the experience as “so cool” and “fascinating,” noting that it “made me realize AI could be a helpful tool to use for demonstrations when teaching about sound.” Several highlighted design challenges, explaining, “background noise skewed our data,” or “we had to rerecord to get it to do what we wanted.” This process helped them see AI as “something that can be taught and can make mistakes.” By the end, preservice teachers  reflected that their perceptions of AI had changed: “Before, I thought AI was bad… now I see it can be used for education.” They began to imagine AI’s role in modeling and simulation-based learning—tools that “show students things not easily described” or “help kids learn about pitch and frequency.” Through these iterative interactions, preservice teachers shifted from viewing AI as an external authority to engaging it as a learnable system that depends on their design, data, and judgment. Theme 3. Framing AI corresponds to patterns of emotion and agency Across both courses, preservice teachers’ emotions and agency were closely tied to how AI was framed  within the learning task. When ChatGPT was introduced as an instructional assistant, students described themselves as evaluators whoneeded to “double-check its accuracy” and “use it smartly,” reflecting both moral tension and ambivalence. Their agency was largely protective and evaluative, as they aimed to preserve professional authenticity while still benefiting from AI’s efficiency. In contrast, when Teachable Machine was presented as a trainable system and an opportunity  to design a sound recognition tool, teachers took on agency as learners who candesign with the tool and see it as a resource that students could design with, with relevance to the content learning goals (attributes of sound). They reported that they “taught the machine different notes,” “had to rerecord the background noise a few times to get it to do what we wanted,” and found “it was cool to see the machine react to the new directions we were giving it.” In this context, emotions shifted from unease and guilt to curiosity and pride. These patterns suggest  that the way AI is framed—whether as an assistant or as a trainable system—is associated with  both the emotional experience and the kind of agency preservice teachers enact in AI-integrated learning environments. Across these two cases, AI tools were positioned in two contrasting ways: as an instructional assistant (ChatGPT) and as a trainable system (Teachable Machine).  Use of a large language model for lesson plandevelopment prompted ethical ambivalence and protective agency, while  the assignment to design a sound recognition tool with Teachable Machine fostered curiosity, experimentation, and reflective control. These contrasts suggest that positioning AI as a trainable  system—not just a productivity tool—can highlight the roles of “thinking with” AI tools rather than asking the tools to “think for” the teachers. The social studies education activity also introduced how bias can emerge when AI is misunderstood, which may have heightened teachers’ ethical awareness and sensitivity to the social dimensions of technology. We argue that teacher education must intentionally address the ethical and social implications of AI. Designing activities that allow preservice teachers to train, test, and critique AI tools can cultivate both epistemic agency and ethical awareness, helping them balance technical literacy  with social and pedagogical responsibility.

We note that these contexts differ in discipline, tool affordances, and task novelty, which limits the extent to which differences can be attributed to framing alone, and that themes arise from self-reported reflections, rather than observed practice. Future work should examine how sustained engagement over time and across varied task designs may reveal different patterns of agency and affect. 3189 Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). 3190 Teaching Kindergarten Students about Seasons through a Lens of Problem Solving and Decomposition Blakely K. Tsurusaki, Rethink Learning, blakely.tsurusaki@rethinklearning.com Chandra Orrill, Rethink Learning, chandra.orrill@rethinklearning.com Abstract: There is increasing interest in how to integrate computational thinking (CT) into K-12 education and a lack of examples of how teachers have done so, especially in non-computer science classes. This study explores how a kindergarten teacher us es problem solving as a lens for kindergarteners to learn about seasons and leverages decomposition, one aspect of CT,  to help students break down the problem into smaller pieces to make the problem easier to solve. Computational thinking (CT) is gaining traction in  K-12 education. However, there are a variety of conceptions of CT (Grover & Pea, 2013; Kafai & Proctor, 2022; Lodi & Martini, 2021). Across the various definitions of CT skills, practices, and attitudes or dispositions, there is agreement that decomposition is an important aspect of CT (Angeli et al., 2016; Cabrera et al, 2024; CSTA & ISTA, 2011; Grover & Pea, 2013; Mills, et al., 2021; National Research Council, 2010; Wing, 2006). Decomposition is breaking or dividing a problem into smaller parts to make it easier to solve. Rich et al. (2018) developed a K-8 computational thinking learning trajectory for decomposition, but this learning trajectory focuses on computer science decomposition-decomposition as both a content topic in computer science and a disciplinary practice of computer science. However, many schools in the United States do not have elementary computer science classes. One report found that based on data from 47% of elementary schools in the United States, approximately 21% of these schools offer foundational computer science (Code.org Advocacy Coalition, Computer Science Teachers Association, and the Expanding Computer Science Pathways Alliance, 2024).  There is also a gap in the literature about CT in early elementary  school, particularly kindergarten, as most research relates to middle or high school (Authors, under review). Furthermore, the extant literature for kindergarteners and CT focus on coding and computer science tools (Silva, Dembogurski, & Semaan, 2023). With the call for integrating CT into K-12 in ways that go beyond coding, we investigate the question: How does a teacher incorporate CT, specifically decomposition, into a kindergarten science lesson?

## Theoretical framework and methods

We draw on Kafai and Proctor’s (2022) three framings of CT – cognitive, situated, and critical – to explore how a teacher enacts a lesson about decomposition in a kindergarten class. A cognitive framing focuses on “…learning as the acquisition of knowledge and skills and emphasizing preparation for future careers” (p. 2). Kafai and Proctor assert that most research and efforts to incorporate CT  into STEM disciplines, including national standards and curricula, take a cognitive approach. A cognitive approach focuses on the individual, rather than how learning is a social and collaborative process. A situated framing of CT  views learning as a social, cultural process. This framing builds on students’ prior interest a nd recognizes that learners are becoming part of a community of practice (Kafai & Proctor, 2022; Lave & Wenger, 1991; Sfard, 1998). A critical framing takes into account cultural aspects such as race, gender, class, and language in learning, and recognizes and challenges power structures. We investigate which CT framing the teacher uses as she teaches decomposition in a kindergarten science lesson. Decomposition is a skill that can help people solve problems by breaking a larger problem down into smaller pieces. Angeli et al. (2016) provide an example of decomposition in their framework for K-2, stating “Break a complex task into a series of simpler subtasks (e.g., break a longer path into a series of smaller paths that a Bee-Bot can follow)” (p. 51). The CSTA & ISTE (2011) CT Vocabulary and Progression Chart states that a PK-2 decomposition example is for students to “Create directions to a location in the school by breaking the directions down into smaller geographical zones. Join the sections of directions together into a whole” (p. 14). Cabrera et al. (2024) include decomposition under their “programming” practice, saying the practice of “Breaking down problems into smaller parts” involves “ finding the successive steps that need to occur to solve a bigger problem and tackling each step individually … can include discussions around how each step in a solution affects the rest” (p. 1342). Their elementary school example is “In aiming to program  a robot to continuously map the ocean (classroom) floor, students determine the tasks of the robot moving forward, being able to turn, avoid obstacles, and make recordings at specific periods” (p. 1342). The examples provided in K-12 CT frameworks are often broad and non-specific (Cabrera, et al., 2023). Furthermore, w hile examples are provided in various 3191 frameworks, the authors agree that the frameworks can be refined through real world examples of teachers teaching decomposition.

This study focuses on one elementary school teacher,  a K-2 STEM specialist,  teaching a lesson on decomposition to a kindergarten class  in the northeastern United States. The focus of the lesson was on seasons and how weather determines what clothing to wear, which aligns to a kindergarten standard focused on preparing for and responding to different kinds of weather (MA DESE, 201 9). The 30-minute lesson was videotaped and transcribed. We used an intrinsic case  study (Stake, 1995) to explore one example of how a teacher integrate d decomposition into a science lesson.

## Findings & Analysis

We found that the teacher used a situated framing of CT, viewing learning as a social process that makes connections to and draws on students’ experiences. As they learned about seasons by solving the problem of what clothing to wear during each season, the teacher asked the students to think about their own clothing and weather they experienced during different seasons.

The lesson began with the teacher showing the students a definition of seasons and four pictures of trees with one showing green trees and grass, another showing snow on the trees and ground, a third showing trees with yellow leaves, and a final picture showing bright green, new growth on trees. This lesson took place in the northeastern US, where the students experience four seasons that include changes in temperature and precipitation (e.g., snow) and where there are deciduous trees that go through seasonal stages with changes in weather and the students were able to draw on their lived experiences to identify the seasons.  The teacher then provided framing for the lesson by saying, “So we are going to help our friends, solving problems today.” The teacher presented the problem: Rainbow Bear and Turtle want to play outside, but it is snowing. She says, “So Rainbow Bear looks ready to go. But Turtle doesn’t look ready to pl ay outside. He has so many clothes in his closet and he doesn’t know what to wear to dress for when it snows. … We are going to be using decomposition to solve that problem together.” There are two important pieces involved in how the teacher framed this lesson. First, she took a lesson that is commonly taught in early elementary school – seasons – and presented it in a way that asks students to use decomposition to solve a problem. Asking students to identify the types of clothing they could wear during different seasons is not a new context for teaching seasons. However, we believe that using this lesson to teach about seasons and decomposition is novel. The teacher took a lesson that is often taught and specifically talked about this as a problem that the students were  going to solve and they were going to use decomposition to solve it. Second, the teacher took a situated approach to teaching about decomposition. Angeli et al. (2016) asserts that CT should be taught in ways that allow  students to solve  real world problems, as this makes learning more authentic and relevant to children’s lives. In this case, how they dress for weather in different seasons is something that the kindergarteners can relate to and candraw on their prior knowledge and experi ences. Learning about the seasons was framed in a way that highlighted its relevance to the lives of kindergartener s, rather than something important purely for conceptual understanding or as learning something important for one’s career. She also said that they would “solve that problem together,” which signifies that learning is a social and collaborative process. Throughout the lesson, the teacher continually asked the kindergarteners to think about decomposition and draw on their experiences to solve the problem. The teacher helped students think about the parameters of the problem they were solving, such as needed warm clothing for cold weather. This helped lead the students in the right direction, so they focus ed on his clothes and not other things that can help keep people warm. Throughout the lesson, the teacher repeatedly talked about how the class was  solving a problem – how to keep warm in the winter. She also continually state d that they were breaking the problem down into smaller parts, which is decomposition. She asked the students to think about what their body parts  are and what they wear in order to stay warm in the winter. The students were encouraged to draw on their own experiences to solve the problem. With increasing interest in including CT in K-12 education and in expanding its reach beyond computer science, we explored how an elementary school  teacher taught decomposition in a science lesson about seasons in a kindergarten class. She taught decomposition using a situated framing (Kafai, Proctor, & Liu, 2019; Kafai & Proctor, 2022), centering the activity in her students’ lived experiences, allowing them to relate to the context of the lesson and draw on their knowledge and experiences of seasons in the northeastern US. As Angeli et al. (2016) argue, it is important for students to solve real world problems because they are multidisciplinary in nature, meaningful, authentic, and relevant to children’s lives. Skills such as decomposition are important for problem-solving that can be useful for use with computational media and without. It is important to include examples that do not draw on computers and coding if we are to integrate CT into K-12 and if CT really should be considered a fundamental aspect of education. This study provides an example of what a kindergarten science lesson that leverages the CT skill of decomposition can look like. More examples are needed, if we are to integrate CT  into K-12 classes.

Any opinions, 3193 Designing STEAM Learning PD for Early Childhood Contexts Lora Cawelti, USC, cawelti@usc.edu Alejandra Alvarez, Elin Anderson, Paul Reimer alejandra@aimscenter.org, elin@aimscenter.org, paul@aimscenter.org AIMS Center Abstract: STEAM is a popular approach to engaging students in learning through the integration of the arts. There are benefits to introducing STEM in ECE but also challenges finding appropriate professional development to support ECE teachers. This poster aims to address that challenge by taking a DBR approach to designing a workshop to support teacher understanding of STEAM. Findings describe the workshop design and teacher descriptions of interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary STEAM learning  with implications for designing STEAM PD for ECE programs.

STEAM in ECE PD STEAM (science, technology, engineering, art, and math) is a popular approach to engaging students in STEM learning through the integration of the arts. While it’s widely used in schools and other learning settings, there are many interpretations of what S TEAM learning actually is and how to do it well (Mejias et al., 2021). From a disciplinary perspective, STEAM could take a multidisciplinary, interdisciplinary, or transdisciplinary approach (Glass et al., 2024). One interdisciplinary way to apply STEAM could be as a form of arts integration, where students learn another topic through engaging in the arts, while a transdisciplinary approach involves more complex processes, like those described by  Beven and colleagues (2019), who conjectured STEAM practices around exploring, meaning-making, and critiquing. In their study on STEM learning in early childhood education (ECE), Aldemir and Kermani (2017) found benefits to introducing STEM in ECE but als o acknowledged a challenge to finding appropriate professional development to support ECE teachers. This poster aims to address that challenge by considering concrete actions that can be taken in teacher learning to support understanding STEAM in ECE settings. To that end we consider the following research questions: How can an early childhood PD program design a workshop for transdisciplinary STEAM learning? How do participants describe STEAM after participating in the workshop?

We take a design-based research (Design-Based Research Collective, 2003) approach to this study and a constructionist approach to the workshop. Our context is the AIMS Center, a nonprofit professional development (PD) provider in California’s Central Valley. In summer 2025, AIMS hosted a week-long professional learning conference in partnership with regional preschool programs using a train the trainer model. Participants in the conference were ECE teacher leaders who were introduced to tools, resources, and materials to take back to their individual schools. AIMS has a reputation for strong programming and leadership in math, science, and literacy. AIMS leaders designed an arts-centered workshop to support participant understandings of STEAM. With support from the first author who is an arts education specialist, AIMS created conjectures and wrote the workshop. After presenting the workshop, we collected 62 participant open-ended survey responses regarding what they would share about STEAM with their home organizations. We analyzed the survey responses by coding them as interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary. Finally, we grouped transdisciplinary responses by their themes. Designing for transdisciplinary learning The AIMS team set a design goal of guiding workshop participants to develop a transdisciplinary understanding of how art experiences inform STEAM learning (see Figure 1). To start, they shared a video of a song in The Lion King musical, followed by a visible thinking routine focused on “on parts, purposes, and complexities.” The visual thinking routine gave participants a chance to observe, interpret, and describe what they saw. This led to a guided connecting. By focusing on processes rather than skills and products, they modeled moving beyond disciplinarity, and into engaging in complex questions, observations, and discussions. 3194 The main activity was focused on reading and bringing a book to life. Participants could choose to make costumes, music, or movement to match an animal character from the book. They rotated through exploration stations, using arts and making materials and creating. This play-based, exploratory, constructionist activity allowed participants to make their own animal and embody their movements and sounds. Finally, they performed alongside their peers, collaboratively bringing the book to life with their characters. The disciplinary learning was implicit in the activity. Participants explored science and nature by becoming animals, considering their traits and habitats. They demonstrated reading and listening comprehension by performing with the book, and they participated in four arts disciplines. This blended approach to learning emphasized the goal of creating a performance; disciplinary learning was embedded within the activity. Figure 1 Conjecture Map of the STEAM Workshop Describing STEAM After participating in the STEAM workshop, participants were asked to share a specific strategy, idea, or tool from this session that they would use with educators in their local community. Their responses shed light on how they were thinking about STEAM and concepts of interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary learning. Of the 62 participants, 32 gave interdisciplinary responses, 26 gave transdisciplinary responses, and four highlighted their enjoyment in participating. The interdisciplinary responses were focused on integrating STEM and arts with responses like, “Integrating all STEM into the art experience as a whole vs isolating art” or “Integration of art, i.e. using the Lion King play, to look at the engineering and design.” The  transdisciplinary responses focus more on processes for learning, rather thandisciplinary learning (see Table 1). 3196 Bridging Rigor and Joy: The MAT Framework as a Design Model for Structured Project-Based Learning Karishma Shanghvi, Lakshmi T G karishma.shanghvi@gmail.com, lakshmi.ganesh@shikhaacademy.org Shikha Institute of Education, Mumbai, India Abstract: This paper introduces the Motivation  (purpose and curiosity) – Ability (knowledge and skill development)– Transfer (application and synthesis) framework as a curriculum design model that integrates the cognitive rigor of explicit instruction with the engagement and relevance of project-based learning (PBL). The framework was implemented in a six-week interdisciplinary unit, “What Conditions Are Necessary for a Nation to Foster a Renaissance?”. Student artifacts demonstrated conceptual transfer, systems thinking, and evidence-based reasoning. Findings suggest that MAT provides a scalable design logic for rigorous, coherent, and relevant project-based learning.

Contemporary curriculum design faces a persistent tension between disciplinary rigor and real-world relevance. Lecture-based instruction enables structured knowledge transmission but often limits motivation and higher-order skill development. In contrast, project-based learning (PBL) promotes engagement and authentic application but can result in shallow understanding when insufficiently scaffolded (Kirschner et al., 2006). The challenge, therefore, is not choosing between these approaches, but designing le arning experiences that integrate both rigor and relevance.

Grounded in learning sciences theories —including Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000), Deliberate Practice (Ericsson et al., 1993), adaptive expertise (Bransford et al., 2000), and the Interest-Driven Creation model (Chan et al., 2021)—the framewo rk demonstrates how structured pedagogy can sustain engagement while ensuring conceptual depth and meaningful application.  This paper introduces the Motivation– Ability–Transfer (MAT) framework as a sequenced design model that addresses this challenge. MAT organizes learning into three phases: Motivation, which activates curiosity and purpose; Ability, which develops conceptual knowledge and disciplinary skills through structured instruction; and Transfer, which supports application in novel contexts. In doing so, the paper argues that MAT represents a structured pedagogy for high-quality PBL— one that offers teachers a practical route and scalable design language to balance explicit instruction with studentdriven inquiry. MAT framework The Motivation phase seeks to ignite learners’ curiosity and sense of purpose by situating content within a meaningful problem, scenario, or role. Rather than treating motivation as an incidental byproduct of good teaching, MAT positions it as the intentio nal starting point of every unit. Learning begins with experiences that provoke emotion and invite identification—role-playing a leader in crisis, exploring a community dilemma, or responding to an unfamiliar but intriguing challenge. This phase provides an affective entry point that frames subsequent instruction as purposeful inquiry rather than imposed content. The Ability phase emphasizes explicit instruction, guided exploration, and opportunities for feedback and rehearsal. Students learn new concepts, analyze examples, and apply strategies in increasingly complex tasks. Importantly, ability-building focuses on the acquisition of knowledge and skill toolkits that can aid in resolving the scenario mentioned earlier. It also leads to the development of transferable mental models —structured understandings of how systems, processes, or phenomena operate. In this way, MAT retains the clarity and progression of direct instruction while remaining anchored to the motivating problem introduced earlier. The phase often culminates in a formative or summative assessment, ensuring that conceptual understanding and disciplinary skills have reached sufficient depth before moving to open-ended creation. In the Transfer phase, learners return to the motivating scenario or problem introduced at the start of the unit—this time equipped with a richer toolkit of knowledge, skills, and conceptual models developed during the Ability phase. Students work collaboratively to analyze the situation through newly acquired frameworks, test alternative explanations, and design solutions or artifacts that demonstrate the flexible application of their learning. This recursive structure —revisiting the initial challenge from a position of mastery —embodies the process of adaptive expertise (Bransford et al., 2000), in which understanding deepens as learners use knowledge 3197 generatively across contexts. The Transfer phase thus closes the learning cycle by transforming curiosity into competence and competence into contribution, ensuring that knowledge gained through structured practice is reinvested in meaningful, real-world problem solving.

Unit design with MAT and student outcomes To show how the MAT framework structures rigorous and relevant learning, it was used in a six-week interdisciplinary unit titled “What Conditions Are Necessary for a Nation to Foster a Renaissance?” The unit was designed for middle-school students and inte grated history, civics, art, and social studies. It helped students explore how societies achieve periods of intellectual and cultural flourishing. The unit showed MAT’s movement from curiosity, to capability, to contribution.

The Motivation phase began with a scenario about an elderly Indian philanthropist who was concerned about India’s cultural and intellectual stagnation. He wanted to use his fortune to support initiatives that could spark a new Indian Renaissance. Before finalizing his will, he invited a youth advisory council to help him decide how to invest his legacy. This framed the project as an act of civic imagination and ethical responsibility. In the Ability phase, from Lessons 2 to 14, students studied the meaning and features of the Renaissance through art, architecture, historical events, cause-and-effect relationships, and its impact on politics, science, and religion. Through videos, guided discussions, short lectures, debates, and research, they developed a causal framework, or a “checklist for a renaissance.” They then tested and refined this framework through Indian history by studying the Indus Valley Civilization, the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka, the Gupta Period, and the Mughal Empire. This helped students build historical analysis, comparison, synthesis, model-building, and evidence-based reasoning.

In the Transfer phase, students returned to the philanthropist’s scenario as informed advisors. They created “Reviving the Renaissance” proposals for modern India, recommending where and how the philanthropist should invest.  At the end of the unit, students worked in four teams on education and innovation, religious tolerance, humanism and polymathy, and wealth and political stability. Their proposals included a digital teaching platform, a “Unity Course,” an interdisciplinary  fellowship, and “Skill Up India.” Across the projects, students showed conceptual transfer, systems thinking, and evidence-based reasoning. Teacher observations and peer reviews showed high engagement, collaboration, content mastery, and the ability to apply knowledge creatively to socially meaningful action.

The implementation of the Motivation –Ability–Transfer (MAT) framework in the Renaissance unit illustrates how structured sequencing can transform project-based learning (PBL) into a more rigorous, knowledge-rich, and transferable form of inquiry. Across it s three phases —Motivation, Ability, and Transfer —MAT provides a coherent design logic that unites engagement with explicit knowledge building and purposeful application. In addressing long-standing tensions between lecture-based instruction and traditional PBL, MAT demonstrates that rigor and relevance need not be pedagogical opposites. The Motivation phase activates curiosity and emotional investment through a meaningful  scenario; the Ability phase consolidates disciplinary knowledge and skills through guided analysis and feedback; and the Transfer phase returns learners to the original problem, now equipped with conceptual models for collaborative problem-solving. This s tructure ensures that learning moves from interest to expertise, closing the gap between doing and understanding. The Renaissance implementation provides initial design evidence for this synthesis. Students displayed higher engagement and deeper historical reasoning, producing causal models and transfer tasks that demonstrated conceptual rigor and relevance of histor ical learning to present day application. MAT offers a repeatable pattern that preserves PBL’s creative affordances while embedding the cognitive precision of explicit instruction. Because it articulates design principles in terms of both learner psychology and teacher workflow, it can be adapted across disciplines, grade levels, and system contexts, including under-resourced environments where structured pedagogy has proven most effective (Piper et al., 2018). Future research can examine MAT’s efficacy through comparative and longitudinal studies measuring engagement, learning outcomes, and transfer across contexts. Design-based iterations may further explore how teachers interpret and customize the framework. At the system level, MAT also provides a foundation for AI-supported teaching serving as a shared design language for curriculum design, feedback and professional development.

RTI International. https://shared.rti.org/content/effectiveness-structuredpedagogy-interventions-developing-countries 3199 From Feedback to Dialogue: Exploring Rubric-Aligned Chatbot Feedback in Human-Centered Design Education Akash Kumar Saini, Saadeddine Shehab, Bill Cope, Mary Kalantzis aksaini2@illinois.edu, shehab2@illinois.edu, billcope@illinois.edu, marykalantzis@illinois.edu University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Abstract: Generative AI tools offer new possibilities for feedback in design education. This study examines student perceptions of a rubric-aligned, multi-agent chatbot integrated into a 16-week Human-Centered Design course. Using post-course survey data (N = 8), we analyzed usability, workflow integration, and feedback quality. Students found the tool moderately usable, with feedback described as clear and actionable, though sometimes misaligned with project context. Findings suggest AI can support dialogic reflect ion, while highlighting challenges of integration and trust.

Human-Centered Design (HCD) is an iterative and reflective approach to problem solving in which learners move between understanding, ideation, prototyping, and evaluation (Brown, 2008; Buchanan, 1992). In educational settings, students engage in open-ended design challenges where feedback plays a central role in supporting reflection and iteration (Shehab et al., 2025). However, providing timely and meaningful feedback in such contexts remains difficult, creating a gap between students’ need for guidance and their ability to act on it. Generative AI (GenAI) offers new possibilities for rubric-aligned, scalable feedback (Kim et al., 2024). In design education, such tools can extend HCD processes by enabling heuristic evaluations, stakeholder simulations, and creative co-generation (Schmidt et al., 2024; Hess et al., 2024). When aligned with educational rubrics and structured for dialogue, such systems might extend feedback beyond the classroom, offering critique that is immediate, iterative, and, at times, surprisingly insightful. We therefore draw on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner to frame how learners engage in reflection-in-action during design and reflection-on-action when revisiting their work. While prior research has examined the quality and consistency of AI-generated feedback, less is known about how such systems function as dialogic, reflective companions in design learning. This study extends the Fall 2024 pilot in which an AI tool provided rubric-aligned feedback on student design artifacts. Reflective discussions revealed that while the feedback was clear and useful, interaction remained one-directional (Saini et al., 2025), meaning students could not question or elaborate on the AI’s reasoning. In response, the Spring 2025 iteration introduced an interactive, rubric-aligned multi-agent chatbot system that enabled students to query, contest, and refine AI feedback through dialogue. This exploratory mixed-method study examines how students experienced the usability, workflow integration, and perceived feedback quality. This paper contributes (1) empirical insight into student engagement with rubric-aligned AI feedback, and (2) a conceptual framing of AI as a dialogic partner in reflective design learning. We ask:  (a) h ow did students experience the usability and workflow integration of the AI feedback tool; and (b) how  did they perceive the quality and efficacy of the AI-generated feedback?

The study took place in a 16-week online Introduction to Human-Centered Design course (Spring 2025). Of 14 enrolled students, 10 consented to participate; 8 completed the post-course survey. Students worked in teams on open-ended design projects and received AI-generated rubric-aligned feedback, including ratings (0– 4) and comments. As designers and deployers of the tool, the authors acknowledge potential bias in interpretation. The CyberScholar platform enabled a Retrieval-Augmented Generation-enhanced, rubric-aligned, multiagent chatbot system that generated feedback across five HCD taxonomy dimensions derived from prior work (Lawrence et al., 2024): Understand, Synthesize, Ideate, Prototype, and Implement. These criteria operationalize stages of the design process and include  descriptors guiding evaluation (e.g., lower ratings in ‘Understand’ reflected surface-level user insights, while higher ratings indicated deeper empathy and evidence-based understanding). The system evaluate d submissions against these criteria to produce  structured, actionable feedback which students could then query and refine through dialogue, positioning it as a reflective interlocutor. Data included Likert-scale items (5-point scale) and open-ended responses. Self-reported perceptions were used as the primary outcome measure, capturing learners’ evaluative and affective responses (Jonsson, 2012), which are linked to engagement and learning approaches (Biggs, 1999). Given the small sample size, 3200 quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and reported as categorical groups, and qualitative responses were inductively coded by the authors following Braun and Clarke’s (2006) thematic analysis framework. Usability and workflow fit Students rated the AI feedback tool as moderately usable, generally intuitive, and largely compatible with their design workflow. The highest ratings were for usefulness of rubric-based chatbot interactions (M = 3.88 out of 5), overall satisfaction (M = 3.75), and ease of use (M = 3.63), while workflow integration was lower (M = 3.25). Qualitative comments confirmed that the tool was straightforward once running but hampered by extra setup steps, clarifying rubric/phase selection, and occasional contextual errors with visual polish. One student mentioned, “Sometimes it gave me responses that were slightly off-topic, and it could also be frustrating when it

## misunderstood the context or repeated generic suggestions.”

Perceived feedback quality and efficacy Perceptions of feedback quality were broadly positive. The AI’s clarity (M = 4.38) and quality (M = 4.00) received the strongest ratings, followed by actionability, alignment with project expectations, and ease of clarification (all M = 3.88). Similarly, fairness, understanding of rubric and task constraints, and key concepts (all M = 3.75) were strong, while motivation (M = 3.50) and consistency with instructor feedback (M = 3.38) were weaker. Students expressed surprise at the breadth and creative utility of AI feedback, noting its role in expanding their thinking and enhancing design processes, shifting initial skepticism toward appreciation of its capabilities. One student said, “What surprised me was how the Generative AI was able to address multiple factors we hadn't initially considered and how it made recommendations for said factors.”  However, feedback was less effective when it failed to align with design intent or creative direction. Additionally, students’ engagement with the chatbot was mixed: half of the groups indicated that criterion-specific bots enabled more in-depth engagement with feedback, typically through clarification (“why this rating?”), rephrasing, improvement planning,  sequencing guidance, and error-checking. Others engaged conditionally (only when confused or when a criterion was scored lower), and a minority used the bot/s rarely or only at the end of the course. However, the feedback was perceived as an augmentative rather than replacement mechanism, widening the range of insights but not fully substituting human mentorship. In many ways, the AI supported rather than supplanted students’ reasoning, prompting them to articulate their design choices and reflect more critically. When feedback becomes dialogic, learners engage not only in revision but in sensemaking, aligning with Schön’s (1983) notion of reflection-in-action and prior work on feedback as a participatory process (Carless & Boud, 2018). Yet this dialogue remained fragile. Students often interacted reactively, seeking clarification only when confused or when a grade felt low, or nearing deadlines, rather than using the chatbot as a continuous co-designer.

This pattern may have been shaped by temporal integration, trust, and pedagogical framing. Feedback was frequently used late in the process, suggesting that reflection was subordinated to deadlines. Perceived issues such as “generic” or “off-topic” responses also limited trust, while positioning the tool as optional led students to treat it as a mechanism for repair rather than exploration. Embedding AI earlier in project cycles and coupling it with instructor-led reflection could normalize its role as a reflective partner rather than a last-minute evaluator. Its value lies not in automating evaluation but in co-constructing reflection, reframing the studio as a human-machine dialogic space where feedback is developed with students rather thandelivered to t hem. These findings highlight that the effectiveness of AI-mediated feedback depends not only on output quality but on how it is integrated into pedagogical workflows and feedback practices. In the language of design, feedback is iteration made visible. CyberScholar extends this visibility by enabling students to externalize and interrogate their design logic. Students found the feedback clear, usable, and insightful, though occasionally abstracted from the lived messiness of their projects, constrained by contextual limitations and timing of use. This study represents an early-stage exploration with a small, self-selected sample and a single data source within one course context. Its findings are therefore indicative rather thandefinitive. Future work will expand data triangulation, linking chatbot logs, instructor reflections, and longitudinal engagement to explore how rubric-aligned AI systems co-evolve with learners and feedback cultures over time. 3201 Biggs, J.
