3202 Power, Identity, Learning, and Shared Values at the Boundaries of Partnerships for Co-Creation Rani Prasad, Homi Bhabha Centre for Science Education-TIFR, Mumbai, India, rani@hbcse.tifr.res.in Sonali Kadam, Foldscope Instruments Inc., sonali.kadam080@gmail.com Avanish Singh, Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai, India, avanish2write@gmail.com Rafikh Shaikh, Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai, India, rafikh.shaikh@tiss.ac.in Abstract: This study explores how power, identity, learning, and shared values unfold within multi-stakeholder partnerships for co-creating Open Educational Resources (OERs) for schools.

The study explores how early-career Research Assistants (RAs) navigate institut ional hierarchical structures. Using collaborative standardised templates, meeting notes, and interactions were analysed guided by the boundary crossing frameworks, focusing on the mechanisms of identification, coordination, reflection, and transformation. Findings show that RAs were able to partially develop hybrid practices and identity through negotiation, resistance, and adaptation. However, transformation and full reflection were constrained by hierarchy. The study suggests that purposeful partnerships, supported by boundary objects, shared values, and dialogues, can foster learning by creating a platform for sustainable and equitable collaboration. Educational partnership is often assumed to be equitable spaces. However, partnerships also hold challenges with respect to participation and spaces of expression and negotiations among participating stakeholders. We view these challenges as boundaries. Power asymmetries rooted in experience, gender, and positional authority shape who learns and whose expertise is valued, often creating unequal spaces and silencing some participants. A boundary can be seen as a socio-cultural difference that leads to discontinuities in action or interaction. The focus should be on overcoming these discontinuities rather than avoiding the differences (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011). Reestablishing these actions or interactions across boundaries is viewed as a valuable resource for learning instead of seeing them as barriers, where knowledge and identities are negotiated through dialogues  between diverse partners in multiple social worlds (Toiviainen et al., 2009; Wenger-Trayner, 2008). Boundaries and learning in educational partnerships In education research, there is an increased formation of partnerships to bring together multiple stakeholders to collaboratively design resources (Hopkins et al., 2018; Penuel et al., 2020). Such collaborations often reinforce power structures and occupational hierarchies (Levina & Orlikowski, 2009). Research–practice partnerships (Coburn & Penuel, 2016; Penuel et al., 2015) and design-based collaborations (Cobb et al., 2003; Hopkins et al.,

2019) explore how learning emerges through negotiation among partners that occupy unequal positions in the

partnership. This study explores power, identity, learning, and shared values within a state-led initiative to co-create OERs and associated wrap-arounds for use on Interactive Flat Panels (IFPs) in government schools. The study examines how stakeholder interactions shape learning, and, and how power shapes RA’s learning, shared values, and identity development as they navigate their roles within this proce ss.

The study is grounded in the boundary crossing framework (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011), which conceptualizes learning at the intersection of diverse practices. It focuses on four dialogical mechanisms: identification, coordination, reflection, and transformation.

## Research design and methodology

The study is situated within a state-led initiative to co-create OERs and associated wrap-arounds for Grades 8-10. The partnership involved state education officials, teachers, external subject matter experts (SMEs), and a research institute team (includin g quality control (QC team), RAs and SME) (Prasad et al., 2025). Within this structure, RAs occupied positions at the lower end of the hierarchy but were responsible for coordinating across stakeholders, translating feedback, and developing instructional materials. Their role positioned them at the boundaries of multiple institutional practices. Data were drawn from 44 versions of collaboratively edited Google documents and notes from 20 online and offline meetings. These data were organized into a chronological interactional timeline to trace how ideas evolved across iterations. The analysis employed thematic coding guided by the four boundary-crossing mechanisms and examined the trajectory of the wrap-around as a boundary object moving across institutional contexts. This approach enabled the study to capture how interactions, decisions, and revisions reflected underlying power relations and learning processes. 3203 This section presents findings from the analysis of interactional data from one representative wrap-around within a larger corpus of 54 co-created OER templates.

Identification: Hierarchical roles and boundary positions The interactions revealed clear hierarchical roles, external SME, government actors, QCs operated from positions of administrative authority, while Pedagogy Expert and RAs enacted the technical and pedagogical labor. For instance, a government education officer’s intervention:  “Who changed these concept names? Respond immediately.” - explicitly indexed positional power, framing RAs as accountable subordinates. QC1 intervened in the same thread with a procedural command: “@RA1 remove these page number references.” RA1 complied but inserted a subtle resistance within deference:“Alright, I will make the changes. Although, the subject group including teachers agreed on these two concepts.” This response marks a momentary assertion of shared authorship, quickly contained by structural hierarchy. The issue was subsequently “marked as resolved,” signaling procedural closure rather than epistemic agreement. This episode exemplifies what (Fischer-Schöneborn & Ehmke, 2023)  calls value dissonance: a moment when differing institutional definitions of “quality” render authentic co-creation impossible. For the RAs, such interactions crystallized their liminal identity as coordinating mediators. Coordination: Operational learning and adaptive expertise Coordination dominated the dataset, with RAs acting as boundary mediators who translated feedback into revisions and aligned resources with state curricular requirements. Across these interactions, coordination functioned less as shared sense-making and more as pragmatic value translation. RAs learned to sustain workflow and design integrity by aligning conflicting institutional expectations, preserving innovation where possible, and conceding conformity where necessary.

Reflection: Uneven and role-dependent Reflective commentary emerged selectively and was shaped by role hierarchy. Teachers’ feedback was  the most pedagogically grounded and reflective in tone, while RAs’ reply includes design reasoning and technical justification, shifting from task compliance toward epistemic dialogue. Across these interactions, value dissonance defined the texture of reflection. Teachers valued usability, SMEs valued quality, and RAs valued a balance between the two. Where values overlapped, reflection became dialogic and generative; where they diverged, it became procedural and hierarchical.

Transformation: Local adaptation without structural change Transformation occurred locally and pragmatically, but not expansively across institutional boundaries. Within the research institute, RAs demonstrated adaptive learning, integrating global OERs into localized formats and designing hybrid wrap-arounds that combined online interactives with offline classroom activities. Transformation in this dataset was negotiated but not expansive, a form of pragmatic settlement that allowed collaboration to continue while preserving the original power and value hierarchies shaping the partnership. This study highlights how learning emerges through interaction in a multi-stakeholder partnership through boundary crossing, where partners move across boundaries to develop hybrid practices. Boundary objects, such as collaborative tools like Google Docs, provide opportunities for learning through ongoing feedback and coordination (Williams & Wake, 2007); however, such learning remains limited when only certain partners engage in boundary crossing. The study underscores the importance of valuing distributed expertise and fostering shared values, dialogue, and reflection to build equitable and sustainable collaborations. Creating spaces for shared decision-making can help move partnerships beyond coordination toward genuine collaboration, enabling transformation and mutual learning that are not constrained by hierarchical power structures.

3205 On Quantifying Qualitative Data: Ethnographic Sensitivity and the Role of Surprise in Learning Robin Samuelsson, Mälardalen University, robin.samuelsson@mdu.se Abstract: New approaches in the learning sciences help to untangle the learning process by quantifying situated learning, for example, by quantifying the traditionally qualitative ethnographic data. This paper illuminates critical pitfalls that can arise if we over-rely on one side of the  data. The role of the unexpected for understanding learning is illustrated from empirical projects that have quantified multimodal ethnographic data. Integrating data while keeping analyses open to surprises is discussed as a key aspect of understanding the naturally complex and messy learning process.

Today, we live in a world where data is becoming a ubiquitous facet of our living and learning. This datafication means that we are tracked, quantified, and assessed in many of our daily activities. With big data, it has become clear that almost all aspects of human life can be quantified and that this information can be used to shape  our future conduct. This is not only impacting how learning can be quantified, but also opening up the methodological landscape tonew methods that capture learning in richer, more nuanced ways that take advantage of the available streams of data.

In the learning sciences, we are seeing increased interest in approaches that leverage the large quantities of educationally relevant data generated and employ increasingly sophisticated ways of understanding the learning process. For example, i n Learning Analytics (LA), data is used to understand the learning process  and n ew technologies have enabled multimodal learning analytics (MMLA), allowing the analysis of multimodal behavioral data from live learning scenarios for detailed insights into embodied and situated learning (Giannakos et al., 2022). An adjacent approach is Quantitative Ethnography (QE), which inherently bridges the traditionally qualitative fieldwork methodology of ethnography with statistical techniques to build robust patterns of data on learning as situated cultural learning settings (Shaffer, 2017). The promise here is a rigorous understanding of learning as it occurs in educational settings, capturing both the local and situational character while quantifying the precise characteristics of the epistemic patterns that emerge in interaction (Kaliisa et al., 2021). These approaches can provide crucial methodological headway without eradicating the schisms between qualitative and quantitative views of learning, which have long been a subject of debate in the educational sciences (Bridges, 2017). However, with the newfound data-heavy approaches and techniques come major challenges, and there is a growing risk that we overlook important aspects of ethnography in our  eagerness to find quantifiable patterns. This paper argues that we  risk forming incomplete pictures of learning and illustrate s why data and methodological sensitivity are key moving forward.

The grand challenges of quantifying qualitative data A major challenge in science stems from the role of ”serendipity”, the element of unexpected findings  (Pievani, 2024). Related to the context of learning more specifically, a challenge arises from the inherent uncertainty of human conduct. Learning happens in cultural environments, that are shaped together with others in social interaction, but is also an individual undertaking (Samuelsson, 2023; Nasir et al., 2021). This means that while we can find patterns in the biological and socio-cultural foundations of learning, we cannot discount the significant discrepancies in learning trajectories that stem from human agency (Tomasello, 2024). While one central outcome of science is to find patterns and replicate findings of these patterns, another goal is to discover the unexpected and what does not fit with current models or paradigms (e.g., Kuhn, 1962). To identify these crucial divergences, we need methods that capture both the general patterns in how learning processes unfold and the outliers in the data (Berland & Garcia, 2024). When it comes to humans, this unexpected side of data can be meaningful for learners themselves and for us as researchers to account for the learning  we study.

In education, what goes beyond the usual patterns can often be useful for understanding the learning process. Thus, if we rely too much on one side of data, say the quantifiable patterns of interaction, we can miss the critical outlier  events that also influence learning (the ”black swans” of learning, e.g. Taleb, 2007). These events are perhaps divergencies from the general patterns of learning, but can greatly affect the learning process. 3206 Next, we look at examples from mixed-methods research where qualitative and quantitative data influenced each other synergistically.

Empirical illustrations Changing communication patterns with digital tablets This project studied children using video-based ethnography techniques and aimed to compare interactions during traditional shared joint reading with similar situations involving digital tablets (Samuelsson, 2025a). A main result of the quantitative findings following analysis of verbal and embodied behavior  was how children talked less during the tablet sessions. Instead, more actions were directed toward the tablet, while the teacher’s action patterns were relatively unchanged (Samuelsson et al., 2022).

A standard interpretation of these results would be that children communicated less with tablets (and this was the finding that caught the media’s attention). However, qualitative and multimodal interaction analysis revealed that children did not communicate less  but did so in using different modes. As the children talked less, many of the screen-directed actions could also be interpreted as communicational. For example, a teacher question would be “answered” by pressing the touchscreen, whereas in traditional shared reading scenarios, it would elicit a verbal response. Thus, we had to redefine our models of communication to understand interaction in an integrated manner. This outcome would not have been reached if we had over relied on the quantitative data; instead, the qualitative side of children’s new multimodal ways of meaning-making proved crucial. Children’s play moves the object of learning This design-based project was developed to create child-friendly computational thinking activities. The project was captured through video-based ethnography for data collection. While the main patterns of learning could be quantified through data coding, many aspects were also less quantifiable (see Samuelsson, 2024, 2025b), related to “surprising” moments in the data (cf. Pievani, 2024), not least evident in the spontaneity of children’s play. For example, when exploring educational robots  in unplanned events, it was observed how children discovered interests and even properties of the technology that were unknown to the teachers and were not planned during design.

Qualitatively observing these, as part of traditional observations, could then feed back into the designbased learning project, where children’s newfound interests were incorporated into the learning process. If we had only stayed with the initial design,  and evaluated its effects quantitatively, we would most likely have missed those critical moments, where children’s spontaneity in effect moved the object of learning. These findings remind us of the importance of finding what is meaningful as the key to quantitative ethnography (Shaffer, 2017), and, furthermore, that meaningful instances can appear in the outliers of our data (Berland & Garcia, 2024). Moving forward This paper is not meant as a refrain from quantifying qualitative data. QE offers a crucial advance in the complex methodological puzzle of understanding the messy processes of situated learning. However, when we advance our methods, it is important that we see both ”sides” of data: what qualitative tools can provide and  what quantitative methods do not,  and vice versa. Mixing methods can be a good design to ”integrate” findings (Bazeley, 2018), but we might alsoneed to work with aspects of rich data sets that also encompass the ”surprising” discoveries of data (Timmermans & Tavory, 2024)  and be sensitive to what theories underpin the quantitative instruments and techniques we use.

Furthermore, an inductive “surprise” in data generated throug h qualitative and abductive methods  can inform a quantitative ethnography and its findings. Vice versa, an epistemic network analysis (ENA) that shows patterns can be informative for qualitative work. Researchers  should be sensitive enough to represent both the patterns and the divergences in the  data as part of robust studies of situated learning. There is no easy recipe for how methods can account for the fundamentally meaningful pieces of the puzzle of learning, in which an outlier event can yield a disproportionately large outcome for an individual (e.g., an “aha-moment”). Moving forward, it is key that we are open to both qualitative and quantitative  data when investigating learning in context. Studying learning in the situated is a complex endeavor that requires understanding the process at multiple  levels simultaneously. Thus, methodological integration is fundamental. Using multiple analytical techniques holds the potential that, if done in a detailed manner, can generate studies where ”1+1=3” (Fetters & Freshwater, 2015). It is crucial, that we can build on the strength of QE.  Combining the richness of qualitative data with the breadth and rigor of the quantitative  can be an important methodological path forward. D oing this will entail looking at both the patterns and the surprises that make up human learning simultaneously. 3207 Bazeley, P. (2018). Integrating Analyses in Mixed Methods Research. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/9780191998294.001.0001 3208 Strengthening Teacher Professional Development through Structured Complex Meetings: Early Learnings from Telangana, India Apurva Sankar, Alokit, apurva.sankar@alokit.org Baidurya Sen, Alokit, baidurya.sen@alokit.org Saipramod Bathena, Alokit, saipramod.bathena@alokit.org Abstract: Teacher professional development (TPD) in India often depends on large-scale training and monthly cluster meetings, which tend to be unstructured and disconnected from classroom practice. This study presents early learnings from two Telangana districts whe re District Resource Persons (DRPs) supported Mandal Resource Persons (MRPs) to plan and facilitate structured, need-based participatory complex meetings. Findings from two meeting cycles show that targeted preparatory support significantly improves facilitation quality, teacher engagement, and the overall effectiveness of complex meetings. The National Education Policy (NEP 2020)  of India  mandates 50 hours of annual Continuous Professional Development (CPD) for every teacher. In Telangana, monthly complex or cluster meetings bringing together 50– 60 teachers from 15 –20 schools serve as key platforms for Teacher Professional Development (TPD). Led by Resource Persons (RPs), these sessions focus on state programs, pedagogy, and creating opportunities for teachers to share best practices and challenges (Guruvu, 2023). Despite their potential, many complex meetings remain administrative and lecture-driven. RPs often receive limited facilitation support while balancing full teaching responsibilities, resulting in low teacher participation and limited classroom relevance. The intervention is anchored in a simple causal pathway: structured support to District Resource Persons (DRPs) improves the facilitation practices of Mandal Resource Persons (MRPs), which in turn strengthens the quality of teacher learning experiences in complex meetings. Improved facilitation and teacher engagement in complex meetings are expected to strengthen classroom instructional practices over time. Intervention: District resource persons (DRP) model Rather than creating a new platform for teacher professional development, the intervention focused on strengthening existing complex meetings to make them more structured and practice-oriented. The emphasis on participatory facilitation and structured preparatory meetings was driven by the need to move beyond one-way information sharing toward active teacher engagement with instructional practices.

To address gaps in structuring and facilitating complex meetings, a District Resource Persons (DRP) model was introduced in Peddapalli and Narayanpet districts, Telangana. A cohort of 5– 6 District Resource Persons (DRPs) trained and supported Mandal Resource Persons (MRPs) to lead participatory, outcome-focused complex meetings (table 1).

Table 1 Resource Persons Cascade Model at District Level Role Role Description Description of geography reached District Resource Person Capacity-building officials supporting teacher training at district level District-level administrative unit covering several hundred schools Mandal Resource Person Capacity-building officials supporting training at mandal and cluster level Each district is divided into sub-units called mandals, which are further divided into clusters. Each district has up to 12-15 mandals and each mandal up to 8-10 clusters These DRPs were responsible for: ● Facilitating preparatory sessions for MRPs on content and participatory facilitation. ● Providing ongoing support through observation, feedback, and content clarification. 3209 ● Using school visits and classroom observations to adapt meeting agendas to district needs. The intervention aimed to create a consistent, reflective, and data-informed structure for teacher learning at the district level. Each complex meeting cycle included a preparatory meeting where DRPs supported MRPs on content and facilitation, followed by complex meetings facilitated by MRPs for teachers. Across two cycles, in each district, a group of 5-6 DRPs trained around 100 MRPs, who in turn led complex meetings for nearly 1,000 teachers. Each complex meeting brought together 50– 60 teachers facilitated by 3 –4 MRPs, creating a cascading but supported s tructure for district-wide TPD. Insights on the effectiveness of these spaces were gathered through a mix of tools, like observations of preparatory meetings and complex meetings by our team members, feedback forms shared at the end of preparatory meetings and complex meetings and informal interviews conducted with DRPs, MRPs and teachers around the effectiveness of these spaces.

## Early results: Signs of change in facilitation and participation

Data were collected through structured observation rubrics and teacher feedback forms during the first two complex meeting cycles.

1. Preparatory meetings strengthened MRPs

Preparatory meetings enabled MRPs to engage with training content, practice facilitation strategies, and plan participatory complex meetings. Special emphasis was placed on adult facilitation techniques to increase teacher engagement and move beyond passive lecture-based training. DRPs demonstrated strategies such as checking for understanding, managing disruptions, and planning hands-on activities, which MRPs later implemented during complex meetings. These preparatory meetings also gave MRPs opportunities to practice facilitation and content delivery, leading to greater confidence and preparedness. MRPs rated the usefulness of preparatory meetings at 3.3 out of 4. In addition, training topics were selected based on prioritized student outcome areas identified through baseline assessments conducted at the beginning of the academic year. MRPs also reported greater clarity on practices such as model reading and question creation.

2. Complex meetings became more structured and participatory

Preparatory meetings contributed to more structured and participatory complex meetings. MRPs demonstrated greater clarity on training content and used activities to create more hands-on learning environments for teachers. Insights generated through DRP school visits and observations were also used to make complex meeting agendas more responsive to district needs.

For example, DRPs identified challenges in teachers’ use of facesheet pedagogy  (a classroom instructional routine) during school visits and observations. In response, MRPs demonstrated effective implementation strategies and provided teachers opportunities for guided practice during complex meetings. Teachers rated the overall usefulness of these complex meetings at 3.4 out of 4. Many teachers were also able to articulate specific instructional practices they planned to implement in their classrooms, including facesheet pedagogy and structured questioning techniques. Data from classroom observations conducted by DRPs across 240 schools showed that 79% of teachers were observed effectively conducting model reading to improve oral reading fluency, while 75% were observed creating 5W1H questions to assess reading comprehension. Both practices were key focus areas of the first two complex meeting cycles. While these findings primarily capture shifts in facilitation quality and teacher engagement, they are viewed as intermediate indicators in a longer causal chain linking professional development to classroom practice and student outcomes.

## Next steps and conclusion

Preliminary findings highlight the value of DRPs and preparatory meetings in making complex meetings more structured and participatory. The model supported MRPs with facilitation, content clarity, and contextualized agendas, contributing to stronger teacher learning spaces. Early outcomes from Peddapalli and Narayanpet suggest promising directions for continuous teacher professional development. 3210 Government of India. (2020). National Education Policy 2020. (1976) framework. Using 21 authentic prompts from the RECIPE4U dataset, we compared

outputs from Original Prompts (OP), ChatGPT Study Mode (SM), and Boosted Prompts (BP). Quantitative content analysis across eight scaffolding dimensions showed that BP consistently produced more structured and process-oriented support than OP and SM (all ps <.001). instructional partners.

With the rapid adoption of LLMs such as ChatGPT in academic writing, students increasingly rely on them for direct text generation, bypassing key cognitive and metacognitive processes. Prior studies show that a large proportion of student prompts request full content generation, and many students struggle to formulate effective prompts (Sawalha et al., 2024; Usher & Amzalag, 2025).  At the same time, LLM outputs are highly sensitive to prompt formulation, making prompt quality a critical factor shaping learning outcomes. While recent work demonstrates that automated prompt refinement can improve model performance (Madaan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023), its role in supporting learning-oriented interaction remains underexplored. To address these challenges, this study introduces Prompt Booster, investigating: RQ1: How do outputs generated from Original Prompts, Study Mode, and Prompt Booster differ in the writing scaffolding they provide?

RQ2: To what extent does Prompt Booster’s automated prompt rewriting enhance the presence of scaffolding features in AI-generated responses?

Prompt booster and its theoretical groundings This study is grounded in Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and Wood et al.’s (1976) concept of scaffolding, which describes how structured support enables learners to accomplish tasks beyond their current ability. We focus on five scaffolding functions—reduction in degrees of freedom, direction maintenance, marking critical features, frustration control, and demonstration—as the analytical framework. Prompt Booster is a Chrome extension embedded in the ChatGPT interface that rewrites cognitively offloading prompts into scaffolding-oriented ones. Acting as an intermediary layer, it uses GPT-5 to apply rulebased transformations grounded in scaffolding theory, encouraging responses that guide learners through structured steps, highlight key writing elements, and provide supportive feedback. After user approval, the rewritten prompt is submitted to ChatGPT-5 to generate the final response. To evaluate Prompt Booster, we used prompts from RECIPE4U, a dataset of 212 college students’ interactions with ChatGPT in an English writing course (Sawalha et al., 2024a), which includes dialogue histories, essay revisions, and annotated writing intentio ns. We selected 21 conversational segments labeled as “Request for Generation” with sufficient surrounding context. For each prompt, three responses were generated using ChatGPT-5 (63 outputs total): (1) an Original Prompt (OP) response, (2) a Study Mode (SM) response using ChatGPT’s built-in mode, and (3) a Boosted Prompt (BP) response, where the original prompt was first rewritten by Prompt Booster before submission.

A quantitative content analysis was conducted to examine writing scaffolding across three conditions (OP, SM, BP) (Chi, 1997). Model outputs were coded using an adapted framework based on Wood et al. (1976), with additional dimensions of Relevance, Richness, and Direct Generation. Each response received a 0–2 ordinal rating for each dimension. The data were analyzed in Python. 3212 Quantitative analyses showed a clear advantage for the Boosted Prompt (BP) mode. BP achieved the highest median ratings on most dimensions with low variability, while OP and SM remained low. Friedman tests (Table

1) indicated significant differences across seven dimensions (ps <.001, Kendall’s W =.46–.80). Pairwise

comparisons followed OP < SM < BP, except for Direct Generation (BP < SM < OP), indicating reduced direct text output in BP. These results collectively indicate that BP elicited responses characterized by stronger and more diverse scaffolding functions than either OP or SM.

Direct Generation. Under the Original Prompt condition, all responses (100%) showed direct text generation (score = 2), indicating that ChatGPT consistently produced ready-made outputs rather than scaffolding. Study Mode showed greater variability (Median = 2, IQR = 1), with some responses including limited explanations (N = 7) while many (N = 14) still generated complete answers. In contrast, the Boosted Prompt condition fully suppressed direct generation (Median = 0, IQR = 0), demonstrating a clear shift toward process-oriented support.

Reduction in Degrees of Freedom. This dimension captures how the model structures tasks into manageable steps. Under the Original Prompt condition, this feature was absent (all scores = 0), while Study Mode showed only occasional and unsustained guidance (Median = 0). The Boosted Prompt condition consistently achieved the highest level (Median = 2, IQR = 0), frequently guiding users through specific writing steps (e.g., refining a thesis before developing arguments). Frustration Control. Responses under the Original Prompt condition lacked any affective support. Both Study Mode and Boosted Prompt introduced encouraging language (e.g., “Let’s plan it together”), but these remained brief and typically appeared at the beginning or end of resp onses. Because such cues were rarely integrated with procedural guidance, affective scaffolding in both conditions remained limited in depth. Richness The Boosted Prompt condition achieved consistently high scores (Median = 2, IQR = 0), providing diverse ideas, structures, and examples that expanded learners’ understanding. In contrast, Original Prompt and Study Mode remained low (Median = 0), with Study Mode occasionally offering stylistic or interpretive choices but rarely extending conceptual possibilities to the same extent. Relevance. This dimension focus on whether the response content is semantically and conceptually aligned with the assigned topic and writing task. The absence of significant differences on Relevance  suggests that prompt rewriting primarily affected the quality and function of scaffolding rather than the topical focus of the responses. This pattern suggests that increasing the informational density of a prompt does not necessarily dilute the model’s topical coherence.

The results show clear differences across conditions. Original Prompt mostly led to direct text generation without scaffolding, and Study Mode showed inconsistent support, often reverting to similar behavior. In contrast, Boosted Prompt consistently shifte d the model toward structured scaffolding, breaking down tasks and supporting idea development. However, this effectiveness should not be interpreted as self-sufficient. Prompt Booster provides an externalized aid rather than a replacement for human prompt ing skill. Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers  (No. arXiv:2211.01910). arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2211.01910 3214 From Classroom to System: A Teacher’s Journey in the Implementation of a Large-Scale Technological Education Program Amanda Reis dos Santos, amanda.rsantos01@rioeduca.net Abstract: The Ginásios Educacionais Tecnológicos (GETs) are a large-scale educational policy in Rio de Janeiro, integrating technology, curriculum, and creativity through constructionist learning and the implementation of maker spaces. Within two years, 200 schools have adopted the model, with 300 more  planned by 2028. Drawing on my experience as a teacher and later as a pedagogical leader for the program, this poster highlights how teachers’ experiential knowledge, purposeful collaboration, and deep listening are key for  such educational network transformations.

The Municipal Department of Education of Rio de Janeiro has a long tradition of experimenting with vocational full-time school models, such as the Olympic Educational Gymnasiums (GEOs), the Carioca Experimental Gymnasiums (GECs), and bilingual schools. Among these, the Technological Educational Gymnasiums (GETs) have emerged as one of the city’s most ambitious educational policies. Since their creation in 2022, GETs have expanded from a small experimental cluster of five schools to a projected 500 units by 2028, encompassing both elementary and middle school levels.

The GET initiative aims to modernize public education by integrating the municipal curriculum with digital technologies and innovative pedagogical practices. Its physical and symbolic core is the Colaboratório — a maker space equipped with 3D printers, robotics kits, VR headsets, sewing machines, vinyl cutters, and other creative tools. These environments enable students to engage in hands-on, project-based learning grounded in STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts & Mathematics) and active methodologies. The initiative also established twonew teaching roles — the Articulating Teacher (PA) and the Teacher of Integrative Projects (PIC)

— supported by extensive professional development programs focused on constructionism (Blikstein, 2016;

Blikstein & Campos, 2020) through partnerships with the Transformative Learning Technologies Lab (TLTL, Columbia University) and Casa Firjan in Rio de Janeiro. In 2024, as an Articulating Teacher in two GET schools, I implemented the constructionist approach by transforming the Colaboratório into a space of creativity, inquiry, and interdisciplinary collaboration. Working alongside other teachers, I mapped the learning objectives of each term and designed maker-based solutions aligned with classroom goals. Each project began with an anchoring phenomenon — an experiment, game, or real-world challenge — and evolved through semi-structured questioning that promoted s tudents’ critical reasoning and agency. The process followed backward design principles (Wiggins & McTighe, 2014), emphasizing evidence of learning, continuous reflection, and pedagogical documentation stored in shared digital archives, in order to share with other teachers what was going on in the Colaboratório. These projects extended beyond the school, featuring in events such as the Senac Rio Summit and the Mathematics Festival, demonstrating the model’s transformative potential.

In 2025, following a year-long professional development program for PAs and the successful implementation of constructionist practices in my schools, I was invited to join the Department of Education’s leadership team responsible  for the expansion and consolidation of the GETs policy. This poster draws from that trajectory, from classroom practice to system-level leadership, to highlight how teachers’ experiential knowledge, purposeful collaboration among educators, school leaders, and policymakers, as well as a culture of deep listening are crucial to sustaining large-scale educational innovation in public school networks. Systemic insights As a PA, while planning, teaching and also facing all the challenges leading Colabs in two schools, I have had the opportunity of building experiential knowledge related to the implementation of the GETs through my daily experiences. Co-designing learning experiences using backward design (Wiggins & McTighe, 2014) and STEAM methodologies with other GET teachers we learned a lot about what it takes for teachers to engage  students in inquiry units where students have agency to investigate, generate questions,  collaboratively prototype solutions, use technology in purposeful and critical ways as well as produce reflective documentation of their learning journeys. Through this hands-on work, several important systemic insights for the broader implementation of the GETs program have emerged, such as: 3215 ● Teachers needed collaborative planning time and structures that value experimentation. ● The Colaboratório requires clearer governance and maintenance protocols. ● Professional development must be continuous. Teachers should experience the learning that is intended for students, while also designing, implementing, discussing and iterating their own teaching plans. ● Assessment systems must evolve to capture processes, progress, reflection, and creativity. Transitioning from classroom practice to system coordination, as I became Pedagogical Leader for the GETs at the municipal level in 2025, allowed me to translate micro-level experiences into macro-level design principles. In this role, with the mission of scaling constructionist  and maker practices across Rio’s public-school network, the largest in Latin America, our team has: ● Opened new GET schools and inaugurated Colaboratórios; ● Designed a new professional development model mirroring the constructionist cycle (hands-on, reflection, integration); ● Trained over 200 teachers and reached 10,000+ students in logic and programming; ● Integrated Mathematics as a transversal subject across Colaboratório projects. ● Focused on learning outcomes built through meaningful learning  and alignment with the curriculum (BNCC and the Rio de Janeiro municipal curriculum, the so-called “Currículo Carioca”). ● Enhanced institutional communication with municipal education administrators, school leaders and teachers across the Municipal School Network.

These collective efforts have positioned the GET program as one of the most ambitious technology-integration initiatives in Latin America. The experiential knowledge I gained as an Articulating Teacher (PA) in two GET schools continues to inform my decision-making and proposals in my current leadership role. Yet, a Herculean task  remains ahead. Strengthening this public policy demands significant structural advances, from establishing clear governance flows among all strategic actors of the GETs, to expanding professional development opportunities aligned with constructionism; from fostering maker and STEAM-oriented practices among all teachers (not only the PAs), to promot ing knowledge-sharing within learning communities and consolidating gains in student learning outcomes.

Having been part of the everyday life of schools is undoubtedly an asset in pursuing these goals. Firsthand understanding of teachers’ realities, students’ profiles, and the complex challenges of public schools allows for more grounded and empathetic leadership. This ongoing connection to the field has been a cornerstone of my work at the Municipal Department of Education, nurturing open communication with school communities and regional offices through technical visits and continuous dialogue. Porto Alegre: Penso. 3217 Enhancing Early Clinical Reasoning through Generative AIsupported Self-explanation: A Design-based Research Study in Preclinical Medical Education Xiaoyu Zhao, Kai Yu Ma, Lizayra Dassen, Marco Antonio de Carvalho Filho, Ligia Cayres Ribeiro x.zhao@umcg.nl, k.y.ma@umcg.nl, l.dassen@umcg.nl, m.a.de.carvalho.filho@umcg.nl, l.m.cayres.ribeiro@umcg.nl Wenckebach Institute (WIOO), Lifelong Learning, Education, and Assessment Research Network (LEARN), University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen, Groningen, The Netherlands Abstract: Early clinical reasoning development is challenging because students struggle to transfer and reorganize biomedical mechanisms into causal models of clinical signs and symptoms. Drawing on illness script theory and g enerative learning theory, this design-based research developed and refined design principles for an innovative generative AI –supported self-explanation intervention. These principles promote early knowledge encapsulation and clarify how generative learning processes can supp ort script formation  in early clinical reasoning development.

Clinical reasoning (CR) is a fundamental yet difficult competence to develop during the early years of medical education (Schmidt & Rikers, 2007). First-year students often learn biomedical mechanisms in isolation and find it hard to explain how these mechanisms account for clinical signs and symptoms. Their reasoning therefore remains descriptive rather than explanatory, delaying the encapsulation of biomedical knowledge into early illness scripts (Custers, 2015). Introducing clinical reasoning early can e ase the transition from basic to clinical understanding, yet educators still struggle to help students connect mechanisms with manifestations and to support the construction of causal explanations rather than memorized descriptions.  This study investigates how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can scaffold self-explanation activities that promote early encapsulation of knowledge. The goal is to identify design principles that guide the use of GAI to support the development of early clinical reasoning.

A Design-Based Research (DBR) methodology was adopted, combining iterative cycles of design, implementation, and reflection. Two complementary theories informed the design. Illness s cript theory (IST) describes how biomedical knowledge becomes clinically meaningful through encapsulation and script formation (Custers, 2015; Schmidt & Boshuizen, 1993). Generative learning theory (GLT) emphasizes that learning deepens when learners actively select, organize, and integrate information through constructive processes such as self-explanation (Chi & Wylie, 2014). Together these theories framed the design of prompts and feedback intended to activate prior knowledge, stimulate causal reasoning, and encourage reflection.

The study was conducted in a first-year biomedical course at a Dutch medical school. Students interacted with a generative AI chatbot designed to guide self-explanation around clinical cases, structured into phases of knowledge activation (selection), narrative construction (organization and integration), and reasoning transfer (application). A total of 181 first-year medical students participated across five design cycles (R1: n=181; R2: n=69; R3: n=79; R4: n=64; R5: n=32). Data sources included conversation logs, questionnaires on motivation and cognitive load, and semi-structured interviews with students and tutors. Conversation logs were analyzed to examine students ’ engagement patterns, including interaction length, number of exchanges, and progression across phases. Interview data were analyzed thematically to complement the process data. The analysis was iterative across design cycles to examine how different scaffo lding designs shaped students ’ engagement in generative reasoning processes and supported early script formation. Across the design cycles, the chatbot intervention evolved into a more coherent learning experience that supported early clinical reasoning  development of students. Analysis of conversation logs indicated that embedding mechanistic prompts within authentic patient vignettes was associated with more integrated explanations, reflected in students more frequently linking underlying mechanisms to clinical signs and symptoms. Logs also 3218 suggested that exposure to multiple related cases supported transfer, with students increasingly applying similar causal reasoning across contexts.

Structuring the interaction into phases of knowledge activation, narrative construction, and reasoning transfer appeared to support a progression in students’ reasoning. Conversation log analysis showed that prompts explicitly requiring “why” and “how” explanations were associated with increased generative engagement, reflected in longer interactions and more elaborated responses rather than isolated factual statements. Adaptive follow-up questions that invited students to refine or extend their responses appeared to sustain elaboration without directly providing answers, while reflective prompts supported the consolidation of understanding across phases.

Interview data further indicated that students experienced a shift from recalling facts to explaining why symptoms occur, describing the activity as supporting “thinking like a doctor.” Students also reported that engaging with conceptually challenging topics and authentic clinical cases helped them better connect mechanisms to clinical findings and apply their reasoning across cases. These patterns suggest early integration of biomedical and clinical knowledge, consistent with initial stages of script for mation. These findings informed a set of theory-informed design principles for AI-supported self-explanation. This study illustrates how a generative AI –supported self-explanation environment can help address a central challenge in early medical education: connecting biomedical mechanisms to clinical reasoning. The findings suggest that the structured dialogue supports a progression from knowledge activation to integration and transfer, aligning with key processes described in generative learning theory and facilitating early script formation as described in illness script theory.

From a theoretical perspective, the results provide insight into how generative learning processes may contribute to early script development. By engaging learners in explaining “why” and “how” mechanisms relate to clinical findings, the intervention appears to support the organization and integration of biomedical knowledge into more coherent, clinically meaningful representations. This suggests that structured self-explanation, when appropriately scaffolded, may initiate aspects of knowledge encapsulation even in preclinical stages. This study contributes by articulating theory-informed design principles that explain how AI-supported scaffolding can foster generative reasoning and early script formation. ## Problem statement

In pre-service teacher training, students are expected to learn how to analyze and solve classroom problems in an evidence-informed manner (Gorard et al., 2020). While searching for literature to solve such problems, pre-service teachers are often confronted with multiple documents. While some of them may st em from scientific sources (e.g., journal articles), others may have been produced by non-scientific sources (e.g., teacher blogs; Kiemer & Kollar, 2021). Also, these documents  may vary with respect to how they fit to the classroom problems teachers and their students currently face by either addressing their causes or symptoms (e.g., comprehension difficulties due to complex learning material can be treated cause-related via decreasing intrinsic load or symptom-related by prompting deeper learning processes through constructive and interactive learning activities). Pre-service teachers need to be able to process such multiple documents to arrive at sound evidence-informed analyses of classroom problems.

Integrating multiple documents in the context of evidence-informed reasoning about classroom problems To conceptualize an ideal way how pre-service teachers integrate multiple documents, the Integrated Framework of Multiple Text Use (IF-MT; List & Alexander, 2019)  claims that learners need to build an inter-textual model for cross-textual linking and reasoning of multiple documents. This model assumes  four steps. First, pre-service teachers need to examine the texts for possible relations (identification). Then, they need to individually represent components of potential ly related documents (separate representation) before they synchronize and re present them in a singular statement with a relational modifier (e.g., "while," "both," or "and") as a simultaneous representation. Finally, they need to explicitly label relations between them (relation designation). However, it is unclear how pre-service teachers manage such integration processes, especially since the documents originate from different sources and vary in their fit to the classroom problem.  Therefore, w e investigated how document type (scientific vs. non-scientific) and the fit of the information for solving the classroom problem (cause-vs. symptom-related fit) affect how pre-service teachers  use and integrat e such documents during the evidence-informed analysis of classroom problems.

## Sample and procedure

A total of N = 453 pre-service teachers (mean age = 22.2, SD = 3.2; 69.31% female) in their M = 4.8 1 semester (SD = 2.43) participated in the study. In four subsequent weeks, participants received one authentic case vignette describing a classroom problem (e.g., students experiencing comprehension difficulties due to complex learning material). After they provided a first intuitive suggestion on how to solve the problem, they were invited to revise it by aid of two documents: (1) a 1-page scientific document summarizing an educational theory as well as a related empirical study, and (2) a 1-page non-scientific document presenting a teacher’ s experience-based recommendation. Both documents varied in their fit to the classroom problem: While one document suggested to 3220 address the problem through cause-related strategies (decrease intrinsic load, see Sweller, 1994, or activate prior knowledge, see Bower, 1981), the other document suggested symptom-related strategies (prompt deeper learning processes through constructive and interactive learning activities, see   Chi & Wylie, 2014, or observation, see Bandura, 1986). Selection of strategies as cause-or symptom-related was based on prior expert ratings of N = 24 educational researchers. To control for sequential effects, the order of classroom problems and the documents including their specific recommendations were counterbalanced.

## Measures

Two independent raters coded participants’ revised suggestions with respect to (1) information use (proportion of sentences that referenced information from each document, 0 to 1,  Gwet’s AC1 =.94), and (2) integration quality (how strongly participants linked information from different sources according to the four-step process of crosstextual linking in the IF-MT model, 0 = no integration to 4 = relational designation, Gwet’s AC2 =.86). With respect to information use, participants used documents that addressed the causes of the problem more often than symptom-related documents, β = 0.33, p <.001. There was no significant difference in use between nonscientific and scientific documents, β = −0.05, p =.335, and no interaction effect, β = −0.04, p =.480 (see Figure 1). Integration quality was significantly influenced by document fit: The relationship followed a linear trend, β = 0.88,  p <.001, indicating that students integrated information most strongly when both documents related to the symptoms of the problems, followed by the documents differing in their fit, whereas integration was least frequent when both documents had a cause-related fit (see Figure 2). Figure 1 Use of Information Predicted by Information Fit and Source of Document Figure 2 Probability of Different Levels of Information Integration dependent on Fit With respect to information use, our results suggest that pre-service teachers do not prefer documents based on their sources. Yet, this effect is somewhat surprising, as preferences for documents of non-scientific sources have been reported (Ferguson et al., 2023; Futterleib et al., 2022; Kiemer & Kollar, 2021), thus possibly indicating context effects: Perhaps, situating the study within a regular university course may have led to desirability effects (Schoor et al., 2023). Additionally, information addressing the problem’s cause were used more often than information with symptom-related fit, suggesting that pre-service teachers seem to understand that cause-related documents offer a higher potential for persistent solutions of classroom problems than symptom-related documents. Yet, their probability of use is less than 20 %. Therefore, pre-service teachers need to be scaffolded to select and effectively apply documents with cause-related fit. Regarding the integration of documents,  our address the symptoms of the problem. One possible explanation is  that pre-service teachers may assess the task relevance of symptom-related documents as rather low  (Rouet & Britt, 2011), which in turn may trigger  deeper processing and integration of the available documents. Additionally,  pre-service teachers seem to spontaneously integrate documents of mixed fit more intensively than of only cause-related fit, indicating that documents with mixed fit might trigger a conflict, which may prompt further processing (Stadtler & Bromme, 2014), possibly leading to a deeper  integration. This may hint at the need of a trigger (e.g., insufficient relevance assessment or conflict) to engage in  active processes that are  necessary to promote integration. However, it is important to discuss whether  unconditional integration is a desired outcome when not a ll information fits equally well, or whether a prior evaluation and careful selection of information should be the goal instead. 3221 Bandura, A. ## Acknowledgments

This work was supported by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft; 395758789. 3222 Empowering School Teachers: Impact of Science Movement Emaya Kannamma, Tata Institute of Social Sciences, emayakannamma@gmail.com Abstract: The impact of People’s Science Movements (PSM) on school teachers  is rarely documented. This qualitative case study, based on 23 teacher interviews, examines the influence of the Tamil Nadu Science Forum (TNSF). TNSF facilitates transformative learning, shifting teachers from 'technicians' to 'change agents’. The networ k cultivates social capital, enabling teachers to overcome personal barriers, gain recognition as authors and consultants, and negotiate significant professional autonomy, thus highlighting a critical model for continuous teacher development.

Teacher education traditionally focuses on individuals, giving less attention to teacher communities and networks (Niez, 2007; Batra, 2005). However, effective teachers do not work in isolation, and professional growth can be hindered by individual efforts  (Schiff et al., 2015; Leana, 2011). Informal communities provide professional recognition, help break isolation, and increase job satisfaction (Latha, 2019; Giordano, 2008; Schiff et al., 2015; Johnson et al., 2011; Leana & Pil, 2006, 2009). Teachers have  chosen the profession due to their involvement in social justice networks, finding it a means to create change and sustain their practice (Ritchie, 2012). Professional communities facilitate social, informal, and voluntary learning vital for identity and agency (Lieberman & MclLaughlin, in Neiz, 2007; Wenger, 1999; Thomas et al., 1998; Grossman et al., 2001). Universities and teacher resource centres increasingly recognise these networks, including virtual communities (Sarangapani et al., 2017; Giordano, 2008; Barab, 2003; Thirumalai & Sarangapani, 2023). Policy and professional development measures show little recognition of existing teacher networks in India. Established in the mid-1980s, Tamil Nadu Science Forum (TNSF) is a voluntary movement dedicated to popularising science and cultivating scientific temper. With around 18,000 members, including many teachers, the movement significantly influences educational reform in Tamil Nadu. Although improving education is a major objective of these PSMs, their impact on school teachers remains scarcely documented. This study seeks to address this gap by examining how participation in such a large, voluntary network shapes teachers' agency. This study employed a qualitative case study approach to provide an understanding of impact it has on school teachers. Semistructured interviews were conducted with 23 movement school teachers, identified as T1-T23, for direct quotes in the sections below.

Teacher learning TNSF facilitates transformative learning, shifting teachers from technicians to change agents and intellectuals. Teachers describe this process as life-changing. The movement actively promotes reading; for instance, T10 overcame hesitation to read, finding it a pivotal journey. Involvement in TNSF exposes teachers tonew literature. T13 helped broadcast introductions to alternative education books on Educational TV, while T6 used reading and travel to gain classroom insights. Reading is central to Thulir Illams (Children's Homes), where students discuss the Thulir magazine. Additionally, TNSF book festivals allow teachers to promote literacy to the public. Change in perspective The TNSF instils fundamental beliefs such as equality and rationality, thereby building a worldview. T1 noted that the TNSF taught the doctrine of equality and eliminated superstitious practices. As TNSF’s main focus is to bring change by building scientific temper among citizens, they have a series of events focused on awareness and debunking myths about the eclipse and self-proclaimed godman’s ‘magic' tricks used to exploit people. T23 overcame the ego of being a "big person," realising they are just one member of society. This shift enabled meaningful participation in the teachers' union; despite the power associated with official posts, T23's TNSF training instilled a commitment to the cause regardless of designation. T23 learned to think beyond the immediate village or caste and consider the impacts globally. This is supported by T11's perspective that the movement teaches how to live simply among the people, without focusing on accumulating assets. T22 articulated a desire to use the movement to transform the political environment to address issues of poverty, corporate exploitation, and inequality. T18 argues that the movement reinforces the fundamental duty of every citizen to promote scientific temper. T23's decision to return election funds to parties that gave them to his mother illustrates a deepseated commitment to ethical civic practice, fostered by the movement's principles. 3223 Professional agency Many teacher members contribute significantly to state-level education; T2, a Government Consultant and author, notes that the movement transformed his view of teaching from just a job into a political act. This influence extends to shaping policy and curriculum, with T7 writing government textbooks and syllabus frameworks, and T13 working with SCERT and DIET to develop content and train resource persons. The movement fosters the personal confidence necessary for professional negotiation. By overcoming severe stage fright, teachers like T1, T10, T12, and T19 gained the self-assurance to address hundreds of colleagues and lead sessions with district officials. This empowerment enables them to secure school-level changes, including student specialisations and positive reinforcement awards. TNSF participation provides teachers with pedagogical shifts. T6 utilised Origami and socio-scientific knowledge, while T3 and T4 used film reviews to develop media critique skills. T18 linked his practice to Article 51A, viewing the promotion of scientific temper as a fundamental duty. Many noted that TNSF teachers encourage students to question and engage with their rights. Increased approachability has led to long-term student mentorship regarding career and personal decisions. Key pedagogical changes include using the immediate environment, real objects, and simple experiments to stimulate inquiry. The movement enables teachers to engage in direct social action. T1 raised awareness about sanitary napkins to improve girls' school attendance, while T19 led programs for women, including a quarry movement. T22 coordinated the Illam Thedi Kalvi program for children affected by the pandemic. T3 and T6 facilitate student access to libraries and book exhibitions, and T21 published a student manuscript book titled Agni, fostering youth writing.

Many events are organised to encourage school students to engage with the science magazines published by TNSF, fostering reading habits. T15 conducted activities such as Thulir magazine reading groups, simple science experiments, and organising talent test s and quizzes for children. T2 proudly stated that students who participated in TNSF events like Quiz and Children's Science Congress have gone on to become leaders. T8 noted that students who participated in projects eventually became successful, including one who became a doctor. Social capital TNSF participation has expanded teacher networks across diverse domains, fostering connections with mentors, colleagues, officials, and the public based on equality and mutual support. Teachers T23 and T11 highlighted the humility of prominent scientists and mathematicians within the movement. T12 noted that TNSF uniquely bridges the gap between farmers and scientists. Many teachers, including T2 and T9, gained recognition as authors through their field experiences.

Mentorship within TNSF is deeply personal; T14 and T16 described relationships akin to family, and T12 received support during a family tragedy. T9 noted the movement's significant presence at his wedding. This inter-professional network also enabled T21 to connect with the public and T19 and T15 to interact with highranking officials. Despite these gains, challenges persist regarding meaningful leadership roles for women. Regarding caste, most teachers rejected notions of internal differentiation, though some acknowledged that societal hierarchies might inadvertently permeate the network. The Tamil Nadu Science Forum (TNSF) transforms teachers from mere technicians into "movement intellectuals" capable of negotiating change across personal, professional, and political domains. By fostering social capital and a worldview centred on equality and rationality, the forum empowers educators to implement child-centred pedagogies and engage in direct social action. Ultimately, TNSF provides a vital support system that enables teachers to exercise autonomy and find fulfilment in creating positive social change, highlighting a model for continuous professional development that the formal education system often overlooks.

The study reiterates that teacher education should move beyond skills training by valuing the informal networks where teachers naturally learn from one another. Programs should focus on building a teacher's confidence, professional identity, and community connections. By involving educators in community action and policy and curriculum decisions, we can keep them motivated and use their expertise. 3224 Aslam, M., Rawal, S., & Kingdon, G. (2019). Cambridge university press. 3225 Fostering Elementary School Students' Productive Disciplinary Engagement through Knowledge-Building Inquiry and Reflective Assessment Yuqin Yang, Central China Normal University, China, yangyuqin@ccnu.edu.cn Shufang Yang, Central China Normal University, China, yangshufang@ccnu.edu.cn Daner Sun, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong S.A.R., dsun@eduhk.hk Xueqi Feng, Southern University of Science and Technology, China, fengxq@sustech.edu.cn Abstract: This study examines how reflective assessment –supported knowledge-building inquiry fosters productive disciplinary engagement (PDE) among elementary students. A design-based study was conducted with 50 sixth-grade students over two semesters in a primary science classroom. Results showed significant gains in conceptual understanding, alongside increases in cognitive, social, and emotional engagement. Epistemic network analysis further revealed strengthened connections between metacognitive processes and higher-order engagement. Findings suggest that integrating reflective assessment into knowledge-building environments supports PDE by enhancing metacognitive awareness and learner agency. This study provides empirical evidence and design implications for fostering productive engagement in elementary education.

Productive disciplinary engagement (PDE) is essential for meaningful learning (Engle & Conant, 2002; Engle, 2012; Sinha et al., 2015; Rogat & Cheng, 2019), as it enables students to participate in disciplinary practices and develop deep conceptual understanding (Engle & Conant, 2002; Engle, 2012). However, cultivating PDE in elementary classrooms remains challenging, as instruction often emphasizes rote learning rather than authentic inquiry (Forman et al., 2014). Knowledge building (KB) provides a promising approach by engaging students in collaborative idea improvement within a community, where ideas are treated as improvable objects (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2003; 2014). Reflective assessment further supports this process by promoting metacognitive awareness (Flavell, 1979), enabling learners to monitor, evaluate, and regulate their inquiry processes (Yang et al., 2016; Lei & Chan, 2018).  Integrating KB and reflective assessment offers a mechanism for fostering PDE across cognitive, social, and emotional dimensions (Fredricks et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2022). While prior research has demonstrated these effects in secondary and higher education, empirical evidence in elementary contexts remains limited.  This study addresses this gap by designing a reflective assessment –supported knowledge-building environment to scaffold elementary students’ PDE in science learning. By examining both learning outcomes and engagement processes, this study aims to contribute empirical evidence and design insights for fostering productive engagement in primary education.

This study addresses the following research questions: RQ1: How does reflective assessment–supported knowledge-building inquiry influence students’ disciplinary understanding?

RQ2: How does students’ productive disciplinary engagement change across the intervention? RQ3: How does reflective assessment support the development of PDE? This study was conducted in a university-affiliated primary school in Central China with one intact Grade 6 class of 50 students. It was integrated into the science curriculum over two semesters (eight weeks each), with three 40-minute lessons per week. A single-group longitudinal design was adopted to trace students’ learning. Students participated in a knowledge-building (KB) environment supported by reflective assessment, working in small inquiry groups with cross-group collaboration. Based on Yang’s pri nciples (Yang et al., 2020), a three-phase design was implemented (Figure 1).  Students’ PDE was examined using Knowledge Forum notes (277 in Semester 1; 454 in Semester 2), organized into thematic threads. Pre-and post-tests were administered each semester, with paired-sample t-tests used to assess learning outcomes (RQ1). To analyze changes in PDE (RQ2), a coding framework covering cognitive, social, and emotional engagement was applied (Table 1), with descriptive statistics and lag sequential analysis (LSA). To examine mechanisms (RQ3), epistemic network analysis (ENA) was conducted.

3226 RQ1: How does reflective assessment–supported knowledge-building inquiry influence students’ disciplinary understanding?

Pre-and post-tests showed significant gains in students’ conceptual understanding across both semesters (p <.05), with greater improvement observed in the second semester, indicating cumulative learning effects. These results suggest that reflective-assessment-supported knowledge-building inquiry effectively enhances elementary students’ disciplinary understanding.

RQ2: How does students’ productive disciplinary engagement change across the intervention? across cognitive, social, and emotional dimensions. Students produced more higher-order contributions, including explanations, summaries, and rise-above ideas, along with more frequent collaborative interactions and positive emotional expressions.

Lag sequential analysis revealed shifts in discourse patterns (Figure 3). Compared to Stage 1, higher-order transitions—from explanation to summarization and to rise-above—became more prominent in Stage 2, while low-level question–response patterns decreased, indicating more coherent inquiry. For example, a student’s initial explanation was taken up by peers, refined through interaction, and developed into a more integrated idea, reflecting a shift from isolated contributions to sustained idea improvement. RQ3: How does reflective assessment support the development of PDE? Epistemic network analysis (ENA) revealed how reflective assessment supported the development of PDE (Figure 4). As shown in Figure 4, the Stage 2 network exhibited denser and more centralized connections than Stage 1, particularly among higher-order nodes such as summarization, rise-above, and curiosity. These nodes were more strongly connected to reflective processes, indicating greater integration of metacognitive reflection with student engagement.

For instance, students revisited earlier ideas, evaluated their adequacy, and incorporated peer feedback to improve their explanations. In one case, a student reformulated an initial idea into a more refined explanation by integrating multiple perspectives. This process illustrates iterative idea improvement supported by reflective assessment. Overall, these patterns suggest that reflective assessment not only enhances individual metacognitive awareness but also facilitates the collective advancement of ideas by linking reflection with higher-order cognitive and social engagement.

Figure1                               Figure2 LSA Transitions (Cognitive Engagement) (Stage 1 vs 2)                     ENA Comparison (Stage 1 VS 2) This study examined the effects of integrating reflective assessment into knowledge-building inquiry on primary students’ disciplinary understanding and productive disciplinary engagement (PDE). Results showed significant gains in conceptual understanding across two semesters, along with increases in cognitive, social, and emotional engagement. Discourse analyses indicated a shift toward more coherent and higher-order inquiry, while network enabling iterative idea improvement in collaborative inquiry. The study also provides practical implications, indicating that embedding reflective assessment within knowledge-building environments can support student agency, collaboration, and formative feedback. However, this study is limited to a single subject context and relies primarily on discourse and test data. Future research should examine its applicability across disciplines and incorporate additional qualitative data to better understand the mechanisms underlying PDE development. 3227 Engle, R. A.
