3228 From Toys to Tools: Collaborative Ingenuity in Learning the Requinto Yared Portillo, University of California, Berkeley, yaredp@berkeley.edu Abstract: This study examines how conviviality, ingenuity, and re-mediation were central to a musical community’s collaborative learning practices. The poster highlights how joint participation in everyday quotidian activities created opportunities to learn the cultural practices of fandango music. Drawing on frameworks of hybridity in informal learning, this study demonstrates how weekend gatherings that blended everyday practices with musical education mediated a collective ingenuity that enabled learners to repurpose a children’s toy into a tool for learning.

Some of the best fandango instrument makers are in Veracruz over two thousand miles from California, where Sandra lived when she decided to learn requinto, the four-string melody instrument that leads the fandango. Sandra was a member of Cascabel de Dos Rí os (CDDR), a California collective offering community-led workshops on the fandango, a celebratory musical gathering where son jarocho music is played. Yet when Sandra wanted her own requinto to learn on, the distance and cost of importing one proved prohi bitive. Drawing from a six-year participatory design study with CDDR, this poster focuses on an eight-month period to examine how relational co-participation supports participants’ ingenuity as a site of learning. Sandra, the focal participant, was a Mexican worki ng-class migratory worker who regularly interacted with CDDR members in formal music workshops and across shared practices of everyday life. By examining how Sandra negotiated geographic and economic constraints, this study reveals how she leveraged availa ble tools, resources, and community knowledge to become a full participant by building and repurposing a children’s toy guitar into a requinto.

The fandango and son jarocho The fandango is a participatory musical gathering where people play “música de cuerdas,” commonly referred to as “son jarocho” (Colectivo Altepee, 2018). Son jarocho, a popular folk music, emerged from Afro-diasporic, Indigenous, and European musical practices that converged in colonial Veracruz, México (García de León, 2009). Fandangos are centered around collaborative and improvisational music-making where people dance to improvised music and verses about their lives. Many fandango communities emphasize how its participatory nature fosters convivencia, “the deliberate act of being with each other as community” (Gonzalez, 2017, p. 17). Informal learning and hybridity in the fandango Fandangos, paired with workshops, offer flexible points of entry for participation, allowing participants to engage as they feel ready (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Drawing on informal learning and hybridity frameworks (Gutiérrez, 2008, 2018; Hall & Jurow, 2015; Rogoff et al., 2016), I examine how learning is organized across both didactic and non-didactic contexts. In this poster, I use formal  and informal to classify the kind of events taking place in CDDR; within each of those spaces there are both didactic and non-didactic practices. Viewing CDDR as a hybrid learning space highlights how intentionally didactic practices coexist with spontaneous, participatory ones across both formal and informal events.

Ingenuity and re-mediation Building on cultural-historical approaches to learning as mediated activity (Cole, 1996, 1998), I draw on instances of re-mediation—shifts in how mediating devices regulate coordination with the environment (Cole & Griffin, 1983, p. 70)—to identify moments  of ingenuity within CDDR. Gutiérrez et al. (2017) describe ingenuity as the “creative responses to constraints” present in everyday practices, like playfulness, resourcefulness, making, tinkering, fixing, or boundary crossing (p. 45). Gutiérrez et al. (2017) further emphasize the importance of looking at ingenuity not as an individualistic skill, but as an everyday practice across families and communities. They “conceptualize ingenuity from a generative frame that takes into account ecological factors and strategies for negotiating the complex and dynamic movement of working-class families,” (p. 45). I turn to these frameworks to make sense of how the music students in this study engaged in collaborative, resourceful practices of ingenuity in response to the economic and geographic constraints of learning requinto. 3229 partnership This poster draws from a six-year Participatory Design Research (Bang & Vossoughi, 2016) (PDR) study documenting the evolving design of CDDR’s community-based son jarocho workshops. Guided by a muli-sited approach to research (Vossoughi & Gutiérrez, 2014), the larger study documents the organization of learning across both formal (workshops, fandangos) and informal (meals, gatherings, “jam sessions”) contexts. This poster focuses on informal learning and convivial practices that unfolded in Miguel’s (another CDDR member) and my home when Sandra began spending weekends with us to study son jarocho. The analytical focus on the convivial gatherings within our home— a site of everyday life and occasional CDDR gatherings—is grounded in PDR’s call for theorization, design, and partnerships that stem from the ways of knowing and being already present within our communities (Bang et al., 2016; Bang & Vossoughi, 2016). As fandango musicians of over 10 years, Miguel and I have long engaged in its practices of convivencia; I have documented and analyzed these practices over the past six years as a practitioner and education researcher through this PDR study. Data, collection, and analysis This study examined the everyday practices of convivencia and musicking through observant participant fieldnotes, member checks, pláticas, and videos collected between October 2024 and May 2025. Pláticas — flexible, translingual conversations that centered r elationships, mutuality, and reciprocity (Flores & Morales, 2021)—and videos were collaboratively facilitated and recorded by participants. This poster highlights two emergent findings from the analysis: (1) Convivencia in everyday life as a space of informal learning; (2) Ingenuity and re-mediation in modifying and repurposing a children’s guitar into a practice requinto. Convivencia in everyday life as a space of informal learning During her last few months in California, Sandra, who lived approximately one hour away from us, began visiting us on weekends to study the fandango. In many of the small communities of Veracruz where the fandango is a central cultural practice, students often visit elders’ homes to learn instruments and hear stories of past fandangos. Although Miguel and I still consider ourselves students, as more experienced members of CDDR, we are regularly positioned as teachers by those around us. This responsibility has often resulted in other students coming to our home to study together, and inevitably, to engage in convivencia. Sandra’s visits exemplified these exchanges. She would arrive Friday nights, often bringing food, and we would spend the weekend together eating, talking, doing daily chores, and playing music. Even when eating, driving, or cleaning we would listen to music, ask questions, and exchange knowledge, creating informal spaces for music education through our everyday convivencia. Through these interactions, Sandra grew interested in the requinto, and Miguel, as a requinto player, began teaching her. Her growing interest led her to want her own requinto with which to practice, which ultimately led her to construct her own requinto out of a toy guitar. Ingenuity and re-mediation: Turning a children’s guitar into a practice requinto When Miguel first learned requinto seven years earlier, instruments were also expensive and hard to find. He used a borrowed requinto but did not feel comfortable practicing for fear of damaging it, as he worked in construction and practiced during his lunch breaks. In response, I took a used plastic children’s toy guitar and converted it into a practice requinto by remaking the nut and bridge. This re-mediation of a toy guitar into a makeshift requinto was a direct response to the environmental constraints that inhibited Miguel’s practicing. When we shared that story with Sandra, she asked us to help her make her own practice requinto. She bought two used children’s toy guitars online and that same weekend, she and I set up a work table outside our garage, pulled out our power tools, and turne d both those instruments into makeshift requintos. One became her practice instrument, and the other was gifted to another emerging requintero who also could not afford a requinto. Sandra’s repurposing of a children’s toy guitar demonstrates how collaborative ingenuity mediated by convivial learning contexts re-mediated both tools and relationships within the fandango learning ecology. Emergent analysis suggests that fandango-centered practices of convivencia supported Sandra’s relational co-participation alongside teachers, students, and researchers within the CDDR collective. Through joint participation in everyday quotidian activities, collaborative ingenuity emerged as a collective practice through which participants responded to the economic, geographic, and environmental constraints of learning the requinto. This representative example reveals how relational co-participation can enable collaborative ingenuity as a site of learning.

Teachers College Record: The Voice of Scholarship in Education, 116(14), 603–632. https://doi.org/10.1177/016146811411601413 3231 Effects of Gender and Group Composition on Higher Education Students’ Application of Collaborative Problem-Solving Skills Luise Mehner, University of Tübingen, luise.mehner@uni-tuebingen.de Babette Bühler, Technical University Munich, babette.buehler@tum.de Björn Rudzewitz, University of Tübingen, bjoern.rudzewitz@uni-tuebingen.de Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, University of California Irvine, pcfuente@uci.edu Nia Nixon, University of California Irvine, dowelln@uci.edu Rossella Santagata, University of California Irvine, r.santagata@uci.edu Ulrich Trautwein, University of Tübingen, ulrich.trautwein@uni-tuebingen.de Enkelejda Kasneci, Technical University Munich, enkelejda.kasneci@tum.de Tosca Daltoe, University of Tübingen, tosca.daltoe@uni-tuebingen.de Kathleen Stürmer, University of Regensburg, kathleen.stuermer@ur.de Tim Fütterer, University of Tübingen, tim.fuetterer@uni-tuebingen.de Abstract: Supporting the development of collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills  without reinforcing existing skill gaps is a crucial task in 21 st-century education. Studies  showed that female students tend to  outperform male students.  However, the complex effects  of gender group composition remain inconclusive.  We investigate the effects of gender  and group composition on higher education students’ CPS skill application with an experimental mixedfactor design leveraging log data from 200-280 pre-service teachers collaborating in an online learning environment.

## Theoretical background

The development of collaborative problem-solving (CPS) skills constitutes a central task of the 21 st-century education system in general and, consequently, of higher education (Fiore et al., 2018; Graesser et al., 2018). According to an established  CPS Ontology (Andrews-Todd & Forsyth, 2020), CPS comprises nine measurable high-level skills, such as sharing information, negotiating, and  executing. Prior studies demonstrated a gender-skill gap in collaborative learning and CPS, with female students consistently outperforming male students (e.g., Bahtiar et al., 2023; Borgonovi et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2019). To support the training of CPS skills without reinforcing this societal-skill gap, it is crucial to establish conditions under which CPS  skills can be applied and thereby practiced regardless of gender.

Gender group composition is a relevant determinant of individuals’ collaborative behavior in educational settings (Scoular et al., 2020). Evidence is mixed. S tudies suggest that female and male students  exhibit more collaborative behavior in groups with more students of their own gender (e.g., Beroíza -Valenzuela et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2023; Kube et al., 2022). At the same time, a higher ratio of female students in small groups is associated with more positive group dynamics and more collaborative behavior in both female and male students (e.g., Curşeu et al., 2018; Dowell et al., 2019; Garcia et al., 2022). Hence, existing findings diverge regarding the effect of gender group composition on collaborative behaviors, especially for male students. Moreover, previous studies focused on different indicators of collaborative processes, whereas findings regarding students’ application of CPS skills are limited.

The present study With this study, we  aim to gain insights into the complex effects of gender and gender group composition on higher education students’ application of CPS skills by investigating the following research question: How do students identifying with different genders apply CPS skills in small groups? To answer this question, we a) investigate how the application of CPS skills differs between fe male and male students, b) explore how gender group composition is related to students’ application of CPS skills, and c) explore how female and male students apply CPS skills across different gender group compositions. In addition, we explore the differentiated application of CPS skills across the nine high-level domains described by AndrewsTodd & Forsyth (2020). Our study is the first step towards educational interventions that enhance the application and, thereby, the  practice of CPS skills for all students, regardless of gender. Moreover, our findings will 3232 contribute to the development of  inclusive teaching practices, including group formation strategies and instructional designs, that enable equitable CPS skill development across students from diverse genders. We refer to gender group composition as the number of a student’s group members with the student’s gender. Based on the literature reviewed, we hypothesize that female students, overall, apply more CPS skills than male students. Furthermore, as prior literature is inconclusive about the effect of gender group composition on collaborative behavior, we explore two contrasting hypotheses (see  Figure 1). The majority-domination hypothesis posits that both male and female students apply more CPS skills in groups with more members of their own gender, implying a main effect of gender group composition. In contrast, the female climate hypothesis posits that groups with more female members foster a more prosocial group environment, with more application of CPS skills in both fe male and male members. This implies an interaction effect of gender and gender group composition.

Figure 1 Explored Hypotheses About Students’ Application of CPS Skills in Small Groups Gender group composition describes the number of a student’s group members with the same gender in groups of four: minority (the student is the only group member with their gender), balanced (one other group member with the same gender), majority (two other group members with the same gender), and single-gender (the group comprises only group members with the student’s gender).

## Method

The study was preregistered and positively reviewed by an ethics committee.  The data collection is ongoing. Based on an a priori power analysis, we plan to recruit a sample of 𝑁𝑁 = 200 − 280 German-speaking higher education students enrolled in teacher training study programs.  The study employs a mixed-factor design with a between-subjects factor, Gender (female and male), and an experimental factor, Group Composition, with random assignment to one of four conditions (minority, balanced, majority, or single-gender). Students who do not identify as female or male are assigned to diverse-gender groups and examined exploratively.

The study is completed in an online learning environment developed based on educational research (Beukman et al., 2025) that allows students to chat with each other, write notes, and collaboratively edit a shared document. All students participate in two collaborative professional vision  tasks (Seidel & Stürmer, 2014)  in randomly assigned groups of four, with a maximum duration of 30 minutes. The tasks involve  collaborative Additionally, we assess  sociodemographic, cognitive, and motivational variables, such as socioeconomic We collect log data on students’ tab switch ing and video playback, as well as the content of their messages, notes, and edits in the collaborative document. We annotate students’ application of CPS skills  in the log data with two independent raters, following the qualitative coding strategy of Andrews-Todd & Forsyth (2020). To this end, we adapted the author’s behavioral indicators for the high-level CPS domains that are included in their ontology to our CPS  task and online learning environment. We test our hypotheses using linear mixedeffect models with the lmer() function in R. At this time, 𝑛𝑛 = 47 (34 female, 13 male, 0 diverse) students participated in the study, approximately half of them bachelor’s students and half of them master’s students. Across both tasks, the students collaborated in 21 groups of four: 6 single-gender groups, 6 balanced groups, and 9 majority-and minority groups. On average, 135 relevant log entries per completed task (almost 3000 entries in total) were extracted from the online environment.

American Educational Research Journal, 51(4), 739 –771. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831214531321 3234 Can GenAI Participate as a Peer in Knowledge Building?

Litong Zeng, University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign, litongz2@illinois.edu Yiqi Xiao, University of California-Irvine, yiqix7@uci.edu Abstract: This study investigates how human– AI collaboration supports Knowledge Building (KB), a process of collective idea advancement. We are trying to conceptualize whether it is possible that generative AI can serve as a collaborator in knowledge creation. Using discourse including one Rise Above where the participant synthesized ChatGPT 5’s ideas. While ChatGPT, as a collaborator, primarily restates human ideas, its elaborations can still catalyze the participants’ higher-level reasoning. The findings indicate that KB can occur in human –AI dialogue, highlighting the need to design more inquiry-driven and epistemically engaged AI for collaborative knowledge advancement.

Knowledge Building (KB) is a pedagogical and epistemological framework that conceptualizes learning as the collective advancement of ideas within a community, where knowledge is considered a collective artifact rather than an individual possession (Scardamalia & Bereiter, 2010). Participants collaboratively improve “improvable ideas” through explanation, questioning, and integration, positioning themselves as co-constructors rather than passive receivers of information. Since generative AI (GenAI) was not part of the original context in which knowledge-building theory was first developed, its roles in KB have yet to be fully conceptualized or empirically investigated. Can GenAI act as a co-constructor, like our peer, in the Knowledge Building process, iterat ively improving ideas? If we see it as a co-constructor, what kind of co-constructor is it in KB? Distributed cognition theory argues that cognition is not confined to individual minds but is distributed across people, tools, and environments (Pea, 1993; Hollan et al., 2000). Within such systems, both human and non-human entities possess a certain kind of agency in shaping knowledge and action (Latour, 2005). This agency implies that knowledge and meaning emerge not solely from individual reasoning but are co-produced through interactions among human and non-human entities. In this sense, GenAI can be understood as a non-human, but equal collaborator whose participation has the ability to reorganize the cognitive and social dynamics of a Knowledge Building community.

However, most studies in CSCL tend to only treat GenAI as a tool or assistant. Cress and Kimmerle

(2023) argue instead that we must explore whether knowledge construction can occur between learners and Gen

AI. Even if GenAI’s responses are based on imitation or prior data patterns, it can still provoke reflection, extend ideas, and co-shape writing or problem-solving processes (Chen et al., 2023; Luther et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2024; Cukurova, 2025). It seems to have the capacity to reorganize and external ize linguistic and conceptual patterns, which could potentially stimulate and inspire learners to construct meaning based on it. But most existing studies still focus primarily on learners, rather than also examining AI as a peer in the collaborative proce ss. Few have analyzed the interactional mechanisms through which human and AI contributions jointly transform ideas, how meaning moves, connects, and “rises above” in Knowledge Building. To address this gap, we propose that KB research should move beyond treating GenAI solely as a tool from the learner’s perspective, and beyond focusing only on how learners interact with or benefit from AI. Importantly, research should also examine GenAI as a peer and epistemic equal within Knowledge Building processes, in order to understand the emerging assemblage in which AI increasingly participates as part of the Knowledge Building community we are entering. Along these lines, this paper examines how ideas are co-produced, transformed, and advanced through human–AI interactions. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for rethinking collaboration, learners’ agency in the age of generative AI, and for designing future learning environments that support hybrid human–AI knowledge advancement.

## Method

The dataset for this study consists of an anonymized human– AI dialogue voluntarily provided by an adult participant. The conversation emerged from the participant's spontaneous interaction with ChatGPT 5 in Chinese, rather than through a pre-designed experimental prompt. The participant initiated the inquiry on “AI and artistic creation” based on personal interest, reflecting a naturalistic, daily use scenario. For analysis, the transcript was coded in its original Chinese form, with selected excerpts trans lated into English for reporting while ensuring semantic equivalence.

This exploratory qualitative study adopted a discourse analytic case study design to investigate how ideas develop within a human-GenAI dialogue. Each utterance in the dialogue was treated as a unit of analysis. 3235 The dialogue was jointly coded by two researchers in real time, resolved any differences immediately through established Divergent Collaboration Learning Mechanisms (Tissenbaum et al.,  2017) and knowledge building discourse (Zeng et al., 2023), refined to fit this study. The final scheme includes six codes: Idea Generation (IG): introducing a new idea or perspective; Clarification (C): explaining, defining, or expanding on an existing idea; Negotiation (N): expressing uncertainty or challenging points, or requesting clarification; Making Suggestion (MS): proposing opinions or solutions; Accepting Suggestion (AS): expressing agreement; and Rise Above (RA): synthesizing multiple ideas to form a new, integrated understanding.

In this interaction, the participant initiates the conversation by asking ChatGPT5 about AI's impact on art creation, and later they discuss how AI lowers barriers and costs, raises copyright concerns, reshapes commercial art markets, and prompts questions about artists becoming prompt-based creators or being replaced. The participant and the GPT each contributed seven turns of talk. The participant’s utterances were generally brief, ranging from one to three sentences, whereas the GPT’s responses were much longer, averaging around twenty sentences per turn. Across the transcript, a total of 66 idea units  were coded-Idea Generation (IG), among which 10 were produced by the participant and 56 by the GPT.

In this interaction, Negotiation (N) appeared four times, with two initiated by GPT and two by the participant, marking moments when both sides clarified or reoriented their shared focus. For example, when GPT framed the future as human–AI collaboration, the participant pushed further by suggesting artists might eventually act mainly as prompt directors (N). When the participant asked whether AI could fully replace artists, GPT acknowledged the idea but emphasized emotional and experiential limits (N). We observed one instance of Rise Above (RA) by the participant and none by GPT, where the participant synthesized multiple ideas into a higher-level concept. GPT suggested that AI would democratize art production, accelerate content creation, enable customization, and reshape creative labor. The participant integrated these points into a broader prediction that the art market may split into a low-end AI-driven tier and a high-end elite tier, with no middle layer, demonstrating a higher-level synthesis of GPT’s ideas. Another thing worth noticing is that the participants tended to ask questions, while the GPT always began its turns with (AS) followed by (C). While GPT mostly followed the participant’s line of thinking, the participant tended to steer the conversation in new directions, though after close examination, we found many of these seemingly independent ideas were sparked by small details in GPT’s Clarification (C). For example, when responding to the question about whether AI disrupts the commercial art market, GPT attempted to clarify its view by noting that AI enables highly flexible and personalized commercial art production (C). Building on this specific detail, the participant jumped and generated an idea, a prediction that seems not related to the GPT’s main point, that the future art market may split into a low-cost, high-volume AI tier and a high-end human–AI tier (IG). The findings suggest that elements of KB did occur within the human– GenAI dialogue. The presence of identifiable (IG) and the (RA) indicates that both parties were actively engaging in idea improvement and conceptual synthesis. Though the participants generally drove the knowledge advancement, ChatGPT-5’s contributions were not trivial. It acted as a responsive and supportive collabor ator, sustaining coherence, reinforcing the participant’s direction, and offering conceptual cues through elaboration and clarification that stimulated the participant’s higher-level reasoning. In this sense, the GPT in this interaction demonstrated the ability to act as a peer to collaborate in the KB processes. However, this raises further questions about what it truly means to have such a “peer” in a KB environment. While the GPT-inspired idea generation and supported cognitive reorganization, its participation remained largely reactive and descriptive, rather than epistemically proactive or inquiry-driven. The interaction pattern, long clarifications following short participant prompts, suggests that the current GenAI with no specific designed prompt, may not yet foster the most inspiring or co-evolving dialogue. The next question to ask is, how can GenAI be designed or prompted to become a better KB peer, one that not only elaborates but also questions, challenges, and builds upon ideas with a human. This leads to further inquiry into what specific qualities we can adjust in a GenAI peer for better Knowledge Building, how different is building knowledge with a GenAI peer to a human peer, and whether established KB theories, originally conceptualized for human-to-human interaction, are sufficient to account for these hybrid partners. Ultimately, addressing these questions requires us to rethink the epistemic roles (Bozkurt, 2024) that GenAI can assume within knowledge communities.

## Acknowledgements

This paper used ChatGPT-5 to assist with academic writing and language refinement. All ideas, interpretations, and arguments presented are original and authored by the researcher. 3237 Design Principles for AI-Supported Chatbots to Scaffold ProblemBased Learning in Undergraduate Nursing Education Seora Kim, Hyunkyu Han, Min Kyu Kim skim359@student.gsu.edu, hhan21@student.gsu.edu, mkim120@gsu.edu Georgia State University Abstract: This study proposes design principles for an AI-supported chatbot that facilitates problem-based learning in undergraduate nursing education. Drawing on constructivist learning environment, transactional distance theory, and scaffolding theory, the design emphasizes authentic problem-solving, interactive communication, and multi-dimensional instructional support. The proposed chatbot features differentiated personas to provide cognitive, procedural, and social scaffolding, promoting learner engagement, self-directed learning, and clinical reasoning.

The American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) identified ten core competencies encompassing disciplinary knowledge, clinical skills, and interpersonal and professional capacities essential for developing competent nurses. Among these, “knowledge for nursing practice” emphasizes the integration and application of interdisciplinary knowledge across contexts rather than rote memorization (AACN, 2021). Similarly, the National Council Licensure Examination (NCLEX) measures a nurse’s ability to apply knowledge and think critically through real-world case studies (NCLEX, n.d.). However, achieving these competencies requires students to navigate cognitively demanding and emotionally intensive learning environments, which often heighten stress and lead to burnout which is a global concern affecting 19–41% of nursing students (Gómez-Urquiza et al., 2023; Rudman & Gustavsson, 2012). Instructor expertise and interpersonal support have been shown to enhance students’ motivation and self-efficacy (Labrague et al., 2020), underscoring the need to integrate cognitive, emotional, and relational supports within nursing curricula to foster both competence and resilience. Problem statements Burnout in nursing students stems not only from emotional exhaustion but also from cognitive –behavioral mismatches, such as incompatible learning styles (Ghods et al., 2023), which hinder the application of theoretical knowledge to clinical contexts. Addressing these challenges requires an integrated framework that combines educational and interpersonal supports. Incorporating social support mechanisms  which have been shown to strengthen grit and reduce academic burnout (Kim & Lee, 2022) into curriculum design can promote persistence, self-directed learning, and overall well-being, aligning with the holistic competency framework of contemporary nursing education.

Theoretical backgrounds Problem-centered nursing class with constructivist learning environment In nursing education, where students encounter complex clinical cases, Jonassen’s constructivist learning environment (CLE) model provides a framework for designing authentic learning experiences that reflect real-world problem-solving demands (Jonassen, 1 999). Grounded in constructivist theory, the model emphasizes active learner engagement in solving ill-structured problems through the exploration of multiple solution paths rather than predetermined answers. Through this process, learners construct understanding by examining, testing, and reflecting on key concepts. The instructor’s role shifts from that of a knowledge transmitter to a facilitator who demonstrates, coaches, and provides scaffolding. Effective problem-based learning, therefore, depends on the thoughtful design of authentic problems and the dynamic instructor-learner interaction that supports students’ problem-solving processes.

Instructional support based on Transactional Distance Theory While the CLE model centers on designing authentic problem contexts, its effectiveness depends on the quality of interaction between learners and instructors. In nursing education, where social support serves as a critical source of student persistence, it  is important to examine the psychological and communicative distance between learners and instructors as well as among peers. Moore’s (1993) Transactional Distance Theory  (TDT) explains 3238 this interactional gap as a function of course structure, dialogue, and learner autonomy. Because nursing education involves highly structured content and limited learner autonomy, meaningful dialogue becomes essential to reduce transactional distance and sustain engagement. Given instructors’ limited availability, AI-supported feedback can complement human interaction by providing consistent, scalable support. AI-supported scaffolding to communicate cases and students Scaffolding serves as a communicative strategy that bridges learners' cognitive and social processes in problem-based learning. Rooted in Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development, it provides adaptive support including cognitive, metacognitive, procedural, strategic, and social  supports that enable learners to accomplish tasks beyond their current abilities (Reiser, 2004; Belland, 2014). Recent advances in AI-powered tutors and conversational agents extend these scaffolding functions by facilitating reasoning, dialogue, and engagement (Holmes et al., 2019). In nursing education, knowledge-based chatbots have shown effectiveness in guiding students through complex clinical cases, supporting self-directed learning and decision-making even in the instructor’s absence (Allen et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2022).  Taken together, these theoretical perspectives underscore the need to implement diverse types of scaffolding in an integrated and dialogic manner. Design principles and proposed intervention Based on the theoretical backgrounds described above, design principles for a chatbot supporting problem-based learning in nursing education were derived. These principles were developed with consideration for courses that integrate both theoretical and practical components, rather than purely theoretical subjects. Table 1 Design Principles for Undergraduate Nursing Courses Building on these principles, the envisioned AI-supported learning environment operates as follows. Students engage in problem-based learning using virtual patient cases and can easily access various resources  such as lecture materials, related NCLEX questions, and research articles  to support problem solving. In addition, a chatbot is continuously available to assist students throughout the process. To enhance authenticity, each chatbot is assigned a distinct persona according to its specific function as follows:

• Professor Bot (Cognitive Scaffold):  Provides conceptual explanations, corrects misconceptions, and

promotes critical reasoning  (e.g. “Tube placement must be verified via X-ray and gastric aspirate pH testing (≤5.5) before any feeding or medication did your lecture identify as the gold standard?”)

• Mentor Nurse Bot (Procedural Scaffold):  Guides step-by-step clinical processes, connecting decisions

to patient outcomes. (e.g. "That's okay. Let's think through it together: what's the very first thing you'd want to confirm before using the tube?")

• Peer Bot (Cognitive and Social Scaffold):  Engages in conversational reflection, prompting students to

articulate understanding and explain concepts to the chatbot back. (e.g. "I wasn't sure about this. I think it involves checking placement with X-ray or pH testing. Could you explain the related concepts?") The theoretical review and design principles proposed in this paper identify key considerations for developing AI-based interventions in nursing education. These principles can be further refined through collaboration with field experts, and future studies  will focus on implementing and evaluating their educational effectiveness.  with careful attention to mitigating hallucination and bias. Beyond cognitive learning outcomes, future research should also examine whether the tool can meaningfully support resilience and sustain persistence throughout the nursing programs.

3240 Connecting the Dots: Designing Curricula for Understanding Machine Learning through Mathematics Hyunju Oh, University of Miami, hxo163@miami.edu Chenglu Li, University of Utah, chenglu.li@utah.edu Rui Huang, University of Florida, rui.huang@coe.ufl.edu Wanli Xing, University of Miami, wanli.xing@miami.edu Abstract: This work-in-progress study examines how integrating machine learning (ML) into math education can make AI concepts more accessible to high school learners. It proposes the concreteness-fading approach to connect ML’s real-world applications with the abstract concepts of math. Using a Design-Based Research framework, the study develops a curriculum to improve conceptual understanding, usability, and attitude in ML-integrated math learning. Learning artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has become increasingly important for all students, as AI/ML literacy helps them  understand and critically engage with the data-driven technologies that shape modern life (Zhou et al., 2025). However, effectively introducing ML concepts to early learners is challenging. Traditionally, AI/ML education has been treated as a specialized computing topic, accessible only to those with advanced programming or math backgrounds. Without these foundations, early learners often struggle to understand how ML systems operate, a challenge compounded by teachers’ limited training and confidence, as well as the scarcity of pedagogical resources and curriculum guidance (Chiu & Chai, 2020; Opel et al., 2019). Recent efforts (e.g. AI4K12 curricula; Touretzky et al., 2019) show that even primary-level students can begin to learn how AI works with age-appropriate tools, but this underscores the need for new pedagogical strategies to bridge the accessibility gap. In other words, rather than only  presenting ML as complex computer science, researchers have suggested in connecting  ML with foundational subjects, such as math and science,  to provide stronger conceptual grounding and coherence (Sanusi et al., 2023) One promising avenue is to leverage the inherent connections between ML and mathematics. ML algorithms are fundamentally built on mathematical principles  and m ath concepts play a critical role in how models learn from data and are optimized (Deisenroth et al., 2020). For example, probability and statistics are deeply integrated in ML, underpinning algorithms in everything from simple classifiers to complex deep learning models. These overlaps suggest that ML can be contextualized within the math curriculum,  giving students concrete illustrations of abstract math concepts in action. Despite these natural linkages, integrating ML into  high school  mathematics education remains non-trivial. A core difficulty is the gap between the abstract formality of school math and the contextual, applied nature of ML. Mathematics instruction often emphasizes symbolic manipulation and formulae in isolation, whereas ML concepts are typically taught through computing exercises or real-world problem scenarios. Thus, a key challenge is how to help high school students build bridges between familiar mathematical ideas and the seemingly complex, computing-heavy world of ML.

To address this challenge, we draw on the concreteness-fading (CF) approach from math  education, a proven pedagogical strategy for linking intuitive understanding with formal abstractions.  Grounded in cognitive science, this approach  involves gradually transitioning  from concrete, physical representations of a concept to increasingly abstract, symbolic representations (Fyfe et al., 2014). In practice, a CF-based lesson starts with handson objects, visual demonstrations, or story contexts, then move to drawings or diagrams that represent the same ideas, and finally arrive at the abstract mathematical notation or algorithms. This concrete-pictorial-abstract sequence ensures that learners have a meaningful context at first, but do not get “stuck” in the context – they gradually generalize the concept beyond the specifics of the concrete examples.  Educators have applied the CF strategy not just in arithmetic but also in teaching more advanced concepts like algebra, functions, and even in science domains where ab stract principles (e.g. in physics) benefit from concrete instantiation  (Kokkonen et al., 2022; Xing et al., 2023; Zhao & Gibson, 2023). In all these cases, the approach helps learners form links between an accessible experience and the formal representation of the idea. For this reason, we propose that a CF approach is a promising way to integrate ML into high school math education. By initially presenting ML ideas through concrete analogies, real-life examples, or interactive visual tools, students – even those without a coding background – candevelop an intuitive sense for what ML does. As the instruction fades toward more abstract representations, students can then encounter the underlying math 3241 concepts in a guided manner, seeing it as a natural extension of the concrete scenario. This approach allows learners to witness how abstract math concepts they learn in class operate within an AI system, thereby reinforcing their math knowledge and simultaneously making ML less “magical” and more comprehensible. In this project, we will explore how the CF framework can be implemented to teach specific ML topics through math and discuss how this approach can lower barriers to AI education for all students.  Specifically, we ask: (1) How does integrating ML concepts through the CF approach influence high school students’ conceptual understanding and attitudes toward mathematics and ML? (2) How do iterative refinements in the Design-Based Research (DBR) process improve the usability and instructional effectiveness of the CF-based ML curriculum? This study employed a DBR methodology, following the framework proposed by Hoadley and Campos (2022), which outlines four iterative and non-linear processes  (See Figure 1): grounding, conjecturing, iterating, and reflecting. These stages are not strictly sequential but dynamically revisited throughout the research process to refine both the theoretical framework and instructional design. Figure 1 DBR based Approach to Develop Curriculum and Platform

(1) Grounding: The research was grounded in the CF instructional approach. Furthermore, a preliminary

pilot study (Oh et al., 2024) conducted in May 2023 contributed to this grounding. In this study, high school students engaged with an image classification module designed using the CF approach. The module also included a generative AI (GAI) -based programming activity. The findings indicated that integrating ML concepts  with math through CF enhanced students’ learning performance. However, despite the low-code design, participants— who had minimal programming experience —struggled to troubleshoot errors due to insufficient foundational coding knowledge. Furthermore, while GAI effectively generated code prompts, its variability across sessions caused confusion among early learners.  Based on these findings, we transitioned from low-code to no-code activities in subsequent iterations. Consequently, the current version introduced ML concepts during the concrete (physical representation) stage, emphasized mathematical principles i n the abstract  (symbolic representation) stage, and used visualizations to bridge the two during the pictorial representation stage.

(2) Conjecture: In the conjecture phase, the research hypothesized that connecting ML concepts with

mathematical principles through the CF approach would improve students’ conceptual understanding and attitudes toward both mathematics and ML. This conjecture guided the iterative design and testing of the learning materials.

(3) Iterating: During the iteration phase, the curriculum was co-designed over three weeks in

collaboration with a high school mathematics teacher to design more engaging and impactful learning experiences. The co-design process unfolded in three stages:  First, the researcher developed a prototype curriculum and identified potential mathematical concepts aligned with national math standards  with the teacher. Second, i n consultation with the teacher, the team reviewed the mathematical appropriateness and adj usted the complexity of tasks to match students’ proficiency levels. Finally, the researcher produced the final curriculum (see Table 1), including instructional materials such as presentation slides, hands-on activities, and worksheets.

(4) Reflecting: After implementation, students will complete attitude, usability, and knowledge

assessments, along with a few open-ended questions. The attitude survey (Faber et al., 2013) will examine perceptions of mathematics and ML, while the usability survey (Sauro & Lewis, 2016) will assess material clarity and accessibility. A knowledge test, aligned with the physical, pictorial, and symbolic stages, will identify learning challenges and evaluate how effectively the CF-based curriculum supports conceptual understanding. 3243 Understanding Students’ Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating: An Instructor Perspective from Online Forums Analysis Iman Mohammadi, Sina Rismanchian, Ali Keramati imohamm1@uci.edu, srismanc@uci.edu, a.kera@uci.edu University of California, Irvine Shayan Salehi, s4salehi@uwaterloo.ca, University of Waterloo Abstract: The extensive adoption of AI has precipitated a crisis in academic integrity. While studies attempt to quantify cheating, less is known about the motivations instructors believe students have for using AI in prohibited ways. We analyze 2.01 million posts on r/Professors to understand how instructors perceive students' justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Our qualitative analyses reveal four primary themes: (1) Academic System Gaming, (2) Digital-Academic Literacy Gap, (3) Performance Anxiety, and (4) Normalization of Dishonesty. Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have rapidly reshaped the educational landscape, challenging conventional notions of authorship, learning, and assessment integrity (Kazley, 2024). Within months of their release, generative AI systems became ubiquitous in higher education, adopted by both instructors seeking innovation and students navigating unprecedented opportunities for automation (Balabdaoui et al., 2024). Yet, this technological disruption has also precipitated an academic integrity crisis, as instructors grapple with detecting and interpreting new forms of AI-mediated misconduct (Yusuf, 2024; von Garrel, 2023). Despite this growing conversation, instructors’ perspectives on student motivations remain underexamined. Most existing research privileges student self-reports, which may obscure how instructors interpret and respond to the motivations they perceive (Sumakul, 2022). Yet, instructors play a crucial role in framing academic integrity, shaping institutional responses, and constructing the moral discourse surrounding AI use in classrooms (Wenger, 1998; Lave & Wenger, 1991). Understanding how instructors conceptualize students’ reasons for cheating with AI provides insight not only for emerging pedagogical challenges, but also into the broader socio-technical negotiation between automation, learning, and trust (Reddy-Lund, 2025; Scardamalia, 2014).

To address this gap, we analyze 2.01 million posts (including threads and comments) from the r/Professors subreddit to examine how instructors discuss, interpret, and theorize their students’ justifications for AI-mediated cheating. Through qualitative the matic analysis, we identify four overarching rationales instructors attribute to students (Braun & Clarke, 2006).

Early responses to AI in education have focused primarily on detection and policy. A significant body of work investigates how to identify AI-generated text or how to craft institutional guidelines that preserve assessment fairness (Shepard, 2000). Parallel efforts have sought to quantify the prevalence of AI cheating through surveys and controlled experiments, revealing widespread use of generative tools across disciplines. However, these quantitative efforts, while informative, leave underexplored the why, the underlying motivations and rationalizations that shape students’ use of AI in prohibited ways (Sozon, 2024). Prior qualitative research has begun to uncover students’ moral reasoning around academic dishonesty more broadly. Studies on plagiarism, contract cheating, and collusion identify themes of instrumentalism, performance pressure, and systemic distrust in hi gher education. With the emergence of AI, these rationales are amplified and transformed: the boundary between legitimate assistance and unethical delegation becomes ambiguous, particularly when AI is framed as a "study aid" rather than a "substitute". Moreover, recent interviews and surveys show that students often misunderstand the epistemic status of AI outputs, treating them as valid sources of knowledge rather than synthetic predictions (Sun, 2025).

To address the mentioned gap, in this study, we used data from the r/Professors subreddit, a public online forum where university instructors discuss teaching, assessment, and classroom challenges. Reddit was chosen because it provides naturally occurring discussions that capture instructors’ real-time reflections and debates about academic integrity in the age of AI.

3244 We searched posts and comments on cheating and AI use published after the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, when public conversation about AI cheating began to rise. Using Reddit’s public API, we collected a total of 2.01 million posts (including threads and comments). To identify relevant discussions, we applied keyword-based searches using terms such as academic integrity, cheating, plagiarism, AI detection, ChatGPT, LLM, GPTZero, Turnitin, AI policy, and academic misconduct.

## Data analysis

From the full dataset, 5 random sample pools, each containing 200 threads and comments combined, were selected to ensure diversity in topics and time periods. The selected posts were analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis to identify patterns in how instructors describe students’ reasons for using AI unethically. Each sample pool was independently coded by two researchers, with disagreements resolved through discussion until consensus was reached. The analysis followed an inductive approach; initial open coding of posts was followed by grouping similar ideas into broader themes and subthemes through iterative review and discussion among the researchers. As shown in Table 1, our analysis finds that instructors attribute students’ AI-related cheating to a range of personal, cognitive, and cultural factors. The findings are organized into four major themes that reflect different ways instructors interpret students’ motivations.

First, instructors believe many students treat education instrumentally, gaming the system to maximize rewards while minimizing effort, often exploiting assignment types or grading structures where AI use is hard to detect. Second, they observe a digital-academic literacy gap, in which students misunderstand academic conventions or overestimate AI’s capabilities, using it as a "study aid" without recognizing its ethical or epistemic limits. Third, instructors perceive performance anxiety and skill deficits as key drivers, describing how students turn to AI as a coping mechanism for insecurity or under-preparedness. Finally, many instructors view dishonesty as becoming normalized, noting that AI-assisted cheating is increasingly seen by students as common, low-risk, and socially acceptable. These four themes, together, reveal how instructors make sense of AI-mediated misconduct not only as individual wrongdoing but also as a symptom of deeper tensions in educational systems and cultures.

Table 1 Thematic Framework of Student Rationales for AI-Mediated Cheating, as Reported by Instructors Sub-themes Academic System Gaming & Instrumentalist

## Motivation

1A: Exploiting Systemic Vulnerabilities Targets low-detection, high-reward assignments.

1B: Efficiency Optimization AI used as a time-saver, bypassing learning.

1C: Gaming Admissions and Credentialing Uses AI to fabricate or enhance application materials.

Digital-Academic Literacy Gap & Misguided Tool Use 2A: Misunderstanding Scholarly Synthesis Believes AI generation is legitimate brainstorming/synthesis.

2B: Over-reliance on "Polishing" Tools Views AI as an advanced grammar/style checker, blurring authorship.

2C: Misunderstanding Evidence and Academic Discourse: Presents AIgenerated fabrications as legitimate evidence.

Performance Anxiety and Capability Deficits 3A: Masking Inadequate Preparation Used due to a lack of foundational knowledge or skills.

3B: Fear of Inadequate Performance Capable students use AI from anxiety that their work isn't "good enough." Normalization of Dishonesty and Diminished Consequences 4A: The "New Normal" of Cheating AI cheating is perceived as a standard, unremarkable student behavior.

4B: Boldness in the Face of Accusation Students persistently deny, obfuscate, or argue when confronted.

Our analysis reveals a complex landscape of student rationales for AI-mediated cheating from the instructors’ perspective, categorized into four primary themes.

3246 Generative AI in Lesson Planning: Effects on Teacher Practice Zhenyi Huang, Samuel Tan, Claudia Chew huang_zhenyi@moe.gov.sg, samuel_tan@moe.gov.sg, claudia_chew@moe.gov.sg Ministry of Education, Singapore Abstract: Teachers increasingly use GenAI platforms like ChatGPT for lesson planning, yet few studies examine its effects on teachers’ technological pedagogical and content knowledge (TPK and TCK). We investigated how teachers use GenAI in English and Science, finding they primarily create resources and assessments for knowledge acquisition. More experienced teachers leveraged GenAI better due to stronger pedagogical knowledge. Professional development could focus on helping teachers leverage GenAI to explore  novel approaches for diverse learners.

Given that 64% of teachers using AI employ it for lesson planning (OECD, 2025), studies show teachers value GenAI's time-saving benefits for creating lesson plans and resources or assessments (Moorhouse & Kohnke, 2024; Chiu, 2023), though concerns exist about over-reliance and deskilling. Learning design  refers to  the order of teaching and learning activities  that enable students to achieve intended learning outcomes (Koper  & Olivier, 2004). Emerging as a field of practice and research in the 2000s  as teaching became viewed as a design science (Laurillard, 2012), technology-enhanced learning (TEL) (Bennett et al, 2014) design requires teachers’ integration of Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) (Koehler & Mishra 2006) with an understanding of students’ needs from learning data.  This study uses an ecological framework for teacher knowledge in TEL design (McKenney et al, 2015), examining transferable knowledge including the know-what (fundamental knowledge base, including tacit knowledge  from experience) and the know-how (TPACK which  influences pedagogical design capacity). This study assesses possible shifts in teachers’ learning design competencies from using GenAI for lesson planning with the following research questions: 1a) How do teachers use GenAI Chatbots to design lessons? 1b) How does the use of GenAI for lesson planning influence/ impact teachers’ integration of technology into their learning designs?  2) How has teachers’ use of GenAI for lesson planning impacted the development of their technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) and technological content knowledge (TCK)? Sampling plan and intervention The study design adopted a stratified sampling strategy  and recruited participants from four schools, with 32 English and Science teachers with a range of teaching experience. Between February and September  2025, the teachers employed GenAI platforms of their choice for lesson planning and preparation, with the most used being ChatGPT, followed by Gemini, Claude, CoPilot, and a customised chatbot with local curricular knowledge bases.

## Data analysis

A sequential mixed methods research approach was employed. Quantitative data was gathered through pre-postintervention surveys, and qualitative data included teacher-AI chatlogs, FGD transcripts, and pre-post lesson plans and artifacts. Table 1 details the data and analysis.

Chatlogs of interactions with GenAI Manual coding for pedagogical intent RQ 1b.  Survey on technology integration  Comparison of pre-post survey ratings FGD transcripts   Thematic analysis: GenAI influence on lesson planning Chatlogs of interactions with GenAI   Manual coding for pedagogical intent and TPACK Pre-post lesson artefacts Inter-rater reliability Cohen-Kappa RQ 2  Survey on impact of GenAI use design skills  Descriptive statistical analysis 3247 FGD transcripts   Thematic analysis: effect on TPK or TCK Chatlog transcript analysis Markov Chain analysis: Transition probability matrix Coding of chatlogs To explore shifts in teacher design process, p edagogical intent and knowledge, a variable-centred analysis was triangulated with a process-oriented approach (Reimann, 2009).  Chatlog analysis provided insights into interaction patterns of pedagogically advanced teachers vis-à-vis novice teachers. Teacher prompts in the Chatlogs were coded according to pedagogical intent (know-what, why & when) and TPACK (know-how) domains. We analysed the coded data for pedagogical intent using a First-order Markov Chain (Green, 200 0), a sequential matrix showing the probability of moving from one design move/pedagogical intent to another, and the top next three moves of the teacher in the group. We compared the design moves of teachers  with sophisticated design knowledge and skills against frequently used patterns and examined differences in design practices. [RQ 1a] How do teachers use Gen AI Chatbots to design lessons? Teachers use GenAI largely for creating digital resources quickly, with Knowledge Acquisition  (KNW) as the type of prompt with the highest frequency: “…to check if the students have learned… ask GenAI to generate … questions…to check their understanding” (S2ELT11). These digital resources include customised interactives and simulations which would have been difficult to create otherwise without necessary technical skills. Teachers also report the ease with which they can generate assessment items and lesson materials with the use of GenAI to cater to a different profile of students. [RQ 1b] How does the use of GenAI for lesson planning influence/ impact teachers’ integration of technology into their learning desig ns? Teachers expressed a growth in confidence in integrating technology into their learning designs, possibly due to an enhanced knowledge of EdTech tools (100% agreement) and enhanced knowledge and skills in designing tech-enabled lessons (88.8% agreement). Using a GenAI chatbot as a sounding board for ideation during lesson design also bolstered teacher confidence in experimenting with EdTech tools and trying out alternative ways of integrating technology into learning design: “…asked ChatGPT...how can I introduce the word(s) “formal” “informal”…for the kids to understand…I would have never come out (up) with it on my own…I link together with GenAI.” (S1ELT5). The analysis of pre-post lesson artefacts showed more purposeful and varied technology integration in teachers’ learning designs, shifting from passive technology use towards student-centric active learning approaches that enhanced learner agency and engagement with the content. [RQ2] How has teachers’ use of GenAI for lesson planning impacted the development of their technological pedagogical knowledge and technological content knowledge? Sequential analysis of teachers’ prompts with GenAI chatbot suggests  the main pattern: knowledge acquisition (KNW), followed by a ssessment (ASM), then disciplinary skills (DISC) acquisition. Most requests focused on creating lesson resources to address knowledge gaps, test understanding, and develop subject skills. However, some teachers demonstrated more varied interaction patterns, using prompts to find out how to better engage specific groups of  diverse learners, provide differentiated support, facilitate collaboration and develop higher-order thinking skills.  An e nhanced understanding of TPK was observed as teachers gained an understanding of how technology can support specific pedagogical strategies and were better able to align technology use with learning outcomes. However, this is dependent on teachers’ existing PCK, as evidenced fr om analysis of their chatlogs and FGD responses: "The alignment is something that I think is very useful for us. Because it knows what is the expected … that means the lesson generated will never go off" (S1SCT9). More experienced teachers were able to  evaluate GenAI’s output due to their tacit knowledge and understanding of students’ learning challenges for the topic. The findings demonstrate that whilst GenAI significantly enhances teachers’ confidence and efficiency in resource creation, its effectiveness in developing teachers’ TPK depends on existing pedagogical  expertise, with more experienced educators better a ble to critically evaluate  GenAI suggestions and prompt with varied pedagogical intents beyond knowledge acquisition. Our research underscores the importance of  t argeted professional development that help educators across all experience levels  maximise GenAI’s potential to deepen their pedagogical expertise whilst maintaining their agency as educational decision-makers in learning design. 3248 Bennett, S., Agostinho, S., & Lockyer, L. ## Acknowledgments

This project is funded by the Ministry of Education, Singapore. We would like to thank teachers from participating schools for their time, effort and opening their classrooms and professional learning sessions for this research. 3249 Enactments of Community-Driven Design Research: Creating a Hybrid STEAM Workshop with a Tribal Nation Dallas Haws, Utah State University, dallas.haws@usu.edu Breanne K. Litts, Utah State University, breanne.litts@usu.edu Marjle Pete, Charlene Pete, Clell Pete, Genevieve Fields marjle.pete@ctgr.us, charlene.pete@ctgr.us, clell.pete@ctgr.us, genevieve.fields@ctgr.us Confederated Tribes of the Goshute Reservation Tifiny Mills, Utah State University, tifiny.mills@usu.edu Christina Morgan, Utah State University, christina.morgan@usu.edu Abstract: In this poster, we share our community-driven design process with a Tribal Nation over the course of two years of their summer youth program. We share specific insights to answer the question: what does it look like to create a hybrid STEAM workshop that is responsive to the needs of a Tribal Nation in a rural community? Our design case provides understanding for how to enact culturally sustaining and revitalizing values throughout community-centered design processes.

As we consider access to STEAM learning opportunities, especially in rural settings, we must also consider the design of the learning environments themselves. In our work, which is built on a collaboration between university researchers and a Tribal Nation, we identified ways to design STEAM learning opportunities that are responsive to the Tribal Nation’s goals to preserve their culture and language through digital technologies. We are guided by the research question: what does it look like to create a hyb rid STEAM workshop that is responsive to the needs of a Tribal Nation in a rural community? Drawing on data from our ongoing partnership, we share our analysis of our process as we collaboratively designed a hybrid STEAM workshop in the context of a youth summer program. We contribute to the growing body of research that promotes mutually benefi cial, respectful, and intentional relationships between researchers and the communities with whom they work. Insights also provide practical design considerations fo r other partnership teams to consider in their design of hybrid learning environments for rural and Tribal communities.

## Theoretical framework

Our culturally sustaining/revitalizing (McCarty & Lee, 2014) orientation toward and relationship with technology and story is also grounded in technological and rhetorical self-determination (Lyons, 2000; Winter & Boudreau, 2018). These stances support the  self-determination for Tribal Nations to decide what technology they use, how they use it, and what they wish to be shared publicly. Moreover, in upholding Tribal sovereignty and self-determination, we are further shaped by Indigenous frameworks of storywork (Archibald, 2008). Storywork encourages intentional listening to Indigenous voices and perspectives and promotes the active embrace of storytelling in education, learning, and other realms, employing the values of “respect, reverence, responsibility, reciprocity, holism, interrelatedness, and synergy” (Archibald, 2008, p. 33). Lastly, in our theoretical grounding, we also embrace the many ways in which people hold relationships with nature and the land as important elements of culture in STEAM learning (Medin & Bang, 2014). Rooted in these frameworks, we designed hybrid STEAM workshops with the goal of supporting youths’ self-determination, storywork, and  technical skills through landbased learning experiences. We follow a community-driven design process (Bang et al., 2016; Quayle et al., 2023) where the Tribal Nation established the goals of our work through a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). Our design team includes University researchers and Tribal Elders and educators from a Tribal Nation. Together, we collaboratively designed and integrated hybrid STEAM learning experiences throughout the Tribal Nation’s summer youth program, which already incorporates rich in-person cultural learning activities and land-based field trips. We present data from two summers of implementation. To construct the design case study (Boling, 2010) presented in this poster, we draw on meeting notes, project communications, design artifacts, and reflective analytic 3250 making analytic approach by identifying areas of resonance (Medico & Santiago-Delefosse, 2014) in our interpretations across partners, perspectives, and documentation.

Our findings present three areas of resonance from our analysis as three design considerations for designing hybrid workshops in rural and Tribal communities that support STEAM learning. Designing for a hybrid rhythm The first design consideration we encountered in our designing for the hybrid STEAM workshops was balancing Zoom-based and in-person participation in the workshops. With the practical geographic constraint that the University research team and designers were a 3-4 hour drive from the Tribal Nation reservation lands, we were immediately faced with the question: how can we support a hybrid rhythm? In response, we designed Zoom workshops and integrated technical lessons into the existing summer youth program. The Zoom workshops focused on teaching technical digital media skills for iPads such as photo and video composition, digital art and animation, and film editing. With grant support, the University team sent a set of iPad Pros and workshop learning materials ahead of the summer program, so that the youth could follow along in real-time on their own devices. As part of this design consideration, we also explored the significance of relationship with the land through recognizing its role as a teacher (Styres, 2011). Thus, we integrated technological learning throughout field trips. For example, while visiting sacred locations on the reservation lands, we taught LiDAR scanning in the field, so youth could learn this skill while capturing 3D images of ancestral rock art. We found that learning some of these technical skills through a land-based approach was an important design consideration in how we designed for hybridity across the workshops. Hence, in our exploration of how to support a hybrid rhythm we found t hat we must weave together Zoom, in-person, and land-based cultural and technical learning experiences. Distributed teaching and learning The second design consideration we encountered was balancing teaching and learning across the hybrid spaces. With the goal of interweaving cultural and technical learning throughout the summer program, we were faced with the question of: who is a teacher? Building from the existing summer program, the Tribal Nation members of our team offered in-person cultural teaching, and the University members of our team designed Zoom-based technical workshops. Early in this arrangement, though, we realized that we ne eded to expand technical learning opportunities, so that youth would have community members and mentors in-person alongside them who could support troubleshooting and technical issues that are difficult to resolve over Zoom. As a result, the University members of our team held consultations with some of the Tribal community members to build their technical skills and self-determination, so they could support in-person troubleshooting needs of the youth in the program. Responsiveness to community needs The third design consideration our team encountered was balancing the need for just-in-time learning that inherently happened outside of scheduled Zoom meetings. With our goal to be responsive to community needs, we face the question: how are the community’s needs evolving throughout the workshop? As an example, in the weeks following the land-based learning portion of the workshop, we not only scheduled more Zoom workshops based on youths' individual plans, but the University researchers also made themselves available for ‘on-call’ needs. We had the flexibility to do this because we had distributed teaching across our entire project team, so each member had familiarity with the technologies the youth were using for their digital creations.  This distributed nature of our availability ensured that at least one person on our team was constantly available to guide the youth in finishing their projects by the community showcase at the end of the summer program.

## Significance

When researchers seek to work with communities in any context, we invite them to deeply consider their design processes and level of community involvement. In our design case, we identified three design considerations that can help design teams to create h ybrid STEAM learning environments for rural and Tribal communities. Specifically, we invite design teams to honor Tribal sovereignty and youths’ self-determination by considering: how can we support a hybrid rhythm?, who is a teacher?, and how are the community’s needs evolving throughout the workshop?. We see these three questions as a starting point for designers of hybrid learning environments to consider the goal of enacting culturally sustaining and revitalizing approaches through their design process and in partnership with rural and Tribal communities.
