3252 Teacher Candidate Experiences on the Translation of Program Equity Principles into Classrooms Mrinalini Mattoo, University of Toronto, mrinalini.mattoo@mail.utoronto.ca Elizabeth Jean Larson, Mount Saint Vincent University, ElizabethJean.Larson@MSVU.CA Kathryn Broad, University of Toronto, k.broad@utoronto.ca Abstract: Program expectations of equity principles for a graduate teacher education program were examined to assess the translation of these principles as graduate students in the program and as practicing teachers in school classrooms. A preliminary qualitative analysis of seven indepth interviews with graduate teacher candidates and alumni was conducted. Findings were categorized into successes and challenges, each with three emerging themes. Our study reiterates the importance of closing the divide between teacher programs and classroom realities.

In 2021, the National Council on Teacher Quality (NCTQ) Program reported that only 21% of teacher education programs exceeded the diversity of the teacher workforce and local community (NCTQ, 2021). Similarly, Cochran-Smith & Reagan (2022) found that teacher education preparation policy documents failed to adequately address equity. In the present political climate, the attack on DEI further discourages the integration of equity principles into education, underscoring the importance of conducting equity-based research in this field (American Civil Liberties Union, 2020). The present study begins to bridge the gap between program expectations and teachers' realities of equity by examining how equity-based program expectations map onto students' experiences within the program and as practicing teachers in schools. While teacher programs aim to equip candidates with relevant theory and practice to address the realities of school classrooms, research underscores a disconnect between the program theory and teacher candidates' experiences (Chang & Tsai, 2019). This stress is intensified when applied to the theory and application of equity principles in teacher education (Gilbert & Choudhry, 2024). Teacher education programs must prepare candidates for classrooms of students with diverse backgrounds with only a few courses (Sleeter, 2017). Assessing preservice teachers through the Cultural Responsive Teaching Readiness Scale, Moore et al. (2021) illuminate the necessity for teacher education programs to connect equity theory with practical field experience. Gorski (2009) reviewed 45 syllabi of teacher education courses, using qualitative content analysis to examine “course descriptions, course goals, course objectives, and other conceptual and descriptive text”. Gorski (2009) criticized the inability of these  courses to prepare teachers for the creation of inclusive and equitable learning environments in schools.

Participants were enrolled in a 2-year graduate teacher program, which qualifies teachers while providing a strong courses, including a mandatory fundamentals of teaching and learning, and an anti-discriminatory education course, provide teacher candidates with knowledge on equitable teaching practices. This graduate teacher program has a strong focus on equity, embedding research-driven equity theory and practices within coursework. The program expectations also explicitly outline the necessity of faculty to create courses with this emphasis. Within the syllabus for faculty, 9 of 29 program expectations refer directly or indirectly to equitable teaching goals. For instance, within the category of professional capacity or autonomy, one program expectation states, “Demonstrate categories and actions that support well-being, equity, social justice, cultural, responsiveness, and environmental sustainability to promote the transformative purposes of education”. All students in the program are full-time and sorted into either Primary/Junior (Junior Kindergarten to Grade 6), Junior/Intermediate (Grades 4 to 10), or Intermediate/Senior (Grades 7 to 12). A total of seven interviews were conducted, five of 2024 graduating teacher candidates and two 2023 alums. Candidates comprised of diverse backgrounds, with a wide distribution in ethnicities, age and prior teaching experience. Interview data is supplemented with program survey data collected from 2023 and 2024. Survey questions about equity program expectations contain scaled and open-ended responses. Data analysis was conducted using NVIVO 15 software. 3253 Interviews were transcribed verbatim, and several open-ended readings of the transcripts were conducted to develop a preliminary inductive understanding of the data. Reflexive thematic analysis revealed six inductive themes, subdivided into successes and challenges  (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Terry, 2017). Our preliminary results revealed six themes, further categorized into challenges and successes regarding the program expectations. The success category also consisted of three themes, including: Professional Confidence, Strength in Diversity, and Classroom Practice. The Professional Confidence theme underlined how the understanding of equity principles allowed teacher candidates to excel in this area during job interviews, practicum placements, and classroom settings. For instance, one participant highlighted their job interview process as, “When I talk to other people from other colleges and like that EDI job interview question, I crush every time, because I know everything I want to say in regards because we've practiced that a lot.” The Strength in Diversity theme emerged from the positive reflections of teacher candidates' equity understandings. Participants engaged in a reflexive process with equity principles during graduate coursework, practicum experiences, or as a classroom teacher, highlighting the importance of diversity. In one instance, a participant describes their graduate course experience, “Like there was a problem with all the white people in my class being like, I don't want to say something and it be taken as racist. And they, they were able to really, really deconstruct that and help us understand what was going on. So I think that was very helpful.” The last success theme that emerged from the data was Classroom Practice. This theme demonstrates how equity principles taught with practical application resulted in subsequent classroom practice and teacher candidate retention. One example of this includes the following quote: “Some of my courses excelled in connecting the theory and the practice because they were very big on like, let's do some practice teaching in the classroom. Here is the best practice. Let's practice it. And when I got to practice best practices based on research, I actually ended up doing it in classrooms”. The challenge category comprised three themes, including: Equity Fatigue, Internal Dissonance, and Overemphasis on Theory. Despite being coined by one of the participants during the interviews, Equity Fatigue emerged as a pertinent theme for several participants across survey and interview data. An apt description of this theme aligns with the following participant quote,  “A week of sitting and listening, yeah, and it-you lose motivation. You don't lose -, like I never felt that it was less important, yeah, addressing sort of equity and addressing anti-oppression within my own teaching like that is still, like, my top priority within the classroom, and like, providing an environment of acceptance and of-of love and about like, trust and safety within my classroom. And like my students know that, but in the program learning about it, there, it was like, I don't know how to explain it. I'll make up a term for fun. It's like, like, anti-oppression fatigue”. Similarly, other participants and survey responses described the exhaustion associated with the continuous stream of equity theory and examples. The Internal Dissonance theme showcases the internal versus external conflict for the acceptance of societal equity norms. Responses within this theme implicitly and explicitly highlight agreement with the theoretical concept of equity while having internal conflicts with the boundary lines of equity application. For instance, one participant says, And I feel like it's very hard in a school to maybe take that stance and be like, hey, like, I absolutely respect and love everybody, but like, I don't, I don't want this to be so heavily associated with me, and that, you know, for whatever reasons. It could be a religious reason, it could be a comfort, it could, you know, for whatever it is”. Finally, the theme of Overemphasis on Theory emerged from several experiences of the inability to transfer theoretical equity knowledge into practical classroom application. Despite being wellversed in equity theory through the program, teacher candidates described the inability to apply this knowledge due to a lack of examples of application, connection to lesson plans and logistical realities like time constraints. These findings highlight the benefits and areas of improvement of a teacher education program in the translation of equity principles from program expectations to classrooms. Challenge themes like equity fatigue and classroom practicality illuminate the ne ed for programs to continue to generate content which reflects the needs of the students while providing safe spaces for them to voice their concerns. Success themes like professional advancement and awareness of diversity demonstrate the significance of i ncorporating equity principles within teacher education programs. Within the present political environment, education that fights for an understanding of equity is critical for the harmony of present and future generations of teachers and students, whether  in universities or school classrooms.

SAGE Publications. 3255 Purpose and Paradox in India’s National Education Policy 2020: The Catch-22s of Learning Reform Anupam Raj, Columbia University, ar5099@tc.columbia.edu Savneet Bains, University of Texas at Austin, s.bains@utexas.edu Antarjot Kaur, Virginia Tech, kaura@vt.edu Abstract: India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisions transformative, learner-centered reform. However, its implementation faces inherent contradictions. Using Deborah Stone’s Policy Paradox  framework, this study identifies three Catch-22s in NEP’s goals: technical expertise versus holistic growth, linguistic rootedness versus global readiness, and formative versus standardized assessment. By framing these tensions as products of democratic negotiation, this study highlights the importance of acknowledging and managing the competing interests and values inherent in any large-scale reform. Education policy is more than an administrative mandate; it is a declaration of societal values and a primary driver of national development (Hanushek & Woessmann, 2008; OECD, 2020). These are inherently value-laden decisions that determine which forms of knowledge are prioritized and how success is measured (Fischer, 2003). In high-performing systems like Finland, success is not attributed to fragmented competitive reforms, but to a systemic coherence that prioritizes equity and professional trust over standardized competition (Sahlberg, 2011). Ultimately, a policy serves as the definitive script for a society's collective aspirations. Yet, most educational frameworks originate in Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) contexts, which may not translate to the complex governance of the Global South (Henrich et al., 2010). India provides a critical site to expand this conversation. As a postcolonial democracy, India is continually negotiating between local philosophical traditions and global market demands (Deshpande, 2011). The National Education Policy 2020 (NEP 2020) captures this dual aspiration: it seeks to modernize the purpose of learning through technical competencies, global linguistic readiness, and standardized accountability while simultaneously reviving ancient ideals of holistic development and cultural rootedness. It is a bold attempt to meet the world without losing the self.

This study also bridges the gap between the learning sciences and education policy, two fields that are increasingly realized to be interdependent (Penuel et al., 2022). While learning scientists often focus on classroom design, policy determines the systemic environments in which those classrooms operate (Coburn & Stein, 2010). although prior studies have examined NEP 2020 from various perspectives (Ashokkumar et al., 2025; Batra, 2020; Deb & Lal, 2026; Govinda, 2020; Kulal et al., 2024; Muralidharan & Singh, 2021), this article argues that impactful reform must be both technically sound and contextually grounded (Fishman et al., 2013). By analyzing the NEP 2020 document, we demonstrate how large-scale reforms enable or constrain learning through the "Catch-22s" they create. Consequently, this paper asks: How does India’s National Education Policy 2020 construct and negotiate paradoxes within its vision for learning and assessment?

## Theoretical framework and methodology

This study is framed by Deborah Stone’s Policy Paradox  (2012). Stone argues that policymaking is a struggle over ideas rather than a rational problem solving exercise. Central to this framework is the tension between the Market logic and the Polis logic. The Market logic focuses on individual rationality, competition, and measurable efficiency. In contrast, the Polis  logic is rooted in community identity, shared values, and collective flourishing (Stone, 2012). These are circular traps where two desirable,  but incompatible goals compete for the same space creating a Catch-22 situation (Heller, 1961). By viewing the NEP 2020 through these dual logics, we interpret its internal contradictions as inherent democratic negotiations between its Market and Polis oriented ambitions. We employed qualitative document analysis to examine the NEP 2020 as a social fact. This approach views the document as a dynamic artifact that both reflects and produces societal meaning (Atkinson & Coffey, 1997). Following Bowen (2009), our interdisciplinary team used open coding to identify recurring contradictions, followed by deductive coding to align these findings with Stone's framework (Saldaña, 2016). Our perspective prioritized the real world implications of policy ideas while recognizing that meaning is co-created through context and dialogue (Berger & Luckmann, 1966; Dewey, 1916). These findings center on three primary sites of contestation: the purpose, the medium, and the measure of learning. 3256 The analysis of NEP 2020 (Government of India [GOI], 2020) reveals three structural tensions where competing democratic goals create implementational "Catch-22s." Using Stone’s (2012) framework, we identify a recurring struggle between the Market logic (efficiency, global competition, and measurable standards) and the Polis logic (community, cultural identity, and holistic flourishing). Theme 1: Technical expertise versus holistic growth NEP 2020 (GOI, 2020) exhibits a deep structural tension between measurable scientific competencies and humanistic development. The policy identifies " universal foundational literacy and numeracy " as its " highest priority," driven by a National Mission (p. 8). This technical strand is reinforced by an emphasis on STEM, noting that “mathematics and computational thinking will be given increased emphasis... Activities involving coding will be introduced in the Middle Stage”  (p. 15). This Market-oriented vision frames schooling as preparation for a "skilled workforce" (p. 3) to meet global economic labor demands. Simultaneously, the policy invokes the Polis logic of ancient Indian traditions, where the goal was the “complete realization and liberation of the self ” (p. 12). It envisions " holistic and well-rounded individuals" (p.

12) through a curriculum that integrates " basic arts, crafts, humanities... and values, in addition to science and

mathematics" (p. 3). The resulting paradox asks the system to be at once expansive and rigorous. In resourceconstrained settings, like a government school in Bihar (Kingdon, 20 20), this creates a dilemma: does a school prioritize hiring a computer teacher for coding or a local artist for Madhubani  painting? These "motherhood issues" (Stone, 2012) —ideals everyone agrees with —become difficult to realize because they require different support, curriculum, and infrastructures. Ultimately, navigating this paradox requires a contextual wisdom that empowers schools to innovatively bridge these interests, perhaps by using digital tools to explore and create local art, ensuring that techn ical training serves as a vehicle for, rather than a competitor to students’ holistic development.

Theme 2: Linguistic rootedness versus global readiness NEP 2020 presents language as both a tool for learning and cultural rootedness, and as a pathway to economic mobility, creating a tension between Polis (identity, belonging) and Market (employability, global access) logics. The policy strongly advocates for the use of the “home language/mother tongue” as the medium of instruction in early years to support conceptual understanding, while also promoting English and foreign languages to “ enrich their global knowledge and mobility ” (pp. 13–15). This dual vision asks schools to ground students in local linguistic contexts while preparing them for participation in a global economy. In practice, this creates a dilemma, particularly where prioritizing mother-tongue/bilingual instruction may improve early learning and inclusion but candelay access to English-mediated opportunities in higher education and employment. Much like Theme 1, this tension reflects competing policy logics that cannot be resolved through one-size-fits-all design. Rather th an prescribing a uniform multilingual model, the policy’s success rests on contextual judgment and the agency  of local actors (students, families, and communities) to navigate trade-offs between identity and opportunity. Theme 3: Assessment for learning versus assessment for accountability Apart from discussing the purpose (Theme 1) and medium (Theme 2) of learning, the NEP 2020 also introduces a dual-track vision to reimagine the measure s of learning. The policy emphasizes shifting toward formative assessments that encourage “ analysis, critical thinking, and conceptual clarity ” (p. 17). Aligned with the Polis logic of holistic growth, it proposes a " 360-degree progress card " and redesigns board exams to test " core capacities" (p. 18). Simultaneously, driven by the Market logic of efficiency and accountability, it establishes the National Assessment Centre (PARAKH) to oversee uniform standards and conduct large-scale testing. This creates a Catch-22: teachers must nurture open-ended, inquiry-driven learning while preparing students for standardized testing. As seen in U.S. state reform models like Massachusetts, high-stakes accountability often undermines the very formative practices a policy seeks to nurture (Massachusetts Secretary of the Commonwealth, 2024). To avoid reproducing this exact pitfall in India, the key takeaway is that the implementation of this dualtrack vision for assessment must structurally buffer schools from top-down testing pressures. Ultimately, NEP 2020’s paradoxes are inherent democratic negotiations between Market  and Polis ideals, not design flaws. Realizing this vision requires moving beyond rigid, top-down mandates. Instead, systemic support must empower educators and communities to balance these competing priorities in practice, granting them the contextual agency to integrate technical and holistic goals for the purpose of learning, exercise linguistic pragmatism in the medium of instruction, and protect formative classroom spaces from the pressures of standardized measurement.

Norton. 3258 Knowledge in New Pieces: How do Material Culture, Object Ecosystems, and Intuitive Knowledge Shape Children’s Cognition? Paulo Blikstein, TLT Lab, Columbia University (USA), Instituto Tecnológico de Monterrey (México), paulob@tc.columbia.edu J.K. Voorhis, TLT Lab, Columbia University (USA), jkv2109@tc.columbia.edu Leah Rosenbaum TLT Lab, Columbia University (USA), leah@tltlab.org Abstract: Young people today grow up immersed in interconnected technological, social, and natural systems that shape how they construct knowledge. Digital environments nurture intuitive understandings—such as perceiving exponential growth through everyday experienc es with social media virality. Grounded in the Knowledge-in-Pieces (KiP) framework, which views cognition as composed of context-sensitive p-prims, this study extends KiP to contemporary, digitally mediated learning contexts. Our analysis situates these technologyinformed intuitions within broader trajectories of conceptual development in mathematics and complex systems thinking, illustrating how youth’s lived experiences with contemporary technologies can provide powerful entry points for formal learning of advanced topics in mathematics and science.

Scholars of Material Culture of Childhood consider childhood as a social and historical construct “readable” through its objects —oriented to piety (1850s), industrial ingenuity (1920s), or consumer conformity (1950s) (Cross, 1997; Jenkins, 1998).  In the mid-19th century, before mass media and consumer markets, children were seen as “miniature adults in training” and shared most objects with adults (Ariès, 1962). By the late 19th century, however, the Merry’s Museum and The Youth’s Companion were already advertising products for children, such as bicycles, photo cameras, telegraphs, gramophones, and microscopes (MerryCoz, n.d.; “The Youth’s Companion,” 1899). The 1920s brought radios and construction toys (Erector, Tinkertoy)  (Hornbake Library, 2024), and by the 1960s, television defined childhood, alongside plastic toys, LEGO, and space-race imagination; Highlights for Children  mixed puzzles, civics, and crafts (Internet Archive, 1960). Even though these changes have been well documented, far less attention has been paid to studying how this evolving material culture shaped children’s cognition and curricula. This work, thus, asks:  How do material culture, object ecosystems, and intuitive knowledge shape children’s cognition? Would children in 1899 find gears and ratios easier because of bicycles? Would “walking amongst microscopes” make the particulate nature of matter more intuitive? We draw on sociocultural theory (Vygotsky, 1978), Constructionism (Papert, 1980), and Actor-Network Theory (Latour, 2005), which considers educational settings as places where agency is distrib uted across human and non-human entities alike, and where objects and technologies structure what is known and created. We build on research on how children think with and on technology (Danovitch, 2019; Hallström, 2022; Jarvis & Rennie, 1998), including their understanding of the internet (Brodsky et al., 2021; Wennås Brante & Walldén, 2021), voice assistants (Oranç & Ruggeri, 2021), and search engines (Murray, 2021; Tong et al., 2022). Our work is grounded in diSessa’s Knowledge-in-Pieces (KiP) framework (diSessa, 1982, 1988), which argues that learners’ minds operate on phenomenological primitives (p-prims)—small abstractions from everyday experience, such as “more effort generates more result.” P-prims are context-dependent, activated by pattern recognition, and can be reorganized through schooling into more robust structures; KiP accounts for both productive intuitions and misconceptions. The framework has been extended to ideology (Philip, 2011), and chemistry (Taber & García-Franco, 2010), with the latter suggesting that intuitive pieces can arise from digital or mediated experiences, not only sensorimotor ones. Given dramatic changes in youth life— ubiquitous computing, social networks, viral content, climate change, and supply chains —we argue that learners today develop and use new p-prims that warrant closer examination. Our framework, Knowledge in New Pieces, extends KiP to intuitions emerging from techno-social experiences (Blikstein et al., 2023, 2024, 2025), many of which did not exist when KiP was first formulated. Next, we explore specific examples of these phenomena, particularly within social media and viral growth.

3259 We interviewed about ten youth between the ages of 8 and 14. Participants were recruited through convenience and snowball sampling, and all lived in the United States. Each interview, lasting about 45 minutes, was conducted on Zoom using a semi-structured protocol developed through three rounds of earlier pilot interviews with youth. Interviews were automatically transcribed and later verified by the authors. The research team reviewed and coded the transcripts to identify recurring ideas and notable patterns across participants. F rom the larger dataset, we selected summative focal themes, and the findings presented below draw from a subset of responses that focused specifically on social media posts. We published more detailed results elsewhere (Blikstein et al., 2024), but our goal in this paper is to exemplify the general findings across a range of studies.

## Summative findings

Children’s reasoning about online virality reflects intuitions about quantity, speed, popularity, and social connectedness, sometimes aligning with mathematical models of exponential growth. Nearly  every child recognized that popular people’s posts spread faster (“more followers mean more views”), but most treated this relationship additively rather than multiplicatively: popularity raised totals, not rates. A few mentioned accelerating growth: one student referenced “curves” from science videos and split v irality into intervals (10% early, 80% mid, 10% late), a nascent “ rate-of-change” idea. Many children invoked word-of-mouth models — content spreads because “people tell their friends”—mirroring diffusion or branching processes; younger children treated this as a simple chain, while more digitally fluent ones imagined branching networks. A third cluster concerned time and growth dynamics, with children describing posts that gain views quickly and level off (“fast at first, then slower”), echoing logistic or e xponential curves. Probabilistic reasoning  surfaced when children invoked algorithms or luck, acknowledging non-deterministic growth. Across interviews, popularity often operated as a cognitive “ stand-in” for feedback. Being famous  is seen as both the cause and the mechanism  of growth, a circular logic that approximately parallels feedback loops in formal systems. Across interviews, children’s level of experience s in the digital world mattered:  in general, those with limited exposure reasoned locally and linearly; moderate users reached for “curves” and “trends;” the most digitally fluent integrated algorithmic, networked, and temporal explanations. Across the sample, we observed a developmental continuum: from linear exposure models (“everyone sees it eventually”) to relational diffusion (friends-of-friends) to popularity feedback (bigger = faster), to algorithmic amplification (systems accelerate the spread). A significant implication of identifying these new “pieces” is that raising awareness of them could help educators rethink curriculum design,  narrowing the gap between students’ lived knowledge and curricular standards. Mathematics instruction could not only explore current curricular topics more effectively  but also introduce new topics that were previously out of reach for children, such as complex non-linear growth. Teachers could leverage viral metaphors to introduce proportionality, rates of change, recursion, and stochastic processes using real data from students’ social media feeds. Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence instruction could move beyond solving puzzles and simple problems toward more critical approaches, discussing how apps choose what to show students, and activating prior intuitions to introduce concepts such as collaborative filtering algorithms. Implementing these connections requires that teachers themselves become aware of these new “pieces.” Thus, professional development  could reposition students’ smartphones as data sources and educational assets rather than only distractions.  However, since t echnology access and experience vary widely, especially outside urban centers, affluent neighborhoods, and the Global North, e ducators must attend to socioeconomic, cultural, and neurodiversity differences, including teens who avoid socia l media.  KiP reminds us that intuitions are not automatically correct. Just as physics teachers anticipate the “heavier objects fall faster” intuition, math teachers might anticipate students imagining viral growth continuing forever, and design instruction that confronts saturation and logistic limits. We are extending this agenda beyond virality to environmental degradation, climate, AI, and supply chains; further terrains include multiverses in physics, economics from online gaming marketplaces, engineer ing from Minecraft, and feedback intuitions from fan fiction and maker forums. A key open question is transfer:  does a teen who grasps viral growth also understand bacterial growth or compound interest? Acknowledging these techno-social experiences as part of children’s cognitive toolkit pushes us toward a more responsive, student-centered education—aligned with Fr eire’s (1970) vision of learning relevant to lived experience, which can also help learners “fight back” against, for example, social media algor ithms. Today’s youth run micro-experiments in complex phenomena every time they share a post; the challenge for the Learning Sciences is to study these intuitions rigorously and integrate them into formal education. 3260 Blikstein, P. & Rosenbaum, L. Nordic Journal of Digital Literacy, 16(1), 7 –26. https://doi.org/10.18261/issn.1891-943x-2021-01-02 3261 Extending Freeze Framing: Designing Equitable Scaffolds for Outof-School Time (OST) Participation Peri Ella Green, Nichole Pinkard peri@u.northwestern.edu, nichole.pinkard@northwestern.edu Northwestern University Abstract: This poster examines a youth-centered incentive design project from Evanston, Illinois’s participatory budgeting process, which allocated $75,000 to support high school students’ access to OST learning. We define incentives not as rewards for thin measures  of participation, but as equitable scaffolds: material, social, and symbolic supports that make meaningful participation more reachable. Using Cultural-Historical Activity Theory, we analyze how a breakdown in Mappenings, the intended geocapture app, beca me a productive contradiction that expanded Freeze Framing beyond a single sociotechnical tool. The pivot to narrative reflections, annotated maps, and privacy-preserving composite personas made visible the connective tissue of youth OST lives-transportation, safety, family labor, belonging, time, and self-directed interest. We argue that Freeze Framing's greater utility lies in its portable activity structure, which can surface youth-authored evidence across multiple mediations and translate that evidence into more dignified, equity-aligned incentive logics. Cities often invest in OST programs as if opportunity is only a matter of program availability. Yet young people can live near libraries, parks, museums, clubs, jobs, or enrichment programs and still not experience those places as reachable, desirable, safe, or meant for them (Green et al., 2025). This gap matters for incentive design. When incentives are framed as rewards for attendance alone, they can reproduce the very inequities they are meant to solve by treating participation as an individual choice rather than a socio-spatial accomplishment. This study grows out of Evanston, Illinois's participatory budgeting initiative. Among seven winning proposals, one funded grants and incentives for marginalized students in grades 3-12; this paper focuses on the co-design of a $75,000 incentive system with high school youth. The work was situated in a research-practice partnership between Evanston Township High School (ETHS) and the Digital Youth Network (DYN). ETHS is a critical site because all 3,570 students in the district attend one public high school, making it possible to examine how students navigate the same dense but uneven opportunity landscape. Our central contribution is not that a technology failed and the study recovered. It is that the failure clarified what Freeze Framing is for: helping youth and adult partners understand how young people access learning opportunities outside school, and how ecosystems can be redesigned so opportunity becomes reachable. The pivot showed that Freeze Framing does not depend on Mappenings, or any single platform, to do that work.

## Theoretical framework

We define incentives as equitable scaffolds for the conditions of participation: transportation, time, safety, recognition, mentorship, and continuity. This distinction matters because OST participation is shaped by what Pinkard (2019) calls the connective  tissue of a healthy learning ecosystem: the relationships, routines, tools, resources, and pathways that enable learning across settings. Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) gives us language for analyzing this connective tissue. Activity is mediated by tools, rules, communities, and divisions of labor; contradictions among these elements are not merely barriers, but possible engines of expansive learning (Cole & Engeström, 1993; Engeström, 2001). We pair CHAT with socio-spatial learning perspectives that treat space as relationally produced rather than neutral (Leander, 2002; Soja, 1996). Together, these lenses support a core design principle: incentive systems should recognize socio-spatial labor, not simply count attendance.

## Method: Freeze Framing as a portable activity structure

Freeze Framing is an iterative socio-spatial surfacing process organized around five linked moves: Conceive, Capture, Behind the Frame, Opening the Frame, and Reframe (Green & Pinkard, 2025). Across these phases, youth surface spatial beliefs, document meaningful OST moments, interpret patterns and absence with peers and maps, and translate insights into design principles and concrete supports. 3262 In the intended six-week design, Mappenings would mediate the Capture phase by allowing students to geopin OST moments, add captions, tag activities, and reflect on why places mattered. Those captures would become shared artifacts for analyzing movement and co-designing incentive rules. Almost immediately, however, the app collided with the conditions of youth digital life: students reported broken buttons, in-app camera issues, and parental controls that blocked data sharing. From a CHAT perspective, the tool intended to mediate youthauthored evidence became an obstacle within the activity system. The team responded through re-mediation while keeping the object constant. Students created annotated Google and Apple Maps, wrote and recorded reflections in DB65, and worked with privacy-preserving composite personas built from anonymized student experie nces. These composites allowed students to analyze realistic constraints without being forced to disclose personally sensitive details. In this sense, ethics were not separate from method (Barton et al., 2020); the design protected refusal, privacy, and re vision while enabling collective Across the pivot, three findings clarify what Freeze Framing contributed to incentive design. ● First, the rupture made mediation visible. The app breakdown did not redirect the study; it exposed the same access conditions Freeze Framing was designed to surface. Access was mediated by rules, devices, permissions, transportation, family expectations, and institutional assumptions. The failed capture process became evidence that youth-centered methods must be designed for permissioned ecologies rather than idealized participation.

● Second, narrative and collaborative mediations widened the evidentiary scope without abandoning the object. Annotated maps showed how places accumulated meaning over time: gyms, parks, fields, homes, online spaces, and informal third places became sites of  identity, memory, and aspiration. Reflections surfaced nostalgia, self-directed interests, parental permission, and hopes for arts-related opportunities. These were not side details; they were the connective tissue of OST engagement. ● Third, composite personas helped students translate lived OST constraints into incentive logics. Megan represented constant negotiation among cheer, babysitting, family needs, and interest in acting. Bob navigated parental rules, curfews, safety, and biking limits. Jules represented self-directed creative labor, online recognition, and paid work to fund art materials. Hector surfaced family translation, sibling care, and the labor of being the dependable oldest child. By authoring schedules and journal entries for thes e personas, students moved from abstract equity talk to concrete design requirements. The resulting incentive ideas moved beyond a simple points-for-prizes model. Students proposed supports such as free transportation, Uber or transit credits, mentorship, internships, tutoring, recognition for consistency, and credit for community service or helping at home. The most important shift was methodological: the project was always oriented toward equitable scaffolds, but the pivot clarified which kinds of evidence were needed to design them. A youth-centered incentive system should recognize the labor of becoming able to participate, including movement, care work, safety negotiation, and sustained self-directed engagement. This case reframes a tool failure as a methodological and theoretical insight. Mappenings remains valuable as a mediating artifact, but Freeze Framing's broader utility is its capacity to travel across mediations while preserving its object: understanding and redesigning the conditions that shape young people's OST lives. That portability matters because youth lives are already mediated by uneven technologies, institutional rules, family responsibilities, and spatial constraints.

For learning sciences researchers, the case offers a contradiction-aware approach to validity. Confidence did not come from one cleandataset; it came from convergence across imperfect but complementary mediations: maps, journals, persona schedules, dialogue, and student proposals. For OST systems, the implication is practical: incentive design should begin by surfacing the connective tissue of youth participation before deciding what to fund, reward, or measure. Otherwise, incentives risk rewarding meaningless or already privileged forms of engagement while ignoring the supports needed to make opportunity reachable. Future work should design for plurality from the start: offline-first capture, analog options, layered consent, stable convening routines, and privacy-preserving visualizations that represent time, travel, safety, cost, and caregiving without exposing students. The broader design challenge is to build ecosystems that recognize youths’ existing pathways and expand their freedom of movement so OST opportunities become more reachable, rather than asking young people to adapt to inequitable landscapes alone. 3263 Barton, A. C., & Tan, E. (2020a). Beyond equity as inclusion: A framework of “rightful presence” for guiding justice-oriented studies in teaching and learning. Educational Researcher, 49(6), 433– 440.
